Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 11, verse 1:

[314]
﴿Alif, Lam, Ra.﴾
What has been said about the disjointed letters (al-huruf al-muqatta'a) at the beginnings of surahs has already been stated at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah and elsewhere among their counterparts, and Surat Yunus is not far from that.

* * *
﴿A Book whose verses have been made firm, then elaborated in detail, from the presence of One who is All-Wise, All-Aware.﴾
The discussion regarding the opening with His words "A Book" (kitab), and its indefinite form, is similar to what occurs in His words ﴿A Book sent down to you﴾ [al-A'raf: 2] in Surat al-A'raf.

The meaning is that the Qur'an is a Book from Allah, so why do the polytheists marvel at this and deny it? Thus "kitab" is the subject (mubtada'), and what made the indefinite form acceptable as a subject is the indefiniteness that indicates a category (lil-nawʻiyya).

And ﴿from the presence of One who is All-Wise, All-Aware﴾ is the predicate (khabar), and ﴿whose verses have been made firm﴾ is an attributive clause (sifa) modifying "kitab." You may also make ﴿whose verses have been made firm﴾ a restrictive attribute (sifa mukhassisa), and it is then what justifies the beginning with an indefinite noun. You may also make "uhkimat" itself the predicate, and make ﴿from the presence of One who is All-Wise, All-Aware﴾ an adverbial phrase of no specific meaning (zarf laghw) related to "uhkimat" and "fussilat."

Al-ihkam (making firm) means perfecting the craft. It is derived from al-hikmah (wisdom), with a kasra on the ha' and a sukun on the kaf. Wisdom is the perfecting of things such that they are free from the defects that afflict their kind. That is, His verses have been made complete in their kind of speech, such that they are free from contradicting reality and from defects in meaning and wording. This was discussed earlier at His words, Exalted is He: ﴿In it are firm verses﴾ [Al 'Imran: 7] at the beginning of Surat Al 'Imran. And in this sense the contrast with His words ﴿from the presence of One who is All-Wise﴾ is indicated.

Ayat al-Qur'an (the verses of the Qur'an) are sentences that are independent in their meanings and concluded with fawasil (closing rhyme-units). The reason for calling the sentences of the Qur'an "verses" (ayat) was discussed earlier at His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And those who disbelieved and denied Our verses﴾ [al-Baqarah: 39] at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah, and in the eighth of the introductions to this commentary.

[315]
Tafsil (elaboration) means clarification and explanation. It is derived from al-fasl (separation), meaning distinguishing one thing from another by what distinguishes it. It thus became a well-known metonymy for explanation, because it involves separating meanings. This was discussed earlier at His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And thus We elaborate the verses, that the way of the criminals may become clear﴾ [al-An'am: 55] in Surat al-An'am.
Its counterpart is al-furq (distinction). It is used as a metonymy for explanation, so the Qur'an is named "al-Furqan." It is also used for separation, so the day of Badr is called "Yawm al-Furqan," and in the mention of the Night of Power is His words: ﴿In it every wise matter is made distinct﴾ [al-Dukhan: 4].

"Thumma" (then) here indicates a delay in rank, as is its function when joining sentences, because elaboration carries importance in the minds of people, since intellects find rest in clarity and explanation.

And ﴿from the presence of One who is All-Wise, All-Aware﴾ means from the presence of the One described as perfecting the craft through His wisdom, and as making things clear through the strength of His knowledge. Al-Khabir is the one who knows the hidden aspects of things. The more things there are, the more difficult it is to encompass them all. Thus al-Hakim corresponds to "uhkimat," and al-Khabir corresponds to "fussilat." Although both are related to knowledge and related to power (since power only operates in accordance with knowledge), the contrast takes into account the act that is the effect of one of the two attributes, which is more immediately evident to people than the other. This is among the eloquent instances of paired correspondence.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 11, verse 2:

﴿That you worship none but Allah. Indeed, I am to you from Him a warner and a bringer of good tidings.﴾

(An) is explanatory (tafsiriyyah), corresponding to what is implied in ﴿Its verses have been perfected and then made detailed﴾ [Hud: 1] of the indication of perfected and detailed statements. It is as if it were said: "It has been revealed to you in this Book that you worship none but Allah." Thus this sentence is explanatory of the verses that were perfected, because the prohibition of worshipping other than Allah and the obligation of worshipping Allah is the foundation of the religion, and to it returns all the attributes of Allah - exalted is He - that have been established by proof, and from it branch out all the details.

For this reason the command to monotheism (tawhid) and the argument for it is repeated in the Qur'an. The first verse revealed contained the command to associate the name of Allah with the first recitation of the Qur'an, in His saying - exalted is He: ﴿Recite in the name of your Lord who created﴾ [al-'Alaq: 1].

The address in ﴿That you worship none﴾ and the pronouns of address that follow it are directed to those who have not believed, namely everyone who hears this speech, the speech that he was commanded to convey to them.

The sentence ﴿Indeed, I am to you from Him a warner and a bringer of good tidings﴾ is a parenthetical clause (i'tiradh) between the sentence ﴿That you worship none but Allah﴾ and the sentence ﴿And that you seek forgiveness from your Lord﴾ [Hud: 3] and so on. It is a parenthesis to warn against opposing the prohibition and to encourage complying with it.

The occurrence of this parenthesis directly after the first sentence, which is among the perfected verses, indicates that its content is among the perfected verses, even though the sentence is not explanatory. This is because the nature of a parenthesis is that it should be suitable to what comes after it and arise from it. The content of "bringer of good tidings" and "warner" comprises the whole of the Messenger's ﷺ work in his mission. He is a bringer of good tidings to whoever believes and obeys, and a warner to whoever turns away and disobeys. This also comprises the principles related to the message, the circumstances of the messengers, and what they reported of the unseen, and thereby the transmitted doctrines (al-'aqa'id al-sam'iyyah) are included. This is exactly what perfection (ihkam) means.

The "min" in His saying ﴿Indeed, I am to you from Him﴾ is for origin (ibtida'iyyah), meaning: "Indeed, I am a warner and a bringer of good tidings to you, coming from Allah."

The combining of warning and good tidings is to correspond to what the first sentence contained: the request to abandon worshipping other than Allah by way of prohibition, and the request to worship Allah by way of exception. Thus warning refers to the first part, and good tidings refers to the second part.

[Page 317]

﴿And that you seek forgiveness from your Lord, then repent to Him; He will let you enjoy a good provision until a specified term, and will give every person of virtue his virtue﴾

This is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon the clause ﴿that you worship none but Allah﴾ [Hud: 2]. It is a second explanation (tafsīr, "elucidation") that returns to what was in the first clause of detailed explanation (tafṣīl). This is the beginning of the detailed explanation, because it is a clarification and guidance toward the means of abandoning the worship of anything other than Allah, the Exalted, together with proofs, examples, and warnings for that. The purpose is the division of the explanation, and this is the reason for repeating the particle of explanation in this clause, rather than relying on what is in the clause it is conjoined to.

Istighfār (seeking forgiveness) is requesting forgiveness, meaning requesting that one not be held accountable for a past sin, and that involves regret.

Tawbah (repentance) is giving up the act of a sin, along with a resolve never to return to it.

Thumma (then) denotes ranked sequence (tartīb rutbī), because acknowledging the corruption of what they were engaged in, namely the worship of idols, is more important than seeking forgiveness. The firm resolve not to return to them is the very meaning of repentance. This is an encouragement to abandon the worship of idols and an explanation of the benefits in that, in this world and the Hereafter.

Matāʿ (provision) is a verbal noun (ism maṣdar) from tamtīʿ, for what one enjoys, meaning what one benefits from. It is also applied to the benefits of this world. It has already been discussed at His saying, the Exalted: ﴿There is for you on earth a dwelling place and enjoyment for a time﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 24], in Surat al-Aʿrāf.

Ḥasan (good) is a restriction of the type of provision as being good in its kind, meaning pure, free from troubles, and lasting long for its possessor, as indicated by His saying: ﴿until a specified term﴾. The intended meaning of provision is continuance, that is, life, and the meaning is that He will not uproot them. Describing it as good indicates that it is a pleasant life.

[Page 318]

﴿Until a specified term﴾ is connected to ﴿He will let you enjoy﴾ and is the endpoint of the enjoyment. This is an admonition and an alert that this provision has an end, and thus it is understood to be the provision of this world. What is meant by the term (ajal) is the term of each individual, which is the end of his life. This is a promise that it is a blessing that lasts throughout life.

The clause ﴿and will give every person of virtue his virtue﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿He will let you enjoy﴾. Ītāʾ (giving) is bestowing, and this indicates that it is part of the good provision, so it is understood to be the bestowal of the bounties of the Hereafter. Faḍl (virtue) is giving good.

It is called faḍl because the usual case is that the doer of good does it with what is surplus to his need; then this meaning was forgotten, and faḍl came to mean giving good.

The first faḍl is righteous deeds, by the indication of its being contrasted with the grace (faḍl) of Allah, who is free of need from people. The second faḍl, which is attached to the pronoun of majesty, is the reward of the Hereafter, by the indication of its being contrasted with the provision of this world. The meaning is: and Allah will give His grace to every person of virtue in his deed.

Since the giving is connected to the two graces, it is understood that the measure of the reward is according to the measure of what is rewarded, because it is connected to "a person of virtue," which has the force of a derived noun (mushtaqq). Thus there is an indication of causation and of proportion. Knowing the exact measure of this belongs to Allah alone, and it is a secret between the servant and his Lord. A parallel to this, with differences in order and additional explanation, is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while being a believer, We will surely cause him to live a good life, and We will surely reward them with their best deeds﴾ [al-Naḥl: 97].

* * *

﴿But if they turn away, then indeed I fear for you the punishment of a great day﴾

This is a conjunction upon ﴿that you seek forgiveness from your Lord﴾, so it is part of what came as explanation of ﴿whose verses were perfected and then elaborated﴾ [Hud: 1], and it is among what was revealed to the Messenger (ﷺ) to convey to the people.

Tawallaw (turn away) originally was tatawallaw, and one of the two tāʾs was dropped for lightness.

[Page 319]

Emphasizing the clause of the conditional with inna (indeed), and with the subject being a noun whose predicate is a verbal sentence, serves to intensify the emphasis on the expectation of punishment.

The indefiniteness of yawm (day) is for awe, so that their souls go to the possible meaning that it could be a day in this world or in the Hereafter, because they used to deny the resurrection, so frightening them with the punishment of this world has a stronger effect on their souls. By this, the indefiniteness of yawm is suitable for it to be placed in opposition to the two rewards in His saying: ﴿He will let you enjoy a good provision until a specified term and will give every person of virtue his virtue﴾. So the listener infers: if you turn away, then I fear for you two punishments, just as I hoped for you two rewards if you sought forgiveness.

Describing it as great is to increase its awfulness, and by greatness is meant metaphorical greatness, namely the intensity of what happens in it, that is, the punishment. So describing the day as great is a rational metaphor (majāz ʿaqlī).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 11, verse 4:

﴿To Allah is your return, and He is over all things Competent.﴾

This clause is in the position of giving the reason for the warning about them, and therefore it is separated (from what precedes, as a full sentence). The meaning is: you are going back to Allah, that is, to His power, not escaping from Him, so He will requite you for your turning away from His command.

So "al-marji'" (the return) is a mīmī verbal noun meaning "the returning." It is used as a metonymy (kināyah) for its customary implication, which is not escaping (Him), even if time is long; and that includes the return after death. The intended meaning is not that alone, because His saying: ﴿and He is over all things Competent﴾ is more fitting to the worldly destiny, since that is what they accept; as for the otherworldly destiny, if they had acknowledged it, there would not have been any strong reason for the addition ﴿and He is over all things Competent﴾.

The fronting of the prepositional phrase (al-majrur) before its governing element is for emphasis and reinforcement, and the intended meaning is not restriction (ḥaṣr), since they do not reckon that they will be returned after death, let alone that they would return to other than Him.

Page 320

The clause ﴿and He is over all things Competent﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿To Allah is your return﴾, meaning: so what is your assumption about returning to the One Who is Competent over all things, when you have disobeyed His command? Will He not punish you with a great punishment?

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 11, verse 5:

﴿Verily they fold their breasts to hide themselves from Him. Yet when they cover themselves with their garments, He knows what they conceal and what they reveal. Indeed He is Knowing of what is in the breasts.﴾

On the manner of the discourse addressing the Prophet (peace be upon him) with what he was commanded to convey, it informs him of a condition of those to whom he was commanded to convey it, in their ignorance of the all-encompassing knowledge of God, may He be exalted, of every state of created beings, of their essences and actions, the apparent and the hidden. He therefore first refuted a delusion among the delusions of the people of polytheism, that they were able to hide some of their states from God, may He be exalted. Thus His saying: ﴿Verily they fold their breasts﴾ etc. serves as a preface to His saying: ﴿He knows what they conceal and what they reveal. Indeed He is Knowing of what is in the breasts﴾, combining their report of the all-encompassing knowledge of God over things with the refutation of their imaginings and their ignorance of the attributes of God. This discourse arose from His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿To God is your return, and He is over all things Competent﴾ [Hud: 4], by way of the connection that the One to whom return is made, being described with complete power over all things, is also described with the all-encompassing knowledge of everything, because of the necessary connection between complete power and complete knowledge.

The opening of the discourse with the particle of alerting, "ala" (indeed/take note), is for emphasis on its content, because of the strangeness of the reported matter of these people, and for attentiveness to teaching the all-encompassing knowledge of God, may He be exalted.

The pronouns of the absent plural refer back to the polytheists to whom the Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded to convey in His saying: ﴿that you worship none but God﴾ [Hud: 26], and this is not an iltifat (shift of address). The pronouns of absence in the singular refer back to the Name of Majesty (Allah) in His saying: ﴿To God is your return﴾ [Hud: 4].

Page 321
Al-thanyu (thanyu) is folding, and its root derivation is from the number two (ithnayn). It is said: "thanahu" (lightened), when he made it second; it is said: "This is one, so make it second," i.e., be second to it. So the one who folds a thing makes one of its two flaps second to the one before it. Thus "thanyu al-sudur" (folding of the breasts) is inclining and bending them, by way of likening it to folding. Its meaning is stooping.

This discourse admits of being taken according to the literal sense of its words, of folding and breasts. It may also be that it is a figure (tamthil) depicting a psychological state by a sensible state.

On the first possibility, this is a marvelling at the ignorance of the people of polytheism, since they measured the attributes of God, may He be exalted, by the attributes of people, and so reckoned that God does not perceive what they hide from Him. It has been narrated that the verse alludes to what the polytheists did: one of them would enter his house, let down the curtain over himself, cover his garment, bend his back, and say: "Does God know what is in my heart?" This was from their ignorance of the greatness of God.

In al-Bukhari, from Ibn Mas'ud: Two Qurayshis and a Thaqafi gathered at the House, many in the fat of their bellies and few in understanding of their hearts. One of them said: "Do you think that God hears what we say?" Another said: "He hears if we speak aloud, and does not hear if we conceal." Another said: "If He hears when we speak aloud, He hears when we conceal." So God revealed: ﴿And you did not conceal yourselves lest your hearing, your sight, and your skins should testify against you, but you thought that God does not know much of what you do﴾ [Fussilat: 22] ﴿And that was your assumption which you assumed about your Lord; it has ruined you, and you have become among the losers﴾ [Fussilat: 23].

All the errors of the people of misguidance in the Jahiliyyah and in the earlier religions flow into their minds from sickly reasoning, corrupt analogies, measuring the lofty realities by the measures of their customary usages and habits, and analogizing the unseen to the seen. Many of the sects of Muslims have strayed along these paths, were it not that they arrive at necessary knowledge of the religion which preserves them, at the extremity, from leaving the circle of Islam; and some of them have indeed come close to falling.

Page 322
On the second possibility, it is a figure for the state of their harboring enmity toward the Prophet (ﷺ) in their souls and their disguising that upon him and upon the believers, by the condition of one who folds his breast to conceal it, and one who covers his garment over what he wishes to conceal with it. This possibility does not fit the verse being Meccan, since the polytheists in that day were not flattering the Prophet (ﷺ). Interpreting it as referring to the hypocrites requires that the verse be Medinan. No one among the early exegetes related this. In al-Wahidi's Asbab al-Nuzul, it was revealed concerning al-Akhnas ibn Shariq al-Thaqafi, ally of Banu Zuhra, who was a man sweet of speech, who showed affection for the Prophet (ﷺ) while concealing enmity, i.e., enmity toward the religion; so God struck the folding of the breasts as a figure for his concealment of hatred for the Prophet (ﷺ). Thus it is a figure and not a literal reality. The plural form on this reading is used for a single intended person, for the purpose of keeping him vague, like His saying: ﴿Those to whom people said﴾ [Al 'Imran: 173], it being said that he is al-Akhnas ibn Shariq.

It occurred in Sahih al-Bukhari that Ibn 'Abbas was asked about this verse and said: Some Muslims used to hide themselves so as to relieve themselves, and so they would disclose themselves to the sky, and so as to have intercourse with their wives, and so they would disclose themselves to the sky; then this verse was revealed. This explanation does not fit the placement of the verse nor the consistency of the pronouns. Perhaps Ibn 'Abbas's meaning is that the verse applies to the conduct of these people, and that their deed was not the cause of its revelation. Know that the way of the call to truth is that it does not go in vain even with those who did not believe in it nor follow it, for it turns their minds to the presumption of its truth or to readiness to repel it, and all of this stirs its reality and spreads its study. How many have turned away from a call to truth and found nothing for it but to rouse themselves to its matter and awaken from their heedlessness of it. Likewise was the state of the polytheists when they heard the call of the Qur'an: they began to ponder means of resisting and refuting it and to understand its meanings in order to find a way to repel it, like the case of al-'As ibn Wa'il, who said to Khabbab ibn al-Aratt when he demanded from him the payment for a sword he had made: "I will not pay you until you disbelieve in Muhammad." Khabbab said: "I will not disbelieve in him until God causes you to die and then brings you back to life." Al-'As said to him: "If God brings me back to life after my death, then I will have wealth, and I will pay you from it." So there was revealed concerning him His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Have you seen the one who disbelieved in Our signs and said: "I will surely be given wealth and children"?﴾ [Maryam: 77]. This was from his misunderstanding of the meaning of resurrection and his supposition that he would be returned to what his state was in this world of family and wealth.

Al-istikhfa' is concealing oneself (ikhtifa'), and the sin and ta' in it are for emphasis, like istajaba and ista'khara.

The clause ﴿Ala hina yastaghshuna thiyabahum﴾ etc. may be a completion of the clause ﴿Ala innahum yathnuna sudurahum﴾, connected to it, in which case the second particle "ala" is an emphasis of its counterpart in the clause before it, for the increase of confirming the matter; the adverbial phrase "hina" is then linked to the verb ﴿yathnuna sudurahum﴾ and shares it with the verb ﴿ya'lamu ma yusirrun﴾, and the described state is one single compound state of folding the breasts and covering oneself with garments.

Al-istighsha' is being covered by what covers, i.e., conceals; the sin and ta' in it are for emphasis, like His saying: ﴿and they covered themselves with their garments﴾ [Nuh: 7], and like istajaba.

The addition of ﴿wa ma yu'linun﴾ is an explicit statement of what was understood from the preceding discourse, to remove the delusion that He knows only hidden things and not the apparent.

The clause ﴿Innahu 'alimun bidhat al-sudur﴾ is a conclusion and a reason for the clause before it, i.e., He knows their secret and their open speech, because He is intensely knowing of what is hidden in souls, and He knows the open a fortiori.

Thus "dhat al-sudur" is an attribute of an omitted noun understood from the context from His saying "'alim": i.e., the things that are the possessors of the breasts.

The word "dhat" is the feminine of "dhu," by which one reaches description with generic nouns; the discussion of this has preceded at His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed He is Knowing of what is in the breasts﴾ and His saying: ﴿and set right the relations between you﴾ [al-Anfal: 1] in Surat al-Anfal.

"Al-sudur" is intended to mean the souls, because the Arabs express the inner senses by the breast.

Page 324
The choice of the intensive form "'alim" is for exhausting the expression of the all-encompassing knowledge over everything that the language established for common human usage can contain, which falls short of words that express lofty realities, by way of comprehending what is suitable among the expressions to approximate the intended meaning.

"Dhat al-sudur": the things settled in souls that do not exceed them. It is therefore annexed to them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 11, verse 6:

Page 5

﴿There is no creature on the earth but that its provision is upon Allah, and He knows its place of rest and its place of storage. All of it is in a clear Record.﴾

This is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon the clause: ﴿He knows what they conceal and what they reveal﴾ [Hud: 5]. The implied sense is: "There is no creature but that He knows its place of rest and its place of storage." The speech was arranged in this style for the sake of variety (tafannun), to convey an explicit statement of generality through negation emphasized by min (مِن), and to incorporate (idmaj) the generalization of Allah's provision for every creature on the earth within the statement of the generality of His knowledge of the circumstances of every creature. For this reason the conjoined verb was postponed, since in reminding that Allah is the Provider of creatures that have no means of acquiring sustenance there is an inference (istidlal) that He is Knowing of their circumstances. Indeed, His being the Provider of creatures is a matter among the established principles accepted by the general run of mankind, and so His providing for them was made a proof of His knowledge of what they need.

The word dabba (دابَّة) in the language is a noun for that which crawls (yadibb), i.e., walks upon the earth, other than humans.

The addition of "on the earth" (فِي الأرْضِ) is an emphasis on the meaning of dabba, to make explicit that the generality is used in its literal sense.

Al-rizq (الرِّزْق) means food, and it was discussed earlier in His saying: ﴿She found with her provision﴾ [Al 'Imran: 37].

The exception (istithna') is from the generality of states, which follows the generality of the essences and what is indicated by mention of their provision, which is one of their states.

The placing of ʿalā Allāh (عَلى اللَّهِ) before its complement, namely "its provision," serves to convey restriction (qasr), i.e., upon Allah and not upon anyone else. It also conveys, through the structure ʿalā Allāh rizquhā, the meaning that Allah has taken on the responsibility for its provision and has not neglected it; because ʿalā indicates obligation and entitlement, and it is known that no one can impose anything upon Allah. So what conveys the meaning of obligation is His binding Himself, in accordance with the attributes that require this for Him, as indicated by His saying: ﴿a promise upon Us﴾ [al-Anbiya': 104] and His saying: ﴿a truth upon Us﴾ [Yunus: 103].

The exception is from the generality of what the provision of creatures is ascribed to, in the apparent view of people, that it is provision from the owners of the creatures and those who raise them. That is, its provision is upon Allah and not upon anyone else. So the excepted element is the being upon Allah, and the excluded element is the absolute being-upon of whatever is imagined to be a provider. Thus restricting provision to being upon Allah is a rational metaphor (majaz 'aqli) in common usage, on the basis that Allah is the causer and determiner of that provision.

The clause ﴿and He knows its place of rest and its place of storage﴾ is a conjunction upon the clause of the exception, not upon the excepted element; that is, "and Allah knows the place of rest and the place of storage of every creature." Thus the ruling of this clause is not included within the scope of the restriction.

Al-mustaqarr (المُسْتَقَرُّ): the place where it settles. Al-mustawda' (المُسْتَوْدَعُ): the place of depositing; al-ida' (الإيداع) is placing and storing. What is meant by its place of storage is its storage in the womb before it emerges onto the earth, as in His saying: ﴿It is He who produced you from a single soul, so there is a place of rest and a place of storage﴾ [al-An'am: 98] in Surat al-An'am.

The tanwin of "kull" (كُلٌّ) is the tanwin of substitution for an omitted genitive complement, i.e., "all of its provision, its place of rest and its place of storage are in a clear Record." Here "Kitab" (الكِتاب) is a verbal noun (masdar), like His saying: "the Decree of Allah upon you" (كِتابَ اللَّهِ عَلَيْكم). It is used to express the determination of knowledge and its establishment, such that it admits no increase, no decrease, and no deviation. Just as writing is intended so that nothing is added to the matter, nothing is subtracted, and nothing is annulled. Al-Harith ibn Hilliza said:

Fearing oppression and deviation; yet can desires alter what is in the scrolls?

Al-mubin (المُبِينُ) is an active participle of abana, meaning "to make manifest," and it is an imaginative image (takhyil) for the metaphor of the Record for determination. It is not meant that it clarifies to whoever reads it, because the knowledge and decree of Allah is not comprehended by anyone.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 11, verse 7:

Page 7
﴿It is He who created the heavens and the earth in six days — and His Throne was upon the water — that He might test you as to which of you is best in deed.﴾
This is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with the clause ﴿And there is no creature on the earth but that upon Allah is its provision﴾ [Hud: 6]. The connection is that the creation of the heavens and the earth is among the greatest manifestations of Allah's knowledge, of the scope of His power, and of the perfection of workmanship. The purpose of this report is therefore its implication, which is contemplation of the breadth of His knowledge and power. The discussion of its like has already occurred in His saying: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is Allah, who created the heavens and the earth in six days; then He established Himself above the Throne﴾ [al-A'raf: 54], in Surat al-A'raf.

The clause ﴿and His Throne was upon the water﴾ may be a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and it may be a parenthetical insertion (iʿtirāḍ) between the verb "created" and the particle of causation (lām al-taʿlīl). As for its being coordinated with the clause ﴿And there is no creature on the earth but that upon Allah is its provision﴾ [Hud: 6], which is presented as evidence for the breadth of Allah's knowledge and power, this is not elegant, because the content of that clause is neither perceptible nor established for the polytheists, since it belongs to the unseen, and part of it has been altered by the creation of the heavens. Thus it is not fitting to make it a proof against the polytheists for establishing the breadth of Allah's knowledge and power derived from the clause "And there is no creature on the earth…" etc. The meaning is that the Throne was created before the heavens and was encompassing the water, or containing the water. Taking the Throne to be a created entity above the heavens is the apparent sense of the verse. That requires that the Throne was created before that, and that the water was created before the heavens and the earth. The detail of that, its manner, and the manner of the "establishment" are things for which minds have no capacity, since expressing it is only an approximation.

It is also possible that by the Throne is meant the kingdom and rule of Allah, as a figure modeled on the throne of sovereignty; that is, the kingdom of Allah was before the creation of the heavens and the earth, a kingdom over the water.

His saying: ﴿that He might test you﴾ is connected with "created," and the lām is for causation. The balw (testing) is ibtila', that is, examining something in order to obtain knowledge of its states, and it is used figuratively to mean the appearance of the effects of His creation upon the created beings. The literal sense of testing is impossible for Allah, since He is All-Knowing of everything, so He does not need to examine it, as in His saying: ﴿except that We might know who follows the Messenger﴾ [al-Baqara: 143], in Surat al-Baqara.

Making the testing a cause of the creation of the heavens and the earth is because it is one of the wisdoms of the creation of the earth, considering that the earth is part of this whole creation. Then, the creation of the earth entails the creation of what the earth has been made populated with, and the variation in the deeds of those addressed is among the states that the creation required, so it was among the wisdom of the creation of the heavens and the earth. The causation here is of several levels, and the cause of a cause is a cause.

"Ayyukum" is an interrogative noun, so it is a subject (mubtada'), and the nominal clause of the subject and predicate fills the place of the necessary circumstantial clause mentioned after the pronoun of address in "yabluwakum," considering that testing does not attach to the essences themselves; so the transitivity of the verb "yabluwa" to the pronoun of the essences does not by itself give complete meaning, and it needed mention of the condition of the restriction of the object of testing. This is a kind of specification, though not its very essence.

In the verse there is an indication that among the wisdom of the creation of the earth is the occurrence of virtuous deeds from the noblest of the creatures upon it. Then that requires recompense for deeds, completing what the wisdom demands; and for this reason it is followed by His saying: ﴿And if you say, "Indeed you will be resurrected after death…"﴾ etc.

* * *

﴿And if you say, "Indeed you will be resurrected after death," those who disbelieve will surely say, "This is nothing but clear magic."﴾
It appears that the "wa" is the wa of circumstance, and the clause is a circumstantial clause relating to the subject of "created the heavens and the earth," in view of what is attached to the verb in His saying "in six days," and His saying "that He might test you." The sense: He did that wondrous creation, while they deny what is less than that, namely the re-creation of people. And they are ignorant that, were it not for recompense, this creation would be vain, as He, may He be exalted, said:

Page 9
﴿And We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them in play﴾ [al-Dukhan: 38]. If the report in His saying "It is He who created the heavens and the earth" is taken in its apparent sense as information, then the circumstance is a presumed (muqaddara) circumstance of the subject of "created," meaning: He created that while foreseeing that you would deny His great power. If the report is taken to be used for admonition and reflection upon the power of Allah, then the circumstance is a concurrent (muqarana) one.

The reason for making it a conditional sentence is to indicate the renewal of denial at every report of resurrection. The lām is a preparatory lām for an oath, and the answer of the oath is "la-yaqulunna" etc., so the lām in it is the lām of the answer of the oath. The answer of the conditional "in" is omitted, being dispensed with by the answer of the oath, as is the custom when a condition and an oath come together: the answer of the latter of the two is omitted.

The emphasis of the clause by the lām preparatory to the oath and the nūn of emphasis that follows it is to treat the listener as one who doubts that such a statement would come from them, given how strange it is for a rational person to say it. So the strong emphasis and this treatment are used to imply its necessary meaning, which is wonder at the state of those who disbelieve, that they deny the re-creation even though they have witnessed the signs of the beginning of creation, which is greater and more wondrous.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read "illa sihrun" (this is nothing but magic), taking "hadha" as a reference to what is indicated by "qulta" (you say), and the report about the statement being magic means that they claim it is a statement of the kind that magicians utter, owing to properties that affect souls.

Ḥamza, al-Kisa'i, and Khalaf read "illa sahirun" (this is nothing but a magician), so "hadha" refers to the Messenger ﷺ, understood from the pronoun in "qulta," meaning that he says words by which he enchants us.

The reason for their calling this statement magic is that among their beliefs and superstitions, the means of magic include impossible statements and slanderous falsehoods. The meaning is that they deny resurrection whenever they are informed of it, not hesitating to hold that it cannot occur, let alone believe in it.

Mubin: an active participle of abana (the hamzated form), which has the meaning of the unaugmented bana, i.e., clear and evident, that it is magic, or that he is a magician.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 11, verse 8:

Page 10
﴿And if We defer the punishment from them until a counted nation, they will surely say, "What is holding it back?"﴾
Its connection to what precedes it is that both verses describe one of the varieties of the obstinacy and mockery of the polytheists toward the Islamic call. When the Messenger (ﷺ) informed them of resurrection and that their polytheism was the cause of their punishment, they treated his speech as sorcery. When he warned them of the punishment for associating partners with God, they asked him to hasten it. When it was delayed from them until a term required by divine wisdom, they asked about the reason for its being withheld from them, as a mocking question, supposing that its delay was incapacity.

The lam is a preparatory lam (lam al-muwatti'ah) for the oath, and the clause ﴿they will surely say, "What is holding it back?"﴾ is the answer to the oath, serving in place of the answer to the conditional.

Ummah (ㅤ'ummah): its basic meaning is a large group of people whose affair is one. It is also used for a period of time, as though they considered it to be the span in which a generation appears, so it was applied to the general notion of a period, meaning "after a period of time."

Ma'dudah (ma'dudah) means determined, that is, deferred. It implies that the period is not long, because it is common in Arabic speech to use counting, reckoning and the like to mean few, since a small amount can be controlled by number. For this reason they say the opposite: "without reckoning," as in ﴿God gives provision to whom He wills without reckoning﴾ [al-Baqarah: 212].

Habs (confinement) means binding a thing to a place it does not exceed. For this reason it is used to mean prevention, as here, that is, "what prevents it from reaching us and befalling us," while they intend mockery.

* * *

Page 11
﴿Surely, on the day it comes to them, it will not be turned away from them, and what they used to mock will encompass them.﴾
This sentence stands in the position of a reply to their statement, when they say, "What holds back the punishment from us?" Therefore it is separated as a dialogue is separated. This is a threat and warning that it will not be turned away from them, but it is deferred.

The speech is opened with the particle of alerting (ala) to draw attention to the news, to affirm it, and to instill awe into their hearts.

Fronting the adverbial phrase (yawma) implies that the coming of the punishment is beyond doubt, to the extent that it is fixed to a specific time.

Al-sarf: repelling and removing.

Al-hawq: encompassing.

The meaning is that it descends upon them in a way from which there is no escape by any means.

The clause "and it encompassed them" is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), or is coordinated with the predicate of laysa.

The past form is used to express certainty, and this is the punishment of killing on the day of Badr.

The phrase "what they used to mock" (ma kanu bihi yastahzi'un) refers to the punishment, and the bi in bihi is causal, meaning "because of its mention," for the mention of the punishment was the cause of their mockery when the Prophet (ﷺ) threatened them with it.

The use of the relative pronoun in place of a pronoun indicates that their mockery was among the causes of God's wrath against them. Its implied sense is that the punishment encompassed them such that they found no escape from it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 11, verse 9:

Page 12
﴿And if We let man taste mercy from Us and then withdraw it from him, indeed he is despairing and ungrateful.﴾ It is a conjunction with the clause "And if We delay the punishment from them until a specified community." When He mentioned that what they are in is enjoyment until a known term with Allah, and that they grew insolent over the blessing of being given enjoyment and mocked the delay of the punishment, this verse clarifies that the people of misguidance are firmly rooted in that state, because they do not reflect on anything other than worldly pleasures, so their emotional responses follow accordingly, without hope that the condition will change. They do not reflect on the causes of blessing and hardship, nor on the dispositions of the Creator of people and the Determiner of their circumstances, and they do not take warning from the changing conditions of nations. Thus the way of the people of misguidance is that if harm befalls them after blessing, despair of good takes hold of them, they forget the blessing, deny it, and disbelieve in its Bestower. Indeed, the delay of punishment is a mercy, and the arrival of punishment is a withdrawal of that mercy. This sentence is in the sense of a concluding generalization (tadhyil). The definite article in "al-insan" is the generic definite used to mean totality (al-istighraq), and by this the sentence acquired the force of a concluding generalization. The criterion of the generality is the exception in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿except those who are patient and do righteous deeds﴾ [Hud: 11], as will come, so the totality is customary, following the terminology of the Qur'an in applying the word "insan" or "nas". And because the two descriptors "despairing, ungrateful" suit the polytheists, the general term is specified by them.

It has been said that the definite article in "al-insan" is for a specific reference (al-'ahd), meaning a particular person. Al-Wahidi related from Ibn 'Abbas that it was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughira. And from him, that it was revealed concerning 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Umayya al-Makhzumi. It is also permissible that what is meant is every person to whom something like this befalls, with variation among people in this despair.

The lam is an introductory lam for the oath (al-lam al-muwatti'a lil-qasam).

The word "adhaqna" (We let taste) is used in the figurative sense of conveying perception, and the root of "adhaqa" was chosen for what it implies of perceiving a loved thing, because a person only tastes what he desires.

Page 13
By "mercy" is meant the mercy of this world, and it is applied to its effect, which is blessing, such as health, security and well-being; what is meant is the blessing that preceded the arrival of harm.

The literal meaning of "naz'" is removing a garment from the body. It is used here for stripping away blessing by way of metaphor, and for this reason it is followed by the preposition "min" rather than "'an", because the meaning is one of stripping and wresting away; the mention of "min" is thus an abstraction (tajrid) of the metaphor.

The clause ﴿indeed he is despairing and ungrateful﴾ is the answer to the oath. It was stripped of the opening lam, being dispensed with by the emphatic particle and the lam of commencement in the predicate of "inna". The answer of the oath was used in place of the answer of the conditional clause that accompanies it, as is the case with speech containing both a condition and an oath, as was previously mentioned in His saying: ﴿And if We delay the punishment from them﴾ [Hud: 8] to its end.

"Yaus" and "kafur" are both intensive patterns for one who despairs and for one who denies blessing, that is, one who rejects it. By "kafur" is meant one who denies God's blessing, because from him proceed statements and thoughts of resentment regarding what has afflicted him, as though He had never bestowed a blessing upon him at all.

The emphasis of the clause by the lam introducing the oath and by the emphatic particle in the answer of the oath is for the purpose of affirming its content, and that it is a firm reality with no exaggeration in it and no generalization.

[p. 14 marker omitted]

This sentence is a *tatmim* (a complementary sentence, one that completes the meaning of what precedes it), because it describes a state opposite to the one described in the sentence before it. It consists of an oath, a conditional clause, and the answer to the oath, as has been explained in similar places earlier.

The pronoun in *adhaqnahu* (We let him taste), which is in the accusative, refers back to *al-insan* (man). Its definiteness is like the definiteness of its antecedent, and it is for comprehensiveness (*istighraq*) in the sense explained earlier.

*Al-na'ma'* (with a fatha on the nun and a long vowel) means *al-ni'mah* (blessing). This word was chosen here, even though *al-ni'mah* is more common, for the sake of the good stylistic effect of matching the two words *al-na'ma'* and *al-darra'* in pattern. The meaning here is the blessing that comes after adversity.

*Al-mass* (touching) is used in the figurative sense of befalling in general. The choice of the verb *adhaqa* (to let taste) in the earlier clause has been explained, and the choice of the verb *massa* (to touch) in relation to experiencing adversity signals that the befalling of adversity is lighter than the befalling of blessing, and that God's gentle kindness encompasses His servants in every state.

The sentence is emphasized by the *lam al-muwatti'ah* (the lam that prepares for the oath) and by the *nun al-tawkid* (the emphatic nun) in the answer to the oath, for the same purpose explained in the previous sentence.

The answer to the oath is given as *al-qawl* (the saying), to indicate that it is boastful and self-exalting. Therefore the statement in His words *dhahaba al-sayyi'at 'anni* (the bad things have gone away from me) is used to express self-satisfaction and conceit. This is what the addition of *'anni* (from me), connected to *dhahaba* (has gone away), requires, to indicate that each person believes he deserves to have the bad things removed from him, out of vanity about himself, as in His words:

﴿And if We let him taste mercy from Us after adversity has touched him, he will surely say, "This is mine, and I do not think the Hour will ever occur. And if I am returned to my Lord, I will surely have the best with Him."﴾ [Fussilat: 50]

The clause *innahu la-fariḥun fakhur* (indeed he is exultant and boastful) is a *isti'naf ibtida'i* (a fresh beginning, a new sentence) to express wonder at his condition. *Fariḥ* (exultant) and *fakhur* (boastful) are both intensive patterns, meaning: greatly exultant and greatly boastful. Extreme exultation is going beyond the limit, and it is *al-bataru* (insolent exultation) and *al-ashar* (overweening pride), as in His words:

﴿Indeed, God does not love the exultant.﴾ [al-Qasas: 76]

*Al-fakhr* (boasting) is a person's showing off over others with the things that people love that he possesses.

The meaning is that he does not thank God for the blessing after hardship and the adversity he was in. He does not reflect on the existence of the Creator of causes, the one who changes conditions, and the one who varies their causes. The meaning of the two verses is also found in His words in Surat al-Shura:

﴿And when We let man taste mercy from Us, he rejoices in it; but if an evil befalls them because of what their hands have sent forward, then indeed man is ungrateful.﴾ [al-Shura: 48]

[Page 15]

﴿Except those who are patient and do righteous deeds; those will have forgiveness and a great reward.﴾

This is a precautionary qualification (*ihtiras*) by way of exception from "man" (*al-insan*). By "those who are patient" (*alladhina sabaru*) is meant the believers in God, because patience (*al-sabr*) is one of the concomitants of faith (*min muqarananat al-iman*). So he referred to the believers by "those who are patient," for faith trains its possessor to abandon desire and to reject the habitual error. God the Exalted said: ﴿Except those who believe and do righteous deeds, and advise one another to truth and advise one another to patience﴾ [al-'Asr: 3].

Among the meanings of patience is awaiting relief (*intizar al-faraj*), and for this reason the description "those who are patient" is preferred here over "those who believe," because the purpose is to contrast their state with the state of the disbelievers in His saying: ﴿Indeed, he is despairing, ungrateful﴾ [Hud: 9]. The exception indicates that they are characterized by the opposite of the attributes of those excepted from them. In this is a warning against falling into what resembles the attributes of the disbelievers, to varying degrees. The verse has been woven in this general manner so that the souls of the believing listeners may go in every possible direction of caution against the two attributes of despair and ingratitude for blessings, and the two attributes of joy and boasting.

The clause ﴿those will have forgiveness and a great reward﴾ is a resumptive independent sentence (*mustaʼnafa ibtida'iyya*). The use of the demonstrative ("those") immediately after describing them with what the exception indicates, and with patience and doing righteous deeds, is an alert that they deserved what is mentioned after the demonstrative because of the attributes mentioned before it, like His saying: ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord, and those are the successful﴾ [al-Baqara: 5].

[p. 16]

This is a consequence (*tafrīʿ*, a branching-off) from His words: ﴿And if you say, "Indeed you will be raised up after death"﴾ [Hud: 7], up to His words "they mock," mentioning their denial and obstinacy. This consequence indicates that the content of the preceding discourse is a cause for directing this expectation, because it is the nature of what is consequent upon it that they have despaired of their turning back, due to the repetition of denial and mockery, a despair that may prompt the abandonment of calling them. All of this is conveyed by the consequential *fā'* (the particle of consequence).

The expectation conveyed by *la'alla* ("perhaps") is used to warn against something that concerns the conveying (of the message). It is permissible to posit an interrogative whose particle has been omitted, the sense being: "Perhaps you (are about to) leave...?" The interrogative would then be used in the sense of negation for the purpose of warning, similar to His words, exalted is He: ﴿Perhaps you would destroy yourself with grief that they do not become believers﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 3].

The interrogative is a metonymy for the condition reaching a degree that makes one expect the matter being asked about, to the extent that the speaker asks about its occurrence. This is a style intended to stir the resolve of the addressee and to kindle his resolve to repel lethargy from him. Therefore, there is nothing in this that permits the Prophet (ﷺ) to abandon conveying some of what is revealed to him. That "some" is what contains their call to faith, their warning of punishment, and their being informed of the Resurrection, as indicated by His words, exalted is He, in another verse: ﴿And when you do not bring them a sign, they say, "Why have you not invented it?"﴾ [al-A'raf: 203]. The meaning is a warning to him against being affected by their obstinacy, denial and mockery; and this entails despairing the polytheists of his abandoning mention of the Resurrection and warning of punishment. Thus the address is used in its literal sense, and it is also intended, together with that, that the hearers know its content.

*Wa-ḍā'iq* is the active participle from *ḍāqa* (to be constricted). The form *ḍayyiq* was deliberately avoided here, in favour of *ḍā'iq*, for the sake of matching the parallel with *tārik* (leaving aside), since that is more eloquent. Also, *ḍā'iq* does not indicate the firm establishment of the attribute of constriction in his breast, unlike *ḍayyiq*, which is an attribute of resemblance (*ṣifa mushabbaha*) and indicates the firm establishment of the attribute in the one described. (Using *ḍā'iq* also) implies that the most that could be imagined as expected of him, (ﷺ), is a slight constriction that befalls him.

The constriction (*ḍayq*) is used figuratively for distress and grief, just as its opposite, expansion (*inshirāḥ*), is used for joy and gladness.

*Wa-ḍā'iq* is conjoined to *tārik*, so it and its subject form a predicate clause concerning *la'alla* ("perhaps"), and therefore the consequence applies to it.

The *bā'* in *bihi* ("by it") denotes causation, and the pronoun governed by the *bā'* refers to what follows it, namely *an yaqūlū* ("that they say"). *An yaqūlū* is a substitute (*badal*) for the pronoun. Such a construction is common in speech, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿And they conceal their private counsel, those who did wrong﴾ [al-Anbiya': 3]. Thus it becomes a warning lest his breast become constricted by their demand for signs, by their saying ﴿"Why has not a treasure been sent down to him, or an angel come with him?"﴾. Along with that, the warning also includes lest his breast become constricted by their saying ﴿"This is nothing but manifest magic"﴾ [Hud: 7], and by their saying, "What holds back the punishment from us?" This is due to *ḍā'iq* being included in the consequence of the warning upon their two preceding statements. The pronoun was introduced and then substituted by a noun in order to achieve a summary that is followed by detail, so that it would be more firmly fixed in the mind. It was also intended to front the prepositional phrase dependent on the active participle over its subject, to draw attention to the importance of what it depends on, since it is the cause of the act proceeding from its agent. Hence the explanatory pronoun was introduced afterwards, because of the length of the wording of the explanation; so by mentioning it there is a separation between the active participle and its nominative, and therefore it was abbreviated into a pronoun referring back to it. Thus concern was achieved and was strengthened by what indicates its firm establishment in the mind.

Most of the exegetes made the pronoun in *bihi* refer to "some of what is revealed to you," on the basis that what is revealed to him is the cause of the constriction of his breast; that is, his breast would not be constricted on its account. They also made *an yaqūlū* ("that they say") governed by a presumed causal *lām* (the *lām* of purpose). Accordingly, the imperfect verb in His words *an yaqūlū* is in the sense of the past, because they did say that. The *lām* is then connected to *ḍā'iq*, but the meaning does not rest firmly on this.

*Lawlā* here is used for urging (*taḥḍīḍ*). *Al-kanz* is wealth that has been hoarded, that is, hidden.

*Inzāluhu* ("its sending down") is its coming from a high place, that is, from heaven.

This statement was made by the polytheists before the revelation of this verse, so the imperfect verb is intended to express the renewal and repetition of this statement by them, by the evidence that it is known to have proceeded from them in the past, and by the evidence of the warning lest that become a cause of constriction of his breast, since the warning relates only to the future.

By their words *jā'a ma'ahu malak* ("an angel came with him") they intend that an angel from among the angels should come bearing witness to his prophethood. This is from their ignorance of the realities of matters, and their assumption that God cares about their aversion and would condescend to answer the proposal of their obstinacy; and from their inability to grasp the divine miracles and the extent of the Lord's support.

The sentence ﴿"You are only a warner"﴾ is in the position of a reason for the warning against his abandoning some of what is revealed to him and his breast being constricted by their speech. It is as if it were said: "Do not abandon conveying to them some of what is revealed to you, and do not let your breast be constricted by their speech, for you are a warner, not a guardian over the attainment of their faith, so that the abandonment of calling them would follow from your despair of their faith."

The restriction derived from *innamā* is a restriction relative to a specific context (*qaṣr idāfī*): you are a warner, not one entrusted with placing faith in their hearts, since that is not up to you but belongs to God, as His words before it indicate: ﴿Perhaps you will leave aside some of what is revealed to you, and your breast will be constrained by it﴾. Thus it is a restriction that reverses a false belief (*qaṣr qalb*). In it is an allusion to the polytheists, rejecting their belief that the Messenger should bring whatever miracles they ask for; so if he does not bring them, they make that a support for their denial of him. This is a rejection that results from the implications of the address, as was mentioned earlier at His words, exalted is He: ﴿Perhaps you will leave aside some of what is revealed to you﴾, since the mention of sentences like this one is frequent in the Qur'an in contexts of rebuttal of the polytheists and disbelievers who asked for miracles according to their own desires.

The sentence ﴿"And God is Guardian over all things"﴾ is a concluding generalization (*tadhyīl*) for His words "Perhaps you will leave aside some of what is revealed to you" up to here. It is conjoined to the sentence ﴿"You are only a warner"﴾, because of what the restriction required, namely the negation that he could be a guardian over compelling them to faith. Among what is included in the generality of "all things" is that God is Guardian over the hearts of the deniers, who are the intended target. The speech was couched in the form of generality so that it would be a concluding generalization and so that the purpose would be achieved with what is like a proof,

[p. 19]

and so that from that generality it might pass on to consoling the Prophet (ﷺ), by (informing him) that God is aware of the scheming of those people, that He is Guardian over their recompense, and that God knows the Prophet's exertion of effort in conveying the message.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 11, verse 13:

﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it." Say: "Then bring ten surahs like it, invented, and call upon whomever you can besides Allah, if you are truthful."﴾

Am (أمْ) here is disjunctive (munqati'ah), with the meaning of bal (بَلْ, "rather"), the particle of turning away (al-idrab) used for moving from one topic to another. However, am is specifically associated with interrogation, so the interrogative hamza (همزة الاستفهام) is to be understood after it. The sense is: "Rather, do they say, 'He has invented it'?" The transitional turning (al-idrab al-intiqali) carries the force of a fresh opening (al-istinaf al-ibtida'i), so the sentence has the status of a new beginning. The connection is clear, since the discourse is about refuting the claims of the polytheists, for they said: "This is invented speech," and He rebuked them with proof.

The interrogation is one of denial (istifham inkari).

Al-iftira' (الافتراء, "invention"): it is lying that its perpetrator has no excuse for, that is, lying deliberately, as was mentioned earlier in His words: ﴿But those who disbelieve invent lies against Allah﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 103], in Surat al-'Uqud.

The clause "Say: 'Then bring...'" is a reply to their statement, and therefore it is separated (fusilat) in the manner customary in dialogue, whether the recounting of the dialogue is in the form of reported speech or is a command to say, as was mentioned earlier at His words, Exalted is He: ﴿They said, "Will You place in it one who causes corruption therein?"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30]. The hidden pronoun in iftarahu refers to the Prophet ﷺ mentioned in His words: ﴿Perhaps you will leave some of what is revealed to you﴾. The manifest attached pronoun in the accusative refers to the Qur'an, understood from His words ﴿some of what is revealed to you﴾ [Hud: 12].

Al-ityan bi al-shay' (الإتيان بالشيء) means bringing it, whether it is obtained by borrowing from another or by originating it from the one who brings it. This is a broadening of the challenge in their favour.

He challenged them here to bring ten surahs, unlike the challenge elsewhere to bring a single surah like it, as in Surat al-Baqarah and Surat Yunus. Ibn 'Abbas and the majority of the exegetes said: the challenge was at first to bring ten surahs like the Qur'an, which is what occurred in Surat Hud, and then it was abrogated (nusikha) by a challenge to bring a single surah, as occurred in Surat al-Baqarah and Surat Yunus. The proponents of this view went further and said that Surat Hud was revealed before Surat Yunus, and this is the view relied upon.

Al-Mubarrad said: He challenged them first with a single surah, then challenged them here with ten surahs, because they were granted leniency here by being allowed to suffice with invented surahs; so when He broadened their situation regarding its description, He increased its number for them. The challenge with a single surah requires that it be similar to the surahs of the Qur'an in the perfection of its meanings, but this is not a strong view.

The meaning of muftariyat (مُفْتَرَيات, "invented") is that they are invented in their meanings, as you claim against the Qur'an, that is, in the manner of the tales and falsehoods of the people of ignorance (jahiliyyah). This is a case of giving free rein and of dialectical concession (al-taslim al-jadali). The similarity in His words "like it" (مِثْلِهِ) is therefore a similarity in the eloquence and fluency of speech, not in the soundness of its meanings. Our scholars said: in this is evidence that its inimitability (i'jaz) and eloquence lie apart from the loftiness of its meanings and the confirmation of some of it by other parts. And this is so.

Al-du'a' (الدعاء): calling out for an action. It is used metaphorically for a request, even without a call.

The object is omitted because the context indicates it, i.e., "and call upon [for that]." The imperative here is for permission (al-ibahah), that is: if you wish, when you have become unable to bring ten surahs of your own accord, then you may call upon whomever you judge to have the ability to do so, and whom you hope will aid you with support from your gods and by facilitating people to help you, like His words: ﴿And call your witnesses besides Allah, if you are truthful﴾ [al-Baqarah: 23].

And ﴿besides Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 23] is a qualifier of ﴿whomever you can﴾. The point of mentioning this qualifier is a reminder that they denied that it was from Allah. When He generalised for them the seeking of help from whomever they could, He emphasised that they were "besides Allah." So if they were unable to bring ten surahs like it, despite their ability to seek help from everyone other than Allah, it became clear that this Qur'an is from Allah.

The meaning of ﴿if you are truthful﴾ is: in your saying "He has invented it." The answer to the condition is His words: ﴿then bring ten surahs﴾. The connection between the condition and its consequence is that if the Qur'an can be produced by invention, then why do you not invent the like of it, so that your argument would stand?

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 11, verse 14:

﴿Then if they do not respond to you, know that it has been sent down with the knowledge of Allah, and that there is no god but Him. Will you then submit?﴾

This is a consequence (tafri') of His words ﴿and call upon whomever you can besides Allah﴾ [Hud: 13], meaning: if those whom you call upon do not answer you, then you are more incapable than they are, because you only call upon them when you feel your own helplessness, without any helper. Therefore, the incapacity of these (idols) necessarily becomes a cause of despair for those who call upon them to produce ten surahs.

Al-istijabah (response) means ijabah (answering), and the sin and ta' in it are for emphasis. It is used here for aid and support in the matter for which one seeks help. It is a metonymy (majaz mursal), because aid generally arises from a call for assistance; when the one sought for help is summoned to assist, he responds to the call by his presence, so it is called istijabah.

Al-'ilm (knowledge) means certain conviction (al-i'tiqad al-yaqin). That is: be certain that the Qur'an has been sent down only with the knowledge of Allah, i.e., accompanied by the knowledge of Allah, meaning, by the effect of knowledge, which is His making it in this arrangement for mankind, because that making is an effect of the power of Allah operating in accordance with His knowledge. The particle innama indicates restriction (al-hasr), i.e., restricting the state of the Qur'an, at the time of its sending down, to being from Allah.

﴿And that there is no god but Him﴾ is coordinated (atf) with "that it has been sent down," because when they have been unable, it becomes evident that those whom they sought as helpers cannot help them. Among those whom they seek for support by requesting aid against the challenge are the idols, so this indicates the negation of divinity from them.

The fa' in ﴿Will you then submit?﴾ is for consequence (tafri') upon "know." The interrogative is used to urge the act and not to delay it, like His words ﴿Will you then desist?﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 91], i.e., from drinking wine and gambling. The meaning: will you then submit after your certainty that this Qur'an is from Allah?

The nominal sentence was used, which indicates the continuity and steadfastness of the act. He did not say "will you then submit" (tuslimun, verbal form) because the state of non-response produces certainty in the correctness of Islam, and so it requires its firm establishment in the souls, and the nominal sentence indicates that firmness.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 11, verses 15–16:

﴿Whoever desires the life of this world and its adornment – We will pay them in full for their deeds therein, and they will not be deprived therein.﴾ ﴿Those are the ones for whom there is nothing in the Hereafter except the Fire; and what they did therein will be nullified, and what they used to do is worthless.﴾

This is a parenthetical resumption (isti'naf i'tirad) between the two sentences, arising from the sentence ﴿So will you then submit?﴾ [Hud: 14], because that sentence was a consequence of the establishment of the proof. If they were seekers of the truth and of success, then what requires the firm settling of Islam in their souls has already been secured for them. But if they only seek greatness and dominion in this world, and disdain to be followers of others, then they are those who desire this world. Therefore they are warned not to be deceived by fleeting enjoyment, and are informed that behind that lies a lasting punishment, and that they are upon falsehood. Thus the purpose of this speech is the second sentence, namely the sentence ﴿Those are the ones for whom there is nothing in the Hereafter except the Fire﴾ etc. And what precedes it is a preparation and an alert to the glittering of delusion and the slippery paths of heedlessness.

Since that was their condition, this parenthesis contains an added clarification of the causes of their obstinacy and their distance from faith. It also contains an alert to the Muslims not to be deceived by the apparent beauty of the state of the disbelievers in this world, nor to think that disbelief necessitates the hastening of punishment. They are awakened from this illusion, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Let not the movement of those who disbelieve in the land deceive you. A brief enjoyment, then their refuge is Hell, and wretched is the resting place.﴾ [Al 'Imran: 196]

The verb of the condition in a rhetorical context indicates the restriction of the agent to that act. So the meaning is: whoever desires only the life of this world, by the indication of His saying: ﴿Those are the ones for whom there is nothing in the Hereafter except the Fire﴾, since their affair is confined to deserving the Fire, which is the meaning of eternal abiding. A parallel to this verse is ﴿Whoever desires the immediate, We hasten for him therein what We will, for whom We wish. Then We assign for him Hell, which he will enter censured and rejected.﴾ [Al-Isra: 18] ﴿And whoever desires the Hereafter and strives for it its due effort while he is a believer – those are the ones whose effort is appreciated.﴾ [Al-Isra: 19]. So the meaning is: whoever seeks only the benefits of life and its adornment. This arises only from disbelievers, because the believer is never free of desiring the good of the Hereafter, and he has not believed except for that. So the context of these verses and their like concerns the state of disbelievers who do not believe in the Hereafter.

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿If you desire the life of this world and its adornment, then come, I will provide for you and release you with a fair release. And if you desire Allah and His Messenger and the Last Abode, then indeed Allah has prepared for the good-doers among you a great reward.﴾ [Al-Ahzab: 28], that is in another sense of the meanings of life and its adornment, namely the luxury of living and the adornment of clothing, contrary to what is implied by the Messenger's ﷺ turning away from much of that luxury and that adornment.

The pronoun in ﴿ilayhim﴾ refers to ﴿man﴾ (the relative pronoun), because what is meant by it is the peoples who are characterized by the content of the relative clause.

Al-tawfiyah: giving a thing in full, i.e., complete and not diminished. That is, We make their deeds in this world full. The meaning of their fullness is that they are not mixed with the demands of the obligations of faith, jihad, and standing for the truth, for all of that is not free of some deficiency in the enjoyment of those who do those deeds, which is the deficiency arising from opposing the desire of the soul. So the meaning is that they are not diminished from their pleasures which they have prepared for themselves, according to their different levels, in enjoying this world, unlike the believers, for whom the means of enjoying this world are prepared according to their different degrees of such preparation; so they leave much of that for the sake of seeking the pleasure of Allah the Exalted, and He warns them of the consequences of that in the Hereafter according to their different ranks in this observance.

The verb nuwaffi is transitive by the particle ilā because it includes the meaning of nuwassil (We deliver) or nublígh (We convey), to give two meanings.

So the meaning of the verse is not that whoever desires life and its adornment is given by Allah what he desires, because the wording of the verse does not indicate that, given His saying: ﴿We pay them in full for their deeds﴾. So tawfiyah is the absence of deficiency. It is connected to deeds, which are efforts. The addition of deeds to the pronoun of them indicates that they are the deeds which they intended and prepared for their own benefit; that is, We leave them to them as they wished, without introducing any deficiency into that. This fullness varies, and the common element shared among them is their freedom from the burdens of faith, the hardships of standing for the truth, and patience against disobedience to desire. So it is as if it were said: We leave them and their affair in that.

His saying: ﴿and they will not be deprived therein﴾, that is, in this world they are not requited for their disbelief with the recompense of the removal of some blessings from them; rather they are left to their affair as a gradual leading and a respite. This complements the meaning of the clause ﴿We pay them in full for their deeds therein﴾, since bakhs is the reduction of a thing and its lessening from what it ought to be, which is injustice. In this verse there is evidence for the view held by al-Ash'ari that disbelief does not prevent one from the blessing of Allah.

The pronoun in ﴿fīhā﴾ may refer to life and may refer to the deeds.

The clause ﴿Those are the ones for whom there is nothing in the Hereafter except the Fire﴾ is a resumed sentence, but the demonstrative pronoun links the two sentences. The demonstrative was used to distinguish them by those described attributes mentioned before the demonstrative. In the demonstrative there is an alert that the one indicated deserves what is mentioned after him, having been singled out, by the judgment due to the attributes mentioned before the demonstrative, as was explained in His saying: ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 5] in the Surah of al-Baqarah.

And ﴿illā al-nār﴾ is an exceptive construction (istithna' mufarragh) from ﴿laysa lahum﴾, meaning: there is nothing for them of what people are given in the Hereafter except the Fire. This indicates eternal abiding in the Fire, and thus indicates that these are disbelievers in our view.

Al-habt: nullification, i.e., annihilation.

What is meant by ﴿mā ṣana'ū﴾ is what they did, and among it is good done in this world, such as feeding the needy and the like, including mutual aid among them; for this reason it is expressed here by ṣana'ū, because good is called ṣani'a (a kindly act).

The pronoun in ﴿fīhā﴾ may refer to the world being spoken of, so the prepositional phrase is connected to the verb ṣana'ū. It may also refer to the Hereafter, so the prepositional phrase is connected to the verb baṭala, meaning its effect is annihilated. The meaning of the statement is an alert that their share of blessing is what comes to them in this world, and that God's mercy toward them does not exceed that. The Prophet ﷺ said to 'Umar when he mentioned Persia and Rome and their enjoyment: "Those, their good things have been hastened to them in the life of this world."

Al-bāṭil: that which goes to waste and loss.
