Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 11, verse 17 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Is he who has a clear proof from his Lord, and whom a witness from Him follows, and before him the Book of Moses as a guide and a mercy? Those believe in it. Whoever of the factions disbelieves in it, the Fire is his appointed place.﴾

The meanings of this verse have been locked shut because of the great number of possibilities surrounding it, from the side of the return of the pronouns and the demonstrative, from the side of the vagueness of what is meant by the relative pronoun, and from the position of the interrogative particle [hamza] and the position of the resultative fa' (fa' al-tafri'). Ibn 'Atiyya related many opinions in his tafsir, without anyone summarizing them as he did, and al-Qurtubi followed him in relating some of them. The points of difference are: who is meant by "he who is upon a clear proof from his Lord"; what is meant by "a clear proof from his Lord"; who is meant by "yatluhu" (follows him); what is meant by "shahid" (witness); the return of the object pronoun in "yatluhu"; the sense of "min" in "minhu"; the return of the pronoun governed by "min"; the position of "min qablihi" relative to "Kitab Musa"; the referent of the demonstrative in "Ulaika yu'minuna bihi"; and the return of the pronoun governed by "bi" in "yu'minuna bihi wa man yakfur bihi min al-ahzab" etc. These are the keys to the interpretation of this verse.

What has become clear to me from this, and from what God has opened to me, and what is clearer in its direction and closer in its resemblance to the intended meaning, is this: the fa' is for the resultative connection to the sentence "Am yaqulun iftarahu" [Hud: 13] up to His saying "fahal antum muslimun" [Hud: 14], and that what lies between them is a parenthetical insertion to establish their persistence in obstinacy and their distance from faith. This resultative connection is the connection of the opposite upon its opposite, in affirming for it the opposite of its judgment; that is, if the state of those deniers is as described, then there are a people in the opposite of their state, for whom the clear proofs and witnesses have benefited, so they believe in the Qur'an, and they are the Muslims. This is what is required by His saying "fahal antum muslimun" [Hud: 14], meaning: just as those who were upon a clear proof from their Lord among you and among the People of the Book submitted.

The hamza is for the interrogative of affirmation (istifham taqriri), meaning: if these disbelieve in it, will he who is upon a clear proof from his Lord believe in it? This is in the manner of the construction of His saying, may He be exalted: "Afaman haqqa 'alayhi kalimatu al-'adhab, afa anta tunqidh man fi al-nar" [al-Zumar: 19], meaning: "Will you rescue from the Fire the one upon whom the word of punishment has come due?"

"Man kana 'ala bayyina" is not intended to refer to a specific person. So the word "man" here functions like the definite article of mental reference (al-'ahd al-dhihni), applying to whoever has the attribute fulfilled, namely that he is upon a clear proof from his Lord. Without this, the reference would not be coherent. The singular forms of the pronouns in "kana 'ala bayyina min rabbihi" follow the wording of the relative "man," and that is one of two usages; the plural in "Ulaika yu'minuna" follows the meaning of the relative "man," and that is another usage. The estimate is: "Afaman kanu 'ala bayyinatin min rabbihim, ulaika yu'minuna bihi." A parallel to this verse is His saying, may He be exalted: "Afaman kana 'ala bayyinatin min rabbihi kaman zuyyina lahu su'u 'amalihi wa-ittaba'u ahwa'ahum" [Muhammad: 14] in the surah of Fighting.

Those who are upon a clear proof from their Lord may be the Christians alone, for they were widespread among the Arabs, and the people of Makkah knew many of them; these are the ones who recognized the truth of Islam, such as Waraqa ibn Nawfal and Dihya al-Kalbi. It may also be that Christians and Jews are intended, such as 'Abd Allah ibn Salam, among those who believed after the Hijra; this indicates their capacity to know the clear proof, because of the soundness of their understanding and the clarity of the proof's indication, so its possessors are believers in it.

By "the clear proof" is meant the proof of the coming of the Messenger ﷺ, who was foretold in the Torah and the Gospel. That the Christians were upon a clear proof from their Lord before the coming of Islam is evident, because they did not deny a truthful messenger. As for the Jews being upon a clear proof, it is only in relation to their awaiting a messenger foretold in their Book, although in their disbelief in 'Isa (peace be upon him) they were not upon a clear proof. So the meaning is a particular clear proof, indicated by the context of the preceding speech, from His saying: "fa'lamu anna ma unzila bi-'ilm Allah" [Hud: 14], and specified by the following: "Ulaika yu'minuna bihi," that is, by the Qur'an.

The "min" in "min rabbihi" is initial (ibtida'iyya) in a metaphorical sense of initiation. The meaning of it being "from His Lord" is that it is from God's revelation and His charge, which is indicated by His saying, may He be exalted: "Wa-idh akhadha Allahu mithaqa al-nabiyyin lama ataytukum min kitabin wa-hikmatin thumma ja'akum rasulun musaddiqun lima ma'akum latu'minunna bihi wa-latansurunnahu" [Al 'Imran: 81], and His saying: "Alladhina yattabi'una al-rasula al-nabiyya al-ummiyya alladhi yajidunahu maktuban 'indahum fi al-Tawrah wa al-Injil" [al-A'raf: 157]. His mention of the Book of Moses and that it came before it indicates that the proof mentioned here is from the Gospel, and this strengthens that the intended meaning of "man kana 'ala bayyina min rabbihi" is the Christians.

The verb "yatluhu" is the imperfect of "talw," which is following, not recitation (tilawa); that is, it follows him. "Ittiba'" is used metaphorically for support and emulation, since the witness for the truth comes behind the one he testifies for. The object pronoun in "yatluhu" refers to "man kana 'ala bayyina min rabbihi."

By "shahid minhu" is meant a witness from his Lord, that is, a witness from God, and it is the Qur'an, because by its inimitability it silenced the obstinate from producing ten surahs like it, and so it was a proof that it came from God's side.

"Min" is initial. The pronoun in "minhu" refers to "rabbihi." It may also refer to "shahid," meaning: a witness to its truthfulness inherent in its essence, which is its inimitability, silencing them from producing the like of it.

"Min qablihi" is a circumstantial clause (hal) of "Kitab Musa." "Kitab Musa" is conjoined to "shahid minhu," and the meaning is to follow it in the argument by way of ascent, for the Christians are guided by the Gospel, then they seek further support for what is in the Gospel from the Torah, because it is its root and in it is its explanation. Therefore, when "Kitab Musa" was conjoined to "shahid," which is the object of "yatluhu," it was qualified as "min qablihi," that is, "and a witness from Him follows him, and the Book of Moses follows him in the state of coming from before the witness," meaning preceding it in descent. If the intended meaning of "man kana 'ala bayyina min rabbihi" is specifically the Christians, then the mention of the Book of Moses is an allusion that the Book of Moses (peace be upon him) is a witness to the truthfulness of Muhammad ﷺ, and it does not mention the people of that Book, namely the Jews, because they were not upon a complete clear proof from their Lord, owing to their non-acceptance of 'Isa (peace be upon him).

"Imaman wa-rahmatan" are two circumstantial clauses, a praise of the Torah for what it contains of the detailed legislation; so it is an imam by which one is guided, and a mercy for people who act by its rulings, so God shows them mercy in this world by establishing justice and in the Hereafter by the reward of uprightness, since an imam is that which is followed and whose model is emulated.

The demonstrative "Ulaika" refers to "man kana 'ala bayyina min rabbihi," that is: those who were upon a clear proof from their Lord believe in the Qur'an, and they are not like you, O assembly of polytheists. This is in the sense of His saying, may He be exalted: "Fa-in yakfur biha ha'ula'i faqad wakkalna biha qawman laysu biha bi-kafirin" [al-An'am: 89].

The insertion of "ulaika" here resembles the insertion of the pronoun of separation (damir al-fasl), and in it is an alert that what follows of the predicate is caused by the attributes mentioned before the demonstrative, namely that they are upon a clear proof from their Lord, reinforced by witnesses from the Gospel and the Torah.

The clause "Ulaika yu'minuna bihi" is the predicate of "man kana 'ala bayyina min rabbihi."

The pronoun in "bihi" refers to the Qur'an, known from the context or from the prior mention of its pronoun in His saying: "Am yaqulun iftarahu" [Hud: 13]. With it the speech is connected to His saying "Am yaqulun iftarahu" up to His saying "fa'lamu anna ma unzila bi-'ilm Allah" [Hud: 14], that is: they believe that the Qur'an is from God.

The "ba'" is for transitivity, not causation. So the transitivity of the verb "yu'minuna" to the pronoun of the Qur'an is from the mode of attributing a judgment to the entities while meaning their attributes, like "Hurrimat 'alaykum ummahatukum" [al-Nisa': 23], that is: they believe in what the Qur'an is described as, that it is from God.

The total meaning of the verse and its connection to what precedes it is "fahal antum muslimun" [Hud: 14], for those who believe in it are those who were upon a clear proof from their Lord, supported by a witness from their Lord and reinforced by the Book of Moses (peace be upon him) before their proof.

Close to the meaning of the verse is His saying, may He be exalted: "Qul ara'aytum in kana min 'indi Allah wa-kafartum bihi wa-shahida shahidun min Bani Isra'il 'ala mithlihi fa-amana wa-istakbartum" [al-Ahqaf: 10]. Thus the interpretation of the verse is straightened to full straightness, and you will not lack the composition of the aspects by which the commentators interpreted it that differ from what we have mentioned, in whole or in part; your sight in them is keen, and in your hand are the keys to opening their locks.

The clause "wa-man yakfur bihi min al-ahzab" is conjoined to the clause "Afaman kana 'ala bayyina min rabbihi," because when He urged the people of Makkah to Islam with His saying "fahal antum muslimun" [Hud: 14], and showed them the example with His saying "Ulaika yu'minuna bihi," He returned to warn against disbelief in the Qur'an, saying "wa-man yakfur bihi min al-ahzab," and turned away from what had become clear to him of the clear proof of his Lord and the witnesses of His messengers: "fa-al-nar mawʻiduhu."

"Al-ahzab" are the groups of nations gathered by a matter on which they assemble: the polytheists are a party, the Jews are a party, and the Christians are a party. He, may He be exalted, said: "Kadhdhabat qablahum qawmu Nuh wa-'Ad wa-Fir'awn dhu al-awtad" [Sad: 12], "wa-Thamud wa-qawmu Lut wa-ashab al-ayka ulaika al-ahzab" [Sad: 13].

The "ba'" in "yakfuru bihi" is like the "ba'" in "yu'minuna bihi."

"Al-mawʻid" is a noun of place or time for a promise. It is used here for the destination to which one goes, because the nature of a specific place for an action is that it is specified by a prior promise.

* * *

"Fa-la taku fi miryatin minhu innahu al-haqqu min rabbika wa-lakinna aktha al-nas la yu'minun"

This is a resultative connection to the clause "wa-man yakfur bihi min al-ahzab fa-al-nar mawʻiduhu," and the address is to the Prophet ﷺ.

The prohibition is used as a metaphorical allusion (kinaya ta'ridiyya) concerning those who disbelieve in the Qur'an, because a prohibition implies the corruption and deficiency of the thing prohibited, so among its implications is the blame of one who is engaged in what is forbidden. Since the addressee is not presumed to be engaged in what is forbidden, so that he would be asked to abandon it, and the prohibition would be a request for the obtaining of what is already obtained, it is necessary that the prohibition not intend stopping and desisting from the forbidden thing, so it is used for its implication by the context. What makes this clearer is His saying, may He be exalted, in the surah of al-Sajda: "Wa-laqad atayna Musa al-kitab fa-la takun fi miryatin min liqa'ihi" [al-Sajda: 23], for if the intended aim were warning the Prophet ﷺ against doubting the tablet, the resultative connection of this to the giving of the Book to Musa (peace be upon him) would have no necessary link. But since the intent is an allusion to those who denied the revelation, He presented to them the argument of the prior revelation to Musa (peace be upon him).

"Fi" is for the metaphorical sense of containment, used for the firmness of engagement, in view of the state of those against whom the prohibition is used as a metaphor for blaming them, for they are engaged in a severe excess regarding the matter of the Qur'an.

The two pronouns of the third person refer to the Qur'an, to which the pronoun of "iftarahu" returned.

The clause "innahu al-haqq min rabbika" is a resumptive sentence (musta'nafa), a confirmation of what the clause "fa-la taku fi miryatin minhu" indicates, that because of the clarity of its truth it is not fitting that its truthfulness be doubted. The particle of emphasis stands in the place of a command to believe in its truth, because of the concern that emphasis indicates.

The Arabic passage uses "المِرْيَةُ" as a term, and I should translate it along with the rest. Here is the translation.

Al-mirya (doubt) means shakk (doubt). It is synonymous with al-imtira' (disputing/doubting) mentioned earlier at the beginning of al-An'am. The prohibition is framed as one against mirya rather than against believing it to be a lie, as is the case with the polytheists, because a prohibition on imtira' concerning it necessarily entails a prohibition on firmly asserting that it is a lie, a fortiori. In this there is an allusion that what the polytheists possess of certainty in the falsehood of the Qur'an is even more blameworthy and abhorrent.

Min (مِن) is ibtida'iyyah (indicating origin/starting point), meaning "in doubt arising from the Qur'an." Doubt arises from it only insofar as it is a doubt regarding its very essence and reality, because the reality of the Qur'an is that it is a Book from Allah. Thus, doubt arising about its revelation is doubt about its totality of reality. This is like the pronoun in His saying ﴿يُؤْمِنُونَ بِهِ﴾ ("they believe in it"), without any need to posit an elided genitive (mudaf) through which the attribution of the judgment would be reinterpreted as attributing it to the entities whose attributes are intended.

The definite article in "al-Haqq" (the Truth) serves to restrict the genus of truth to the Qur'an. It is a restriction of hyperbole (qasr mubalaghah), affirming the perfection of the genus of truth in it, to the point that it is as if no truth exists other than it, like your saying: "Hatim is the generous."

The istidrak (contrastive continuation) with His saying ﴿ولَكِنَّ أكْثَرَ النّاسِ لا يُؤْمِنُونَ﴾ ("but most of the people do not believe") arises from the implication of the restriction, for restriction implies that everyone who has received it should believe in it, but most people do not believe.

Iman (faith) is tasdiq (affirmation) of what the Messenger ﷺ brought of the religion.

The object of yu'minun (they believe) is omitted because the intent is the negation of the reality of faith from them in everything for which faith in the truth is demanded; that is, in the natures of most people is the dominance of desire over truth, so when something comes that opposes their desires, they do not believe.

[Page 32]

﴿And who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against God? They will be presented before their Lord, and the witnesses will say, "These are the ones who lied against their Lord. Surely, the curse of God is upon the wrongdoers, ﴿who bar [people] from the way of God and seek to make it crooked, and they are disbelievers in the Hereafter."﴾

When the discourse concluding the refutation of their claim that the Prophet ﷺ fabricated the Qur'an and attributed it to God had finished, and when they were shown to be unable to produce proof for what they claimed, [the verse] turned back upon them, making clear that they were the ones who fabricated lies against God in several respects, among them their denial that the Qur'an was sent down from Him.

The clause ﴿And who is more unjust than one who fabricates﴾ is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to the clause ﴿And whoever among the factions disbelieves in it, the Fire is his promised place﴾ [Hud: 17], to explain that they deserve the Fire for their disbelief in the Qur'an, because they disbelieved in it by way of fabrication against God, since they attributed the Qur'an to other than the One who sent it down, and claimed that the Messenger ﷺ had fabricated it. Thus they had reached the utmost degree of injustice, to the extent that one asks about the existence of a party more unjust than them, in a rhetorical question of denial that amounts to negation, meaning: no one is more unjust. A parallel to this has already occurred in His words, exalted is He: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who prevents the mosques of God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 114] in Surat al-Baqarah. And in Surat al-A'raf, in His words: ﴿So who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against God or denies His signs?﴾ [al-A'raf: 37].

Their fabrication against God is what they invented of the religion of polytheism, such as their saying that the idols are their intercessors with God, and their saying in many matters of their religion, ﴿God commanded us to do it﴾ [al-A'raf: 28]. And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿God did not ordain any bahirah, nor sa'ibah, nor wasilah, nor ham; but those who disbelieve fabricate lies against God﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 103], meaning: by their saying, "God commanded us to do that."

The clause ﴿They will be presented before their Lord﴾ is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf). Its opening with the demonstrative noun (ism al-ishara) serves to draw attention to the fact that they deserve what will follow the demonstrative, of the news, on account of what preceded the demonstrative, of the description, and this is the most severe injustice, as has already been mentioned regarding ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 5] in Surat al-Baqarah.

And because the demonstrative noun implies a meaning of causal explanation of what precedes by what follows, it is known that their being presented before their Lord is a presentation of reproach and retribution.

The verb ʿaraḍa, when it is followed by the preposition ʿalā, conveys the meaning of bringing forth with intention.

The choice of describing them by the cause serves to indicate the power over them.

The conjoining of the verb ﴿says﴾ to the verb ﴿they will be presented﴾, which is the predicate, makes it a conjunction on a part of the preceding sentence; here it is the beginning of conjoining one sentence to another, so both verbs are intended as information about the demonstrative noun.

The meaning: they will be presented before God for punishment, and the witnesses will proclaim that they lied against their Lord, as an exposure of them.

Al-ashhad (the witnesses) is the plural of shahid in the sense of present, or the plural of shahid in the sense of one who informs about the truth that is due from them. These witnesses are from among the angels.

Summoning them by way of the demonstrative noun serves to single them out for all the people, so that what will be said about their state becomes well known, and the intended purpose of that is their being notorious for evil and their public disgrace.

The use of the relative pronoun in the report about them is an indication that the description contained in the relative clause is the cause of the judgment that follows them, namely ﴿Surely, the curse of God is upon the wrongdoers﴾, while the intended purpose is their exposure rather than the testimony. The intended purpose of announcing this attribute is their disgrace and humiliation, not the establishing of their lying, because the establishing of that is already present in their records of deeds. For this reason the presentation was not attributed to their deeds, but was attributed to their very persons in His words: ﴿They will be presented before their Lord﴾.

The clause ﴿Surely, the curse of God is upon the wrongdoers﴾ is part of the speech of the witnesses. Its opening with the particle of alerting suits the situation of exposure. The predicate is used in the sense of supplication, for their humiliation and belittlement.

[Page 33]

Something that confirms that it is part of the speech of the witnesses is the occurrence of a parallel to it in Surat al-A'raf, in which this is explicitly stated: ﴿Then a caller will proclaim among them that the curse of God is upon the wrongdoers﴾ [al-A'raf: 44], and so on.

As for His words: ﴿who bar [people] from the way of God and seek to make it crooked, and they are disbelievers in the Hereafter﴾, a parallel to it has already occurred in Surat al-A'raf.

The feminine pronoun in His words ﴿and seek to make it crooked﴾ refers to the way of God, because sabil (way) may be treated as feminine.

The meaning: they seek to make the way of God crooked. Thus it is known that the way of God is straight, and that they attempt to make it crooked, because they want the Prophet ﷺ to follow their religion, and they become angry at his opposition to them. Here the speech of the witnesses ends, because the parallel to it in Surat al-A'raf, in His words: ﴿Then a caller will proclaim among them that the curse of God is upon the wrongdoers﴾ [al-A'raf: 44], and so on, ends with something similar to the end of this verse.

This verse is distinguished from its parallel in al-A'raf by the addition of the pronoun hum in His words: hum kafirun (they are disbelievers). This is an emphasis (tawkid) that conveys the strengthening of the judgment, because the context here is one of recording their denial of resurrection and affirming it, indicating what awaits them of fitting punishment. Thus there is quoted from the speech of the witnesses what fits this. What is in Surat al-A'raf is a report of what was said concerning a people who were admitted into the Fire and whose punishment became manifest, so there is no purpose in reporting what contains emphasis from the speech of the witnesses. Both statements are true, and an eloquent speaker, in what he reports, reports what has a fitting relation to the situation of the report.

﴿Those will not be able to escape [Allah] on earth.﴾ This is an explanatory resumptive clause (*istīnāf bayānī*, a clause that answers a question the preceding statement naturally raises). It arises from the fact that the threat was limited to describing part of their punishment in the Hereafter. That description provokes in the listener's mind the question: are they then safe from the punishment of this world? The answer is that they will not be unable to escape [Allah] in this world. That is, they cannot get out of Allah's power to punish them in this world, should His wisdom require hastening their punishment.

Repeating the demonstrative "those" (*ulā'ika*), after it had already been used in His words, ﴿Those will be presented before their Lord﴾ [Hud: 18], serves to confirm the purpose of the earlier demonstrative. The meaning is: they will come to the judgment of their Lord in the Hereafter, and they will not be able to escape Him, that He would punish them in this world whenever He wills. Rather, He intended to give them respite.

*Mu'jiz* here means one who escapes from someone who seeks to harm him. Its explanation has already been given at His words, ﴿What you are promised is surely coming, and you cannot escape it﴾ [al-An'am: 134], in the chapter of al-An'am.

"Earth" (*al-ard*) means this world. The benefit of mentioning it is that they have no refuge from Allah if He wishes to take vengeance upon them. They will find no place on earth where they can seek protection. This is a negation of the shelters and strongholds in which a fugitive seeks refuge. In my view, the pairing of "on earth" (*fī al-ard*) with "unable to escape" (*mu'jizīn*) functions as a proverbial expression in the Qur'an, as in His words, ﴿And whoever does not answer the caller of Allah, he cannot escape on earth﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 32]. Perhaps it is also something that operates in this way in the speech of the Arabs, as indicated by the verse of Iyas ibn Qubayṣa al-Ta'i, one of the poets of the Jahiliyya:

*Have you not seen that the earth is vast and spacious,
so can any patch of its lands make me unable to escape?*

* * *

﴿And they had no allies besides Allah.﴾ The "allies" may be understood as helpers, meaning they had no supporter who would aid them apart from Allah. Thus [the verse] combines the negation of the two means of escape from the punishment of the All-Powerful: a place that the Almighty cannot reach, or the opposition of another powerful being that prevents Him from inflicting His punishment. "Besides Allah" (*min dūni Allāh*) is connected to "allies" (*awliyā'*), because the word *walī* here carries the meaning of a barrier or one who keeps away, as in His words, ﴿And whoever takes Satan as a *walī* besides Allah has certainly incurred a clear loss﴾ [al-Nisa': 119].

It is also possible that "allies" refers to the idols which they took as allies, meaning they devoted to them love and worship.

Page 36

The negation of allies from them in this sense is the negation of the effect of this attribute. That is, their idols and gods did not benefit them.

"Besides Allah" in this sense means "other than Allah." *Dūn* is a noun that is not a adverb of place (*ghayr ẓarf*), and the *min* preceding *dūn* is extra (*zā'ida*), which is added to non-declinable adverbial nouns. The *min* preceding *awliyā'* is also extra, for the purpose of encompassing the negated category, meaning: they had not a single member of the class of allies.

The "doubled punishment" (*al-'adhāb al-muḍā'af*) is the punishment of the Hereafter, by the indication of His words, ﴿they will not be able to escape on earth﴾, which implies a delay of punishment for them in this world, not because of incapacity.

* * *

﴿Their punishment will be doubled.﴾
This is a predicate of the demonstrative. It is also possible that the clause ﴿they will not be able to escape on earth﴾ is the first predicate and the clause "will be doubled" is the second predicate. It is also possible that the clause ﴿they will not be able to escape﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) and the clause "will be doubled" is the first predicate.

* * *

﴿They were not able to hear, nor were they able to see.﴾
This may be a predicate of the demonstrative or a circumstantial clause of it. In that case, the negated "ability to hear" is a metaphor for their aversion to hearing the Qur'an and the sayings of the Prophet (ﷺ), just as ability was negated in the verse of al-A'sha:

*And can you bear farewell, O man?*

He meant by negating the capacity to bear farewell that he grieves so much over parting that it resembles something that cannot be borne. Here he expresses it with "ability" (*istiṭā'a*) because the Prophet (ﷺ) was calling them to listen to the Qur'an, but they turned away, because they disliked hearing it. He says, ﴿Woe to every sinful liar﴾ [al-Jathiya: 7], ﴿who hears the verses of Allah recited to him, then persists arrogantly as if he had not heard them﴾ [al-Jathiya: 8]. And He says, ﴿Those who disbelieve say: Do not listen to this Qur'an, and make noise during it, that perhaps you will overcome﴾ [Fussilat: 26]. This is because if they had listened and understood, they would have been guided, since the spoken speech contains the composition of proofs and their conclusions, so hearing it is sufficient for attaining guidance.

The negated "seeing" (*ibṣār*) is contemplation of created things which indicate the Oneness [of Allah], meaning they did not direct their gaze to created things with the direction of reflection and contemplation. Rather they looked at them with the gaze of one heedless of the subtleties within them. For this reason, He did not say here, "they were not able to see," because they did see them; but mere seeing is insufficient for achieving inference unless reflection is added to it. This differs from hearing in His words, ﴿they were not able to hear﴾.

It is also possible that the clause is a circumstantial clause of "allies," and what permitted its being a circumstantial clause of an indefinite noun is that the indefinite noun occurs in a negative context. The meaning is: they took them as gods for themselves while they (the idols) are unable to hear or see.

The return of the plural pronoun for rational beings to the idols in this manner is viewed as based on the fact that the polytheists believed they understand. In this employment of the pronoun, together with the negation of hearing and seeing from them, there is a form of mockery of them.

The use of the verbs of being (*af'āl al-kawn*) in these clauses four times, beginning from His words, ﴿Those will not be able to escape﴾ up to His words, ﴿nor were they able to see﴾, serves to convey what the verb of being indicates of the firm establishment of the event reported. So His words, ﴿they will not be able to escape﴾ (*lam yakūnū mu'jizīn*) are more emphatic than "they do not escape," and similarly for its counterparts.

The variation between the forms of the verbs of being, in that the first is in the present form (with *lam*) and the three following it are in the past form, is because the jussive present with the particle *lam* carries the meaning of the past. So the variation among them is nothing but stylistic variety.

ʾUlāʾika alladhīna khasirū anfusahum wa ḍalla ʿanhum mā kānū yaftarūn (Qur'an 11:21)... [translation of the quoted verses follows below]

**Translation**

Page 38

﴿Those are the ones who have lost their souls, and what they used to fabricate has gone astray from them.﴾ ﴿Undoubtedly, in the Hereafter, they are the greatest losers.﴾

This is a resumptive sentence (istiʾnāf). The demonstrative "those" (ʾulāʾika) here is a second emphasis of the demonstrative in His words: ﴿Those are presented before their Lord﴾ [Hud: 18].

The relative pronoun in ﴿those who have lost their souls﴾ [al-Anʿam: 20] is meant to denote the category known by this description; that is, it reaches you that a people lost their souls, and they are the ones who fabricate lies against Allah. The loss of their souls means the failure to benefit from them in being guided; when they went astray, they indeed lost them.

The discussion of "they lost their souls" has already been presented under His words, exalted is He: ﴿Those who have lost their souls, so they do not believe﴾ [al-Anʿam: 20], in Surat al-Anʿam.

Ḍalāl (going astray) is the error of the intended path.

And ﴿what they used to fabricate﴾ [al-Anʿam: 24] refers to what they used to claim: that the idols would intercede for them and ward off harm from them in times of hardship. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Why did those they had taken as gods besides Allah, as a means of approach, not help them? Rather, they went astray from them; that was their lie and what they used to fabricate﴾ [al-Aḥqāf: 28].

In attributing the going astray to the idols there is a mockery of their worshippers. Their idols are likened to one who takes a road to reach someone he sought help from, and then gets lost on the way.

The clause ﴿Undoubtedly, in the Hereafter, they are the greatest losers﴾ is a resumptive, concluding and consequential sentence following the preceding clauses from His words: ﴿Those are presented before their Lord﴾ [Hud: 18], because what has been gathered for them of being driven to punishment, of the exposure of their affair, and of their turning away from hearing the warnings and from reflecting on the signs of God's oneness, necessarily entails certainty that they are the greatest losers in the Hereafter.

Lā jaram is a word of certainty and conviction that has taken the place of a proverb. I suppose that jaram is derived from something that has been forgotten. The grammarians of Arabic have differed about its composition, and the most apparent of their views is that

﴿Those are the ones who have lost their souls, and what they used to fabricate has gone astray from them.﴾ ﴿Undoubtedly, in the Hereafter, they are the greatest losers.﴾

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 11, verse 23:

﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds and humble themselves before their Lord - those are the companions of Paradise; they will abide therein eternally.﴾

When he had mentioned the states of those who reach the utmost extremes of loss, he mentioned their counterparts, those who attain the highest degrees of happiness. The sentence is a resumptive clause (istી'naf bayani, a sentence that begins a new topic to answer a question the listener naturally forms), because when people hear the judgment on one thing, their souls strain to know the judgment on its opposite.

Al-ikhbat (الإخبات) means submission and humility; that is, they obeyed their Lord in the best obedience.

The position of ﴿ulaika﴾ (أولئك, "those") here is like its position in the verse before it.

The clause ﴿hum fiha khalidun﴾ (هم فيها خالدون, "they will abide therein eternally") is in the position of explanation for the phrase ﴿ashab al-jannah﴾ (أصحاب الجنة, "companions of Paradise"), because abiding eternally in a place is the most appropriate of states for applying the description of "companion" to someone in that place, since places are sought only for the sake of dwelling in them. Thus the clause is a resumptive clause explaining what precedes it, and its status is that of an explicative apposition ('atf al-bayan, a noun or clause that clarifies the one before it). It is not to be parsed (i'rab, grammatical analysis) as a second predicate (khabar thani) of the demonstrative noun. A parallel of it has already occurred in surah al-Baqarah in His saying: ﴿Those who believe and do righteous deeds - those are the companions of Paradise; they will abide therein eternally.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 82]. So return to that passage and add to it what is here.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 11, verse 24:

﴿The likeness of the two parties is like the blind and the deaf, and the seeing and the hearing. Are they equal in likeness? Will you not then be mindful?﴾

After the difference between the state of the polytheists, who fabricate lies against God, and the state of those who believed and did righteous deeds, in the abodes of the Hereafter, was made clear, there followed an explanation of the comparison between the two states of the two parties, the polytheists and the believers, by way of depicting what each deserves of blame and praise.

The sentence is therefore a summary (fadhlaka) of the discourse, a consolidation of it, and a warning against falling into its cause.

Al-mathal, with a vowel on the first letter, means the condition or attribute, as in God's words, ﴿The likeness of the Garden which the righteous have been promised﴾ (Surah al-Ra'd, 35), and the verse that follows it in Surah al-Ra'd. That is: the condition of the two parties, the polytheists and the believers, resembles the condition of the blind and the deaf on one side, and the condition of the seeing and the hearing on the other side. The statement is therefore a simile (tashbih), not a metaphor (isti'arah), because the particle of comparison (kaf al-tashbih) is present; and it is also a simple (mufrad) simile, not a compound (murakkab) one.

The two parties are those mentioned in this discourse, namely the party of the polytheists and the party of the believers, since what indicates these two parties has already preceded in God's words, ﴿Who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against God?﴾ (Surah al-An'am, 21), and then His words, ﴿Indeed, those who believed and did righteous deeds and humbled themselves before their Lord﴾ (Surah Hud, 23), and the verse that follows it.

[Page 41]

Al-fariq (party) is a group that is distinguished, that is, whose condition differs from the condition of another group in action or creed. It was discussed earlier at God's words, ﴿So which of the two parties is more deserving of security, if you know?﴾ (Surah al-An'am, 81).

He likened the state of the party of disbelievers, in their failure to benefit from reflecting on the clear evidences of God's oneness in His creation, to the state of the blind; and they were likened, in their failure to benefit from the proofs of the Qur'an, to the state of one who is deaf.

And He likened the state of the party of believers, by contrast, to the state of one who has sound sight and sound hearing, so he is upon guidance and certainty regarding what he perceives.

The arrangement of the two likened states in mention, following the order in which the two parties were mentioned earlier, indicates the intended meaning of each party in the manner of ordered correspondence (al-nashr al-murattab, "ordered unfolding"). Order in laff wa nashr (the arrangement of wrapping and unfolding) is the basic and predominant pattern.

It is known that those likened to the blind and the deaf are the party about whom it is said, ﴿They were not able to hear, and they did not see﴾ (Surah Hud, 20).

The waw in His words, "and the deaf," is for coordination with "the blind," coordinating one of the two likened items with the other. Likewise, the waw in His words, "and the hearing," is for coordination with "the seeing."

As for the waw in His words, "and the seeing," it is for coordinating the second comparison with the first, which is the unfolding after the wrapping. It coordinates one of the two parties with the other, and the coordination by it is for division (taqsim), and the indication is clear.

One who looks at this might think that the appropriate course is to omit coordinating the attribute of the deaf with the attribute of the blind, just as their counterparts were not coordinated in God's words, ﴿Deaf, dumb, and blind﴾ (Surah al-Baqarah, 18) in Surah al-Baqarah, supposing that the subject of both verses is the same, namely that the intent is to liken those who combined the two attributes. That is one of two aspects mentioned by the author of al-Kashshaf (Zamakhshari's commentary). The commentators on the margins of al-Kashshaf have answered that the coordination is based on treating the difference of attributes as the difference of essences. They did not mention a reason for this treatment; perhaps they meant that it is merely a usage in speech, like the words of Ibn Zayyaba:

"Alas for Zayyaba for al-Harith, the one who rises at dawn, the one who takes booty, the one who returns."

[Page 42]

In my view, the reason for coordinating the attribute of the deaf with the attribute of the blind is that it is intended that the party of disbelievers has two states, each of which is worthy of being likened by one of those two attributes separately. They liken the blind in failing to be guided to the evidences whose path of apprehension is sight, and they liken the deaf in failing to understand beneficial admonitions whose path of understanding is hearing. Thus they are, in two states, each of which is likened separately. In God's words, ﴿like the blind and the deaf﴾, there are two separate similes, as in the words of Imru' al-Qays:

"As if the hearts of birds, moist and dry, beside their nest are 'unnab berries and a decayed dry date-stalk."

What is in the verse is the likening of intelligible things to perceptible things. Considering each of the two states of the party of disbelievers is unavoidable, because the occurrence of either of the two states is sufficient to draw misguidance upon them, let alone both together, since the thing likened to them is a negative matter and thus is in the sense of the negated.

As for the reason for coordination in the two attributes of the seeing and the hearing with respect to the state of the party of believers, it is different from what we have established regarding the state of the party of disbelievers. The state of the believers resembles the state of the combined two attributes of the seeing and the hearing, since guidance is attained only through the combination of the two attributes. If one of the two attributes were established and the other were absent, guidance would not be attained, since the two matters likened to them are existential matters, and so they are in the sense of affirmation. Therefore, it is determined that the reason for coordinating the hearing with the seeing in likening the state of the party of believers is the pairing (muzawaja) in expression, so that the expression about the state of the believers would be parallel to the expression about the state of the disbelievers within the context of the discourse. Pairing is among the embellishments of speech (muhassinat al-kalam), and it returns to its eloquence.

[Page 43]

The clause, ﴿Are they equal in likeness?﴾, stands in the position of explanation of the purpose of the simile, which is the negation of the equality of their states. The negation of equality is a metonymy (kinayah) for preference, and the one preferred between them is known from the context, that is, the preference of the party depicted by the hearing and the seeing over the party depicted by the blind and the deaf is known. The interrogative is one of denial (istifham inkari).

"Likeness" (mathalan) is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz), that is, with respect to their state; and al-mathal means the state.

The intent is to alert the polytheists to the misguidance they are in, so that perhaps they might remedy their affair. For this reason, the clause ﴿Will you not then be mindful?﴾ follows it with the particle fa' (then).

The hamza is an interrogative, and it denies the absence of their remembrance and the continuation of their misguidance.

The majority of readers recite tadhakkarun with a shadda on the dhal. Its original form is tatadhakkarun; the ta' was changed to dal because the two articulation points are close, and in order to facilitate idgham (assimilation) for lightness. Hafs, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i recite it with a light dhal, by omitting one of the two ta's from the beginning of the verb.

The pairing of the blind and the deaf with the seeing and the hearing is an embellishment of antithesis (tibaq).

[Ibn 'Ashur, *al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir*, on verses 25–26]

﴿And We certainly sent Noah to his people: "Indeed, I am to you a clear warner, that you worship none but Allah. Indeed, I fear for you the punishment of a painful day."﴾

This is a transition from warning the polytheists, describing their conditions and what is related to that, to admonishing them with the calamities that befell those who denied before them. This also consoles the Prophet ﷺ with what the messengers, peace be upon them, faced from their peoples before him.

The conjunction here is the conjunction of one narrative to another, which is called the *waw al-ibtida'iyya* (the initial *waw*, used to begin a new narrative).

The sentence is emphasized with the *lam al-qasam* (the lam of oath) and *qad*, because the addressees, having failed to take heed of what happened to the people of Noah, despite the similarity of their own circumstances, were treated as one who denies the occurrence of his message.

[Page 44]

Nafi', 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir and Hamza read *innī* with a kasra on the hamza, so that it is reported by a verb of saying that is omitted and is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*), meaning "saying."

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, al-Kisa'i, Abu Ja'far, Ya'qub and Khalaf read it with a fatha on the hamza (*annī*), presupposing a preposition, which is the *bā'* of accompaniment (*lil-mulābasa*), meaning: We sent him while associated with that, i.e., with the meaning of the verbal noun derived from "that I am a warner," that is, while clothed in clear warning.

The discussion of Noah, peace be upon him, and his people has already been given in the commentary on His words, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah chose Adam and Noah﴾ [Al 'Imran: 33] in Surat Al 'Imran, and at His words: ﴿We certainly sent Noah to his people﴾ [Al A'raf: 59] in Surat Al A'raf.

The clause ﴿that you worship none but Allah﴾ explains the clause "We sent," because sending contains the meaning of saying without its letters. It is also permissible for it to explain *nadhīr* (warner), because "warner" contains the meaning of saying, as in His words in Surat Nuh: ﴿He said: "O my people, indeed I am to you a clear warner, that you worship Allah and fear Him"﴾ [Nuh: 2–3]. This possibility is definite in the reading with a fatha on the hamza of *annī*, if *an* is taken as explanatory (*tafsīriyya*).

It is also permissible to take *an* as the lightened form of the heavy *anna*, so that it is a substitute for "that I am to you a clear warner," in the reading with a fatha on the hamza. Its subject is an omitted pronoun of the matter (*ḍamīr sha'n*), meaning: that it is, "You shall not worship except Allah."

The clause ﴿Indeed, I fear for you the punishment of a painful day﴾ gives the reason for "warner," because it is the nature of warning to weigh heavily upon souls and to humiliate them. So it was fitting to be given a reason, to remove the discomfort of what they encounter.

Describing the day as painful is a metaphor in the attribution (*majāz 'aqlī*), and it is more eloquent than describing the punishment itself as painful, because when the severity of the punishment reached its utmost, its time was described as painful, meaning causing pain.

The clause "I fear for you" and similar expressions, such as "I fear for you" (*akhshā 'alayka*), are used to express apprehension about a matter that is supposed or certain, considering the possibility of escaping what is certain. As Labid said:

*I fear for Arbad the calamities of death,*
*yet I do not fear for him the winds and the rain.*

So the verb is transitive to the thing feared by itself, and it takes the object feared for by the preposition *'alā*, as in the verse and in Labid's line.

[Page 45]

The punishment here is indefinite in meaning, because it is attributed to an indefinite noun, so it may refer to the punishment of this world or the punishment of the Hereafter. As for the punishment of this world, its descent upon them is not certain, but it is supposed by Noah, peace be upon him, based on his knowledge of Allah's care for the faith of his people and what was revealed to him of his zeal in conveying the message. So he knew that it is the nature of such matters that Allah does not leave those who disobey Him without punishment. For this reason he said in his subsequent speech: ﴿It is only Allah who will bring it to you, if He wills﴾ [Hud: 33], as will come there. The punishment also included the punishment of the Hereafter if they remained in disbelief, and this is certain, because Allah joins the threat with the call. For this reason Noah, peace be upon him, said in his subsequent speech: ﴿And you cannot escape﴾ [Hud: 33]. The punishment of this world came readily to the minds of his people, because they did not believe in the Resurrection, so they said in their subsequent speech: ﴿Then bring us what you threaten us with, if you are among the truthful﴾ [Hud: 32]. Perhaps in Noah's speech, peace be upon him, there is what indicates to them that he threatened them with a punishment in this world, which was the Flood.
