He joined the statement of the chiefs (al-mala'), those among his people, with the particle *fa* (then) to the verb *arsalna* (We sent), to indicate that they rushed to reject him with futile disputation when he said to them: ﴿Indeed I am to you a clear warner﴾ (Hud 11:25), and so on to the end of it. The narration of the beginning of their dialogue with him is not given with *qala* (he said) standing alone without *fa*, as occurs in al-A'raf, because the beginning of his dialogue with them here did not take the form of the word "qawl" (saying). Therefore their reply was not related in the manner of dialogues, unlike the verse in al-A'raf.

Al-Mala' means the nobles of a people. It was discussed earlier at His saying, ﴿The chiefs of his people said: Indeed we see you in clear error﴾ (al-A'raf 7:60), in the commentary on Surah al-A'raf.

They were determined to reject him, so they put forward premises from which they drew his rejection. These premises were false, and they built them upon the false sophistries that were common among them, which habit and custom had promoted. They reckoned superiority by nobility (al-su'dud), a status conventionally defined whose foundation is courage and generosity. They made the causes of nobility material and bodily, so they made lords of those with handsome bodies, as if they were propped-up pieces of wood. Because of the simplicity of their intellectual faculties, they magnified the beauty of physical forms. They made lords of the wealthy, because they hoped for their largesse, and they made lords of the champions, because they prepared them to defend against their enemies. Then they came to know the bearers of those qualities either by associating with them or by associating with their followers. When they heard of a lord of a people whom they did not know, they came to know his followers and supporters. If they were of the nobles and lords, they knew that they had followed him only because they saw in him the requisites of lordship. These causes are suited to the conditions of the people of error, since they have no concern for the soul-related side of the human frame.

When Nuh (peace be upon him) called them with a call from which they knew that he was leading them to obedience to him, they reflected and calculated, and they saw that the causes of nobility familiar among them were absent in Nuh (peace be upon him) and in those who followed him. So they were certain that he was not worthy of lordship over them, and they were certain of rejecting him in what he claimed of prophethood, with lordship over the community and leadership of it.

These people, because of the weakness of their minds and the feebleness of their perceptions, did not reach the realization of the true causes of perfection. Instead they sought perfection in accidental attributes that befall people by chance: abundance of wealth, strength of followers, or the might of a tribe. These are things whose effect does not consistently bring general benefit, nor do they indicate the perfection of their possessor, since the least intelligent of people share them, and so do dumb animals, such as the cow with the milk in its udder or the sheep with the wool on its back. Indeed, their usual state is the opposite of that.

Sometimes they sought perfection in unfamiliar kinds, such as the jinn, or in extra bodily features that have no effect on the work of the one who possesses them, such as beauty of form and perfection of stature. Although these accompany what they describe, they do not benefit them in becoming sources of perfections,

**Page 47**

since many dumb animals share them, such as gazelles, oryxes, and peacocks. If they rose above that, they sought perfection in the causes of strength and might, such as the breadth of the body, skill in archery, wrestling, and courage in facing the enemy. These are more fitting to be counted among the causes of perfection, but they are complements to human perfection, because they are instruments for executing lofty aims in the view of people of sound intellect and of divine wisdom, such as prophets and righteous kings. Without that, they become instruments for executing evil aims, like the courage of brigands, highwaymen, and vagabonds, and like the strength to tear off doors in order to storm the homes of the secure.

The true perfection is the purification of the soul (zaka' al-nafs) and the uprightness of the intellect (istiqamat al-'aql). These two are the consistent cause of delivering general benefits to what is in this world. Through them the executive powers become servants, like courage for those who defend the truth and for those who compel tyrants to submit to the religion. Yet that is exposed to error and to the absence of correctness, so it cannot be safeguarded from that except when it is surrounded by infallible divine guidance, and this is the station of prophethood and messengership.

Thus these disbelievers of the people of Nuh, when they fell short of realizing the causes of perfection and sought causes from other than their proper place, looked at Nuh (peace be upon him) and his followers. They did not see him as of a kind other than human, and when they considered him and his followers, they did not see in their bodies anything distinguishing them from people. Perhaps among the community in general there were those whose faces were more beautiful or whose bodies were taller.

For this reason they erred in inference, and so they said: ﴿We do not see you except as a human like us﴾, so they grounded their inference in sight. Here "sight" means ocular sight, because they made their inference a necessity drawn from the sensible features of bodies. That is, "We do not see you as anything other than a human, one who is similar to people and does not have extra limbs or additional appendages."

Al-bashar, with a short vowel on the first letter and a sukun on the second, means the human being, male or female, singular or plural. Al-Raghib said: "The human being is called bashar in consideration of the visibility of his skin (bashara), which is his hide, free of hair, unlike animals that have wool, hair, or fur," that is, or feathers. Al-bashar is a synonym of al-insan, so it is applied as al-insan is applied, to the singular and the plural, the feminine and the masculine. It may also be made dual, as in His saying, ﴿Shall we believe in two humans like us?﴾ (al-Mu'minun 23:47).

They also said: ﴿And we do not see that those who follow you are other than our lowly ones﴾. They made the followers of people, whom they counted as lesser in their customs, lowly and despised, as evidence that he had no distinction over their lords, whom the nobles and the strong of the people take refuge with. So they negated from him the cause of lordship from two directions: his own person and his followers. This is an insinuation that they do not follow him because they hold themselves above mixing with the likes of those, and that if he drove those away from him, they would follow him. For this reason there came after it: ﴿And I am not one to drive away those who believe﴾ (Hud 11:29), and so on.

Al-aradhil is the plural of arzal, which has become a noun and not an adjective, plural in that way by analogy; or it is the plural of radhil, against analogy. Al-radhil means the despised. They meant that they are among the common mass of the people, not lords and not wealthy. The annexation of "aradhil" to the pronoun of the first-person plural serves to specify the tribe, that is, "the lowly ones of our people." He expressed them with the relative pronoun and its clause rather than saying "except our lowly ones," to convey that in the speech of those who disbelieved there is an allusion to the fame of Nuh's followers among their people by the description of baseness and vileness. Nuh's followers were among the weak of the people, but they were of pure souls, among those who had already been granted guidance.

*Badi'* was read by the majority with a yā' at its end, as derived from *bada* (to appear), a defective verb, and its alif is converted from a wāw, since it moved and the letter before it was opened. When the pattern *fā'il* was formed from it, the wāw came in final position after a kasra and was converted to a yā'. The meaning is what appears to them of opinion, without investigating its hidden and subtle aspects.

Abu 'Amr alone read it with a hamza at its end, as derived from *bada'* (beginning), which is the first of a thing. The meaning is: in what occurs at the first opinion, that is, without re-examining to know the truth from the deception. The outcome of both meanings is one.

Al-ra'y is the intellect's view, derived from the verb *ra'a* (to see), just as *ra'a* is used with the meaning of *zanna* (to suppose) and *'alima* (to know).

**Page 49**

They mean that these people have been deceived by your call, so they hastened to follow you; if they had reconsidered and reflected, they would have known that you do not deserve to be followed.

The accusative of *badi' al-ra'y* is by way of substitution for the adverb of time, that is, "at the time of opinion" without investigating its hidden aspects, or "at the first opinion" without re-examination.

The annexation of *badi'* to *al-ra'y* is an annexation of the attribute to the thing described. The meaning of their statement is: their rightful guidance will not delay in returning to your followers, so they will reconsider at another time, and their error will be exposed to them.

When they described each of the two groups, the follower and the followed, with what negates the lordship of the followed and the purification of the follower, they combined the comprehensive description covering both. This was the intended meaning of the two separate descriptions. That is their saying, ﴿And we do not see for you any superiority over us﴾. Thus they denied that Nuh (peace be upon him) and his followers had any superiority over those who did not believe in him, such that Nuh would be a lord over them and his followers would be preferred by the lordship of their leader.

Al-fadl is excess in nobility and perfection. What is intended here is its effects and signs, because they are what is seen. So they made the absence of any visible superiority in them over those others evidence of the absence of their superiority, because a thing whose effects are not hidden may rightly be taken to have the absence of seeing them as evidence of its absence, since if it were established it would have been seen.

The clause ﴿But we think you are liars﴾ is a refutation of the entire negated content, which indicates the truth of his claim by establishing the opposite of what was negated. That opposite is their supposition that they are liars, because when a thing is refuted, its opposite is established. So they asserted that Nuh (peace be upon him) was a liar in his claim of messengership, and that his followers were liars in their claim of having attained certainty about the truthfulness of Nuh (peace be upon him). Rather, that from them was a false belief. This supposition they claimed rests on the sensible evidence as they believed.

Here *al-zann* (supposition) is used in the sense of knowledge, as in His saying, ﴿Those who suppose that they will meet their Lord﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:46). This usage is widespread in speech.

[Page 50]

﴿He said: "O my people, tell me, if I have a clear proof from my Lord, and He has granted me mercy from Himself, yet it has been concealed from you, shall we compel you to accept it while you are averse to it?"﴾

The sentence "He said, O my people" is detached from the preceding sentence, following the manner of relating speech in dialogues, as we have explained previously at His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And when your Lord said to the angels, "Indeed, I will place upon the earth a successor"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30] in Surat al-Baqarah. Here, because it corresponds to a reported statement, the sentence is detached and not joined by a conjunction ('atf). This differs from what came earlier in His words: ﴿The eminent ones among those of his people who disbelieved said﴾ [Hud: 27].

The opening of his reply with the vocative (al-nida') is to solicit the attention of their minds to understand his words, as was discussed for its counterpart in Surat al-A'raf. Choosing to address them with the title "his people" serves to draw down the bird of their aversion, reminding them that he is one of them and therefore wants nothing but good for them.

Since their objection to his mission was based on the claim that they saw in him no distinction or superiority, and saw only the weak among their people following him, and that this is a sign of his falsehood and the misguidance of his followers, Noah (peace be upon him) followed in his argument two methods: first a general method to nullify their doubt, and then a detailed method to refute their statements. As for the general method, he followed the method of reversal (qalb), by saying that if they do not see in him and his followers anything that compels belief in his mission, then likewise he cannot compel them to see the meanings that indicate his truthfulness, nor can he prevent those who believed in him from following him and being guided by the guidance he brought.

So his saying: ﴿If I have a clear proof from my Lord﴾ to the end of the verse means: if I possess a clear demonstration and am endowed with the mercy of God through the mission and the guidance, yet the proof and the indications of guidance have not become manifest to you, then shall I and my followers compel you to accept them, that is, to submit to them and affirm them,

[Page 51]

while you are averse to accepting them? This is an allusion (ta'ridh) that if they had reflected with an unbiased consideration, free from aversion and hostility, they would have known the truth of his call.

"Ara'aytum" is an interrogation about seeing in the sense of believing. It is a rhetorical interrogation (istifham taqriri) when the verb of seeing does not govern a single noun; it is then a confirmation of the content of the clause that takes the place of the two objects of ra'aytum. For this reason its meaning returns to "inform me," but it is used only when addressing someone whose state is that of one who denies the report. Its meaning has already been discussed at His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: "Tell me, if the punishment of God comes upon you suddenly or openly"﴾ [al-An'am: 47] in Surat al-An'am.

The clause ﴿If I have a clear proof from my Lord﴾ up to His words ﴿it has been concealed from you﴾ is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraḍ) between the verb "ara'aytum" and what takes the place of its two objects.

The interrogation in ﴿shall we compel you to it﴾ is a denial (istifham inkari), meaning: we do not compel you to accept it. The compulsion is attached to the pronoun referring to the proof or the mercy. What is meant is that it is attached to acceptance of it, as indicated by the context.

Bayyinah (clear proof) means a manifest argument, and it may also be applied to a miracle. Thus his miracle could be the Flood, and it is also possible that he had other miracles not mentioned, since the sending of messengers (peace be upon them) is never free of miracles.

By mercy is meant the blessing of prophethood and the distinction over them which they denied, together with the clear proof that accompanied it, since it is part of its completion. Thus the conjoining of mercy with proof requires that the two be different. The difference is one of generality and specificity, for mercy is more general than proof, since the proof of his truthfulness is part of the mercy granted to him. For this reason, when the pronoun was repeated in His words "it has been concealed" (fa-'ummiyat), it referred back to mercy, because it is the more general.

The phrase "upon you" ( 'alaykum) is connected to "concealed" ('ummiyat). It is a particle through which verbs indicating the meaning of hiddenness are transitive, such as "khafiya 'alayka" (it was hidden from you). Since 'ummiya has the meaning of khafiya, it takes "'ala," which denotes figurative elevation, meaning firm establishment, that is, the strength of the proof's and mercy's constant adherence to him.

The choice of the description "Lord" instead of the proper name of majesty (Allah) is to indicate that His granting of the proof and the mercy is a bounty from God; he intended by this to show His gentleness and care towards him.

The meaning of "fa-'ummiyat" is "fa-khafiyat" (it became hidden). This is a metaphor (isti'arah), in that the proof that the addressees did not perceive is likened to the blind, in that it did not reach their minds, just as a blind person cannot find the way to reach his destination, and so does not arrive at it. Since "'ummiya" was given the sense of "khafiya," the verb "fa-'ummiyat" is construed with the particle "'ala" in order to strip the metaphor down (tajrid). In contrast to this metaphor comes His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And We gave Thamud the she-camel as a visible sign﴾ [al-Isra': 59], meaning We gave them a clear sign that could not be denied, because it was a perceptible sign. For this reason their denial of it was called injustice, as He said: ﴿they wronged themselves by it﴾.

Among the excellences of this metaphor here is that it contains an antithesis (tibaq) corresponding to their statements in their dispute: ﴿We see you only as a human being﴾ [Hud: 27], and "we do not see that anyone followed you," and ﴿we do not see for you any superiority over us﴾ [Hud: 27]. Noah (peace be upon him) answered their words with a counterpart both in meaning and in wording, for he made their not seeing a kind of blindness.

The conjunction of "'ummiyat" with the particle fa' of sequence (ta'qib) indicates that there was no interval between his being given the proof and the mercy and their becoming hidden from them. It is also an allusion to them, that they hastened to deny before reflecting.

The clause ﴿shall we compel you to it﴾ takes the place of the two objects of "ara'aytum," because the verb has been suspended from acting by the entry of the interrogative hamzah.

The answer to the conditional is omitted, indicated by the verb "ara'aytum" and what took the place of its two objects. The sense of the discourse is: O my people, if I have a clear proof from my Lord, up to the end, do you see that we would compel you to accept the proof while you are averse to it?

The pronoun of the speaker, who is included with them here, is used to indicate that if compulsion were supposed to occur, he would have helpers in it, namely his followers. So he wanted not to neglect mention of his followers, and that they are supporters for him should he wish to call upon them. The purpose of this is to exalt their status in contrast to the contempt of the others toward them.

[Page 53]

The interrogation is a denial, meaning: it was not for us to do that, because God did not command him to compel them. This is a turning away from concern for them, so he left their affair to God, and that is more intense in provoking fear of a great punishment.

The one who is averse (al-kari) is the one who hates something. It is made transitive by the particle "li" (to) to its object, to strengthen the attachment of aversion to the mercy or the proof, meaning: while you are hating to accept it because of your turning away from reflecting upon it.

The placing of the prepositional phrase before "averse" (karihun) is for the sake of the rhyme (fasilah), together with attention to its matter. The purpose of his speech is to urge them to reconsider the signs, to lower their self-assertion, and to bring them down to fairness. The intent is not to excuse them for what they did, nor to desist from repeating his call to them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 11, verse 29:

﴿And O my people, I do not ask you for wealth in return for it. My reward is only from Allah. And I am not one to drive away those who have believed. Indeed, they are going to meet their Lord, but I see you as a people who are ignorant.﴾

The repetition of the address "O my people" (yā qawmi) is for emphasis on the meanings mentioned earlier in the address. As for joining the address with the conjunction "wa" (and), although the one addressed is one person, the rule for conjoining an address is that it occurs when the one called upon differs, as in the verse of al-Ma'arri:

O watcher of the lightning, wake the sleeper of the Samur (trees); perhaps at al-Jizʿ there are helpers against the sleeplessness.
Then he said:

And O captive of her two anklets, I see it as foolishness, carrying jewelry for one who is blind to sight.

But when the addressed is one and the same, the rule is non-conjunction, as in the story of Abraham (peace be upon him) in Surah Maryam: ﴿When he said to his father, "O my father, why do you worship that which neither hears nor sees?"﴾ [Maryam: 42] up to his saying "and a friend," for the address was repeated four times.

Page 54
Thus it is determined here that the conjunction is part of Noah's (peace be upon him) own speech, not part of Allah's narration about him. Then it is possible that it serves as an alert to the connection of the addresses to one another, and that one of them does not suffice in place of the other; and this is not of the kind of conjunction (wasl) because the address is an opening of speech, so its clause is independent, and its conjunction when conjoined is merely a verbal conjunction. It is also possible that this is an Arabic stylistic variation (tafannun) in speech when the address is repeated, favoring the variation between the emphasis and the emphasized. Something similar will come shortly in the story of Hud (peace be upon him) and the story of Shu'ayb (peace be upon him).
Of this is what occurred in Surah al-Mu'min in His saying: ﴿And said the one who believed, "O my people, indeed I fear for you a day like the days of the factions"﴾ [Ghafir: 30] ﴿like the custom of the people of Noah and 'Ad and Thamud and those after them. And Allah does not intend injustice for the servants﴾ [Ghafir: 31] ﴿And O my people, indeed I fear for you the Day of Calling Out﴾ [Ghafir: 32] ﴿the Day you will turn back in retreat; you will have from Allah no protector﴾ [Ghafir: 33]. Then He said ﴿And said the one who believed, "O my people, follow me; I will guide you to the way of right conduct"﴾ [Ghafir: 38] ﴿O my people, indeed this worldly life is but a provision, and indeed the Hereafter is the abode of permanence﴾ [Ghafir: 39] ﴿Whoever does an evil deed will not be recompensed except by its equivalent; and whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while being a believer—those will enter Paradise, being provided therein without account﴾ [Ghafir: 40] ﴿And O my people, what is [wrong] with me that I invite you to salvation while you invite me to the Fire?﴾ [Ghafir: 41]. So he conjoined "wa yā qawmi" at one time and left the conjunction at another.

As for when the attribute of the one addressed differs, conjunction has come, and it is more apparent, because of the semblance of difference in the attribute of the one addressed, as in the saying of Qays ibn 'Asim, or it is said Hatim al-Ta'i:

O daughter of ʿAbd Allah and daughter of Malik, and O daughter of the one of the two cloaks and the red horse.
So his saying "wa-bnata dhi al-burdayn" is a conjunction of address upon address, and the one addressed by both is one and the same.

When Noah (peace be upon him) made clear to them that he would compel them to a faith they dislike, he moved to bringing them closer to considering the purity of what he brought them, and that he does not seek worldly gain, in that he does not ask them for anything they would not give him; so what would they accuse him of, to the extent that they decisively call him a liar?

Page 55
The pronoun in His saying "ʿalayhi" refers to what was mentioned, in the position of a demonstrative, as in His saying "and whoever does that," for the pronoun is treated as a demonstrative.

The clause ﴿in ajriya illa ʿala Allah﴾ is a precaution (ihtiras), for when he negated that he asks them for wealth, and wealth is a reward, the supposition arose that he does not ask any recompense for the call, so he brought the clause ﴿in ajriya illa ʿala Allah﴾ as a precaution. The variation between the two expressions in His saying "mālan" and "ajriya" indicates that he does not ask wealth from Allah, but he asks a reward. And "ajr" is the compensation for a deed. The reward of Allah is called "ajr" because it is a recompense for righteous deeds.

He conjoined the clause ﴿wa ma ana bi-tārid alladhina amanu﴾ to the clause ﴿la as'alukum ʿalayhi mālan﴾, because its content is like a result of the content of what it is conjoined to, since negating his desire regarding the addressees entails that he does not harm his followers for the sake of pleasing these people. For this reason he expressed his followers by way of the relative form with His saying "alladhina amanu," because of what the relative clause indicates regarding the blame of his people in their exposing him to driving them away on the grounds that they do not sit with people like them, signifying that their faith necessitates preferring them over others who have not believed, and desiring them, so how could he drive them away? This is a refutation of what their saying "and we do not see you followed except by those who are our lowest" [Hud: 27] implied, of the insinuation that they are not equal to them in following him.

Ṭard (driving away) is the command to distance oneself from the place of presence, in contempt or rebuke. It was mentioned earlier at His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord﴾ [al-An'am: 52] in Surah al-An'am.

The clause ﴿innahum mulaqu rabbihim﴾ is in the position of a justification for negating that he would drive them away, on the ground that they are going to Allah in the Hereafter, so whoever drives them away will be called to account. This holds if "meeting" is literal. Or he meant that they call upon their Lord in their prayers, so Allah will support them if "meeting" is figurative. Or [it means] that they will meet their Lord when they attend the gathering of my call, because I call to Allah, not to something that belongs to me, so they are at my meeting like those who meet their Lord, because they receive what Allah has revealed to me. This is like the saying of the Prophet ﷺ regarding the story of the three men who

Page 56
came to the gathering of the Prophet ﷺ: one of them sat down, one of them was shy, and the third turned away. "As for the first, he sought refuge in Allah, so Allah sheltered him; as for the second, he was shy, so Allah was shy of him; as for the third, he turned away, so Allah turned away from him."

The emphasis of the predicate with "inna" is, if the meeting is literal, to refute their denial of resurrection; and if the meeting is figurative, the emphasis is for attention to that meeting. This emphasis has been further emphasized by the clause "wa lakinni ara-kum qawman tajhalun" (but I see you as a people who are ignorant).

The place of the istidrak (corrective contrast) is that the content of this clause is the opposite of the content of the one before it, namely the clause ﴿innahum mulaqu rabbihim﴾: that is, there is no doubt about that, but you are ignorant, so you suppose they have no presence and that there is no consequence for driving them away.

The omission of the object of "tajhalun" is because it is known, i.e., you are ignorant of that.

The addition of the word "qawman" (a people) indicates that their ignorance is an inseparable attribute of theirs, as if it were one of the constituents of their peoplehood, as was mentioned earlier at His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Surely there are signs for a people who reason﴾ [al-Baqarah: 164] in Surah al-Baqarah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 11, verse 30:

﴿And O my people, who would help me against Allah if I drove them away? Will you not then take heed?﴾

The repetition of "O my people" is like its repetition in the verse before it.

The interrogation is one of denunciation (istifham inkari). Al-nasr (help) is the assistance of one who opposes an adversary or enemy, and it has been used here with the sense of deliverance (al-injaʼ), so it takes "min" (from): meaning, "who would rescue me from Allah," that is, "who would save me from His punishment." This is because driving them away would be a humiliation that harms them without any valid cause recognized by Allah, and Allah does not love the humiliation of His friends.

He then builds on this a denunciation of his people for their neglect of taking heed (al-tadhakkur), that is, reflecting upon the evidences and what they indicate, and upon causes and their effects.

The majority of readers recite "tadhakkarun" with the dhal doubled (tashdid).

The original form of "tadhakkarun" is "tatadhakkarun," in which the second ta was changed into dhal and merged into the dhal. Hafs recited it as "tadhakkarun," with the dhal lightened (takhfif) and one of the two ta's deleted. The meaning of tadhakkur was discussed earlier, at His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who fear Allah, when an impulse from Satan touches them, remember (tadhakkaru)﴾ [al-A'raf: 201], at the end of Surat al-A'raf.

This is a detailed explanation of what he rejected in the claim of his people, in summary form. They argued against his prophethood by saying they saw no superiority in him over them. In reply, he took the position of *al-qawl bi-l-mujib* (accepting the premise of an argument while showing it does not lead to the conclusion), saying that he did not claim any superiority apart from the revelation sent to him. This is how God related the words of His Prophets, peace be upon them, in His saying: ﴿Their messengers said to them, "We are only humans like you, but God bestows His favour upon whom He wills of His servants"﴾ [Ibrahim: 11]. For this reason he denied that he had claimed anything beyond that. He limited himself to some of what they imagined to be consequences of prophethood, namely that he would be richer than them, or that he would know the unseen matters. The word *qawl* here means claim. He expressed the denial in the present tense to indicate that this was not true of him at present. As for its negation in the past, it was known to them, since he had never said it. That is, do not suppose that I secretly intend to claim it, even though I have not said it.

*Khaza'in* (treasuries) is the plural of *khizana*, with a kasra on the kha'. It is a room or a large niche with a door, used for storing wealth or food, that is, for protecting it from being lost. The mention of treasuries here is an implicit metaphor (*isti'ara makniyya*): blessings and beneficial things are likened to precious wealth that is stored in treasuries, and this comparison is signalled by mentioning something that belongs to the likened-to term, namely the treasuries. The attribution of the treasuries to God is for God's exclusive possession of them.

[Page 58]

As for His saying: ﴿Nor do I say, "I am an angel"﴾, it is a negation of the doubt in their saying: ﴿We see you only as a human like ourselves﴾ [Hud: 27]. For this reason he repeated the verb *yaqul* (say) with it, because it is a rejection of another claim they attached to him. Its emphasis with *inna* is because it is a statement that no one would make except with emphasis, given how strongly it would be denied if someone claimed it. So when he negated it, he negated the form of its affirmation. When he wanted to refute their saying: ﴿And we see that none follows you except those who are our lowest-ranked﴾ [Hud: 27], he refuted it by way of *taghlit* (showing a faulty inference), because they made their weakness and poverty a reason for the absence of their superiority. So he refuted it by saying that their weakness is no barrier between them and the good from God, since there is no connection between weakness in worldly matters, such as poverty and lack of means, and being deprived of attaining spiritual and religious perfections. He repeated the verb *qala* (say) with it because he meant by the word a sense different from what was meant in what was said before. So *qala* here is a metonymy (*kinaya*) for belief, because a person only says what he believes. It is also allusive (*ta'ridiyya*) toward the addressees, because they hold this in their hearts and presume it.

*Al-izdira'* (scorning) is a reflexive form (*iftial*) from *al-zary*, which means contempt and attributing a fault. Its original form is *izterā'*, and the *ta'* of the reflexive form was changed into *dal* after the *zay*, as it was changed in *al-izdiyad*.

The attribution of scorning to the eyes, though it is actually an act of the soul, is a rational metaphor (*majaz 'aqli*), because the eyes are usually the cause of scorning, since scorning arises from seeing lowly attributes in the one who looks. A parallel is the attribution of distinguishing to the eyes in the verse of al-A'sha:

*So do this as long as you live, when they gather, and advance when the people's eyes are distinguished.*

A parallel is also His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They bewitched the eyes of the people﴾ [al-A'raf: 116]. They actually bewitched their minds, but the eyes see the movements of the sorcerers, so seeing them takes precedence over the minds of those who look.

In the negation he used the particle *lan*, which indicates emphasis on negating the action in the future. This is allusive toward his people, because they made the weakness and poverty of Noah's followers, peace be upon him, a proof that good had been denied them. Thus the continuation of that state would be implied as long as they remained weak and poor. Their unspoken position says: they will not obtain any good. So his reply to them was that he does not say ﴿God will not bestow any good upon them﴾.

[Page 59]

The clause ﴿God knows best what is in their souls﴾ is a justification for his denial that he would say ﴿God will not bestow any good upon them﴾. For this reason the clause is detached and not joined with a conjunction. The meaning of ﴿God knows best what is in their souls﴾ is that their affair is entrusted to their Lord, who knows what He has placed in their souls of good, and who guided them to faith. That is, He treats them according to what He knows of them. Connecting it to the souls is a warning to his people about their error in saying ﴿And we do not see in you any superiority over us﴾ [Hud: 27], since they looked at the physical, worldly side and ignored the spiritual virtues and perfections and the gifts from the presence of God, which God knows best.

The superlative form here (*ism al-tafdil*, "more knowing") is stripped of comparison, and what is intended by it is the intensity of knowledge.

The clause ﴿Then indeed I would be among the wrongdoers﴾ is a second justification for his denial that he would say ﴿God will not bestow any good upon them﴾. *Idhan* is a particle of answer and consequence, responding to a statement. That is, if you said that, you would be among the wrongdoers. This is because he would wrong them by passing judgment on them with what he does not know of their reality, and he would wrong himself by plunging into speech without knowledge that could be believed.

His saying "among the wrongdoers" is more emphatic in affirming wrongdoing than "I am a wrongdoer," as was mentioned before in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He said, "I seek refuge in God from being among the ignorant"﴾ [al-Baqara: 67] in Surat al-Baqara.

He emphasized it with three emphatic devices: *inna*, the *lam* of initial emphasis, and the conditional particle. This is to establish the wrongdoing of those who slandered the believers with baseness and denied them superiority, because he intended by this an allusion toward his people concerning that. Another occasion of Noah, peace be upon him, with his people concerning these believers will be mentioned in Surat al-Shu'ara'.

[Page 60]

﴿They said, "O Noah, you have argued with us and multiplied your arguments with us. So bring us what you threaten us with, if you are among the truthful."﴾ ﴿He said, "Only Allah will bring it to you, if He wills, and you cannot escape."﴾

This sentence is detached (fasl) in the manner of recounting speech within a dialogue, as was previously explained in the story of Adam (peace be upon him) in Surat al-Baqarah.

Al-mujadalah (arguing) means contending in speech and presenting proof against the other party. It may be used for good, as in His words, ﴿He argues with us concerning the people of Lot﴾ [Hud: 74], and for bad, as in His words, ﴿nor is there any disputing during the Hajj﴾ [al-Baqarah: 197]. They only meant that he argued with them about what was evil, so they expressed their intended meaning with the word jidal in its general sense. This was discussed earlier at His words, ﴿and do not argue on behalf of those who betray themselves﴾ [al-Nisa: 107], in Surat al-Nisa.

This statement came directly after his argument reported in the preceding verse. It is therefore established that that argument was the last of the arguments he presented to his people, and that their weariness and boredom at the repetition of his argument arose at that very moment, so they uttered this statement. All of his arguments had thus passed. The final argument was the one that provoked their indignation at the striking force of his reasoning, until they grew weary of the refutation of their opposition and their opinions, as the falsifier does when proof has overwhelmed him. For this reason they wanted to bring the debate to an end, and they wanted to silence him by asking for the hastening of the punishment he had threatened them with, which would descend upon them, as in his earlier words, ﴿Indeed I fear for you the punishment of a painful day﴾ [Hud: 26].

Their words, ﴿you have multiplied our arguments﴾, are a declarative statement used to express complaint, impatience, and despair of being convinced. He answered them by hastening to explain the punishment, because that is more effective in admonition, so he hastened to it and then returned to explaining his argument.

Bringing a thing (al-ityan bi al-shay') means presenting it. By it they meant hastening it and not granting them respite.

﴿what you threaten us with﴾: its fulfilment is the painful day's punishment.

The restriction (qasr) in His words, ﴿Only Allah will bring it to you, if He wills﴾ is a restriction by reversal (qasr qalb), based on the apparent meaning of their request. This interprets their words according to their outward sense, in the manner of matching the opponent's claim in debate. Otherwise, they were certain that he could not bring them what he had promised, since they considered it false, and they were certain that Allah had not threatened them. Perhaps they did not believe in the existence of Allah. His words, ﴿if He wills﴾, are a precautionary qualification (ihtiras) referring to understanding the punishment as the punishment of this world.

The meaning of ﴿and you cannot escape﴾ is that you cannot escape or elude the threat, meaning that the punishment is certain to occur. Perhaps Noah (peace be upon him) had no revelation from Allah that the punishment of this world would befall them, and for this reason he left the matter to the will of Allah. Or perhaps he was certain that it would descend upon them, in which case the conditional "if He wills" is to be understood with regard to whether the punishment would be hastened or delayed.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 11, verse 34:

﴿And my advice will not benefit you, if I wished to advise you, if Allah intends to lead you astray. He is your Lord, and to Him you will be returned.﴾

This is a conjunction with his admonition of them about the descent and impending arrival of the punishment. It explains the nature of his debate with them, which they resented, saying that it was a debate for their benefit and well-being. In this there is an implicit rebuke of them, a mockery of their opinions, since they disliked what was beneficial to them.

Naṣīḥ (sincere advice): a statement or action whereby the one who does it intends the well-being of the one for whose sake it is done. It is most often applied to beneficial statements that rescue from harm. It can also be by action, as in His saying, ﴿when they are sincere to Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Tawbah: 91] in Surat al-Tawbah. And in the hadith, "Religion is sincere advice (naṣīḥah) to Allah, to His Messenger..." meaning sincerity in acting for them both, because Allah is not informed of anything He does not know. It has already been discussed in His saying, ﴿I advised you, but you do not love those who advise﴾ [al-A'raf: 79] in Surat al-A'raf. So what is meant by advice here is what his people called debate. That is, it is more appropriate to call it advice, because debate may be for good or for evil, as has already been explained.

[p. 62]
The conditional clause in His saying, ﴿if Allah intends to lead you astray﴾, is the intended point of the speech. Its answer is in the sense of His saying, "my advice will not benefit you." However, the structure of the speech was built on the report that advice does not benefit, out of concern for this point. So it was made coordinate with what precedes it, and the conditional was introduced as a restriction on it.

As for His saying, ﴿if I wished to advise you﴾, it is a conditional inserted between the first conditional and the evidence of its answer. This is because it is not the intended point of the stipulation, but rather a stipulation upon a stipulation, and it is not intended to restrict at all. Therefore this is not the kind of conditional found in the hypothetical conditions posed in the questions of jurisprudence and its principles, such as the saying of one who says: "If you eat, if you drink, then you are divorced," because those are posed as one condition restricting another condition. Moreover, when the verbs of both conditions are combined, the intended meaning is the content of both answers. They illustrated this with the verse of the poet:

"If you seek help from us, if you are terrified, you will find from us strongholds of honour, adorned by generosity."

As for His saying, ﴿if I wished to advise you, if Allah intends to lead you astray﴾, each of the two conditionals is intended as a stipulation. The answer of one of them has been omitted, because the answer of the other indicates it.

The stipulation in His saying, ﴿if I wished to advise you﴾, indicates his determination to renew the advice in the future, because his duty is conveyance, even if they dislike that.

By His saying, ﴿if Allah intends to lead you astray﴾, he pointed to their state of disliking the call of Nuh, peace be upon him. Its cause is that Allah has abandoned them, and had it not been for that, his advice would have benefited them. But Nuh, peace be upon him, did not know what Allah intended by their misguidance, nor the extent to which their deviation would continue. Therefore it was incumbent upon him to advise them until the end of the matter.

The discussion of the entry of the lam upon the object of naṣaḥa has already been addressed at His saying, ﴿when they are sincere to Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Tawbah: 91] in Bara'ah.

[p. 63]
Al-ighwā' (leading astray): making a person one of ghiwayah, which is error away from the truth and right guidance.

The sentence ﴿He is your Lord﴾ is a fresh statement, to teach them that Allah is their Lord if they do not believe in the existence of Allah, or to remind them of this if they believe in His existence yet associate with Him Wadd, Suwa', Yaghuth, Ya'uq and Nasr.

The fronting in ﴿and to Him you will be returned﴾ is for emphasis and for the sake of the rhyme (fāṣilah), and not for restriction. This is because they do not believe in resurrection at all, let alone claim that they will be brought before Allah or before anyone else.

What was narrated by Allah about the story of Nuh, peace be upon him, with his people, embodies a clear picture of the thinking of people of foolish minds, over whom error has cast its veil, so that their reasoning has been turned into a hideous crookedness. This is the picture that appears among nations whose minds have not been refined by religious guidance, so that being carried away after the caller of desire overcomes them. Delusion overtakes them, taking error to be correct, and they flatter whoever has the eye of insight blurred despite the clear light, whoever calls them to close it. They lack the inner restraint, so they heed only sensible forms and concern themselves only with pleasures and self-love. They do not weigh, by the true standard of criticism, the purity of souls from the taint of deficiencies.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 11, verse 35:

﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it." Say: "If I have invented it, then upon me is my crime, and I am innocent of what you commit."﴾

This is a parenthetical sentence (jumla mu'taridha) placed between the sentences of the parts of the story, and it is not part of the story itself. Whoever takes it as part of the story has strayed far. It is an emphatic confirmation of its earlier counterpart at the beginning of the surah. The occasion for this parenthetical sentence is that the details of the story, which those being addressed do not know, are wondrous details that call the deniers to recall their denial and repeat their mention of it.

That these details correspond to what happened in the time of Noah, peace be upon him, and that the books of the Children of Israel bear witness to them, indicates the truthfulness of the Prophet ﷺ. This is because his knowledge of that, despite his being unlettered and his people's distance from the People of the Book, is a sign that it is a revelation from God, "falsehood cannot approach it from before it or from behind it."

The interrogation that is indicated by the particle (am) (أم), which is specific to conjoining an interrogation, is a rebuking interrogation (istifham inkari). The placement of the denial is marvellous, because it contains the proof against them.

Here, am (أم) is for transition (lil-idrab), meaning a shift from one purpose to another.

The object pronoun refers to the Qur'an, understood from the context.

The clause "Say" (qul) is separated from the one before it because it occurs within the context of dialogue, as has been mentioned more than once.

The Prophet ﷺ was commanded to turn away from disputing with them by means of proof, because they are not people deserving of that, since the proof has been established against them more than once, and it did not avail them anything. Therefore they were answered that, even if that were supposed, the consequence of his fabricating against himself would not reach them at all.

The fronting of "upon me" (alayya) (عَلَيَّ) indicates restriction (qasr), meaning: my crime is upon me, not upon you. So why do you multiply the claim of fabrication as if you were going to be held accountable for its consequence? This is in keeping with the method of gradually drawing them on (istidraj) and of fair speech.

As for making the fabrication the verb of the conditional: its meaning is that if the fabrication had occurred, as in His saying: ﴿If I had said it, You would surely have known it﴾ (al-Ma'idah 5:116).

Since fabrication against God is a crime, he changed in the answer from expressing it as "fabrication," although he is the one making the claim, to expressing it as "crime." So there is no need to estimate: "then upon me is the crime of my fabrication."

The mention of the particle "upon" (ʿala) with "crime" indicates that the crime is held to account, as the root of the word "crime" (ijram) requires.

The crime (ijram) is the acquiring of a sin (jurm), which is a wrongdoing; so it necessarily requires being held to account.

The sentence "and I am innocent of what you commit" is conjoined to the conditional and its consequent sentence, so it is an independent sentence (ibtida'iyya). Its apparent sense is that it is a concluding statement (tadhyil) to the speech and a reinforcement of it by its opposite: meaning, my crime is upon me, not upon you, just as your crime does not reach me with any consequence. There is no need to estimate a genitive-modified noun in His saying "of what you commit," meaning "its consequence." It is an estimation of meaning, not an estimation of i'rab (grammatical analysis). A thing is emphasised by its opposite, as in His saying: ﴿I do not worship what you worship﴾ and ﴿nor are you worshippers of what I worship﴾ (al-Kafirun 109:2–3).

In this sentence there is a marvellous implication: it conveys the clearing of his own self from fabricating the Qur'an. The claim that he fabricates the Qur'an is a false assertion they put forward against him, so it is a crime on their part against him. Thus the meaning is: "and I am innocent of your saying, which you commit against me as falsehood."

[Page 64]

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 11, verse 36:

﴿And it was revealed to Noah: "None of your people will believe except those who have already believed, so do not be distressed by what they have been doing."﴾

This is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon the clause ﴿They said, "O Noah, you have argued with us"﴾ [Hud: 32]. That is: after that, it was revealed to Noah, peace be upon him, ﴿that none of your people will believe except those who have already believed﴾.

The particle (anna) with its noun being a pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-shaʾn) indicates that what follows it is a grave matter, because it is a declaration of despair regarding the faith of the rest of his people. Likewise, the particle (lan), which conveys the perpetual negation of the future, indicates this. That is very hard upon him, and for this reason it is followed by consolation (tasliya) in the clause ﴿so do not be distressed by what they have been doing.﴾ The fāʾ (so) is for deriving the consolation from the sad news.

Al-ibtiʾas (ابتئاس) is an iftiʿal form derived from al-bu's (البؤس), which is worry and grief; that is, "do not grieve."

The meaning of the iftiʿal here is being affected by the misery that the mentioned news has caused. And (what they have been doing) is their persistence in disbelief and their turning away from considering the call up to the time when this was revealed to him. God, exalted, said, relating about him: ﴿But my call has only increased them in flight﴾ [Nuh: 6], ﴿And indeed, every time I have called them, that You may forgive them, they have put their fingers in their ears, covered themselves with their garments, persisted, and been arrogant with extreme arrogance﴾ [Nuh: 7].

The emphasis of the verb with (qad) in His saying ﴿those who have already believed (man qad āmana)﴾ is to specify that what is meant is those from whom faith has come about with certainty, not those who wavered.

When his prohibition against grieving over their actions, given the severity of their wrongdoing, indicated that God would grant him victory, He followed it with the command to build the ark, to prepare his salvation and the salvation of those who had believed in him from the punishment that God had decreed for his people. This is as God related about him: ﴿So he called upon his Lord, "I am overcome, so help [me]."﴾ [al-Qamar: 10] ﴿So We opened the gates of heaven with water pouring forth.﴾ [al-Qamar: 11], and so on. Thus the clause ﴿And build the ark﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿so do not grieve﴾ [Hud: 36], and by this it falls within what was revealed to him. It therefore indicates that God revealed to him the manner of building the ark, as His words "and by Our revelation" also show. For this reason, Noah (peace be upon him) was the first to build the ark, and this was not known to mankind. That was many centuries ago, which none can count except God, Exalted is He. Nothing found in the Isra'iliyyat (narrations of Israelite origin) concerning the enumeration of those centuries should be relied upon.

Al-fulk (the ark) is a noun that applies equally to the singular and the plural. It was discussed earlier, at His words, ﴿and the ships that sail through the sea with that which benefits people﴾ [al-Baqarah: 164], in Surah al-Baqarah.

The bā' in bi-a'yununa is for accompaniment (al-mulabasah), and it occupies the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to the pronoun in iṣna' (build).

Al-a'yun (eyes) is a metaphor for watchfulness and observation. The plural form in (a'yununa) carries the meaning of the dual, that is, bi-'aynayna (with Our two eyes), as in His words: ﴿And be patient for the judgment of your Lord, for indeed you are in Our eyes﴾ [al-Tur: 48]. The intended meaning is a kinaya (allusion) through the figurative sense, referring to its necessary implication, which is protection from defect and error in the making.

The meaning of revelation (al-waḥy) here is the revelation through which He described the manner of building the ark, as indicated by its conjunction with the object of the bā' of accompaniment attached to the command to build.

The prohibition in His words ﴿and do not address Me concerning those who have wronged﴾ indicates that a severe punishment will befall his disbelieving people. This is because the address being forbidden is the address that would lift their punishment, so that it would be for their benefit, like intercession and a request to lighten the punishment, not mere address in general. Perhaps this is a preparation for his prohibition against addressing Him concerning his disbelieving son, before it occurred to Noah (peace be upon him) to ask for his salvation, so that the response would be gentler when the request is made.

The clause ﴿indeed they are to be drowned﴾ is a report of what will happen and an explanation of the reason for the command to build the ark. The emphasis of the statement with the particle of emphasis in this verse is an example of directing speech contrary to what the apparent situation requires, by treating the non-questioner who is hesitant as if he were a questioner, when something has been presented to him that hints at the genre of the statement, so that he becomes eager to have it specified, an eagerness resembling that of one who asks about the precise content of the statement.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 11, verses 38–39:**

﴿And he was building the ark, and whenever a group of chiefs from his people passed by him, they mocked him. He said: "If you mock us, then we mock you just as you mock.﴾ ﴿You will soon know who will receive a punishment that disgraces him and upon whom will descend a lasting punishment.﴾

This is coordinated ('atf) with the clause ﴿Build the ark﴾ [Hud: 37]. That is, it was revealed to him, "Build the ark" [al-Mu'minun: 23:27], and he built the ark. The action is expressed in the present tense (mudari') to bring the situation to mind (istihdar al-hal), so that the listener imagines Nuh, peace be upon him, being engaged in the work at that very moment. This is like His saying: ﴿It is Allah who sends the winds, and they stir up clouds﴾ [Fatir: 35:9], and His saying: ﴿He argues with Us concerning the people of Lut﴾ [Hud: 11:74].

The clause ﴿whenever a group of chiefs passed by him﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (haal) relating to the pronoun in "he was building" (yasna'u).

*Wa-kullama* is a compound word made of *kull* and *ma*, the temporal and verbal *ma* (ma al-zarfiyya al-masdariyya). *Kull* is in the accusative of time (zarfiyya) because it acquired the temporal sense through its annexation to a temporal noun, namely the verb *sakhiru* (they mocked), which is its object-related complement in one respect and its answer in another. The meaning is: a group of chiefs from his people mocked him at every time they passed by him.

Because *kullama* contains the sense of generality together with the sense of time, it has taken on the meaning of a conditional, like *idha* (whenever). Therefore it requires an answer, and its answer is ﴿they mocked him﴾.

The clause ﴿He said: "If you mock us"﴾ reports what he replied to their mockery. It is phrased in the manner of the verb "to say" when it occurs within the context of a dialogue, because the clause "they mocked" implies statements that express their mockery or reveal words in their hearts.

The use of the plural pronoun in His words ﴿us﴾ indicates that they mocked him for the building of the ship and also mocked those who believed with him, since they were around him, confident that he was doing a great deed. Likewise, the plural in His words ﴿we mock you﴾ is used in the same way.

*Al-sukhriyya* means mockery (istihza'). It is contemptuous amazement, mixed with belittling and considering someone a fool. It was discussed earlier at His words: ﴿so there befell those who mocked them what they used to mock﴾ [al-An'am: 6:10], at the beginning of Surat al-An'am. Its verb takes *min* (from) as its complement.

Their mockery of him meant treating his action as futile, based on their belief that what he was making could not confirm his claim.

The mockery of Nuh, peace be upon him, and the believers by the disbelievers arose from the foolishness of their minds and their ignorance of Allah and His attributes. Thus the two mockeries coincide in time.

With this, the point of the comparison in His words ﴿just as you mock﴾ becomes clear. It is a comparison in the motive that prompts the mockery, even though there is a great difference between the two motives.

*[Page 69]*

It is also permissible to take the *kaf* of comparison (kaf al-tashbih) as conveying the sense of causation (ta'lil), as in His words: ﴿And remember Him as He has guided you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2:198]. In that case it indicates a difference between the two mockeries, because the mockery that has a cause is more deserving than the other. The disbelievers mocked Nuh, peace be upon him, for an action whose purpose they did not understand, while Nuh, peace be upon him, and his followers mocked the disbelievers because they knew that they were ignorant and deluded, as His words indicate: ﴿You will soon know who will receive a punishment that disgraces him﴾. Thus this is a consequence (tafri') of the clause ﴿then we mock you﴾, meaning: it will become clear who is more deserving of being mocked.

Attributing the knowledge to the pronoun of the addressees ("you will know"), rather than to the inclusive pronoun, as in "we will know" (fa-sawfa na'lamu), is a hint that the addressees are the ones most deserving of knowing this. This conveys a noble lesson: one who is certain that he is upon the truth does not let his confidence be shaken by the foolish mocking his beneficial actions, and that he and his followers should mock those who mock.

*Al-khizy* means humiliation (al-ihana). It was discussed earlier at His words: ﴿Our Lord, indeed whoever You admit into the Fire, You have disgraced him﴾ [Al 'Imran: 3:192], at the end of Surat Al 'Imran.

*Al-'adhab al-muqim* ("lasting punishment") is the punishment of the Hereafter. That is, the one upon whom will come the punishment of disgrace in this worldly life, and the everlasting punishment in the Hereafter.

*Man* is an interrogative (istifhamiyya) that suspends (mu'allaqa) the verb of knowledge from acting on its object. *Hulul al-'adhab* means its occurrence (husul). The occurrence is described as the arrival (hulul) of a newcomer at a place, which is a widespread figurative usage that has become almost equal to the literal meaning.
