With this, the point of the comparison in His words ﴿just as you mock﴾ becomes clear. It is a comparison in the motive that prompts the mockery, even though there is a great difference between the two motives.

*[Page 69]*

It is also permissible to take the *kaf* of comparison (kaf al-tashbih) as conveying the sense of causation (ta'lil), as in His words: ﴿And remember Him as He has guided you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2:198]. In that case it indicates a difference between the two mockeries, because the mockery that has a cause is more deserving than the other. The disbelievers mocked Nuh, peace be upon him, for an action whose purpose they did not understand, while Nuh, peace be upon him, and his followers mocked the disbelievers because they knew that they were ignorant and deluded, as His words indicate: ﴿You will soon know who will receive a punishment that disgraces him﴾. Thus this is a consequence (tafri') of the clause ﴿then we mock you﴾, meaning: it will become clear who is more deserving of being mocked.

Attributing the knowledge to the pronoun of the addressees ("you will know"), rather than to the inclusive pronoun, as in "we will know" (fa-sawfa na'lamu), is a hint that the addressees are the ones most deserving of knowing this. This conveys a noble lesson: one who is certain that he is upon the truth does not let his confidence be shaken by the foolish mocking his beneficial actions, and that he and his followers should mock those who mock.

*Al-khizy* means humiliation (al-ihana). It was discussed earlier at His words: ﴿Our Lord, indeed whoever You admit into the Fire, You have disgraced him﴾ [Al 'Imran: 3:192], at the end of Surat Al 'Imran.

*Al-'adhab al-muqim* ("lasting punishment") is the punishment of the Hereafter. That is, the one upon whom will come the punishment of disgrace in this worldly life, and the everlasting punishment in the Hereafter.

*Man* is an interrogative (istifhamiyya) that suspends (mu'allaqa) the verb of knowledge from acting on its object. *Hulul al-'adhab* means its occurrence (husul). The occurrence is described as the arrival (hulul) of a newcomer at a place, which is a widespread figurative usage that has become almost equal to the literal meaning.

﴿Until, when Our command came and the oven overflowed, We said: "Load into it two of every pair, and your family, except those against whom the word has already preceded, and those who believe." But only a few believed with him.﴾

*hattā* is a limit (ghāya) for *yaṣna'u al-fulk* (he was building the ark), meaning he continued building it until the time of the coming of Our command. *Idhā* is an adverb that carries the meaning of a conditional (sharṭ), and for this reason it is given an answer (jawāb), which is the clause *"qulnā uḥmil fīhā"* (We said: "Load into it").

He made the conditional and its answer a limit, in view of the meaning of time contained in the conditional particle and its being attached to the conditional clause. Thus the meaning of a limit is achieved when the content of the answer clause occurs. This is a wondrously concise construction.

*Ḥattā* here is inceptive (ibtidā'iyya).

The word *amr* here may refer to the command of creation (amr al-takwīn) concerning the flood, and it may refer to the matter (sha'n), which is the occurrence of the drowning. Its attribution to the Name of Majesty (ism al-jalāla) is to magnify it, that it is beyond what they know.

The "coming" of the command (majī' al-amr) means its taking place.

*Al-fawarān* is the boiling of the cooking pot, and it is applied to a spring of water gushing forcefully, by way of comparison with water boiling in a pot when it bubbles. They interpreted it in accordance with what came in other verses about the story of Noah (peace be upon him), such as His saying: ﴿And We caused the earth to gush forth with springs﴾ [al-Qamar: 12]. For this reason it was not clear to them that it is attributed to *al-tannūr*. For *al-tannūr* is the oven in which bread is baked. The opinions regarding the interpretation of *al-tannūr* became numerous, and some of them reached a level that should not be accepted, while some have a valid basis, though they vary.

Among the exegetes is one who kept *al-tannūr* in its literal sense, so he made the bubbling the gushing of water from one of the ovens, and that this was a sign which God set for Noah (peace be upon him): when water bubbles up from his oven, he would know that this is the beginning of the flood. So he boarded the ark and caused those with him to board.

Among them is one who took *al-tannūr* in the single figurative sense (al-majāz al-mufrad), and interpreted it as the surface of the earth. That is, the water gushed forth from all the earth until the surface of the earth became like the mouth of the oven.

Among them is one who interpreted it as the highest part of the earth.

Among them is one who took *fāra* and *al-tannūr* in their literal senses, and put the statement in the mode of a figurative expression (tamthīl) to convey the intensity of the situation, as one says: "*ḥamiya al-waṭīs*" (the fight grew hot). The account of this is in the *Tafsīr* of Ibn 'Aṭiyya on this verse, and in al-Kashshāf on the commentary of Sūrat al-Mu'minūn. Al-Ṭabarsī cited the verse of the poet, who is al-Nābigha al-Ja'dī:

*"Their cooking pot boils over us, so we keep its fire going, and we calm it for us when its pot has boiled."*

He means by the pot war, and *nafthi'uhā* means we quiet it. It is said: *fathi'a al-qidr* when the boiling of the pot subsides by pouring water into it. This is the best of what has been related from the exegetes.

What appears to me is that His saying: ﴿and the oven overflowed﴾ is a proverbial expression (mathal) for something reaching the furthest extent that such a thing can bear, as one says: "The torrent reached the *zubā*" (the highest rock/limit), "the measure was filled," "the cup overflowed," and "it became grave."

*Al-tannūr* is the place of the valley's bank (maḥfil al-wādī), that is, its edge, so it is like the phrase "the valley overflowed," from the same category as "the torrent reached the *zubā*." The meaning is that the execution of Our command upon them occurred, and they had reached, through the length of the period of disbelief, a point at which no pardon is granted to them thereafter, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So when they angered Us, We exacted retribution from them﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 55].

*Al-tannūr* is a name for the fire-hearth used for baking bread. Al-Layth claimed that it is among the words on which the languages agree, that is, like *al-ṣābūn* (soap) and *al-sammūr* (sable). Al-Khafājī, in *Shifā' al-Ghalīl*, attributed this to Ibn 'Abbās. Abū Manṣūr said: the statement of al-Layth indicates that it is originally non-Arabic (a'jamī).

The evidence for this is that it is *fa'ūl* derived from *tanara*, and we do not know *tanara* in the speech of the Arabs, because it is unused (muhmal). Others said: there is no *nūn* before *rā'* in the speech of the Arabs, for *narjis* is also an arabized word. It has been counted among the arabized words found in the Qur'an. Ibn al-Subkī versified them in his commentary on the Mukhtaṣar of Ibn al-Ḥājib, the original, and attributed this to Ibn Durayd. Abū 'Alī al-Fārisī said: its pattern is *fa'ūl*. And from Tha'lab that it is Arabic. He said: its pattern is *taf'ūl* from *al-nūr* (that is, the *tā'* is extra), and its original form is *tanūwur* with two *wāws*. The first *wāw*, being pronounced with *ḍamma*, was changed into a *hamza*, then the *hamza* was deleted for ease, then the *nūn* was doubled as a substitute for what was deleted, like His saying *taqaḍḍā al-bāzī* meaning *taqaḍḍaḍa* (the falcon swooped).

Al-Jumhūr read *min kulli zawjayn* with the *idāfa* (annexation) of *kull* to *zawjayn*.

*Al-zawj* is a thing which is second to another in a given state. Its original meaning is a name for what joins a single thing so that it becomes its pair, and each of the two is a pair for the other. What is meant by *zawjayn* here is the male and female of the species, as the annexation of *kull* to *zawjayn* indicates; that is, "Load into it of the mates of all the kinds."

*Min* is partitive (tab'īḍiyya), and *ithnayn* is the object of *uḥmil*, and it is an explanation lest one suppose that he should load of each pair only one of the two, since the *zawj* is one of two connected things, as previously mentioned in His saying: ﴿eight pairs﴾ [al-An'ām: 143] in Sūrat al-An'ām. And lest he should load more than two of one kind, so that the ship would be cramped and heavy.

Ḥafṣ read *min kullin* with *tanwīn* on *kullin*, so it is *tanwīn al-'iwaḍ* (the nunation of substitution) for a omitted genitive, that is, "of all created things," and *zawjayn* is the object of *uḥmil*, and *ithnayn* is an attribute of *zawjayn*, that is, "do not add to two."

*Ahl* of a man are his kinsfolk and the people of his household, and it is a collective noun with no singular. His wife is the first thing that comes to mind from the word, and the word *ahl* is also applied to a man's wife, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So when Moses had completed the term and set out with his family﴾ [al-Qaṣaṣ: 29], and He said: ﴿when you went out early from your family﴾ [Āl 'Imrān: 121], that is, from 'Ā'isha's house (may God be pleased with her).

And ﴿those against whom the word has preceded﴾ means those upon whom the word of God has passed, that is, His threat. The definiteness in *al-qawl* is for a known reference, meaning: except whoever among your family was a disbeliever. The one that exemplifies this is one of his two wives mentioned in Sūrat al-Taḥrīm, and his son by her, mentioned at the end of this story. Noah (peace be upon him) had two wives.

*Sabaqa* is construed with *'alā* because *sabaqa* is made to imply the meaning of *ḥakama* (to decree), just as it is construed with *lām* in His saying: ﴿And Our word had already preceded to Our servants, the messengers﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt: 171], because it implies the meaning of beneficial commitment.

[Page 73]

*Man āmana* (those who believed) is all the believers.

The clause ﴿and none believed with him except a few﴾ is a parenthetical insertion (i'tirāḍ) to complete the benefit of the story in the fewness of the righteous. It was said: all the believers with him, from his family and others, were over seventy, among men and women, so most of the ship's cargo was animals.

* * *

[The words of His, exalted is He: "And he said: Board it, in the name of God be its course and its mooring..."]

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 11, verse 41:

﴿And he said: "Embark therein; in the name of Allah is its course and its mooring. Indeed, my Lord is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful."﴾

It is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with the clause ﴿We said: "Load therein..."﴾ [Hud: 40], meaning: We said to him that. And Nuh (peace be upon him) said to those who were commanded to be carried: "Embark" (ارْكَبُوا).

The pronoun in "fīhā" refers to something understood from the context, namely the ship (al-safīnah), as in His saying: ﴿And We carried him upon a [vessel] of planks and nails﴾ [al-Qamar: 13], meaning a ship.

The verb "ārkabū" is construed with "fī" (in) in accordance with eloquent usage, for one says "rakiba al-dābbah" (he mounted the animal) when he rides upon it. As for boarding a ship (rukūb al-fulk), it is construed with "fī" because the application of the term "rukūb" to it is figurative; it is in fact sitting and settling. Thus one does not say "rakiba al-safīnah" (he mounted the ship). They intended to distinguish between true riding and that which resembles it, and this is a fine distinction.

The "bāʾ" in "bi-ism Allāh" is for accompaniment (al-mulābasah), like what preceded in the explanation of the basmalah. It is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in "ārkabū", meaning: accompanied by the name of Allah, this being the accompaniment of a speech to its speaker, i.e., saying: "In the name of Allah."

"Majrāhā wa mursāhā" is read with a ḍammah on both mīms in the reading of the majority. They are both verbal nouns (maṣdar) of "ajrā al-safīnah" when he made it flowing, i.e., he moved it swiftly, and "arsāhā" when he made it anchored (rāsiyah), i.e., standing still on the shore. One says "rasā" when it became firmly fixed in place.

صفحة ٧٤
Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī, and Ḥafṣ from ʿĀṣim, and Khalaf read "majrāhā" alone with a fatḥah on the mīm, as a noun of place or time or a verbal noun formed on the pattern "mafʿal". As for "mursāhā", it is with a ḍammah on the mīm like the majority, because one does not say "marsāhā" with a fatḥah on the mīm. The avoidance of the fatḥah in "mursāhā" in Arabic speech, although it is analogically similar to "majrāhā", has as its purpose the prevention of ambiguity, lest it be confused with the name "al-marsā", which is the place prepared for ships to anchor.

It is also permissible for "majrāhā wa mursāhā" to be in the position of an accusative by substitution for an adverb of time, meaning: at the time of its sailing and at the time of its anchoring. It is also permissible for it to be in the position of a nominative as the agent (fāʿil) of the prepositional phrase because of the verbal sense it contains; this is the view of the grammarians of Kufa, and it is not far-fetched.

The clause ﴿Indeed, my Lord is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful﴾ is a justification for the command to embark, which is qualified by the accompaniment of mentioning the name of Allah the Exalted. In justifying it by forgiveness and mercy there is an allusion to the fact that Allah promised him their deliverance, and that is from His forgiveness and mercy. He emphasised it with "inna" and the lām of commencement, to confirm for his followers that Allah had shown them mercy by delivering them from drowning.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 11, verses 42–43:**

﴿And it sailed with them through waves like mountains.﴾

This is a parenthetical sentence (*jumlah mu'taridah*), whose insertion here was prompted by the mention of its course (*majraha*), to complete the benefit, describing the greatness of that day and the wondrous power of God, exalted is He, in facilitating their salvation.

The subject (*musnad ilayh*) is placed before the verbal predicate (*khabar fi'li*) to strengthen and confirm the judgment.

He shifts from the past tense verb to the present tense (*mudari'*) to make the situation present to the mind, like His saying: ﴿And it is Allah who sends the winds, and they stir up clouds﴾ [Fatir: 9].

The *mawj* (wave) is that which rises from the water on its surface when it is agitated. It is compared to mountains in its immensity. This is either due to the abundance of winds that raise the water, or due to the thrust of the water-surges (*dafaqat*) coming from floods and the meeting of valleys with the water that preceded them. The event of the Flood was nothing but the result of earthquakes through which the waters of the earth burst forth, and abundant rains whose torrents met with the waters of the springs, mixing, gathering, and pouring into the water that was there before, until the water covered the whole earth whose people God intended to drown, as will come later.

* * *

﴿And Noah called out to his son, who was apart, "O my son, board with us and do not be with the disbelievers." He said, "I will take refuge on a mountain that will protect me from the water." [Noah] said, "There is no protector today from the decree of Allah, except for whom He has mercy." And the wave came between them, and he was among the drowned.﴾

The sentence "And Noah called out" is conjoined (*'utifat*) to the most closely connected of the sentences before it, which is "And he said, 'Board it'" [Hud: 41], because his calling to his son occurred before the ship sailed through waves like mountains, since it would be impossible to stop it after it had set off, as all the riders were settled in the hold of the ship.

The son of Noah here is the fourth of his sons from a second wife of Noah, whose name was Wa'ilah, who drowned, and she is the one mentioned at the end of Surah al-Tahrim. It is said that his son's name was Yama, and it is said his name was Kan'an, which is different from Kan'an son of Ham, the grandfather of the Canaanites. The Torah that exists today has omitted mention of this son and the matter of his drowning, and whether he had a wife or was unmarried.

The clause "who was apart" is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) referring to his son. The *ma'zil* is the place of seclusion, i.e., separation, meaning apart from the believers, either because he had not believed in Noah, peace be upon him, and so he did not affirm the occurrence of the Flood, or because he had apostatized, denied the occurrence of the Flood, and thereby disbelieved by denying the Messenger.

The clause "O my son, board with us" explains the clause "called out" and is guidance for him and gentleness toward him.

As for the clause "and do not be with the disbelievers," it is conjoined to the clause "board with us," informing him that his refusal to board places him in the ranks of the disbelievers, since his refusal to board would only be a result of his denial of the occurrence of the Flood. Thus Noah's saying to him "board with us" is a metonymy (*kinayah*) for calling him to faith through the method of presentation and warning. His son's disbelief in the Flood was further shown by his mocking words: ﴿I will take refuge on a mountain that will protect me from the water.﴾

"My son" (*bunayya*) is the diminutive (*tasghir*) of *ibn* (son) when attached to the first person pronoun "my." Its diminutive form here is the diminutive of compassion (*tasghir shafaqah*), whereby he is treated as a little one in being the object of mercy and tenderness.

Its original form is *bunayw*, because the original of *ibn* is *bany*. When they dropped the *waw* from it, because it is heavy at the end of a triliteral word, and it fell short of three letters, they compensated by adding a hamzat al-wasl at its beginning. When the dropped *waw* returned, because the reason for dropping it disappeared, the hamzat al-wasl was discarded. Then when the diminutive was to be attached to the first-person pronoun, the *waw* had to take a kasra, becoming *bunayawi*. When the *waw* fell between two *ya's*, it was changed into a *ya* and assimilated (*idgham*) into the *ya* of the diminutive, so it became *bunayyi* with two *ya's* at its end, the first of which is shaddah-ed. Since the vocative (*munada*) attached to the first-person pronoun may drop the first-person *ya* and keep the kasra, it became *bunayy*, with a kasra on the doubled *ya*, which is the reading of the majority (*al-Jumhur*). 'Asim read it *bunayya* with a fatha on the first-person *ya* attached to it, because its fatha is permissible in the vocative. Its original is *ya bunayyiya*, with two *ya's*, the first of which is kasra-ed and shaddah-ed, being the *ya* of the diminutive together with the root letter of the word, whose original is *waw*, and then the first-person *ya* was attached to it and the original *ya* was dropped.

The clause "He said, 'I will take refuge'" and the clause "He said, 'There is no protector'" are separated (*fusilat*) because they occur within the context of a dialogue.

His saying "I will take refuge on a mountain" was before the water reached the peaks of the mountains. *Aawi* means "I will descend," and its verbal noun is *al-Awiyy*, with a damma on the hamzah, a kasra on the *waw*, and a shaddah on the *ya*.

The clause "that will protect me from the water" is either an attributive clause (*sifah*) of "mountain," meaning a high mountain, or a resumptive explanatory clause (*isti'naf bayani*), because he sensed that Noah, peace be upon him, would ask why he takes refuge on a mountain, since his son had heard him warning people of a great flood. So the son assumed that the highest mountains could not be reached by the water, and that his father only meant the water reaching the higher elevations other than the towering mountains.

For this reason Noah, peace be upon him, answered him that ﴿there is no protector today from the decree of Allah﴾, i.e., from His commanded thing, which is the Flood, ﴿except for whom He has mercy.﴾

The exception "except for whom He has mercy" is an exception from an object implied in "protector," since a protector requires a protected person, who is the excepted-from element. By "whom He has mercy" he meant whom God had decreed salvation from drowning through His mercy. This decree was made manifest by the revelation about building the ark and guidance on how to board it.

The *mawj* (wave) is a collective noun (*ism jam'*) of *mawjah*, and it refers to quantities of water from the sea or river that rise on the surface of the water from its agitation due to strong winds, or from an increase of water pouring into it. It is said: "the sea surged" (*maja*) when its water was agitated. And they said: "the people surged" (*maja al-qawm*), by analogy with the mixing and agitation of people to the agitation of the sea.

The wave coming between them at the end of the dialogue points to the rapidity of the rising of the water at the moment of the attempt.

His saying "and he was among the drowned" indicates that he drowned, and with him drowned all whom he had threatened with drowning. This is a wondrous brevity (*ijaz badi'*).

The *mawj* (wave) is a collective noun (*ism jam'*) of *mawjah*, and it refers to quantities of water from the sea or river that rise on the surface of the water from its agitation due to strong winds, or from an increase of water pouring into it. It is said: "the sea surged" (*maja*) when its water was agitated. And they said: "the people surged" (*maja al-qawm*), by analogy with the mixing and agitation of people to the agitation of the sea.

The wave coming between them at the end of the dialogue points to the rapidity of the rising of the water at the moment of the attempt.

His saying "and he was among the drowned" indicates that he drowned, and with him drowned all whom he had threatened with drowning. This is a wondrous brevity (*ijaz badi'*).

[p. 75] [p. 76] [p. 77]

[p. 78]

﴿And it was said: "O earth, swallow your water, and O sky, withhold." The water subsided, the matter was concluded, and the ark came to rest on al-Judi. And it was said: "Away with the wrongdoing people!"﴾

When His words ﴿So he was among the drowned﴾ [Hud: 43] had established, in concise form, the occurrence of the promised drowning, as you have known, the discourse moved on to the end of the Flood.

The construction of the verb ﴿qila﴾ (it was said) in the passive here is an abbreviation, because the agent of the saying is evident: such a command could only come from God. The "saying" here is the command of creation (amr al-takwin). The addressing of the earth and the sky by way of the vocative and the imperative is a metaphor (isti'ara) for the connection of the command of creation to modes of action within their very essences, and their being affected by it, just as a rational being is addressed with a task he performs, which he accepts in obedience and awe. Thus the metaphor here lies in the vocative particle, and it is a subsidiary (tab'iyya) metaphor.

*Al-bal'*: its literal meaning is the passage of food and drink into the throat without lodging in the mouth. Here it is a metaphor for the entry of a thing into the interior of another thing swiftly. The meaning of the earth's "swallowing" its water is its entering into the earth's interior swiftly, like the swiftness of a swallower's gulping, such that the earth's drying did not come about through the heat of the sun or the winds, but through a swift earthly action. This may have been by God's causing earthquakes and subsidence, whereby the earth's crust split in many places until the waters that were on the earth's surface sank away.

The attribution of the water to the earth is due to the slightest connection, namely that it was upon its surface.

The "withholding" (iqla') of the sky is a metaphor for the cessation of rain's descent from it, because when the descent of rain ceases, it does not add to the water that had sunk into the earth. For this reason, the command to swallow was placed first, since it is the greatest cause of the water's subsiding.

In the pairing of the earth and the sky there is the embellishment of antithesis (tibaq). In the correspondence of *ub-la'i* with *aqli'i* there is the embellishment of paronomasia (jinas).

[p. 79]

﴿And the water subsided﴾ dispenses with dwelling on the fact that the sky had withheld and the earth had swallowed. The verb *ghiida* (subsided) is in the passive with a deputy subject, as with *qila* and *fu'ila*, in view of the cause of the subsiding, or because it has no real agent, since its occurrence is caused by a cause. *Al-ghayd* is its drying up within the earth. What is meant is the water that arose through the Flood, in excess of the earth's seas and valleys. *Qada' al-amr* is its completion. The construction of the verb in the passive is because it is known that its agent is none other than God, exalted is He.

*Al-istiwa'*: settling.

*Al-Judi*: the name of a mountain between Iraq and Armenia, which today is called (Ararat). The wisdom in the ark's coming to rest on a mountain is that the side of a mountain is more feasible for the ark's stability when the riders disembark, because it becomes lighter when most of them alight; then when it tilts, it leans against the side of the mountain.

*Bu'dan* is a verbal noun from *ba'ida* on the pattern of *karuma* and *fariha*, in the accusative as an absolute object. It stands in place of the verb, as is the usage in contexts of supplication and the like, such as praise and blame, like: *tabban lahu* (ruin to him), *suhqan* (destruction), *suqyan* (may he be watered), *ra'yan* (may he be pastured), *shukran* (thanks). *Al-bu'd* (distance) is a metonymy for contempt, by way of the implication of disliking a thing; therefore one says *ba'uda* or similar of someone who has been lost, when he is hated, as here. And one says the negation of distance of what is desired, even if it has been distant, so it is said of the dear deceased, as Malik ibn al-Rayb said:

They say, "Do not be distant," while they bury me, and where is the place of distance except my place?

And Fatimah bint al-Ahjam said:

My brothers, do not ever be distant, ***
And yet, by God, they have been distant.

The more common usage is *ba'ida* with a kasra on the 'ayn for figurative distance in the sense of destruction and death, and *ba'uda* with a damma on the 'ayn for real distance.

The wrongdoing people are those who disbelieved and so drowned. The speaker of *bu'dan* may be from God's saying, in following the manner of His saying ﴿And it was said: "O earth, swallow your water"﴾, and it is permissible that the believers say it,

[p. 80]

as a contempt for the disbelievers and a way of relieving themselves of them and finding rest. Thus the verb *(wa-qila)* is constructed in the passive, because there is no need to know its speaker.

Al-Zamakhshari said in *al-Kashshaf*, after he mentioned some subtleties of which we have given most: "When we have mentioned the meanings and subtleties, the scholars of rhetoric have found this verse eloquent and have nodded their heads in admiration of it, not because of the harmony of the two words *ub-la'i* and *aqli'i*, although that does not leave the discourse without beauty; rather, it is like what is not regarded in comparison with those beauties which are the core, while the rest is husk." End of quotation.

Al-Sakkaki addressed, in *al-Miftah*, in his discussion of eloquence (balagha) and fluency (fasaha), an explanation of some of the distinguishing features of eloquence in this verse, following the lead of *al-Kashshaf*, as we see, and he said:

"The consideration of this verse is from four aspects: from the aspect of the science of rhetoric (*ilm al-bayan*), from the aspect of the science of meanings (*ilm al-ma'ani*), from the aspect of semantic fluency (*al-fasaha al-ma'nawiyya*), and from the aspect of verbal fluency (*al-fasaha al-lafziyya*). As for its consideration from the aspect of the science of rhetoric . . . we say: when He, mighty and majestic, wished to make a meaning clear, we wished to return what had burst forth from the earth into its belly . . . and to cut off the Flood of the sky . . . and to make the water subside . . . and to complete the matter of Noah (peace be upon him), which is the fulfilment of what We had promised regarding the drowning of his people . . . and to set the ship upon al-Judi . . . and We left the wrongdoers drowned, the discourse was built upon likening the intended to the commanded . . . and likening the bringing-into-being of the intended to the command . . . and that the heavens and the earth . . . follow His will . . . as if they were rational discerning beings . . . then he built upon this likening the composition of the discourse, so He, exalted and high, said *qila* (it was said) by way of metaphor for the will, from which the saying of a speaker results, and He made the evidence of the metaphor the address to the inanimate . . . so He said: ﴿O earth﴾ and ﴿O sky﴾ . . . Then He used metaphor for the subsidence of the water in the earth as *al-bal'* (swallowing), because of the resemblance between them, which is going to a hidden place. Then He used metaphor for water for nourishment, a metaphor by way of allusion (*isti'ara bi-l-kinaya*), likening it to food in that the earth is strengthened by water for growth . . . as the eater is strengthened by food; and He made the evidence of the metaphor the word *ub-la'i* . . . Then He commanded, by way of metaphor, for the resemblance mentioned earlier, and addressed in the command, as a reinforcement (*tarshih*) of the metaphor of the vocative, then He said *ma'aki* (your water), attributing the water to the earth by way of metaphor, likening the connection of the water to the earth with the connection of ownership to the owner, and He chose the pronoun of address for the sake of reinforcement. Then He chose for the restraint of the rain *al-iqla'* (withholding), which is the agent's leaving off of the act, because of the resemblance between them in the non-existence of what had been. Then He commanded by way of metaphor and addressed in the command, saying *aqli'i* (withhold), in the same manner as what preceded in *ub-la'i*. Then He said: ﴿And the water subsided, and the matter was concluded, and it settled upon al-Judi﴾. ﴿And it was said: "Away with . . . "﴾, and He did not specify who made the water subside, nor who concluded the matter and levelled the ship, and He said *bu'dan* (away), just as He did not specify the speaker of ﴿O earth﴾ and ﴿O sky﴾ at the beginning of the verse, following in each of these a path of allusion (*kinaya*), that such great matters are not accomplished except by one of power who cannot be comprehended, the Subduer who cannot be overcome, so there is no room for the mind to go to the idea that other than Him, whose greatness is exalted, is the one saying ﴿O earth﴾ and ﴿O sky﴾, or making subside what subsided, or completing such a terrifying matter; or that the levelling of the ship and its settling were by the levelling of another and his settling."

Then He concluded the discourse with an indirect allusion (ta'rid), as a warning to those who follow their path in denying the messengers, wronging themselves and nothing else, a concluding that shows the place of wrath and the aspect of their deserving it, and that the calamity of the Flood and that terrifying scene occurred only because of their wrongdoing.

As for its consideration from the aspect of the science of meanings, which is the consideration of the contribution of each word in it, and the purpose of each anteposition and postposition among its clauses: it was chosen to use *ya* (O) over its other sisters because it is more frequent in usage, and because it indicates the distance of the one called, which the situation of displaying greatness requires . . . and it is the distancing of the one called, which signals indifference toward him . . .

*Ub-la'i* was chosen over *ibtali'i* because it is more concise, and because the portion of paronomasia between it and *aqli'i* is greater. *Ma'aki* was said in the singular rather than the plural, because the plural carries an image of multiplicity which results in the situation of displaying pride and might. And *ub-la'i* was not said without the object so that its omission would not entail leaving out what is not intended of the generality of swallowing the mountains, hills, seas, and all still waters, in view of the situation of the command's occurrence, which is a situation of greatness and pride.

Then, since He had made the intended clear, He abbreviated the discourse with *aqli'i* to avoid superfluity that is dispensable. This is the reason why He did not say: "It was said: O earth, swallow your water, and it swallowed, and O sky, withhold, and it withheld." Likewise the command, rather than saying: "The command of Noah (peace be upon him), which is the fulfilment of what God had promised Noah (peace be upon him) of the destruction of his people," for the purpose of brevity and of relying on the definite article to dispense with that.

Then it was said: ﴿Away with the wrongdoing people!﴾ rather than saying "Let the people be distant," seeking emphasis with brevity, as *bu'dan* stands in the place of *li-yab'ad al-qawmu bu'dan* (let the people be distant, a distancing), with an additional benefit, which is the use of the *lam* with *bu'dan*, indicating the meaning that distance is due to them.

Then He made the wrongdoing absolute, to encompass every kind, so that their wronging of themselves enters it, for the sake of further alerting to the atrocity of their evil choice in denying the messengers.

As for the consideration of the arrangement of the clauses: He placed the vocative before the imperative, so it was said ﴿O earth, swallow﴾ and ﴿O sky, withhold﴾, rather than saying "swallow, O earth, and withhold, O sky," following what is required for one who is truly commanded: the preceding of the alerting, so that the command that follows it may settle in the soul of the one addressed, intentionally, for the purpose of reinforcement.

Then He placed the command of the earth before the command of the sky and began with it, because the Flood began from it, and its descent in the narrative is in the position of the root, and the root is more deserving by precedence. Then He followed it with His words ﴿And the water subsided﴾, because it is connected to the subsiding of the water and its taking hold of its tail. Do you not see that the original discourse is: "It was said: O earth, swallow your water, and it swallowed its water; and O sky, withhold from sending the water, and it withheld from sending it; and the water that descended from the sky subsided, and it subsided." Then He followed it with what is the purpose of the narrative, which is His words, exalted is He: ﴿And the matter was concluded﴾, that is, the promise was fulfilled. Then He followed it with the account of the ship, which is His words: ﴿And it settled upon al-Judi﴾, then the narrative was concluded with what it was concluded with . . .

[p. 83]

As for its consideration from the aspect of semantic fluency, it is, as you see, an arrangement of meanings that is subtle, and an expression of them that is condensed and clear, with no intricacy that trips up thought in seeking the intended meaning, nor any twisting that obscures the road for the seeker. Rather, when you test yourself upon hearing it, you find its words racing ahead of its meanings and its meanings racing ahead of its words.

As for its consideration from the aspect of verbal fluency, its words, as you see, are Arabic, in common use, conforming to the rules of the language, free from harshness, far from ugliness, sweet to the sweetest, smooth to the smoothest. . . This is the end of the words of *al-Miftah*.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 11, verses 45–47:**

﴿Noah called out to his Lord and said, "My Lord, indeed my son is of my family, and indeed Your promise is true, and You are the most just of judges."﴾ ﴿He said, "O Noah, indeed he is not of your family. Indeed, he is one whose deed is other than righteous. So do not ask Me about that of which you have no knowledge. Indeed, I admonish you lest you be among the ignorant."﴾ ﴿He said, "My Lord, indeed I seek refuge in You from asking You about that of which I have no knowledge. And unless You forgive me and have mercy on me, I will be among the losers."﴾

The context of the verse requires that this call of Noah, peace be upon him, took place after the ark had settled on al-Judi. It was a call prompted by the impulse of compassion, and he intended by it to benefit his son in the Hereafter, after despairing of his salvation in this world. This is because God had informed him that there is no salvation except for those who board the ark. Moreover, when Noah, peace be upon him, had called his son to board the ark and he refused, and the ark sailed, Noah knew that there was no means to his son's salvation, so how could he ask God for it? Therefore it is determined that he asked God to forgive him. This is indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So do not ask Me about that of which you have no knowledge﴾, as will come.

It is also permissible that this supplication of Noah, peace be upon him, occurred before the people were drowned, meaning: he called out to his Lord that He would save his son from drowning.

[Page 84]

It is also permissible that it was after those who were drowned had drowned, meaning: he called out to his Lord that He would forgive his son and not treat him as the disbelievers are treated in the Hereafter.

The calling out here is a calling out of supplication, as if it were said: "And Noah supplicated his Lord," because supplication is usually introduced by a calling out. Referring to the Divine Name by the description "Lord" added to Noah, peace be upon him, is an honouring of Noah and an allusion to God's compassion towards him, and that His subsequent prohibition is a prohibition of reproach.

The clause ﴿My Lord, indeed my son is of my family﴾ is an explanation of the calling out. The apparent requirement is that it should not be joined with the particle of consequence (fa’), just as the explanatory clause is not joined in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When he called out to his Lord with a secret call﴾ [Maryam: 3] ﴿He said, "My Lord, indeed my bones have weakened within me"﴾ [Maryam: 4]. This rule is departed from here. Al-Zamakhshari, in al-Kashshaf, explained its being joined with fa’ by saying that the verb "called out" (nada) is used to mean intending to call out, like the verb "you stood" (qumtum) in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, when you stand up for prayer, wash your faces﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 6], and so on. He means that this is a departure from the apparent requirement, since the presence of fa’ in the clause that explains the calling out is evidence that the verb "called out" is used figuratively for the meaning of intending to call out, i.e., he intended to call out to his Lord, so he followed his intention with the act of calling out. This indicates that he intended to call out, then hesitated to take that step because he knew from His saying, exalted is He: ﴿except those among them against whom the word has already preceded﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 27]. His hesitation did not last long, for compassion for his son overcame him, so he went ahead and called out to his Lord. For this reason he put forward the excuse in his words: ﴿indeed my son is of my family﴾. So his saying: ﴿indeed my son is of my family﴾ is a declarative statement used for excuse and preparation, because he wishes to ask a request whose acceptance he does not know, but he ventured into it because the one for whom he asks is of his family, so he has the excuse of compassion for him. The emphasis of the statement with ﴿indeed (inna)﴾ is for the sake of giving it importance.

Likewise, the clause ﴿and indeed Your promise is true﴾ is a declarative statement used for a necessary implication, namely that he knows that the promise of God is true.

What is meant by the promise is what is in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿except those among them against whom the word has already preceded, and do not address Me concerning those who have wronged; indeed they are to be drowned﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 27], since this indicates that some of his family had already been decreed by God not to board the ark. This exception is determined to refer to his son, since there was no one else of his family whom he asked to board the ark and who refused. And whoever God's knowledge has already determined will not board the ark from among people is a wrongdoer, i.e., a disbeliever, and is destined to drown, so his not boarding the ark and his drowning were a sign that he was a disbeliever. The meaning is: Noah, peace be upon him, was not ignorant that his son was a disbeliever. Therefore his asking forgiveness for him was with knowledge that he was a disbeliever, but he hoped that perhaps God would pardon him because of his kinship with him. So his asking forgiveness for him is equivalent to intercession for him with God, exalted is He, and that is taking the utmost of the motives of compassion and mercy toward his son.

The indicator of all of this is his saying: ﴿and You are the most just of judges﴾, which indicates that there is no one who can reject what He has decided and decreed, and that no one among His creation has any claim against Him. But it is a station of humble supplication and asking for what is not impossible.

Noah, peace be upon him, had not been forbidden from this, and the knowledge that God does not forgive the disbelievers had not been established in his law. So the state of Noah, peace be upon him, was like the state of the Prophet (ﷺ) when he said to Abu Talib: "I will surely ask forgiveness for you as long as I have not been forbidden from you," before the revelation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is not for the Prophet and those who have believed to ask forgiveness for the polytheists﴾ [al-Tawbah: 113], and so on.

Limiting the supplication to these three sentences is an allusion to the thing requested, since he did not mention it explicitly. This is a kind of courtesy and hesitation in proceeding to ask what is asked, relying on the knowledge of the one asked, as if he were saying: "Shall I ask You or leave it?" Like the verse of Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt:

"Shall I mention my need, or has your modesty sufficed me, since your nature is modesty?"

The meaning of ﴿the most just of judges﴾ is the one who is most intense in judgment. The superlative form relates to the reality of the act, so it indicates that His judgment is not unjust and that no one can nullify it.

The meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿indeed he is not of your family﴾ is the negation that he is of the family of his religion and belief. This is not a refutation of Noah's statement, peace be upon him: ﴿indeed my son is of my family﴾, but rather an informing that the kinship of religion, with respect to the people of faith, is kinship. This meaning is common in usage.

[Page 85]

Al-Nabighah said, addressing 'Uyayna ibn Hisn:

"If you try to commit wickedness against the Asad, then I am not of you and you are not of me."

And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And they swear by God that they are indeed of you, but they are not of you; rather they are a people who are fearful﴾ [al-Tawbah: 56].

The emphasis of the statement is for confirming it, because of its strangeness.

The clause ﴿indeed he is one whose deed is other than righteous﴾ is a justification for the content of the clause ﴿indeed he is not of your family﴾, so ﴿indeed (inna)﴾ in it is only for the sake of emphasis.

The word "deed" (ʿamal), in the reading of the majority, with a fatha on the mim and tanwin on the lam, is a verbal noun (masdar) whose predicate is stated for the sake of intensification, and "other than" (ghayr) is raised as an attribute of "deed". Al-Kisa'i and Ya'qub read it ("ʿamila") with a kasra on the mim in the past tense form, and "other than" (ghayr) in the accusative as the object of the verb "ʿamila". The meaning of "the deed other than righteous" is disbelief. Disbelief was called a "deed" because it is an act of the heart, and because its effect appears in the action of its possessor, such as the refusal of Noah's son to board, which indicates his denial of the warning of the flood.

It follows from this that His prohibition, that he should not ask about that of which he has no knowledge, is a prohibition of reproach. Because when it was said to him: ﴿indeed he is not of your family﴾, with its cause being his explanation that he is one whose deed is other than righteous, what he had prepared for in order to have his request answered collapsed, so he was deserving of not asking Him and of reflecting on what he wanted to ask from God.

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Abu Ja'far read ("fa-la tas'alanni") with a shadda on the nun, and these are the nun of emphasis (nun al-tawkid al-khafifah) and the protective nun (nun al-wiqayah), which have been assimilated. Apart from Ibn Kathir, those named read with the first-person ya' affirmed. As for Ibn Kathir, he read ("fa-la tas'alanna") with a heavy fatha-vowelled nun.

Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Ya'qub and Khalaf read ("fa-la tas'alni") with a sukun on the lam and a kasra on the nun, lightly, as not emphasised by the nun of emphasis, and transitive to the first-person ya'. Most of them omitted the ya' in pausal (wasl) position, while Warsh from Nafi' and Abu 'Amr affirmed it in connected speech.

Then, if Noah, peace be upon him, had not previously received a revelation from God that God does not forgive the polytheists in the Hereafter, his prohibition from asking about that of which he has no knowledge was a prohibition of disapproval for the likes of him, because the rank of prophethood requires that one not proceed to ask his Lord a request whose answer one does not know. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and intercession does not benefit with Him except for one whom He has permitted﴾ [Saba': 23], and His saying: ﴿They will not speak except one whom the Most Merciful has permitted, and he says what is correct﴾ [al-Naba': 38]. And even if it had been revealed to him about that before, as His saying indicates: ﴿and indeed Your promise is true﴾. His asking forgiveness for his son was a request to specify him from the general. And his prohibition was a prohibition of blame and reproach, since it had not been made clear to him from his Lord that this was permissible.

His saying: ﴿of which you have no knowledge﴾ was open to its apparent meaning and also open to being a metonymy for knowledge of its opposite, i.e., "do not ask Me about what you know will not occur."

Then, if Noah's statement, peace be upon him, ﴿indeed my son is of my family﴾ to its end was an allusion to the thing requested, the prohibition in His saying: ﴿So do not ask Me about that of which you have no knowledge﴾ was a prohibition against insistence or returning to asking Him. And if Noah's statement, peace be upon him, was merely a preparation for the request, in order to test the state of God's responsiveness to his request, then His saying, exalted is He: "so do not ask Me" is a prohibition against carrying out the request for which he had prepared with his speech. The purpose of the prohibition is to exempt him from exposing his request to refusal.

In all of these views, His saying: ﴿Indeed I admonish you lest you be among the ignorant﴾ is an admonition against neglecting deliberation before proceeding.

The ignorance here is the opposite of knowledge, and this is what suits its being contrasted with His saying: ﴿that of which you have no knowledge﴾.

[Page 88]

Noah, peace be upon him, then answered his Lord's words with what indicates his disavowal of what he had asked, and so he sought refuge that he should not ask about that of which he has no knowledge. If Noah, peace be upon him, had intended by his first statement an allusion to the request, then it is a matter that has already occurred, so the seeking of refuge relates to the consequence of that or to returning to the like of it in the future. And if he had only intended it as a preparation for the request, then the seeking of refuge is evident, namely, restraining oneself from carrying the request through.

His saying: ﴿And unless You forgive me and have mercy on me, I will be among the losers﴾ is a request for forgiveness first, because clearing away (al-takhliyah) precedes adornment (al-tahliyah). He then followed it with a request for mercy, because whoever is in the station of God's approval is worthy of mercy.

The commentators, in their interpretation of these verses, have followed the path that Noah's request, peace be upon him, was a request for the rescue of his son from drowning. This led them to encounter rugged and distant paths, and they suffered hardship in connecting them together, while the verse is far removed from them. Perhaps we have taken the straight road in interpreting it.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 11, verses 45–47:**

﴿Noah called out to his Lord and said, "My Lord, indeed my son is of my family, and indeed Your promise is true, and You are the most just of judges."﴾ ﴿He said, "O Noah, indeed he is not of your family. Indeed, he is one whose deed is other than righteous. So do not ask Me about that of which you have no knowledge. Indeed, I admonish you lest you be among the ignorant."﴾ ﴿He said, "My Lord, indeed I seek refuge in You from asking You about that of which I have no knowledge. And unless You forgive me and have mercy on me, I will be among the losers."﴾

The context of the verse requires that this call of Noah, peace be upon him, took place after the ark had settled on al-Judi. It was a call prompted by the impulse of compassion, and he intended by it to benefit his son in the Hereafter, after despairing of his salvation in this world. This is because God had informed him that there is no salvation except for those who board the ark. Moreover, when Noah, peace be upon him, had called his son to board the ark and he refused, and the ark sailed, Noah knew that there was no means to his son's salvation, so how could he ask God for it? Therefore it is determined that he asked God to forgive him. This is indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So do not ask Me about that of which you have no knowledge﴾, as will come.

It is also permissible that this supplication of Noah, peace be upon him, occurred before the people were drowned, meaning: he called out to his Lord that He would save his son from drowning.

[Page 84]

It is also permissible that it was after those who were drowned had drowned, meaning: he called out to his Lord that He would forgive his son and not treat him as the disbelievers are treated in the Hereafter.

The calling out here is a calling out of supplication, as if it were said: "And Noah supplicated his Lord," because supplication is usually introduced by a calling out. Referring to the Divine Name by the description "Lord" added to Noah, peace be upon him, is an honouring of Noah and an allusion to God's compassion towards him, and that His subsequent prohibition is a prohibition of reproach.

The clause ﴿My Lord, indeed my son is of my family﴾ is an explanation of the calling out. The apparent requirement is that it should not be joined with the particle of consequence (fa’), just as the explanatory clause is not joined in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When he called out to his Lord with a secret call﴾ [Maryam: 3] ﴿He said, "My Lord, indeed my bones have weakened within me"﴾ [Maryam: 4]. This rule is departed from here. Al-Zamakhshari, in al-Kashshaf, explained its being joined with fa’ by saying that the verb "called out" (nada) is used to mean intending to call out, like the verb "you stood" (qumtum) in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, when you stand up for prayer, wash your faces﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 6], and so on. He means that this is a departure from the apparent requirement, since the presence of fa’ in the clause that explains the calling out is evidence that the verb "called out" is used figuratively for the meaning of intending to call out, i.e., he intended to call out to his Lord, so he followed his intention with the act of calling out. This indicates that he intended to call out, then hesitated to take that step because he knew from His saying, exalted is He: ﴿except those among them against whom the word has already preceded﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 27]. His hesitation did not last long, for compassion for his son overcame him, so he went ahead and called out to his Lord. For this reason he put forward the excuse in his words: ﴿indeed my son is of my family﴾. So his saying: ﴿indeed my son is of my family﴾ is a declarative statement used for excuse and preparation, because he wishes to ask a request whose acceptance he does not know, but he ventured into it because the one for whom he asks is of his family, so he has the excuse of compassion for him. The emphasis of the statement with ﴿indeed (inna)﴾ is for the sake of giving it importance.

Likewise, the clause ﴿and indeed Your promise is true﴾ is a declarative statement used for a necessary implication, namely that he knows that the promise of God is true.

What is meant by the promise is what is in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿except those among them against whom the word has already preceded, and do not address Me concerning those who have wronged; indeed they are to be drowned﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 27], since this indicates that some of his family had already been decreed by God not to board the ark. This exception is determined to refer to his son, since there was no one else of his family whom he asked to board the ark and who refused. And whoever God's knowledge has already determined will not board the ark from among people is a wrongdoer, i.e., a disbeliever, and is destined to drown, so his not boarding the ark and his drowning were a sign that he was a disbeliever. The meaning is: Noah, peace be upon him, was not ignorant that his son was a disbeliever. Therefore his asking forgiveness for him was with knowledge that he was a disbeliever, but he hoped that perhaps God would pardon him because of his kinship with him. So his asking forgiveness for him is equivalent to intercession for him with God, exalted is He, and that is taking the utmost of the motives of compassion and mercy toward his son.

The indicator of all of this is his saying: ﴿and You are the most just of judges﴾, which indicates that there is no one who can reject what He has decided and decreed, and that no one among His creation has any claim against Him. But it is a station of humble supplication and asking for what is not impossible.

Noah, peace be upon him, had not been forbidden from this, and the knowledge that God does not forgive the disbelievers had not been established in his law. So the state of Noah, peace be upon him, was like the state of the Prophet (ﷺ) when he said to Abu Talib: "I will surely ask forgiveness for you as long as I have not been forbidden from you," before the revelation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is not for the Prophet and those who have believed to ask forgiveness for the polytheists﴾ [al-Tawbah: 113], and so on.

Limiting the supplication to these three sentences is an allusion to the thing requested, since he did not mention it explicitly. This is a kind of courtesy and hesitation in proceeding to ask what is asked, relying on the knowledge of the one asked, as if he were saying: "Shall I ask You or leave it?" Like the verse of Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt:

"Shall I mention my need, or has your modesty sufficed me, since your nature is modesty?"

The meaning of ﴿the most just of judges﴾ is the one who is most intense in judgment. The superlative form relates to the reality of the act, so it indicates that His judgment is not unjust and that no one can nullify it.

The meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿indeed he is not of your family﴾ is the negation that he is of the family of his religion and belief. This is not a refutation of Noah's statement, peace be upon him: ﴿indeed my son is of my family﴾, but rather an informing that the kinship of religion, with respect to the people of faith, is kinship. This meaning is common in usage.

[Page 85]

Al-Nabighah said, addressing 'Uyayna ibn Hisn:

"If you try to commit wickedness against the Asad, then I am not of you and you are not of me."

And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And they swear by God that they are indeed of you, but they are not of you; rather they are a people who are fearful﴾ [al-Tawbah: 56].

The emphasis of the statement is for confirming it, because of its strangeness.

The clause ﴿indeed he is one whose deed is other than righteous﴾ is a justification for the content of the clause ﴿indeed he is not of your family﴾, so ﴿indeed (inna)﴾ in it is only for the sake of emphasis.

The word "deed" (ʿamal), in the reading of the majority, with a fatha on the mim and tanwin on the lam, is a verbal noun (masdar) whose predicate is stated for the sake of intensification, and "other than" (ghayr) is raised as an attribute of "deed". Al-Kisa'i and Ya'qub read it ("ʿamila") with a kasra on the mim in the past tense form, and "other than" (ghayr) in the accusative as the object of the verb "ʿamila". The meaning of "the deed other than righteous" is disbelief. Disbelief was called a "deed" because it is an act of the heart, and because its effect appears in the action of its possessor, such as the refusal of Noah's son to board, which indicates his denial of the warning of the flood.

It follows from this that His prohibition, that he should not ask about that of which he has no knowledge, is a prohibition of reproach. Because when it was said to him: ﴿indeed he is not of your family﴾, with its cause being his explanation that he is one whose deed is other than righteous, what he had prepared for in order to have his request answered collapsed, so he was deserving of not asking Him and of reflecting on what he wanted to ask from God.

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Abu Ja'far read ("fa-la tas'alanni") with a shadda on the nun, and these are the nun of emphasis (nun al-tawkid al-khafifah) and the protective nun (nun al-wiqayah), which have been assimilated. Apart from Ibn Kathir, those named read with the first-person ya' affirmed. As for Ibn Kathir, he read ("fa-la tas'alanna") with a heavy fatha-vowelled nun.

Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Ya'qub and Khalaf read ("fa-la tas'alni") with a sukun on the lam and a kasra on the nun, lightly, as not emphasised by the nun of emphasis, and transitive to the first-person ya'. Most of them omitted the ya' in pausal (wasl) position, while Warsh from Nafi' and Abu 'Amr affirmed it in connected speech.

Then, if Noah, peace be upon him, had not previously received a revelation from God that God does not forgive the polytheists in the Hereafter, his prohibition from asking about that of which he has no knowledge was a prohibition of disapproval for the likes of him, because the rank of prophethood requires that one not proceed to ask his Lord a request whose answer one does not know. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and intercession does not benefit with Him except for one whom He has permitted﴾ [Saba': 23], and His saying: ﴿They will not speak except one whom the Most Merciful has permitted, and he says what is correct﴾ [al-Naba': 38]. And even if it had been revealed to him about that before, as His saying indicates: ﴿and indeed Your promise is true﴾. His asking forgiveness for his son was a request to specify him from the general. And his prohibition was a prohibition of blame and reproach, since it had not been made clear to him from his Lord that this was permissible.

His saying: ﴿of which you have no knowledge﴾ was open to its apparent meaning and also open to being a metonymy for knowledge of its opposite, i.e., "do not ask Me about what you know will not occur."

Then, if Noah's statement, peace be upon him, ﴿indeed my son is of my family﴾ to its end was an allusion to the thing requested, the prohibition in His saying: ﴿So do not ask Me about that of which you have no knowledge﴾ was a prohibition against insistence or returning to asking Him. And if Noah's statement, peace be upon him, was merely a preparation for the request, in order to test the state of God's responsiveness to his request, then His saying, exalted is He: "so do not ask Me" is a prohibition against carrying out the request for which he had prepared with his speech. The purpose of the prohibition is to exempt him from exposing his request to refusal.

In all of these views, His saying: ﴿Indeed I admonish you lest you be among the ignorant﴾ is an admonition against neglecting deliberation before proceeding.

The ignorance here is the opposite of knowledge, and this is what suits its being contrasted with His saying: ﴿that of which you have no knowledge﴾.

[Page 88]

Noah, peace be upon him, then answered his Lord's words with what indicates his disavowal of what he had asked, and so he sought refuge that he should not ask about that of which he has no knowledge. If Noah, peace be upon him, had intended by his first statement an allusion to the request, then it is a matter that has already occurred, so the seeking of refuge relates to the consequence of that or to returning to the like of it in the future. And if he had only intended it as a preparation for the request, then the seeking of refuge is evident, namely, restraining oneself from carrying the request through.

His saying: ﴿And unless You forgive me and have mercy on me, I will be among the losers﴾ is a request for forgiveness first, because clearing away (al-takhliyah) precedes adornment (al-tahliyah). He then followed it with a request for mercy, because whoever is in the station of God's approval is worthy of mercy.

The commentators, in their interpretation of these verses, have followed the path that Noah's request, peace be upon him, was a request for the rescue of his son from drowning. This led them to encounter rugged and distant paths, and they suffered hardship in connecting them together, while the verse is far removed from them. Perhaps we have taken the straight road in interpreting it.
