**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 11, verse 48:**

﴿It was said: "O Noah, descend with peace from Us and blessings upon you and upon nations among those with you. And there will be nations whom We will provide for, then a painful punishment from Us will touch them."﴾

The sentence is disconnected (fasl) and not joined by a conjunction, because it occurs within the context of the dialogue between Noah, peace be upon him, and his Lord. When Noah answered with his words, ﴿My Lord, I seek refuge in You from asking You about that of which I have no knowledge﴾ [Hud: 47], to the end of the passage, his Lord addressed him to complete the dialogue with what would calm his heart.

The expected form would have been "He said: O Noah, descend," but it departs from this to the passive construction (bina' al-fi'l lil-na'ib, the passive voice) so that it follows the rhythm of the narration of the earlier parts of the story, from His words ﴿And it was said: O earth, swallow your water﴾ [Hud: 44] ... ﴿And it was said: Away with the wrongdoing people﴾ [Hud: 44]. Thus the passive construction fulfils the need to indicate a part of the story, just as the disconnection fulfils the need to indicate that this saying is part of the dialogue.

The address "O Noah" is for the purpose of honouring him before the assembly.

Al-hubut (descending) means descent. It has already occurred in His words ﴿Go down to a city﴾ [al-Baqarah: 61] in Surat al-Baqarah. What is meant here is descent from the ship, since it was higher than the earth.

Al-salam (peace) is a greeting, and it is also used when parting. They say: "Go with peace" (idhhab bi-salam). From this is the verse of Labid:

*"Until the year turns, then the name of peace upon you both."*

His address with peace at that moment is an indication that he was under God's hospitality (dayf Allah, the protection of God, Exalted), since He had guaranteed him salvation, as He, Exalted, said: ﴿And We carried him upon one of planks and nails﴾ [al-Qamar: 13] ﴿running under Our eyes﴾ [al-Qamar: 14].

The origin of al-salam is safety (al-salamah). It was used at meeting to signal that a person grants security to the one he meets and does not intend him harm. Then it spread and became a formula of greeting at meeting, for honour. On this basis the Prophet ﷺ forbade those who said "Peace be upon God" [a reference to the early practice of greeting]. So His words here, ﴿descend with peace﴾, are like His words ﴿Enter it with peace, secure﴾ [al-Hijr: 46], since peace is clearly a greeting, as it is restricted by "secure" (aminin). If peace meant safety, then restricting it with "secure" would be a reinforcement, which is contrary to the original usage.

"From Us" (minna) is an emphasis on directing the peace toward him, since "min" is here for origin (ibtida'iyyah, indicating source). The meaning is: with peace originating from Us, like His words ﴿Peace, a word from a Lord, Merciful﴾ [Ya-Sin: 58]. Such usage is common in their speech. This emphasis is intended to convey an increase in favour and honour, so it is more emphatic than the form in which "min" is not mentioned.

The "ba'" (with) is for accompaniment, meaning: descend accompanied by peace from Us. The accompaniment of peace, which is a greeting, is a figurative accompaniment.

Al-barakat (blessings) are growing goods. Its singular is barakah. It is one of the words of greeting, used in supplication.

Since those who greet one another with the formula of greeting only ask God through one another's supplication, the issuing of this supplication from Him stands in place of the answering of a supplication. It is thus an outpouring of blessings upon Noah, peace be upon him, and those with him. Through this they are honoured, secured, and favoured.

"Upon you" (alayka) is connected to "peace" and to "blessings", and likewise ﴿and upon nations among those with you﴾.

Al-umam (nations) is the plural of ummah. The ummah is a large group of people united by descent from one common ancestor. It is said: "the Arab ummah", or a language-community such as "the Turkish ummah", or a homeland such as "the American ummah", or a religion such as "the Islamic ummah". So "umam" indicates a large number of nations that will come after Noah, peace be upon him. Those who rode in the ship were not nations, because of their small number, as He said: ﴿And none believed with him except a few﴾ [Hud: 40]. The indefiniteness of "umam" is because it is not intended to be general, as a preparation for His words ﴿and nations We will provide for﴾.

The "min" in ﴿among those with you﴾ is for origin, and the relative "man" (those) refers to those who rode with Noah, peace be upon him, in the ship. Among them were his three sons. So the statement is good news to Noah, peace be upon him, and those with him, that God will make of them many nations who will be the place of His honour and blessings. It also indicates that He will make of them nations of a different kind, and for this reason His words ﴿And nations We will provide for, then a painful punishment from Us will touch them﴾ are conjoined to this sentence.

This arrangement implies that God began Noah with peace and blessings and associated with him in these, nations originating from those who were with him. Among them are those who originated from Noah, peace be upon him, since among those with him were his three sons, through whom his offspring was confined after him. Thus it is established that those with him are included in the peace and the blessings, first and foremost, before their offspring. He referred to them by the description of being with Noah, peace be upon him, to draw attention to the cause of their honour. Since the mention of the descendants is an indication that their special honour is because they originated from a group honoured through companionship with Noah, peace be upon him, the honouring of Noah, his companions, and their offspring is achieved through a brief and wondrous expression.

[p. 90]

The clause ﴿And nations We will provide for﴾ etc. is conjoined to the clause ﴿descend with peace from Us﴾ to its end. It is an explanatory resumption (istinaf bayani), since it explains what the indefiniteness in His words ﴿upon nations among those with you﴾ conveyed, namely a distinction from other nations. This waw is called the resumptive waw (istinafiyyah), and its origin is the conjunctive waw. Some trace it back to an extra waw. It is also possible that the waw is for division, and the intended aim is to warn the people of Noah against following the path of those who were drowned. The purpose of relating this in the Qur'an is an allusion to the polytheists among the Arabs, since they are from the offspring of Noah and did not follow the path of their forefather. So they were informed that they are among the nations of whom God informed Noah that He would provide for them and then a painful punishment would touch them. A parallel to this is His words: ﴿The offspring of those We carried with Noah; indeed he was a grateful servant﴾ [al-Isra': 3], meaning that those spoken of were not thankful for the blessing.

The use of al-mass (touching) for a strong affliction has already occurred at His words: ﴿And if God touches you with harm, there is none to remove it except Him﴾ [al-An'am: 17] in Surat al-An'am.

The mention of "from Us" with "will touch them" corresponds to His words in its opposite: "with peace from Us", so that they know that what befalls a nation of conditions beyond the ordinary, whether good or evil, is an announcement from God of His pleasure or His anger. This prevents them from supposing that it is a matter of the customary sequence of effects following their causes. For people ought to reflect upon events and discern whether the course of their affairs is in accordance with God's intent for them, and know that God addresses them through the evidence of created things when His address to them through the tongues of the messengers has ceased. The messengers explain to them the ways of inference and leave to them the consideration of placing the signified things at the moment of their signs. An example of this is what is here: He made clear to them, through the tongue of Noah, peace be upon him, that He gives provision to nations and then a painful punishment will touch them for what they do.

[Page 92]

﴿That is among the tidings of the unseen which We reveal to you. Neither you nor your people knew them before this. So be patient; indeed the good outcome is for the God-fearing.﴾ This is a resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*, a sentence beginning a new thought) intended to convey divine favour (*imtinan*) upon the Prophet ﷺ, admonition (*maw'iza*), and consolation (*tasliya*).

The favour is in His words: ﴿you did not know them﴾.

The admonition is in His words: "so be patient," and so on.

The consolation is in His words: ﴿indeed the good outcome is for the God-fearing﴾.

The demonstrative ﴿tilka﴾ ("that") refers to the account of Noah (peace be upon him) mentioned earlier. The feminine form of the demonstrative is used by interpreting (*ta'wil*) the referent as "the story."

*Anba'* is the plural of *naba'*, which means "news" or "report." "Tidings of the unseen" (*anba' al-ghayb*) are reports hidden from people, or from a group of them. These tidings were hidden from all the Arabs, since they had no knowledge of most of their details. Those details are that there was in ancient times a prophet called Noah (peace be upon him), whose people were struck by a flood. Anything beyond that is unseen, as His words indicate: ﴿you did not know them, neither you nor your people, before this﴾. They did not deny this, nor did they claim to know it. Moreover, some of its contents are unseen even to all the nations, such as the story of Noah's fourth son, his disobedience to his father, and his drowning; the words of the Lord to Noah (peace be upon him) when he descended from the ark; the mockery of his people toward him while he was building the ark; and the dialogue that took place between Noah (peace be upon him) and his people. All of this has not been mentioned in the books of the People of the Book.

The clauses ﴿among the tidings of the unseen﴾, *nuhiyha* ("We reveal it"), and ﴿you did not know them﴾ are predicates about the demonstrative. Alternatively, some of them are the predicate and some are circumstantial clauses (*hal*). The pronoun *anta* ("you") makes explicit the hidden pronoun in *ta'lamuha* ("you know it") so that the coordination with it (*'atf*) is grammatically correct.

[Page 93]

The coordination in ﴿nor your people﴾ is an ascending progression (*tarruq*), because among his people were some who associated with the People of the Book and some who could read and write, yet none of them knew much of what was revealed to him in this story.

The demonstrative in His words ﴿before this﴾ may refer to the Qur'an, or to the time, with regard to the additional details in this story beyond what is mentioned in similar accounts revealed earlier. Or it may refer to *tilka* by interpreting it as "the report," in which case the masculine reference after the feminine is similar to a shift (*iltifat*).

The reason the command to patience is attached to this story is that it contains a comparison between the Prophet's situation with his people and Noah's situation with his people. Just as Noah (peace be upon him) was patient and the good outcome was his, so too the good outcome will be yours over your people. The account of Noah (peace be upon him) is drawn from what is related of his people's opposition and his steadfastness in calling them, since that steadfastness in the face of such opposition is itself a form of patience.

The clause ﴿indeed the good outcome is for the God-fearing﴾ is the cause (*'illa*) for the commanded patience. That is: be patient, because the motive for patience is present, namely that the good outcome belongs to the God-fearing. So it will belong to you and to the believers with you.

*Al-'aqiba* is the state that follows another state. It has become customary, when used without qualification, to refer to a good state, as in His words: ﴿and the good end belongs to piety﴾ [Ta-Ha: 132].

The definite article in *al-'aqiba* is generic (*li-l-jins*).

The *lam* in *lil-muttaqin* ("for the God-fearing") indicates exclusive possession and ownership. It implies that the God-fearing possess the category of good outcome. It is therefore established for them and will not escape them, and it is negated for their opposites.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 11, verse 50–52:

Page 94
﴿And to 'Ad [We sent] their brother Hud. He said, "O my people, worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him. You are but fabricators.﴾ ﴿O my people, I do not ask of you any compensation for it. My compensation is only from the One who originated me. Then will you not reason?﴾ ﴿And O my people, seek forgiveness of your Lord and then repent to Him; He will send down the sky upon you in abundance and increase you in strength upon your strength. And do not turn away as criminals.﴾

This is an conjunction (ʿatf) upon ﴿And We had certainly sent Noah to his people﴾ [Hud: 25], so "to ʿAd" is conjoined to "to his people." And "their brother" is conjoined to "Noah," and the estimated sense is: "And We sent to ʿAd their brother Hud." This is conjunction upon two complements of a single governing verb.

Fronting the prepositional phrase serves to alert that the conjunction is of single terms (ʿatf al-mufradat), not of clauses (ʿatf al-jumal), because the preposition must have a complement; and it serves the requirement of concision (ijaz), so that the mention of ʿAd is present twice, once by its name and once by its pronoun.

Describing Hud as "brother of ʿAd" is because he was of their lineage, as one says, "O brother of the Arabs," meaning, "O Arab."

The mention of ʿAd and Hud has already occurred in Surat al-A'raf.

The clause "He said" explains the implied clause "We sent," which is omitted.

The reason for explicitly stating the verb of saying is that the verb "We sent" is deleted; had it been explained by the clause ﴿O my people, worship﴾, as was explained in His words ﴿And We had certainly sent Noah to his people, [who said], "Indeed, I am to you a clear warner"﴾ [Hud: 25], it would have been an explanation of a non-existent thing, which is not clear.

Opening his call with addressing his people serves to capture their hearing, indicating the importance of what he is about to convey to them.

Page 95
The clause ﴿you have no deity other than Him﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "worship" or from the name of Allah. The bringing of the circumstantial clause serves to emphasize the nullification of their polytheism, that they associated others in His worship while in a state in which they have no deity other than Him, or in a state in which there is no deity for them other than Him. This is a reproach of shirk.

The clause ﴿You are but fabricators﴾ is a rebuke and denunciation. It is an explanation of the clause ﴿you have no deity other than Him﴾, meaning: you are nothing but liars in claiming divinity for other than Allah, the Exalted.

The clause ﴿O my people, I do not ask of you any compensation for it﴾: if he said it together with the preceding clause, then repeating the address in the course of speech is an emphasis of importance, intended to magnify the matter and capture attention, out of concern for what they are listening to; and the address is the linking element between the two clauses. If it was said at a time other than that in which the first clause was said, then its being the beginning of a speech is evident.

The explanation of ﴿I do not ask of you any compensation for it﴾ has already been given in the story of Noah, peace be upon him, meaning: I do not ask you for any reward for what I have told you.

The expression by the relative ﴿Who originated me﴾ rather than the proper name serves to further affirm that he does not ask them any reward for guidance, since he knows that the One who created him drives his provision to him; for the speaker's manifesting his knowledge of the causes gives his speech about the effects strength and affirmation.

Therefore, His saying ﴿Then will you not reason?﴾ is conjoined to that, with the particle of consequence, as a conjunction interrogative of denial concerning their failure to reason, meaning: their failure to reflect on the indication of his state for his truthfulness in what he conveys and his sincerity toward them in what he commands them. And "reason" (ʿaql) means knowledge.

The conjunction of the clause "And O my people" is like its counterpart in the story of Noah, peace be upon him, earlier.

Seeking forgiveness (istighfar) is requesting forgiveness for sin, meaning requesting that they not be held accountable for what has passed of their shirk. It is here used as a metonym for abandoning the creed of shirk, because seeking Allah's forgiveness entails acknowledging His existence and entails the seeker's acknowledgment of a sin on his part; and they had no sin before Hud, peace be upon him, came to them except the sin of association, since there was no law for them before. As for the sin of association, it is established from all the previous laws, so it was known by necessity. Thus the command to seek forgiveness comprised all these meanings, explicitly and implicitly.

Page 96
Repentance (tawba) is abandoning the sin in the future and regret for what has passed. In the essence of repentance is the resolve not to return to the sin, which leads to the command to persist in monotheism and the negation of association.

And "then" (thumma) is for graded sequence, because persisting in abandonment is more important than seeking pardon for what has passed.

And ﴿He will send down the sky upon you﴾ is the answer to the command in "seek forgiveness."

Sending (irsal) is dispatching from a distant place; so "sending" was applied to the descent of rain because it occurs by Allah's decree, and so it was likened to sending something from the place of the sender to the one to whom it is sent.

"Sky" (sama') is among the names of rain, designating a thing by the name of its source. In a hadith: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ addressed us upon a sky (rain)."

"Abundantly" (midrar) is a circumstantial clause from "sky"; it is an intensive form from pouring (durur), which is flowing, meaning copiously. He made their reward for seeking forgiveness and repenting the supplying of them with rain, because that is among the greatest blessings upon them in this world, since ʿAd were people of crops and vineyards, so they were in need of water, and they used to construct dams to store water. The more evident view is that Allah withheld rain from them for years, so their offspring and provision diminished as a recompense for shirk after He sent Hud, peace be upon him, to them; so the statement "He will send down the sky" is a promise and an alert to Allah's anger upon them. Their dwellings had been, from Hadramawt to al-Ahqaf, cities, encampments, and domes.

They were also self-admiring of the strength of their nation, and they said, ﴿Who is mightier than us in strength?﴾ [Fussilat: 15]. Therefore Allah made their reward for abandoning shirk an increase in their strength through multiplicity of numbers, soundness of bodies, and abundance of

Page 97
provisions, because all of that is strength for a nation, making it free from other nations and capable of preserving its independence, and making many nations in need of it.

"Upon your strength" (ila quwwatikum) is connected to "will increase you" (yazidkum). It was construed with "ila" only because it is implicitly used in the sense of "joining" (yadumm). This is a promise to them of the good state in this world; may Allah be pleased with them.

He conjoined to it ﴿And do not turn away as criminals﴾ as a warning against returning to shirk.

"Turning away" (tawalli) is departing, and here it is a metaphor for turning aside.

"Criminals" (mujrimin) is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "turn away," meaning characterized by crime, which is turning aside from accepting the command of Allah, the Exalted.

**Ibn 'Ashur's commentary on Surah Hud, verse 53:**

﴿They said, "O Hud, you have brought us no clear proof, and we will not abandon our gods on your word, nor will we believe you.﴾ ﴿We say only that some of our gods have struck you with evil.﴾ [Hud: 54]

This is a dialogue from them to Hud (peace be upon him), as a reply to his call. For this reason the sentence is left without a conjunction (*'atf*).

Their opening of speech with the vocative (*nida'*) indicates concern with what they are about to say and that it deserves attention. They treated him as if he were distant because of his heedlessness, so they called out to him. It is therefore used in its metonymic meaning (*kinaya*) as well. It may also be intended, along with that, to rebuke and blame him, which makes it a second metonymy, or the vocative is used in both its literal and figurative senses.

Their statement ﴿You have brought us no clear proof﴾ is a falsehood (*buhtan*), because he brought them miracles. This is based on the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And that was 'Ad, who denied the signs of their Lord﴾ [Hud: 59]. Although the Qur'an does not mention a specific sign for Hud (peace be upon him), perhaps his sign was that, at the time of his mission, he promised them abundant provision and children and continuous fertility, a steady abundance in which no calamity or misfortune would reach them, to a degree that was extraordinary compared with the usual state of blessing among nations. This is indicated by the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And they said, "Who is mightier than us in strength?"﴾ [Fussilat: 15].

In the authentic hadith, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "There is no prophet among the prophets except that he was given signs of the kind upon which mankind believed," and so on.

They only meant that the clear proofs which Hud (peace be upon him) brought them did not conform to their demands. They made this the reason for their insistence on worshipping their gods, so they said, ﴿and we will not abandon our gods on your word﴾. They did not make ﴿and we will not abandon﴾ a consequence of their statement ﴿You have brought us no clear proof﴾.

The *'an* in ﴿on your word﴾ indicates separation (*mujawaza*), meaning: we will not abandon them in a manner that proceeds from your word. It is like His saying: ﴿And I did it not of my own accord﴾ [Al-Kahf: 82]. The meaning, on this reading, is that his speech is the cause of their abandoning their gods.

The clause ﴿We say only that some of our gods have struck you with evil﴾ [Hud: 54] is an explanatory resumption (*isti'naf bayani*). Their saying ﴿nor will we believe you﴾ naturally raises a question in the minds of the listener and those with him: "If you do not believe in what he brought, that it is from Allah, then what do you consider his call among you to be?" They answered: we say that you are possessed by some of our gods. They also made this an action of some of the gods, as a threat to the people, that if all the gods confronted him, they would utterly crush him.

*Al-i'tira'* means to descend upon and to afflict. The *ba'* is for accompaniment (*mulabasa*), meaning: it struck you with evil. There is no doubt that they meant that their gods had afflicted him with madness before he began calling to reject their worship, due to another cause. This is a statement that does not follow the coherence of argument, since it is a patched-together utterance of the kind that proceeds from the sophists. They called him mad and made the cause of his madness a touch from their gods. They did not notice the flaw in their speech, which is that how could the gods be the cause of stirring up a rebel against them.

[Page 99]

The word "qawl" is used here for spoken utterance, and it requires that they believed what they were saying.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 11, verses 54–56:

﴿He said: "Indeed, I call Allah to witness, and bear witness yourselves that I am free of what you associate with Him, apart from Him. So scheme against me, all of you together, and give me no respite.﴾ ﴿Indeed, I have put my trust in Allah, my Lord and your Lord. There is no creature but that He holds its forelock. Indeed, my Lord is on a straight path.﴾

When they, in their speech, rejected what he called them to, denied His signs, insisted on persisting in worshipping their idols, and extolled the power of their gods, Hud (peace be upon him) answered them by saying that he calls Allah to witness against them, that he had conveyed the message to them, and that they had shown arrogance and denied His signs.

The clause ﴿I call Allah to witness﴾ is an act of performative speech (inshā'), expressed in the form of a report (ikhbār), because every performative utterance whose effect does not appear in creation is, by its nature, expressed in the form of a report, since a report carries the purpose of informing the listener of what the speaker intends. For this reason, the meaning of the formulas of contracts (ṣīghat al-'uqūd) is performative while expressed in the wording of a report. Then he charged them to bear witness that he is free of their partners, hastening to reject the wrong, even though they had brought it up incidentally. Therefore his addressing its refutation is like an interjection between the clause ﴿I call Allah to witness﴾ and the clause ﴿But if they turn away﴾, based on the view that the clause ﴿But if they turn away﴾ through its end is part of Hud's speech, as will come. The meaning of his calling them to witness is that the matter be established from their partners, and that he does not waver regarding a definite matter that the one witnessed against has made obligatory upon himself. He used the imperative form in his calling them to witness because he intended the flavor of the act of calling to witness without the scent of the meaning of a report.

The "mā" in His saying ﴿of what you associate﴾ is a relative pronoun (mawṣūlah), and its returning pronoun is omitted. The estimate is: "of what they associate with Him."

The referent of the relative is the idols, as indicated by the emphasized plural pronoun in His saying ﴿so scheme against me, all of you together﴾. And since disassociation from the partners entails the belief in their inability to inflict harm upon him, he made the clause ﴿so scheme against me, all of you together﴾ a consequence of the disassociation. He directed the address to his people, lest his address be to something that does not understand and does not hear, so he commanded his people to scheme against him. He included their idols in the pronoun of those who scheme, in accommodation to their belief and in thoroughly establishing their incapacity; that is, you and your idols, as indicated by the consequence drawn from the disassociation from their idols.

The imperative in ﴿kīdūnī﴾ is used to express permission, as a metaphor (kināyah) for their incapacity, both with respect to the idols and with respect to his people, as in His saying ﴿So if you have a scheme, then scheme against me﴾ [al-Mursalat: 39]. This is a refutation of their saying ﴿We say only that some of our gods have struck you with evil﴾.

The "thumma" (then) indicates a rank-based delay: he challenged them to scheme against him, then rose in the rank of incapacitating and belittling them, forbidding them from delaying their scheme against him. That is the utmost of belittling their idols and themselves, and a metaphor for their not being able to reach that.

The clause ﴿I have put my trust﴾ is a causal explanation of the content of ﴿so scheme against me﴾, namely the incapacitation and belittling. That is: he is confident of their inability to scheme against him because he relies upon Allah. This is an ancient religious meaning.

The attribute of lordship (rubūbiyyah) is applied to the name of Allah as proof of the soundness of trusting in Him to repel their harm from him, because He is the owner of them all, who repels the injustice of some of them against others.

The clause ﴿There is no creature but that He holds its forelock﴾ is in the position of a qualifier of the name of Allah, or a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from it, and its purpose is similar to the purpose of the attribute of lordship.

The akhdh (taking hold) is restraint.

The nāṣiyah (forelock) is that part of the hair of the head that hangs down over the forehead. The taking hold by the forelock here is a figurative expression (tamthīl) for complete control, likened to the state of a person holding another by his forelock, where his head is in the hand of the one who holds it so that he cannot escape. It is a figurative expression only because many creatures have no forelocks, so taking hold by the forelock does not fit with the generality of ﴿there is no creature﴾; but when it became a proverb, it came to be equivalent to: "there is no creature but that He disposes of it."

Among the wonders of this proverb is that it is more specifically applicable to the intended kind out of the general class of creatures, namely the human kind. The intended meaning is that He is the owner and dominant over all that crawls on the earth; His being the owner of all requires that none of them escape Him, and His being dominant over them requires that none of them be able to overcome Him.

The clause ﴿Indeed, my Lord is on a straight path﴾ is a causal explanation of the clause ﴿Indeed, I have put my trust in Allah﴾; that is, I trust in Him because He is worthy of my trust in Him, since He is characterized by carrying out His acts in the way of justice and by supporting His messengers.

The "ʿalā" (upon) is for figurative elevation, like His saying ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 5]; it is borrowed to express a moral establishment, namely a firmly established attribute that does not change.

The "al-ṣirāṭ al-mustaqīm" (the straight path) is a metaphor for an act proceeding according to the requirement of justice and wisdom, because justice is likened to straightness and evenness. He said: ﴿So follow me; I will guide you to an even path﴾ [Maryam: 43]. Therefore, the one whom He is relied upon does not hand over those who wrong.

A consequence (*tafrīʿ*) of the statement ﴿Indeed I call Allah to witness﴾ [Hud: 54]. What lies between them is a parenthetical insertion (*iʿtirāḍ*) required by the intent to hasten the refutation of their falsehood, because the content of this sentence is an elaboration of the content of the sentence ﴿Indeed I call Allah to witness﴾ [Hud: 54], on the basis that this is from the speech of Hud, peace be upon him.

On this view, the original form of *tawallaw* is *tatawallaw*, and one of the two *tā*'s is elided for brevity. It is therefore a present-tense verb, and it is Hud's address to his people. This is the apparent sense, since the pronouns follow one uniform pattern.

[p. 102]

It is also permissible that it be a past-tense verb, with the *wāw* referring to the people of Makkah. Then it is like a parenthetical insertion within the parts of the story, for the purpose of drawing a lesson, in the same position as the parenthetical insertion in the story of Noah, peace be upon him, with His saying: ﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it"? Say, "If I have invented it..."﴾ [Hud: 35], and so on. Allah addressed His Prophet (ﷺ) and commanded him to say to them: "I have indeed conveyed to you." The first *fāʾ* marks the consequence of the admonition as drawn from the preaching, and the clause ﴿so I have indeed conveyed to you﴾ is from the speech of the Prophet (ﷺ), being the object of an implied verb of speech that was commanded, which the context indicates. The estimate is: "So say: I have indeed conveyed to you." This style belongs to speech that is directed in a way admitting two meanings that do not contradict one another, and it is among the marvellous styles of inimitability (*iʿjāz*). For its sake the verb *tawallaw* came with one *tā'*, unlike what is in His saying: ﴿And if you turn away, He will replace you with another people﴾ [Muhammad: 38].

*Tawallī* means turning away (*iʿrāḍ*). It was mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿And whoever turns away, We have not sent you as a guardian over them﴾ [al-Nisa: 80], in Surat al-Nisa.

The answer to the condition of turning away was made to be His saying ﴿so I have indeed conveyed to you﴾, even though conveying precedes the turning away that was made the condition. This is because the intended meaning of this answer is the necessary consequence of that conveying, namely the removal of the responsibility for their turning away from him and his innocence of their crime, since he has discharged what was obligatory upon him of conveying. If it is from the speech of Hud, peace be upon him, then "what I was sent with" refers to what has preceded. If it is from the speech of the Prophet (ﷺ), then what he was sent with is the admonition through the story of the people of Hud, peace be upon him.

On both views it is a *kināya* (allusion) to warning them of the consequence of turning away and the descent of punishment upon them. For this reason He conjoined ﴿and my Lord will replace you with another people﴾, meaning He will remove you and substitute you with other people who do not turn away from their messenger. This is like His saying: ﴿And if you turn away, He will replace you with another people, then they will not be the likes of you﴾ [Muhammad: 38].

The *rafʿ* (nominative) of *yastakhlifu* in the reading of all the readers is because it is conjoined to the answer, which admits both *rafʿ* and *jazm* (jussive). The *rafʿ* is more preferable here because it gives the verb the status of an independent new statement, so that it is intended in itself and not as a follow-up to the answer. Thereby its purpose is to inform them, warning them of total extirpation.

[p. 103]

Likewise the clause ﴿and you will not harm Him at all﴾, meaning you do not harm Allah at all by your turning away. *Shayʾan* is an accusative of emphasis for the negated verb *tadurrūnahu*.

Its indefiniteness is for minimization, as is generally the case with the indefiniteness of the word *shayʾ*. The purpose of the emphasis is to specify generality by negating harm, because it is an indefinite noun within the scope of negation. That is, Allah inflicts upon you extirpation, which is the greatest harm, while you do not harm Him even the least harm. For it is known in contests and disputes that the dominant party who harms its opponent is not free from suffering some harm itself in the course of the contest and fighting.

The clause ﴿Indeed my Lord is over all things Guardian﴾ is a causal justification for the clause ﴿and you will not harm Him at all﴾, so the position of *inna* in it is the position of the *fāʾ* of consequence.

*Al-ḥafīẓ*: its origin is the intensive form of *al-ḥāfiẓ*, the one who places the protected thing where no one other than its guardian can reach it. Here it is a *kināya* for power and dominance.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 11, verse 58:

﴿And when Our command came, We saved Hud and those who believed with him by mercy from Us, and We saved them from a harsh punishment.﴾

The use of the past tense in His saying "when Our command came" (jā'a amruna) is in the sense of the coming being near, because the salvation occurred before the punishment descended.

The word "command" (al-amr) has been applied to the effect of the command, which is what Allah commanded by a command of creation (amr takwin); that is, when the coming of the effect of Our command drew near, and that effect is the punishment, namely the great wind.

صفحة ١٠٤
The first object of "We saved" (najjayna) is omitted, meaning: from the punishment, which is indicated by His saying "when Our command came." The manner of the salvation of Hud, peace be upon him, and those with him has already been mentioned in the commentary on Surah al-A'raf.

The "bi" in "by mercy from Us" is causal (li'l-sababiyya), so Allah's mercy toward them was the cause of their deliverance. What is meant by mercy is Allah's favour upon them, because if He had not shown them mercy, annihilation would have encompassed them, and it would have been a vengeance upon the disbelievers and a trial for the believers.

The clause "and We saved them from a harsh punishment" is coordinated (ma'tufa) upon the clause "when Our command came." The sense is: "and also We saved them from a harsh punishment," and this is the salvation from the punishment of the Hereafter, which is the "harsh punishment." Thus there is in this a second favour, upon a second salvation: We saved them from the punishment of this world by mercy from Us, and We saved them from a harsh punishment in the Hereafter. For this reason the verb "We saved them" was coordinated upon "We saved." These two salvations correspond to the doubling of the punishment for 'Ad in His saying: ﴿And they were followed in this world by a curse, and on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [Hud: 60]. Here the object of the salvation is mentioned and the cause is omitted, the reverse of the first clause, because it is evident that salvation from the punishment of the Hereafter was due to faith and obedience to Allah, as is indicated by its contrast with His saying: ﴿And those were 'Ad, who denied the signs of their Lord and disobeyed His messengers﴾ [Hud: 59].

Ghalidh (harsh) in its true meaning is the rough, the opposite of the smooth (raqiq), and it is used figuratively for the severe. The past tense was used in "and We saved them" in the sense of the future, to affirm the certainty of the promise's occurrence.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (*al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir*) on Surah 11, verses 59–60:

﴿And that was ʿĀd, who denied the signs of their Lord, disobeyed His messengers, and followed the command of every obstinate tyrant.﴾ ﴿And they were pursued by a curse in this world, and on the Day of Resurrection. Indeed, ʿĀd disbelieved in their Lord. Away with ʿĀd, the people of Hūd!﴾

The demonstrative *tilka* ("that") refers to something present in the mind because of the account that has been given of it, until it is as if it were present to the senses and to direct observation. Like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Those are the cities; We relate to you some of their news﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 101].

[p. 105]

And like His saying: ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 5]. It is also similar to it in that the use of the demonstrative after the mention of past reports about those pointed to serves to alert that they are deserving of what follows the demonstrative in the predicate, because of those previously mentioned attributes.

The feminine form of the demonstrative noun (*ism al-ishārah*) is in accordance with interpreting the group as a nation (*umma*).

*ʿĀd* is an explanatory apposition (*bayān*) of the demonstrative noun.

The clause *jaḥadū* is the predicate of the demonstrative noun. It and what follows it form a preamble (*tamhīd*) for the conjoined clause, which is ﴿And they were pursued by a curse in this world﴾, in order to further establish the preamble through the earlier crimes, which is what the demonstrative noun required, as mentioned above; for all of that is among the causes of their being given both punishments.

*Al-Jaḥd* means strong denial, like denying things that are evident and observed. This indicates that Hūd came to them with signs, and they denied their indication. *Jaḥadū* is followed by *bi-* although it is transitive by itself, either to emphasize the transitivity, or because it is implicitly used in the sense of *kafarū* ("they disbelieved"), so that it is equivalent to saying: "they denied the signs of their Lord and disbelieved in them," like His saying: ﴿And they denied them while their souls were convinced of them﴾ [al-Naml: 14].

In His saying ﴿and disobeyed His messengers﴾ the word "messengers" is in the plural, though they disobeyed only one messenger, Hūd, peace be upon him. This is because the purpose is to mention their crimes, and it was fitting to attribute the crime to disobedience toward the category of messengers, because their rejection of Hūd was not specific to his person. For they said to him: ﴿We will not leave our gods on your word﴾ [Hūd: 53]. So every messenger who came with the command to abandon the worship of idols, they rejected. Similar to this is His saying: ﴿ʿĀd denied the messengers﴾ [al-Shuʿarāʾ: 123].

The meaning of *ittibāʿ al-amr* ("following the command") is obeying what they are commanded. So *ittibāʿ* is a figurative expression for acting upon what is dictated to the follower, because the command resembles the guide for the traveller on the road, and the one who complies resembles the follower of the traveller.

[p. 106]

*Al-Jabbār* is the arrogant one. *Al-ʿAnīd* is an intensive form of obstinacy (*al-muʿānada*). It is said: *ʿanada*, with the *nūn* having any of its three vowels, when one transgresses; and whoever has arrogance as his character, and the one who is obstinate, does not command good and calls only to falsehood. Thus their following the command of obstinate tyrants indicates that they obeyed the callers to disbelief, misguidance, and wrongdoing.

Each of them is among the forms of generality. If *kull jabbārin ʿanīd* is meant as every obstinate tyrant from among their people, then the generality is literal. If the category of tyrants is meant, then *kull* is used to mean a large number, as in the saying of al-Nābigha:

*"There, every one who drags his garment, and the wide-eyed doe, graze."*

From this is His saying: ﴿They will come to you on foot and on every lean camel﴾ [al-Ḥajj: 27], in Surat al-Ḥajj.

The "following" of the curse after them is a metaphor for its striking them swiftly without delay, as one who walks is followed by someone who catches up with him. What adds to the beauty of this metaphor is the *mushākala* in it (correspondence between the terms), and the equivalence of the punishment to the crime, because they followed the accursed, so they were followed by the curse.

The verb *utbiʿū* ("they were pursued") is in the passive, since there is no purpose in specifying the agent. The verb was not attributed to the curse, although that would have been a figurative attribution, so as to indicate that its pursuit of them was by a command from an agent, to convey that it followed them as a punishment from God, not merely as a coincidence.

*Al-Laʿna* ("the curse") is expulsion with humiliation and contempt.

He joined *al-dunyā* ("this world") with the demonstrative noun in order to belittle its matter in comparison with the curse of the Hereafter, as in the saying of Qays ibn al-Khaṭīm:

*"When this death comes, it will not find a need in my soul except that I have already fulfilled it."*

He hinted that he does not care about death and does not fear it.

The clause ﴿Indeed ʿĀd disbelieved in their Lord﴾ is a new independent sentence (*istiʾnāf ibtidāʾiyya*), introduced by the particle of alerting in order to amplify the report, and emphasized with *inna* to convey the reason for the clause ﴿And they were pursued by a curse in this world and on the Day of Resurrection﴾, as an allusion to the polytheists so that they may take warning from what befell ʿĀd.

[p. 107]

*Kafarū rabbahum* ("disbelieved in their Lord") is transitive without a preposition, either because it is implicitly used in the sense of *ʿaṣaw* ("disobeyed"), in contrast to ﴿and followed the command of every obstinate tyrant﴾, or because the intended meaning is an implied noun, that is, "the blessing of their Lord," since the root *kufr* ("disbelief") does not extend to the essence itself but extends to a non-material matter.

The clause ﴿Away with ʿĀd﴾ is an independent sentence for creating a censure of them. The discussion of *buʿdan* ("away") has already been given in the account of Noah, peace be upon him, at His saying: ﴿And it was said: Away with the wrongdoing people﴾ [Hūd: 44].

*Qawm Hūd* ("the people of Hūd") is an explanatory apposition of *ʿĀd*, or a descriptive attribute of *ʿĀd*, in view of the meaning of description contained in the word *qawm* ("people"). The benefit of mentioning it is to indicate that it has an effect in the censure, through their turning away from obeying their messenger; thus it is an allusion to the polytheists of the Arabs. Its mention is not meant to exclude another ʿĀd, namely Iram, as al-Zamakhsharī permitted in *al-Kashshāf*, because among the Arabs no ʿĀd is known other than the people of Hūd, who were Iram. He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Have you not seen how your Lord dealt with ʿĀd, Iram of the lofty pillars?﴾ [al-Fajr: 6–7].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (*al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir*) on Surah 11, verses 59–60:

﴿And that was ʿĀd, who denied the signs of their Lord, disobeyed His messengers, and followed the command of every obstinate tyrant.﴾ ﴿And they were pursued by a curse in this world, and on the Day of Resurrection. Indeed, ʿĀd disbelieved in their Lord. Away with ʿĀd, the people of Hūd!﴾

The demonstrative *tilka* ("that") refers to something present in the mind because of the account that has been given of it, until it is as if it were present to the senses and to direct observation. Like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Those are the cities; We relate to you some of their news﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 101].

[p. 105]

And like His saying: ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 5]. It is also similar to it in that the use of the demonstrative after the mention of past reports about those pointed to serves to alert that they are deserving of what follows the demonstrative in the predicate, because of those previously mentioned attributes.

The feminine form of the demonstrative noun (*ism al-ishārah*) is in accordance with interpreting the group as a nation (*umma*).

*ʿĀd* is an explanatory apposition (*bayān*) of the demonstrative noun.

The clause *jaḥadū* is the predicate of the demonstrative noun. It and what follows it form a preamble (*tamhīd*) for the conjoined clause, which is ﴿And they were pursued by a curse in this world﴾, in order to further establish the preamble through the earlier crimes, which is what the demonstrative noun required, as mentioned above; for all of that is among the causes of their being given both punishments.

*Al-Jaḥd* means strong denial, like denying things that are evident and observed. This indicates that Hūd came to them with signs, and they denied their indication. *Jaḥadū* is followed by *bi-* although it is transitive by itself, either to emphasize the transitivity, or because it is implicitly used in the sense of *kafarū* ("they disbelieved"), so that it is equivalent to saying: "they denied the signs of their Lord and disbelieved in them," like His saying: ﴿And they denied them while their souls were convinced of them﴾ [al-Naml: 14].

In His saying ﴿and disobeyed His messengers﴾ the word "messengers" is in the plural, though they disobeyed only one messenger, Hūd, peace be upon him. This is because the purpose is to mention their crimes, and it was fitting to attribute the crime to disobedience toward the category of messengers, because their rejection of Hūd was not specific to his person. For they said to him: ﴿We will not leave our gods on your word﴾ [Hūd: 53]. So every messenger who came with the command to abandon the worship of idols, they rejected. Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 11, verse 61:

﴿And to Thamud [We sent] their brother Salih. He said, "O my people, worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him. He has produced you from the earth and settled you therein, so seek His forgiveness and then repent to Him. Indeed, my Lord is near and responsive."﴾

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And to Thamud [We sent] their brother Salih﴾ up to His saying ﴿other than Him﴾. The discussion regarding it is like that in His saying: ﴿And to 'Ad [We sent] their brother Hud﴾ [Hud: 50], etc.

The mention of Thamud and Salih, peace be upon him, has already preceded in Surat al-A'raf.

Thamud is the name of an ancestor after whom the tribe was named, and for this reason it is not inflected (diptote), by way of interpreting it as a tribe.

The clause ﴿He has produced you from the earth﴾ is in the position of giving the reason for the command to worship Allah and the negation of the divinity of any other. It seems they were like the polytheists of Quraysh, who did not claim that their idols created or provided sustenance, and therefore the proof against them was decisive and clear.

Al-insha' (producing) means bringing into existence and originating, and it has preceded in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We produced after them another generation﴾ [al-An'am: 6] in Surat al-An'am.

He made the two predicates about the pronoun verbs rather than saying "He is your producer and your settler," in order to convey restriction (qasr), meaning: no one produced you from the earth except Him, and no one settled you therein except Him.

The producing from the earth is the creation of Adam from the earth, because the producing of him is a producing of his offspring. The connection of their creation to the earth is mentioned because they were people of orchards and crops, as He said in Surat al-Shu'ara': ﴿Will you be left in what is here, secure?﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 146] ﴿among gardens and springs﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 147] and crops and palm trees whose spathes are soft [al-Shu'ara': 148]. And because they used to hew houses out of the mountains of the earth and build palaces in the land, as He said in the other verse: ﴿And He settled you in the land, taking from its plains palaces and hewing the mountains into houses﴾ [al-A'raf: 74]. So there were benefits for them from the earth that correspond to the blessing of their being produced from the earth; for the sake of their benefits in the earth, the blessing of creation was restricted to being from the earth from which they were produced. For this reason, ﴿and settled you therein﴾ is conjoined to it.

Al-isti'mar means al-i'mar, that is, He made you its inhabitants (a'miriha). The sin and ta' are for intensification, like those in istabqa and istafaqa. The meaning of i'mar is that they made the earth populated through building, planting and sowing, since that is considered the making of the earth prosperous, to the point that tilling was called 'imarah because its purpose is the prosperity of the earth.

Having reminded them of these blessings, He made the command to seek His forgiveness and repent to Him a consequence (tafri'), that is, to seek the forgiveness of their transgressions and to desist from what He does not approve of, namely polytheism and corruption. And among the variety of style is that these blessings were made a cause for their command to worship Allah alone by way of the explanatory clause, and were also made a cause for the command to seek forgiveness and repent by way of consequence.

The command to repent is conjoined with the particle of delay (thumma), for the reason previously stated in His saying: ﴿And O my people, seek forgiveness of your Lord, then repent to Him﴾ [Hud: 52] in the preceding verse.

The clause ﴿Indeed, my Lord is near and responsive﴾ is an explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani), as if they regarded it as too great that their crime could be pardoned by seeking forgiveness, so they were answered that Allah is near and responsive. By this it becomes clear that the clause is not a reason. The particle (inna) in it is for emphasis, treating them, in their magnifying of their crime, as one who doubts the acceptance of his seeking forgiveness.

Nearness here is metaphorical for compassion and honour, because distance is used metaphorically for harshness and aversion. Jubayr ibn al-Adbat said:

"Mitahal drew far from me when I called upon him, 'Ameen'; so Allah increased the distance between us."

Likewise its opposite is used metaphorically for its opposite. It has preceded in His saying: ﴿Indeed I am near; I respond to the invocation of the supplicant﴾ [al-Baqarah: 186] in Surat al-Baqarah. The responsive one here is the responder to supplication, which is seeking forgiveness. The answering of a supplication is the giving to the petitioner what he asks.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 11, verse 62:

﴿They said, "O Salih, you were indeed among us a figure of hope before this. Do you forbid us to worship what our fathers worshipped? Indeed, we are in grave doubt about that to which you invite us."﴾

This is their reply to his eloquent and concise call, which is full of guidance and direction. It is a reply filled with misguidance, obstinacy, and weakness of argument.

The opening of the speech with the vocative (al-nida') is for the purpose of reproach (al-tawbikh) or blame (al-mala'am) and alerting (al-tanbih), as was mentioned earlier in His words: ﴿They said, "O Hud, you have not brought us any clear proof"﴾ [Hud: 53]. The indication of reproach here is more evident, and it is their saying ﴿you were indeed among us a figure of hope before this﴾, for it is an allusion to the disappointment of their hope in him, and so it is a rebuke.

And (qad) is for emphasizing the statement.

The object of (marjuwwan) has been omitted, because the verb of hoping (al-raja') indicates that it is the anticipation of good, i.e., "a figure of hope for good." That is, "and now despair of your good has set in." This implies that they regard what he calls them to as evil. They addressed him in this manner because he was sent among them while he was a young man (so said al-Baghawi in his tafsir of Surat al-A'raf), meaning: you were a figure of hope for the qualities of leadership, the protection of the tribe, and the support of their gods.

The indication in (before this) refers to the speech with which he addressed them when God sent him to them.

The clause ﴿Do you forbid us to worship what our fathers worshipped?﴾ is an explanation of the clause ﴿you were indeed among us a figure of hope﴾ in terms of its indication of blame, and because it contains the demonstrative which is also clarified by the clause ﴿Do you forbid us to worship what our fathers worshipped?﴾.

The interrogation is one of denial and reproach.

They expressed their idols by the relative pronoun (ma), because of what the relative clause carries of indication that those idols deserve to be worshipped in their assumption, following their fathers, since the fathers are a model for them; and this increases the denial's direction in their belief.

The clause ﴿and indeed we are in grave doubt﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿O Salih, you were indeed among us a figure of hope﴾. After they mentioned their despair of the goodness of his state, they mentioned that they doubt the truth of his being sent to them, and they reinforced that with the particle of emphasis. Among the fine points here is the affirmation of the nun of (inna) together with the nun of the pronoun of plurality, because that is an increase in the manifestation of the particle of emphasis, and manifestation is a kind of confirmation, unlike what is in Surat Ibrahim in the saying of the nations to their messengers ﴿And indeed we are in doubt about that to which you invite us﴾ [Ibrahim: 9], because the narration there is about nations differing in degrees of denial, and because what is in this verse is a single address; so (tad'una) there was with one nun, the nun of the speaker along with others, and thus no more than three nuns occur in the sentence, unlike what is in Surat Ibrahim, since the narration there is about a group of messengers in (tad'unana), so if (inna-na) had come there, four nuns would have gathered.

The murib: an active participle from arabah, when one is cast into doubt. It is said: rabahu and arabahu with the same meaning. Describing doubt with it is an emphasis, like their saying: "jadda judduhu" (his fortune was truly great).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 11, verse 63:

﴿He said: "O my people, tell me, if I have a clear proof from my Lord and He has given me mercy from Himself, then who will help me against Allah if I disobey Him? You would only increase me in loss."﴾

This is a reply to their speech, so the clause (qala) is not joined by a conjunction, and this is the usual pattern in reported dialogues, as has been mentioned more than once before.

The reply begins with the vocative to draw attention to what he is about to say, giving it importance.

He addressed them with the description "my people" (qawm), for the purpose already mentioned in the story of Nuh.

What is said about His words, ﴿Tell me, if I am upon a clear proof from my Lord and He has given me mercy from Himself﴾, is like what is said about its counterpart in the story of Nuh.

What calls for inquiry here is the reason for placing (minhu, "from Himself") before (rahmah, "mercy") here, while (min 'indihi, "from His presence") comes after (rahmah) in the earlier story of Nuh.

The answer is that this, along with the variety it brings by not keeping to one pattern when repeating similar speech, is also more conducive to clarity in indicating meaning and removing ambiguity. When the object of min (the "min" of origin, ibtida'iyyah) is a locative adverb ('inda, "at/from the presence of"), it explicitly describes the mercy with an attribute indicating the Lord's special care for it and for the one who receives it. Here the object of min is the pronoun of the Majesty (ism al-jalalah, the Divine Name "Allah"), so it is better for it to come directly after the verb (atani, "He gave me"). This makes the restriction of the giving to its being "from Allah" point to a particular giving marked by care for the one who receives it. Otherwise, its being "from Allah" would merely be a confirmation of what is conveyed by attributing the giving to Him. So it is determined that the intended meaning is a particular giving. Had (minhu) been placed right after (rahmah), the hearer might have supposed that this was a substitute for the possessive construction, that is, for saying "and He gave me His mercy," as in His words, ﴿And that We may make him a sign for the people and a mercy from Us﴾ [Maryam: 21], meaning "and Our mercy to them," that is, so that We might admonish them and show them mercy.

The clause ﴿Who will help me against Allah﴾ is the response of the conditional, and the conditional is ﴿if I am upon a clear proof﴾.

The meaning is an argument and a debate: if you deny my prophethood and reproach me for my call, then I affirm that I am upon a clear proof from my Lord. Do you think that I would turn away from my certainty toward your doubt? How could you expect that from me, when you know that my certainty makes me fearful of the punishment of Allah if I disobey Him, and no one will help me?

What is said about His words, ﴿Who will help me against Allah if I disobey Him﴾, is like what is said about His words, ﴿Who will help me against Allah if I drive them away﴾ [Hud: 30], in the story of Nuh.

He made the clause ﴿so you would only increase me in loss﴾ a consequence of the denying interrogative, meaning: since this is the case, your calling me is nothing but an effort to bring about my ruin.

By "increase" is meant the occurrence of a state that did not exist before, because that is an addition to a person's conditions. That is, what would befall me if I followed you and disobeyed Allah is nothing but loss, as in His words, may He be exalted, relating about Nuh, peace be upon him, ﴿But my calling them only increased them in flight﴾ [Nuh: 6], meaning: I was calling them while they were hearing, and when I repeated my call to them they increased in what they were already doing, so they fled. The meaning is not that they were already fleeing and then increased in fleeing, for if that were the case it would have said there, "my calling them only increased them in flight," with (min, "from") added, and here it would have said, "you only increase me in (min) loss."

Al-takhsir (causing loss, "making one a loser") is the verbal noun of khasira, when one makes him a loser (khasir).

[Page 112]

This is a commentary on verses 64–65 of Surah Hud, and it refers back to earlier discussions in Surah al-A'raf. Translating it below.

﴿O my people, this is the she-camel of Allah, a sign for you. So leave her to eat in Allah's earth, and do not touch her with harm, lest a near punishment seize you.﴾ ﴿But they hamstrung her, so he said, "Enjoy yourselves in your homes for three days. That is a promise not to be denied."﴾

This is a response to their saying, ﴿And indeed, we are in disquieting doubt about that to which you invite us﴾ [Hud: 62]. So he brought them a miracle that removes doubt.

The repetition of "O my people" (يا قوم) is for the same purpose already mentioned in his words in the story of Noah, ﴿O my people, who will support me against Allah if I drive them away?﴾ [Hud: 30].

The demonstrative "this" (هذه) refers to the she-camel at the time they witnessed the rock splitting open to bring her forth.

The attribution of the she-camel to the Name of Majesty (Allah) is because she was created by the power of Allah that breaks customary norms.

"A sign" (آيةً) and "for you" (لكم) are two circumstantial clauses (ḥāl) relating to "she-camel," and a parallel of this circumstantial construction has already been mentioned in Surah al-A'raf. A discussion of its grammatical analysis will come at His words, ﴿And this is my husband, an old man﴾ [Hud: 72], in this surah.

He admonished them to avoid attacking her, anticipating that they would confront her out of their obstinacy in their stubborn opposition. Her hamstringing has already been mentioned in Surah al-A'raf.

Al-tamattu' (التمتع) means benefiting from provisions (المتاع). It has already been discussed at His words, ﴿and provision for a time﴾ [al-A'raf: 24] in Surah al-A'raf.

Al-dar (الدار) means the land or town, as has already been discussed at His words, ﴿so they were found lying prostrate in their homes﴾ [al-A'raf: 78] in Surah al-A'raf. This postponement is an extension of the opportunity given to them in calling them to the truth.

Al-maktub (المكذوب) is that which a liar reports. It is said: "He lied about the news" (كذب الخبر) when he fabricated it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 11, verses 66–68:

﴿So when Our command came, We saved Salih and those who believed with him, by a mercy from Us, and from the disgrace of that day. Indeed your Lord is the Strong, the Mighty.﴾ ﴿And the blast seized those who did wrong, so they became prostrate in their homes,﴾ ﴿as if they had never lived therein. Unquestionably, Thamud disbelieved in their Lord. Unquestionably, away with Thamud!﴾

The discussion of the parallels of part of this verse has already preceded in the story of Hud in Surat al-A'raf.

The object of "najjayna" (We saved) is omitted.

The conjunction of "wa min khizyi yawmi'idhin" (and from the disgrace of that day) is upon the omitted object of "najjayna", meaning: We saved Salih - peace be upon him - and those with him from the torment of annihilation and from the disgrace that characterizes the torment, for torment occurs in modes, some of which are more disgracing than others. So the purpose of the conjunction is the conjunction of one favour upon another favour, not the conjunction of one saving upon another saving. For this reason it conjoined the object (of the verb) and did not conjoin the verb itself, as in the story of 'Ad: ﴿We saved Hud and those who believed with him by a mercy from Us, and We saved them from a severe torment﴾ [Hud: 58], because that is a saving from a torment different from the one conjoined to.

The tanwin of "yawmi'idhin" is the tanwin of substitution (tanwin 'iwad) for the genitive noun that is added to it. The estimate is: "the day when Our command came."

Al-khizy: humiliation, that is, the humiliation of the torment, and the discussion of it has preceded shortly.

The clause "Indeed your Lord is the Strong, the Mighty" is a parenthetical insertion (mu'tariḍah).

The report has been emphasized with three emphatic particles, for the sake of giving it importance. He expressed Thamud by "those who did wrong" to indicate, by the relative form, the cause for the ruling's application, that is, because of their wrongdoing, which is the wrongdoing of polytheism. In this there is an allusion to the polytheists of Makkah, warning them lest there befall them the like of what befell those, because they too are wrongdoers.

صفحة ١١٥
Al-sayhah: the thunderbolt that struck them.
The meaning of "ka'an lam yaghnaw fiha" (as if they had never lived therein) is: as if they had never dwelt there.

Shu'ayb has preceded in al-A'raf.

The majority read "ala inna Thamudan" (unquestionably, Thamud) with tanwin, considering Thamud the name of the ancestor of the nation. Hamzah, Hafs from 'Asim, and Ya'qub read it without tanwin, considering it the name of the nation or tribe. Both are well-known methods of the Arabs regarding the names of tribes named after their great forefathers.

The discussion of "bu'dan" (away) has preceded in the story of Nuh: ﴿It was said: Away with the wrongdoing people!﴾ [Hud: 44].
