[p. 116]

This is a continuation of one story after another (*'atf qissah 'ala qissah*).

The verse is emphasized with the particle *qad* to draw attention to the report, as it was earlier in His words: ﴿And We certainly sent Noah to his people﴾ (Hud: 25).

The purpose of this story is admonition, through the fate of the people of Lot, who disobeyed the messenger of their Lord, so the punishment descended upon them, and the disputation of Abraham did not avail them. The story of Abraham was placed first for this reason, and to honor his station with his Lord, by way of *idmaj* (interweaving, embedding one theme within another). For this reason the style of narration was changed from the stories before and after it, such as (*wa-ila 'Ad*), etc.

*Al-rusul* (the messengers) are the angels. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Who made the angels messengers﴾ (Fatir: 1).

*Al-bushra* (the glad tidings) is a noun for giving good news (*tabshir*) and glad tidings (*bishara*). It was discussed at His words: ﴿And give glad tidings to those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ (al-Baqarah: 25), at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah. This glad tiding is the one mentioned in His words: ﴿So We gave him good news of Isaac﴾, because the good news of a son to his wife is also good news to him.

The *ba'* in (*bi-l-bushra*) is for accompaniment (*musahabah*), because they came with the glad tidings, so it accompanies them, like the accompaniment of a message to the one who carries it.

The clause ﴿They said, "Peace!"﴾ is in the position of an explanation of *al-bushra*, because their saying that is the beginning of the glad tidings. What was placed between them is a narration of circumstances, and it reaches its conclusion in His words: ﴿So We gave him good news of Isaac﴾ up to His words ﴿Indeed, He is Praiseworthy and Glorious﴾.

*Al-salam* is the greeting. It was discussed in His words: ﴿And when those who believe in Our verses come to you, say, "Peace be upon you"﴾ (al-An'am: 54), in Surat al-An'am.

*Salaman* is an absolute object (*maf'ul mutlaq*: a verbal noun in the accusative that reinforces or specifies the verb), which stands as a substitute for the verb. The estimate is: "We greeted with a greeting" (*sallamna salaman*).

The nominative *salamun* is a verbal noun in the nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject. Its estimate is: "My affair is peace" (*amri salam*), meaning: for you, like (*fa-sabrun jamil*: "patience is beautiful"). The nominative form of the verbal noun is more emphatic than its accusative form, because in the nominative there is a sense of the continuity of the verb's meaning, so it indicates permanence and stability. For this reason he differentiated between the two, to indicate that Abraham, peace be upon him, returned the greeting with a phrase better than the phrase of the messengers, as an increase in honor.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "The Friend (Abraham) greeted with better than what he was greeted with," meaning, in view of the divine etiquette that He taught us in the Qur'an through His words: ﴿When you are greeted with a greeting, greet with better than it, or return it﴾ (al-Nisa': 86).

[p. 117]

So this was related with the most concise wording in Arabic, to render the meaning of Abraham's speech, peace be upon him, in Chaldean.

The majority (*al-Jumhur*) read ﴿qala salam﴾ with a *fatha* on the *sin* and with an *alif* after the *lam*. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Khalaf (the readers of the Qur'an, i.e., the canonical reciters) read (*qala silm*), with a *kasra* on the *sin* and without an *alif* after the *lam*, and *silm* is the noun for peace (*al-musalamah*). The greeting was also named with it, just as it was named with its synonym *salam*. So this is from the pattern of the agreement of the form *fa'al* and *fi'l* in some attributes, such as *haram* and *harm*, and *halal* and *hall*.

The *fa'* in His words, *fa-ma labitha*, is for indicating sequence (*ta'qib*), with haste in honoring the guest. Hastening to provide hospitality (*ta'jil al-qira*) is an Arab custom. Abraham, peace be upon him, thought they were people, so he hastened to their hospitality.

*Al-lubth* in a place implies moving away from it, meaning: he did not delay. The phrase (*an ja'a*) may be the subject of (*labitha*), meaning: his coming with a roasted calf did not delay, i.e., his coming accompanied by it was not slow, rather he hastened. It is also possible to take the subject of *labitha* as the pronoun of Abraham, peace be upon him, and then a preposition is estimated for (*ja'a*). The estimate is: "He did not delay in bringing it." The negation of delay is an exaggeration in haste.

*Al-hanidh* is the roasted, and it is the *mahnudh* (roasted). Roasting is faster than cooking, so it is more helpful in hastening the presentation of food to the guest.

(﴿They do not reach it﴾) is stronger in indicating the non-taking than (*la tatanawaluh*, "they do not partake of it").

It is said: *nakira al-shay'* when he denied it, meaning he disliked it.

He disliked them only because he supposed that their abstention from eating was for the purpose of disassociating themselves from his food. This happens, in the custom of people in that time, when the one who enters the house intends evil toward its host, because eating the food of hospitality is like a covenant of safety from harm, since reciprocating kindness with kindness is inherent in human nature. So when someone refrains from accepting kindness, that is because he does not want peace and does not accept being ungrateful for kindness.

[p. 118]

For this reason he followed His words *(nakirahum)* with: ﴿he sensed fear of them﴾, meaning he perceived fear of them within himself and concealed it. Its verbal noun is *ijas*. That was because he feared that they were intending harm to him, i.e., he considered them brigands, and they were three while Abraham, peace be upon him, was alone.

The clause ﴿They said, "Do not fear"﴾ is separated from what precedes it, because it resembles an answer: when he sensed fear of them, its trace appeared on his features, so the appearance of its trace was like his saying, "I feared you." For this reason they answered what was in his soul by saying, "Do not fear." This was related in the manner in which dialogues are related. Or it is a response to an estimated speech indicated by His words: ﴿So he sensed fear of them﴾ (al-Dhariyat: 28), meaning: and he said to them, "I fear you," as was related in Surat al-Hijr: ﴿He said, "Indeed, we are fearful of you"﴾ (al-Hijr: 52). It is the custom of people that when someone refuses to accept their food, they say to him, "Perhaps you are a treacherous one or an enemy," and they used to say to the arriving visitor, "Is it war or peace?"

Their saying ﴿Indeed, we have been sent to the people of Lot﴾ is a disclosure to him that they are angels. The clause is a resumptive explanation (*istinaf*) clarifying the reason for their coming.

The wisdom in this is the honoring of Abraham, peace be upon him, and that they spoke from knowledge that he had.

The object of (*arsalna*), i.e., "with what," was omitted for brevity, since it is clear from this story and others.

He expressed the peoples whose punishment was intended by way of the idafah (genitive construction), "the people of Lot," since those peoples had no name that gathered them, nor did they trace back to one lineage. Rather, they were a mixture of tribes known by the names of their villages, and the most famous of them was Sodom (*Sadum*), as was mentioned earlier in al-A'raf.

The clause ﴿And his wife was standing, so she laughed﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*) relative to the pronoun in (*awjasa*), because the wife of Abraham, peace be upon him, was present, serving the food to them, for the custom of them, like the custom of the Arabs after them, is that the mistress of the house serves the guests. In a hadith: "And the bride is their servant." Murrah ibn Mahkan al-Tamimi said:

[p. 119]

*O mistress of the house, rise, not humbled,
Gather to yourself the men of the people and the strangers.*

The story has been abbreviated here in a remarkable manner, because it occurs within the dialogue between the messengers and Abraham, peace be upon him. And relating that dialogue required completing it with the relation of their saying, ﴿Do not fear, indeed we have been sent to the people of Lot.﴾ As for the glad tidings, they had already occurred before they informed him that they had been sent to the people of Lot, as in the verse of Surat al-Dhariyat: ﴿So he sensed fear of them. They said, "Do not fear." And they gave him glad tidings of a knowing boy﴾ (al-Dhariyat: 28). When the order of the dialogue required placing the clause ﴿They said, "Do not fear"﴾ first, the story of the glad tidings and what followed it of dialogue was related in the manner of a circumstantial clause (*hal*), because the *hal* can express priority, simultaneity, and subsequence, and it is the *hal muqaddarah* (the anticipated circumstance).

The wife of Abraham, peace be upon him, laughed at the angels' announcement to Abraham, peace be upon him, of a boy, and her laughter was the laughter of wonder and disbelief. It occurred in the Torah, in chapter eighteen of the Book of Genesis (*Sifr al-Takwin*): "And they said to him, 'Where is Sarah your wife?' He said, 'Here she is in the tent.' And they said, 'Sarah your wife will have a son.' And Sarah was listening at the door of the tent, and Sarah laughed within herself, saying, 'Shall I in truth bear a child, when I am old?' And the Lord said, 'Why did Sarah laugh?' Sarah denied it, saying, 'I did not laugh,' for she was afraid. He said, 'No, but you did laugh.'"

The branching of ﴿So We gave him good news of Isaac﴾ upon the clause *"she laughed"* is with regard to the conjunct, which is ﴿and after Isaac, Jacob﴾, because she did not laugh except after the angels had given her the good news of a son. When she marveled at that, they gave her the good news of a son's son, as an increase in the glad tidings. The wonder was that a son would be born to her, and that he would live and she would live until a son would be born to her son. That is more amazing, because the nature of the sons of old people is that they are sickly and generally do not live except in weakness, and generally children are not born to them. Also, the nature of old people to whom children are born is that they do not live to see the youth of their children, let alone the children of their children.

When they gave her this glad tiding, she expressed her wonder that she had concealed with laughter, and she said:

[p. 120]

﴿"O woe is me! Shall I give birth while I am an old woman and this is my husband, an old man? Indeed, this is an astonishing thing!"﴾ So the clause *qalat* ("she said") is the response to the glad tiding.

*Ya'qub* is the subject (*mubtada'*), and ﴿and after Isaac﴾ is the predicate (*khabar*), and the clause on this reading is in the position of a circumstantial clause. This is the reading of the majority. Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, and Hafs read *Ya'qub* with a *fatha* (in the accusative), and then it is conjoined to *Isaac*. The conjunction particle and the conjoined noun were separated by the adverbial phrase (*zarf*), and its matter is easy, though the grammarians of the literal school, such as Abu Hayyan, considered it a serious matter, by analogy with the conjunction particle standing here in place of the preposition upon the same preposition. This is a weak analogy, since a word having the meaning of another word does not require giving it all the rulings of that word, as in *Mughni al-Labib*.

The vocative in (*ya wailata*) is a *isti'arah tab'iyyah* (a contiguous or verbal metaphor): the word *wailah* is treated as a being that understands, so that it may be called, as if she were saying, "O my woe, be present here, for this is your place."

*Al-wailah* is the terrible event and disgrace. It is perhaps the single instance of *wail*. It is used in situations of wonder, one says, "O my woe!"

The readers agreed on reading *ya wailata* with a prolonged *fatha* at its end with an *alif*. The *alif* at the end of (*ya wailata*) here may be a substitute for the first-person possessive *ya'* in the vocative. The more apparent view is that it is the *alif* of *istighatha* (invocation for help), which replaces the *lam* of *istighatha*. Its origin is: *ya li-wailata* ("O for woe!"). This *alif* most often occurs in expressions of wonder with the word *'ajiba* ("he marveled"), as in: *ya 'ajaban* ("O wonder!"), and with the name of a thing that is wondered at, as in: *ya 'ushban* ("O grass!").

It is written in the Mushaf with an *imalah* (a vocalic inclination toward *ya'*), but it was not read with *imalah*. Al-Zajjaj said: "It was written in the form of a *ya'*, according to the original form of the *ya'* of the first-person possessive."

The interrogative in ﴿Shall I give birth while I am an old woman?﴾ is used for wonder. The clause *wa-ana 'ajuz* ("while I am an old woman") is in the position of a circumstantial clause, and it is the basis of the wonder.

*Al-ba'l* is the husband. Its explanation will come when interpreting His words: ﴿And let them not reveal their adornment except to their husbands﴾ (al-Nur: 31), in Surat al-Nur, so refer to it there.

[p. 121]

She reinforced the expression of wonder with the clause ﴿Indeed, this is an astonishing thing﴾, which is a clause emphasizing the form of wonder, and for this reason it was separated from the one before it because of its complete connection. It seems she was hesitant as to whether they were angels, so she was not reassured regarding the verification of their good news.

The clause *(hadha ba'li)* ("this is my husband") is composed of subject and predicate, because the meaning is: "this one indicated is my husband," i.e., how can he have a child when he is as you see? The word *shaykh* ("old man") is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause from the demonstrative noun, clarifying what is intended by the indication.

Ibn Mas'ud read (*wa-hadha ba'li shaykhun*) with a *raf'* on *shaykhun*, so that *ba'li* is an explanatory apposition of *hadha*, and *shaykhun* is the predicate of the subject. The meaning of the two readings is one.

On this reading there occurred a delicate anecdote, which our shaykh, the distinguished master Salim Bu Hajib, related to us: that Abu al-'Abbas al-Mubarrad was invited by some notables in Baghdad to a banquet. When they had finished eating, a slave-girl of the host sang from behind the curtain with two verses:

*They said to her, "This your beloved is turning away,"
She said, "Ah, his turning away is the easiest of matters."
Then there is nothing but a glance and a smile,
Then his legs tremble and he falls on his side.*

The sorcery-free fervour of the gathering: all those in the assembly were moved (fa-taraba) except Abu al-'Abbas al-Mubarrad, who did not stir. The master of the house said to him, "What is the matter with you that this did not move you?" The slave girl said, "He is excused. He thinks I made a grammatical error when I said *mu'rid* with the nominative (*bi-l-raf'*), and he did not know that 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud recited (*wa-hadha ba'li shaykhun*) with the nominative, [reading *shaykhun* as the predicate of *ba'li*]." Al-Mubarrad was moved by this answer.

The angels' reply to her with the sentence ﴿Do you wonder at the command of Allah?﴾ is a denial of her amazement, because it is an amazement intended to express astonishment. "The command of Allah" is the command of creation (*amr al-takwin*, the divine command by which things come into being). That is, "Do you wonder at the power of Allah to break customary patterns (*kharq al-'adat*, i.e., miracles)?" Their answer proceeds from their confidence that their report is true and that it conveys the command of Allah.

The sentence ﴿The mercy of Allah and His blessings be upon you﴾ gives the reason for denying her amazement. The denial is in the sense of a negation, so the meaning becomes: "There is no wonder in the command of Allah, because granting you a child is a mercy from Allah and a blessing. Therefore there is no wonder in the connection of Allah's power to it, and you are people fit for that mercy and blessing, so there is no wonder in its occurrence among you."

The way in which the denial of wonder is explained by this is that the amazement could be either at the occurrence of this thing from Allah, or at Allah's singling out Ibrahim, peace be upon him, and his wife for it. The angels' words ﴿The mercy of Allah and His blessings be upon you﴾ therefore serve to explain the absence of both kinds of wonder.

The definite article in *al-bayt* ("the house") is the definite article of presence (*ta'rif al-huduur*), referring to the house present among them in which this exchange took place, that is, the house of Ibrahim, peace be upon him. The meaning is "the people of this house."

The purpose of the address (*al-nida'*) is to honour them (*al-tanwih*). It may also be a case of specification (*ikhtisas*), to clarify more precisely what is meant by the pronoun of address.

The sentence ﴿Indeed, He is Praiseworthy and Glorious﴾ gives the reason for the descent of His mercy and blessings upon them: Allah praises those who obey Him, and He is glorious, that is, of great station, with no limit to His bounties. So it is not difficult for Him to grant them a child. In choosing the attribute *al-Hamid* ("the Praiseworthy") from among the Most Beautiful Names, there is an allusion (*kinaya*) to Allah's pleasure, may He be exalted, with Ibrahim, peace be upon him, and his household.

And relating that dialogue required completing it with the relation of their saying, ﴿Do not fear, indeed we have been sent to the people of Lot.﴾ As for the glad tidings, they had already occurred before they informed him that they had been sent to the people of Lot, as in the verse of Surat al-Dhariyat: ﴿So he sensed fear of them. They said, "Do not fear." And they gave him glad tidings of a knowing boy﴾ (al-Dhariyat: 28). When the order of the dialogue required placing the clause ﴿They said, "Do not fear"﴾ first, the story of the glad tidings and what followed it of dialogue was related in the manner of a circumstantial clause (*hal*), because the *hal* can express priority, simultaneity, and subsequence, and it is the *hal muqaddarah* (the anticipated circumstance).

The wife of Abraham, peace be upon him, laughed at the angels' announcement to Abraham, peace be upon him, of a boy, and her laughter was the laughter of wonder and disbelief. It occurred in the Torah, in chapter eighteen of the Book of Genesis (*Sifr al-Takwin*): "And they said to him, 'Where is Sarah your wife?' He said, 'Here she is in the tent.' And they said, 'Sarah your wife will have a son.' And Sarah was listening at the door of the tent, and Sarah laughed within herself, saying, 'Shall I in truth bear a child, when I am old?' And the Lord said, 'Why did Sarah laugh?' Sarah denied it, saying, 'I did not laugh,' for she was afraid. He said, 'No, but you did laugh.'"

The branching of ﴿So We gave him good news of Isaac﴾ upon the clause *"she laughed"* is with regard to the conjunct, which is ﴿and after Isaac, Jacob﴾, because she did not laugh except after the angels had given her the good news of a son. When she marveled at that, they gave her the good news of a son's son, as an increase in the glad tidings. The wonder was that a son would be born to her, and that he would live and she would live until a son would be born to her son. That is more amazing, because the nature of the sons of old people is that they are sickly and generally do not live except in weakness, and generally children are not born to them. Also, the nature of old people to whom children are born is that they do not live to see the youth of their children, let alone the children of their children.

When they gave her this glad tiding, she expressed her wonder that she had concealed with laughter, and she said:

[p. 120]

﴿"O woe is me! Shall I give birth while I am an old woman and this is my husband, an old man? Indeed, this is an astonishing thing!"﴾ So the clause *qalat* ("she said") is the response to the glad tiding.

*Ya'qub* is the subject (*mubtada'*), and ﴿and after Isaac﴾ is the predicate (*khabar*), and the clause on this reading is in the position of a circumstantial clause. This is the reading of the majority. Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, and Hafs read *Ya'qub* with a *fatha* (in the accusative), and then it is conjoined to *Isaac*. The conjunction particle and the conjoined noun were separated by the adverbial phrase (*zarf*), and its matter is easy, though the grammarians of the literal school, such as Abu Hayyan, considered it a serious matter, by analogy with the conjunction particle standing here in place of the preposition upon the same preposition. This is a weak analogy, since a word having the meaning of another word does not require giving it all the rulings of that word, as in *Mughni al-Labib*.

The vocative in (*ya wailata*) is a *isti'arah tab'iyyah* (a contiguous or verbal metaphor): the word *wailah* is treated as a being that understands, so that it may be called, as if she were saying, "O my woe, be present here, for this is your place."

*Al-wailah* is the terrible event and disgrace. It is perhaps the single instance of *wail*. It is used in situations of wonder, one says, "O my woe!"

The readers agreed on reading *ya wailata* with a prolonged *fatha* at its end with an *alif*. The *alif* at the end of (*ya wailata*) here may be a substitute for the first-person possessive *ya'* in the vocative. The more apparent view is that it is the *alif* of *istighatha* (invocation for help), which replaces the *lam* of *istighatha*. Its origin is: *ya li-wailata* ("O for woe!"). This *alif* most often occurs in expressions of wonder with the word *'ajiba* ("he marveled"), as in: *ya 'ajaban* ("O wonder!"), and with the name of a thing that is wondered at, as in: *ya 'ushban* ("O grass!").

It is written in the Mushaf with an *imalah* (a vocalic inclination toward *ya'*), but it was not read with *imalah*. Al-Zajjaj said: "It was written in the form of a *ya'*, according to the original form of the *ya'* of the first-person possessive."

The interrogative in ﴿Shall I give birth while I am an old woman?﴾ is used for wonder. The clause *wa-ana 'ajuz* ("while I am an old woman") is in the position of a circumstantial clause, and it is the basis of the wonder.

*Al-ba'l* is the husband. Its explanation will come when interpreting His words: ﴿And let them not reveal their adornment except to their husbands﴾ (al-Nur: 31), in Surat al-Nur, so refer to it there.

[p. 121]

She reinforced the expression of wonder with the clause ﴿Indeed, this is an astonishing thing﴾, which is a clause emphasizing the form of wonder, and for this reason it was separated from the one before it because of its complete connection. It seems she was hesitant as to whether they were angels, so she was not reassured regarding the verification of their good news.

The clause *(hadha ba'li)* ("this is my husband") is composed of subject and predicate, because the meaning is: "this one indicated is my husband," i.e., how can he have a child when he is as you see? The word *shaykh* ("old man") is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause from the demonstrative noun, clarifying what is intended by the indication.

Ibn Mas'ud read (*wa-hadha ba'li shaykhun*) with a *raf'* on *shaykhun*, so that *ba'li* is an explanatory apposition of *hadha*, and *shaykhun* is the predicate of the subject. The meaning of the two readings is one.

On this reading there occurred a delicate anecdote, which our shaykh, the distinguished master Salim Bu Hajib, related to us: that Abu al-'Abbas al-Mubarrad was invited by some notables in Baghdad to a banquet. When they had finished eating, a slave-girl of the host sang from behind the curtain with two verses:

*They said to her, "This your beloved is turning away,"
She said, "Ah, his turning away is the easiest of matters."
Then there is nothing but a glance and a smile,
Then his legs tremble and he falls on his side.*

The sorcery-free fervour of the gathering: all those in the assembly were moved (fa-taraba) except Abu al-'Abbas al-Mubarrad, who did not stir. The master of the house said to him, "What is the matter with you that this did not move you?" The slave girl said, "He is excused. He thinks I made a grammatical error when I said *mu'rid* with the nominative (*bi-l-raf'*), and he did not know that 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud recited (*wa-hadha ba'li shaykhun*) with the nominative, [reading *shaykhun* as the predicate of *ba'li*]." Al-Mubarrad was moved by this answer.

The angels' reply to her with the sentence ﴿Do you wonder at the command of Allah?﴾ is a denial of her amazement, because it is an amazement intended to express astonishment. "The command of Allah" is the command of creation (*amr al-takwin*, the divine command by which things come into being). That is, "Do you wonder at the power of Allah to break customary patterns (*kharq al-'adat*, i.e., miracles)?" Their answer proceeds from their confidence that their report is true and that it conveys the command of Allah.

The sentence ﴿The mercy of Allah and His blessings be upon you﴾ gives the reason for denying her amazement. The denial is in the sense of a negation, so the meaning becomes: "There is no wonder in the command of Allah, because granting you a child is a mercy from Allah and a blessing. Therefore there is no wonder in the connection of Allah's power to it, and you are people fit for that mercy and blessing, so there is no wonder in its occurrence among you."

The way in which the denial of wonder is explained by this is that the amazement could be either at the occurrence of this thing from Allah, or at Allah's singling out Ibrahim, peace be upon him, and his wife for it. The angels' words ﴿The mercy of Allah and His blessings be upon you﴾ therefore serve to explain the absence of both kinds of wonder.

The definite article in *al-bayt* ("the house") is the definite article of presence (*ta'rif al-huduur*), referring to the house present among them in which this exchange took place, that is, the house of Ibrahim, peace be upon him. The meaning is "the people of this house."

The purpose of the address (*al-nida'*) is to honour them (*al-tanwih*). It may also be a case of specification (*ikhtisas*), to clarify more precisely what is meant by the pronoun of address.

The sentence ﴿Indeed, He is Praiseworthy and Glorious﴾ gives the reason for the descent of His mercy and blessings upon them: Allah praises those who obey Him, and He is glorious, that is, of great station, with no limit to His bounties. So it is not difficult for Him to grant them a child. In choosing the attribute *al-Hamid* ("the Praiseworthy") from among the Most Beautiful Names, there is an allusion (*kinaya*) to Allah's pleasure, may He be exalted, with Ibrahim, peace be upon him, and his household.

[Page 122]

[p. 123]

﴿So when fear had left Abraham and the good news had reached him, he began to argue with Us concerning the people of Lot.﴾ ﴿Indeed, Abraham was forbearing, plaintive, and turning back (to God).﴾ ﴿O Abraham, turn away from this. Indeed, the command of your Lord has come, and a punishment that cannot be averted is coming upon them.﴾

The definite article in "al-rawʿ" (fear) and "al-bushra" (the good news) is the definiteness of reference back to what was previously mentioned (*taʿrif al-ʿahd al-dhikri*, definiteness that refers back to an antecedent). They are the two things mentioned just before, so "al-rawʿ" is synonymous with "al-khīfah" (fear).

His words "yujādiluna" (he argues with Us) is the answer to what was phrased in the present tense in order to bring the astonishing situation before the mind, as in His words: ﴿and he was making the ark﴾ [Hud: 38]. *Al-mujādalah* means debate. It has already been discussed in His words: ﴿and do not argue on behalf of those who betray themselves﴾ [al-Nisa': 107], in Surat al-Nisa'.

His words ﴿concerning the people of Lot﴾ imply an omitted noun, that is, "concerning the punishment of the people of Lot." This is attaching a judgment to the name of the essence, while what is meant is one of its states, determined by the context, as in His words: ﴿Carrion is forbidden to you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3], meaning its eating.

*Al-mujādalah* here is supplication and intimate conversation, by which Abraham, peace be upon him, asked his Lord to pardon the people of Lot, fearing the destruction of the believers among them.

The debate may also have been with the angels. It was linked to the pronoun of Majesty because the purpose of the angels' argument was to bring the matter before God's command to avert the punishment from the people of Lot.

*Al-ḥalīm* is one characterized by forbearance (*al-ḥilm*), an attribute that requires forgiveness and bearing harm.

*Al-awwāh* originally means one who frequently says "awwah" (an expression of pain or sorrow). "Awwah" is a verb-substitute (*ism fiʿl*) standing in place of "I suffer pain," and here it is a metaphor (*kināyah*) for the intensity of his concern for people's afflictions.

[p. 124]
*Al-munīb* is one who *anāba*, meaning returns. It is derived from *al-nawb*, which means descent. What is meant is repentance from shortcoming, that is, one who takes account of himself regarding what he fears.

The real meaning of *al-ināba* is returning to a thing after separating from it and leaving it.

The clause ﴿O Abraham, turn away from this﴾ is a saying that has been omitted, indicated by the context, and it is one of the remarkable forms of concision. It is either revelation from God to Abraham, peace be upon him, or the answer of the angels to Abraham, peace be upon him. If it is from the words of God, then His words ﴿the command of your Lord﴾ use the explicit noun in place of the pronoun, in order to bring the fear into the hearing of the listener.

The command of God is His decree, that is, the command of His bringing into being.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 11, verse 77:

﴿And when Our messengers came to Lot, he was distressed on their account and felt helpless for them, and said, "This is a trying day."﴾

It is known that the angels were going to the people of Lot, from His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have been sent to the people of Lot﴾ [Hud: 70]. So the implied sense is: they parted from Ibrahim and went to Lut, peace be upon them both, and when they came to Lut... The omission of what the context indicates is a wonderful Qur'anic brevity (ijaz).

They came to Lut just as they came to Ibrahim, peace be upon them both, in the form of humans. He thought them to be men, and he feared that his people would assault them with their vile practice, so he was distressed on their account.

The meaning of ﴿felt helpless for them﴾ is: his ability (dhar') was constrained on account of them, that is, on account of their coming. He shifted the attribution to the genitive complement and made the grammatical subject a specification (tamyiz), because attributing constriction to the possessor of the dhar' is more fitting to the figurative meaning, and it is closer to stripping the metaphor of its figurative (tajrid) form, which is a metaphorical allegory (isti'arah tamthiliyyah).

Al-dhar' is the extension of the arm. When it is attributed to a human, it means the measure of distance. When it is attributed to a camel, it means the stretching of its two forelegs in walking according to the width of its stride. So it is possible that ﴿felt helpless (dharʿan)﴾ is an image of the person who wants to extend his arm but cannot extend it as he wishes, so his dhar' is narrower than its usual state. It is also possible that it is an image of the camel burdened with a load beyond its capacity, so it cannot extend its two forelegs as is customary. Either way, it is a metaphorical allegory for the state of one who finds no means in a matter he wants to accomplish, likened to one who cannot extend his arm as he wishes.

His saying ﴿This is a trying day﴾ he said to himself, as a person confides in himself when a matter grows hard for him.

Al-'Asib: that which is severe in what is not pleasing. It is said: "a trying day" when a great matter occurs in it, from the conditions of people or the conditions of the weather, such as severe cold or severe heat. It is on the pattern of fa'il in the sense of fa'il (active), and no unaugmented verb is known for it; rather it is said: i'sawsaba al-sharr, meaning the evil intensified. They said: it is derived from your saying: 'asabtu al-shay' idha shaddadtahu (I bound the thing when I tied it tight). The root of this material conveys tightening and pressing; it is said: 'asaba al-shay' idha lawahu (he twisted the thing), and from it comes al-'isabah (the bandage). It is said: 'asabathumu al-sununu idha aja'athum (the years of drought gripped them when they starved them). I have not found an unaugmented verb used to describe a day as 'asib. He intended: that it would be trying, because he knew the evil practice of his people, and this implies that they came to him in the daytime.

Among the excellence of the arrangement of these sentences is that they came in the order of their occurrence in existence, for the first thing that comes to the mind of one who dislikes a matter is that he is distressed by it and seeks a way out of it; when he knows there is no way out, he feels helpless about it, and then he gives expression to the meanings and, as a consequence, utters words that relieve his soul.

This verse is suitable to serve as an example of a writer's composition arranged according to the order of occurrence in reality, and this is the basic principle of composition, unless there are in the speech reasons for advancing and delaying, and reasons for omission and addition.

[p. 126]

﴿His people came rushing towards him, and before that they had been doing evil deeds. He said: "O my people, these are my daughters; they are purer for you. So fear God and do not disgrace me concerning my guests. Is there not among you a single rightly-guided man?"﴾

That is, some of his people came to him. The coming was attributed to "the people" because such coming was their habit, and they had colluded in it. So when some of them came, others would follow them at another time. This is an instance of attributing an act to a tribe when some of its members perform it, as in the saying of al-Harith ibn Wa'lah al-Jarmi:

My people killed Umaymah, my brother;
so when I shoot, my arrow strikes me.

"Yuhra'un" (they come rushing), with a damma on the yā' and a fatha on the rā' in the passive form, was explained by the commentators as walking like one being driven, somewhere between a trot and a leap. It can only be in the passive form, because its origin is the walk of a captive who is hurried along. This form implies that *har'* is the pushing of a walker while he walks. However, this sense has been forgotten, and *ahra'a* remained with the meaning of moving at a pace like that of one being pushed. For this reason a group of lexicographers said that it is among the verbs that are obligatorily used in the passive form, because originally they are attributed to an unidentified agent. In *al-Sihah* and *al-Qamus*, it is explained as trembling from anger or fear. On both interpretations, the clause "yuhra'un" is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl).

The Qur'an has omitted mention of the purpose for which they came, while pointing to it with the words: ﴿and before that they had been doing evil deeds﴾. Their evil had become their habit, so they strove for nothing except that.

The clause "He said: O my people, etc." is a resumptive clause of explanation (*istiʾnāf bayānī*) arising from the clause "﴿His people came to him﴾", since the listener already knows their purpose in coming, so he wants to know what Lot said to them in response.

Lot, peace be upon him, forestalled them with the words: ﴿O my people, these are my daughters; they are purer for you﴾. Opening the speech with the vocative and with the statement that they are his people is a softening of their hearts towards him, because he knew how obstinate they were in their vile custom, as shown by their words: ﴿You know well that we have no claim on your daughters﴾, as will come later.

[p. 127]

The demonstrative "these" (*hāʾulāʾ*) refers to "my daughters" (*banātī*). "My daughters" is an apposition to the demonstrative, and the demonstrative is used to present an offer; the implied meaning is: "so take them."

The clause ﴿they are purer for you﴾ is a justification of the offer. The meaning of "they are purer" is that they are lawful for you, and they will stand between you and indecency. The comparative form has lost its sense of comparison; it is intended to express the strength of purity.

"These" (*hāʾulāʾ*) refers to a plurality, since it is clarified by "my daughters."

It is related that he had only two daughters. Therefore, the apparent meaning of using "daughters" here is a form of eloquent simile (*tashbīh balīgh*): i.e., "these are their women, like my daughters." He meant women from among his people, equal in number to the people who came rushing to him. This is the meaning given by Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr, and Qatadah, and it fits the making of them lawful to his people when he said ﴿they are purer for you﴾, since the people who were present with him were many. The meaning then is: "These women, so marry them." This is the best of the interpretations.

It has also been said that he meant the daughters of his own loins, which is a narration from Qatadah. Since it is well known that Lot, peace be upon him, had two daughters, the plural came to be used for the two, on the basis that two is treated as a plural in speech, as in God's saying: ﴿Your hearts have indeed inclined﴾ [al-Tahrim 66:4].

It has also been said that he had three daughters.

Two difficulties confront this interpretation.

The first: the people were a large number, so how could two or three daughters suffice them?

The second: his saying ﴿These are my daughters﴾ is an offer to them, as you have just understood. So what would be the nature of this making available between the people and the daughters, when they were a large number? If it were a marriage, it would not suffice the people; and if it were not a marriage, what would it be?

As for the answer to the first: it is possible that the number of people who came to him was equal to the number of his daughters, or that his daughters were with him in addition to some of his people.

As for the answer to the second: it is possible that Lot's disposal of his daughters was in the capacity of fatherhood, and it is possible that it was a disposal in the capacity of prophethood by revelation, for the sake of a benefit. It may be that in the law of Lot, peace be upon him, it was permitted for a father to give his daughters in possession whenever he wished. If those men were partners in the possession of his daughters, then each man's enjoyment of each of them would be lawful in his law, in the manner that prostitution was one of the remnants of pre-Islamic ignorance at the beginning of Islam, before it was abrogated.

As for the attribution of lineage to the children of those women who conceive: it is possible that the child is attributed to the man whom his mother claims to have had intercourse with from among the men who entered upon her, as was the case with prostitutes at the beginning of Islam. It is also possible that the children are not attributed to fathers, and so they are attributed to their mothers, like the son of adultery and the child of li'an (mutual cursing). This permission would be granted as the lesser of two harms, and it is among the things legislated in a temporary way, like the legislation of temporary marriage (*nikāḥ al-mutʿa*) at the beginning of Islam, according to the view that it was later prohibited, which is the view of the majority.

The commentators have occupied themselves, instead of clarifying this, with the question of marrying believing women to disbelievers, which is superfluous.

Following his saying ﴿they are purer for you﴾, he made it a consequence that he commanded them to fear God, because if they complied with what the women offered them, they would then fear God.

The majority read ﴿do not disgrace me﴾ [al-Hijr 15:69] with the omission of the first-person yā' for lightness. Abu 'Amr retained it.

*Al-khizy* means humiliation and abasement, and it has been mentioned earlier. He meant his abasement.

The "fī" (in) is for figurative place. He made the guest like a container, meaning: do not make me disgraced in the presence of my guests, for they would suffer harm in my hospitality; hospitality is a neighbourhood with the master of the house, so if the guest suffers humiliation, it becomes a shame upon the master of the house.

The *ḍayf* (guest) is the one who arrives, i.e., one who alights at someone's house for a non-permanent stay, for the purpose of passing through on a journey or answering an invitation.

[p. 129]

The root of *ḍayf* is the verbal noun of the verb *ḍāfa, yaḍīfu*, and for this reason it is applied to one or to more than one, and to the masculine and the feminine with a single form. It may also be treated as other than a verbal noun and so pluralized, as 'Amr ibn Kulthum said:

You alighted in the place of guests among us.

Lot, peace be upon him, had thought the angels to be men passing by his house, so they alighted with him for rest, food, and lodging.

The interrogation in ﴿Is there not among you a single rightly-guided man?﴾ is a denial and a reproach, because humiliating a guest is a disgrace that only the foolish would commit.

His saying "among you" (*minkum*) means "some of you." He denied their colluding in falsehood and the absence of a rightly-guided man among them. This is an incitement to them to use their reason, so that there might appear among them someone who perceives the corruption of what they are engaged in and forbids them. The appearance of a rightly-guided person within a misguided group opens the door of guidance for them, and conversely, their colluding in falsehood increases them in its pursuit.

[p. 126]

﴿His people came rushing towards him, and before that they had been doing evil deeds. He said: "O my people, these are my daughters; they are purer for you. So fear God and do not disgrace me concerning my guests. Is there not among you a single rightly-guided man?"﴾

That is, some of his people came to him. The coming was attributed to "the people" because such coming was their habit, and they had colluded in it. So when some of them came, others would follow them at another time. This is an instance of attributing an act to a tribe when some of its members perform it, as in the saying of al-Harith ibn Wa'lah al-Jarmi:

My people killed Umaymah, my brother;
so when I shoot, my arrow strikes me.

"Yuhra'un" (they come rushing), with a damma on the yā' and a fatha on the rā' in the passive form, was explained by the commentators as walking like one being driven, somewhere between a trot and a leap. It can only be in the passive form, because its origin is the walk of a captive who is hurried along. This form implies that *har'* is the pushing of a walker while he walks. However, this sense has been forgotten, and *ahra'a* remained with the meaning of moving at a pace like that of one being pushed. For this reason a group of lexicographers said that it is among the verbs that are obligatorily used in the passive form, because originally they are attributed to an unidentified agent. In *al-Sihah* and *al-Qamus*, it is explained as trembling from anger or fear. On both interpretations, the clause "yuhra'un" is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl).

The Qur'an has omitted mention of the purpose for which they came, while pointing to it with the words: ﴿and before that they had been doing evil deeds﴾. Their evil had become their habit, so they strove for nothing except that.

The clause "He said: O my people, etc." is a resumptive clause of explanation (*istiʾnāf bayānī*) arising from the clause "﴿His people came to him﴾", since the listener already knows their purpose in coming, so he wants to know what Lot said to them in response.

Lot, peace be upon him, forestalled them with the words: ﴿O my people, these are my daughters; they are purer for you﴾. Opening the speech with the vocative and with the statement that they are his people is a softening of their hearts towards him, because he knew how obstinate they were in their vile custom, as shown by their words: ﴿You know well that we have no claim on your daughters﴾, as will come later.

[p. 127]

The demonstrative "these" (*hāʾulāʾ*) refers to "my daughters" (*banātī*). "My daughters" is an apposition to the demonstrative, and the demonstrative is used to present an offer; the implied meaning is: "so take them."

The clause ﴿they are purer for you﴾ is a justification of the offer. The meaning of "they are purer" is that they are lawful for you, and they will stand between you and indecency. The comparative form has lost its sense of comparison; it is intended to express the strength of purity.

"These" (*hāʾulāʾ*) refers to a plurality, since it is clarified by "my daughters."

It is related that he had only two daughters. Therefore, the apparent meaning of using "daughters" here is a form of eloquent simile (*tashbīh balīgh*): i.e., "these are their women, like my daughters." He meant women from among his people, equal in number to the people who came rushing to him. This is the meaning given by Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr, and Qatadah, and it fits the making of them lawful to his people when he said ﴿they are purer for you﴾, since the people who were present with him were many. The meaning then is: "These women, so marry them." This is the best of the interpretations.

It has also been said that he meant the daughters of his own loins, which is a narration from Qatadah. Since it is well known that Lot, peace be upon him, had two daughters, the plural came to be used for the two, on the basis that two is treated as a plural in speech, as in God's saying: ﴿Your hearts have indeed inclined﴾ [al-Tahrim 66:4].

It has also been said that he had three daughters.

Two difficulties confront this interpretation.

The first: the people were a large number, so how could two or three daughters suffice them?

The second: his saying ﴿These are my daughters﴾ is an offer to them, as you have just understood. So what would be the nature of this making available between the people and the daughters, when they were a large number? If it were a marriage, it would not suffice the people; and if it were not a marriage, what would it be?

As for the answer to the first: it is possible that the number of people who came to him was equal to the number of his daughters, or that his daughters were with him in addition to some of his people.

As for the answer to the second: it is possible that Lot's disposal of his daughters was in the capacity of fatherhood, and it is possible that it was a disposal in the capacity of prophethood by revelation, for the sake of a benefit. It may be that in the law of Lot, peace be upon him, it was permitted for a father to give his daughters in possession whenever he wished. If those men were partners in the possession of his daughters, then each man's enjoyment of each of them would be lawful in his law, in the manner that prostitution was one of the remnants of pre-Islamic ignorance at the beginning of Islam, before it was abrogated.

As for the attribution of lineage to the children of those women who conceive: it is possible that the child is attributed to the man whom his mother claims to have had intercourse with from among the men who entered upon her, as was the case with prostitutes at the beginning of Islam. It is also possible that the children are not attributed to fathers, and so they are attributed to their mothers, like the son of adultery and the child of li'an (mutual cursing). This permission would be granted as the lesser of two harms, and it is among the things legislated in a temporary way, like the legislation of temporary marriage (*nikāḥ al-mutʿa*) at the beginning of Islam, according to the view that it was later prohibited, which is the view of the majority.

The commentators have occupied themselves, instead of clarifying this, with the question of marrying believing women to disbelievers, which is superfluous.

Following his saying ﴿they are purer for you﴾, he made it a consequence that he commanded them to fear God, because if they complied with what the women offered them, they would then fear God.

The majority read ﴿do not disgrace me﴾ [al-Hijr 15:69] with the omission of the first-person yā' for lightness. Abu 'Amr retained it.

*Al-khizy* means humiliation and abasement, and it has been mentioned earlier. He meant his abasement.

The "fī" (in) is for figurative place. He made the guest like a container, meaning: do not make me disgraced in the presence of my guests, for they would suffer harm in my hospitality; hospitality is a neighbourhood with the master of the house, so if the guest suffers humiliation, it becomes a shame upon the master of the house.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 11, verse 80:

﴿They said: "You certainly know that we have no desire for your daughters, and you certainly know what we want."﴾ [Hud: 79] ﴿He said: "If only I had power against you, or could take refuge in a strong support!"﴾

The clause (qalu, "they said") is disjoined from the one before it because it occurs in the position of a dialogue with Lut, peace be upon him.

The phrase (laqad 'alimta, "you certainly know") is an emphatic affirmation that he knows. It is emphasized by treating him as one who denies that he knows, because his conduct in offering his daughters to them is like the conduct of one who does not know their character. The same emphasis appears in ﴿wa innaka la-ta'lamu ma nuridu﴾ [Hud: 79]. Both statements are used to convey a necessary implication of the message: we know that you already know that we have no desire for your daughters, and that you know what we want.

A similar example is his words, relating the account of the people of Abraham: ﴿laqad 'alimta ma ha'ula'i yantiqun﴾ [al-Anbiya': 65]

The first (ma) is a negation particle that suspends the verb of knowledge from acting, and the second (ma) is a relative pronoun.

Al-haqq (right, claim) is that which is due: it is what is required for someone or upon someone. One says "he has a right (haqq) in such-and-such" if he deserves it, and one says "he has no right in such-and-such" meaning he does not deserve it. Apparently the word is used here as a metonymy for having no attachment to something and for keeping away from it. This is a usage I have not seen the like of, and the exegetes have differed considerably in explaining it. The meaning is: we have no desire for your daughters.

Its response, with ﴿law anna li bikum quwwatan﴾, is the response of one who has despaired of their returning to reason.

The particle (law, "if only") is used here to express wishing, and this is the utmost he was able to do to change this evil.

The (ba') in bikum is for elevation, meaning "over you." One says: ma li bihi quwwa (I have no power over it) and ma li bihi taqa (I have no capacity for it). From this is His statement, exalted is He: ﴿qalu la taqata lana al-yawma bi-Jalut﴾ [al-Baqarah: 249]

And they say: ma li bihadha al-amr yadan, meaning I have no power or means over it.

The meaning is: "Would that I had a power by which I could repel you," and by this he means the power of helpers, because he was a stranger among them.

The meaning of ﴿aw a'wi ila rukn shadid﴾ is: "or I take refuge in what has a stronghold," that is, in a place or a person of authority who would protect me from you.

Al-rukn: the side of a mountain that is joined to the ground.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 11, verse 81:

[Page 131]
﴿They said, "O Lut, indeed we are messengers of your Lord; they will never reach you. So set out with your family during a portion of the night, and let none of you look back, except your wife. Indeed, she will be struck by what strikes them. Indeed, their appointed time is the morning. Is not the morning near?"﴾

This is the speech of the angels to Lut, peace be upon him. They made themselves known to him that they were angels sent from Allah, the Exalted. Since they were in the form of humans and were present in the dispute, Allah related their speech in the manner in which dialogues are related, so their words came without a conjunction, in the same way as the words of Lut, peace be upon him, and the words of his people were related. This speech with which they addressed Lut, peace be upon him, was a revelation that Allah sent to Lut, peace be upon him, through the angels. When Lut's apprehension of harm to his guests reached the point of distress and exhaustion of means, Allah's help came to him, in accordance with Allah's way, the Exalted, with His messengers: ﴿until, when the messengers despaired and thought that they had been denied, Our help came to them﴾ [Yusuf: 110] (3).

The angels began their address to Lut, peace be upon him, by introducing themselves, so as to hasten tranquility into his soul, for when he knew that they were angels, he knew that they had come down only to manifest the truth. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿We send not the angels except with truth, and then they would not be reprieved﴾ [al-Hijr: 8]. Then they attached to this introduction the good tidings in their saying ﴿they will never reach you﴾. The particle of emphasis for negation was used to indicate that they addressed him with what removes doubt from his soul. Allah had turned the disbelievers away from Lut, peace be upon him, so they returned from where they had come. Had Allah removed from the angels the assumption of human bodies and hidden them from the eyes of the disbelievers, they would have thought that Lut, peace be upon him, had hidden them, and so they would have harmed Lut, peace be upon him. Therefore the angels told him ﴿they will never reach you﴾ and did not say "they will never touch you," because that is already known; when they informed Lut, peace be upon him, that they were angels, he did not doubt that the disbelievers could not reach them, but he feared their fury, lest they accuse him of having hidden them.

It occurs in the Torah that Allah blinded the eyes of those who sought to seduce Lut, peace be upon him, from his guest, until they said: "The guest of Lut is a sorcerer," and they departed. This is the apparent meaning of His saying, Exalted is He, in Surah al-Qamar: ﴿And they had already sought to seduce him from his guests, so We obliterated their eyes﴾ [al-Qamar: 37].

[Page 132]
The clause ﴿they will never reach you﴾ explains the general statement in the clause ﴿Indeed, we are messengers of your Lord﴾, and therefore it is separated and not joined by a conjunction, since it stands in the position of an explicative apposition (ʿatf al-bayan).

The command to travel by night (al-sura) is made consequent upon the clause ﴿they will never reach you﴾, because the particle "lan" contains a guarantee of his safety in the entire future. When he saw the beginning of his safety from them through their departure, it was fitting to explain to him the way of his safety in the future from them, through their annihilation and his deliverance; this is the position of the consequential fa'.

(Asri) is an imperative from al-sura, with a dammed sin and shortened form. It is the verbal noun for travelling at night until morning. Its verb is sara, said without a hamza at its beginning, and also asra, said with a hamza.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, and Abu Ja'far read it with a hamza of wasl, as an imperative from sara. The rest read it with a hamza of qat', as from asra.

They combined the command concerning his family with him, because if he travelled with them, he himself travelled as well; for had he sent his family and remained himself, it would not be correct to say "asri bihim" (travel with them), because of the distinction between "adhhabtu Zaydan" (I made Zayd go) and "dhahabtu bihi" (I went with him).

Al-qitʿ (with a kasra on the qaf) means a portion of the night.

The clause ﴿and let none of you look back﴾ is parenthetical between the exception and that from which it is excepted. The looking back that is forbidden is looking back at the place which he was commanded to leave, as the context indicates.

The reason for the prohibition on looking back is thoroughness in realizing the meaning of migration, out of zeal for the sanctities of Allah, so that one severs attachment to the homeland, even attachment of sight. The specification of the night for departure was so that they would not encounter opposition from his people or his wife, which would make it difficult for him to defend them.

[Page 133]
The phrase ﴿except your wife﴾ is an exception from "your family." According to the majority reading, it is in the accusative, considering that it is an exception from "your family," and that is an affirmative statement, and the meaning is: do not travel with her. It was intended that he not inform her of his departure, because she was loyal to her people and would inform them about her husband. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read "imra'atuka" in the nominative, as an exception from the implied subject within the context of the prohibition, which carries the sense of negation. It is said: his wife went out with them, then turned toward the city and yearned for her people, so she returned to them. The meaning is that he forbade them from looking back and they complied, but his wife did not comply with the prohibition and looked back. On this reading, the exception is from an implied statement indicated by the prohibition. The estimated sense is: "they shall not look back, except your wife, who will look back."

The clause ﴿Indeed, she will be struck by what strikes them﴾ is a resumptive explanatory clause arising from the exception within the implied statement.

In His saying "what has struck them," the past tense is used in the sense of the present, whereas the apparent expectation would be "what strikes them." The use of the past tense serves to bring the time of the past near to the present, like His saying, Exalted is He: (﴿When you rise to prayer, wash your faces﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 6]) and so on; or it is used in the sense of the future, to alert to the certainty of its occurrence, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The command of Allah has come﴾ [al-Nahl: 1].

The clause ﴿Indeed, their appointed time is the morning﴾ is a new, independent sentence, cut off from what precedes it for emphasis and to convey awe.

Al-maw'id means the time of the promise. Al-wa'd is more general than al-wa'id, so it applies to specifying evil in the future. What is meant here by the appointed time is the appointed time of the punishment, which Lut, peace be upon him, knew either through earlier revelation, or through circumstantial indication, or through information from the angels in that situation, which the verse here omits for brevity. By these considerations, it is correct to define "al-wa'd" by its being attached to their pronoun.

The clause ﴿Is not the morning near?﴾ is a new explanatory sentence, uttered by the angels in answer to a question welling up in his soul about the delay in the descent of the punishment.

The interrogation is confirmatory (taqriri), and for this reason in such usage confirmation is made of a negation, relaxing the reins with the addressee so that he may recognize his error. They said this at the beginning of the night.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 11, verses 82–83:

﴿So when Our command came, We turned it upside down and rained upon it stones of hardened clay, layered one upon another,﴾ ﴿marked from your Lord. And they are never far from the wrongdoers.﴾

The discussion of the like of "فَلَمّا جاءَ أمْرُنا" has already passed.

And His saying: ﴿We turned its high parts to its low, and rained upon it stones of sijjil﴾. The three pronouns in the genitive construction and with the preposition (ʿalā) refer to the town (qaryah) understood from the context.

The meaning is that the town was overturned upon them with an overturning of collapse, until its high houses became low. That is, its low parts became high, and this is from the overturning of the earth with them.

He mentioned only the making of the high part low because it is more deeply humiliating.

As for sijjil (sijjīl): it has been explained as a valley of fire in Hell, and it is said "sijjīl" with a lām, and "sijjīn" with an nūn. The min here is partitive (tabʿīḍiyyah), and it is an eloquent simile, meaning: with stones as if they were from the sijjil of Hell, like the saying of Kaʿb ibn Zuhayr:

"And its hide is of the ṭuwm of the house"

It has come in the Torah that God sent down upon them brimstone and fire from the heaven. Perhaps the collapse caused volcanoes to erupt from the earth, hurling down upon them stones of burning minerals like brimstone; or perhaps a volcano that was near their cities erupted through earthly upheavals and then subsided from that place through events that followed one another over the centuries; or the sea overflowed over it, and the trace of the sea remained upon it until now, and this is what is called the Lake of Lot or the Dead Sea.

It has also been said: sijjīl is an arabized word (muʿarrab) from the Persian (sang-gil), meaning a stone mixed with clay.

Al-manḍūd: that which is placed one upon another. The meaning here is that they are successive, following one another in descent, with no gap between them. The description is meant for the stones, but since the stones were made of sijjīl, the description was applied to sijjīl, and it leads to describing the stones because they are from it.

Al-musawwamah: that which has a sīmā, which is a mark. Marks are placed for various purposes, among them avoiding confusion, and among them ease of summoning; and here it is used as a metonymy for what is prepared and readied, because preparation is a necessary consequence of marking, by the indication of His saying "from your Lord," since its being marked by God is His determining them for them.

The pronoun in "wa-mā hiya" (and it is not) may refer to what the preceding genitive pronouns referred to, namely the town (al-madīnah), so the meaning would be: that town is not far from the polytheists, i.e., the Arabs; so whoever wishes may go to it and look at its fate. Here the intended distance is spatial. It may also refer to the stones, meaning: those stones are not far, i.e., God is able to strike the polytheists with the like of them. Distance here means the difficulty of attainment, and its negation indicates the possibility of its attainment. This is among the speech that admits two directions, while both meanings are sound; yet it is distant.

"Baʿīd" is stripped of the feminine tāʾ although it is a predicate of "al-ḥijārah" (the stones), which is feminine in form, and although "baʿīd" here has the sense of the active participle (fāʿil), not the passive (mafʿūl); the rule is that it agree with its referent in gender. But the Arabs sometimes treat the faʿīl that has the sense of fāʿil as they treat the faʿīl that has the sense of mafʿūl when it is predicated of a feminine noun that is not truly feminine, for the sake of lightness, as in His saying, exalted is He, in Sūrat al-Aʿrāf: ﴿Indeed, the mercy of God is near to the doers of good﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 56], and His saying: ﴿And what will make you know? Perhaps the Hour is near﴾ [al-Aḥzāb: 63], and His saying: ﴿He said, "Who will give life to bones when they are decayed?"﴾ [Yā-Sīn: 78]. It has also been said:

Ibn ʿAshur's text continues: It has been said that His saying ﴿And your mother was not unchaste﴾ [Maryam: 28] is of this type, meaning bāghiyah (unchaste). It has also been said that its origin is faʿūl, baghūy, and then substitution and assimilation occurred. Al-Zamakhsharī interpreted what is here as an adjective of an omitted noun, meaning "at a distant place" or "at a distant thing," according to the two possibilities regarding the referent of the pronoun (hiya).

[p. 137]

Its statement: ﴿And to Madyan [We sent] their brother Shu'ayb﴾ up to His statement ﴿…you have no god other than Him﴾ is similar to His statement ﴿And to Thamud [We sent] their brother Salih﴾ [Hud: 61], and so on.

He commanded them with three matters:

The first: correcting belief, which is part of correcting the intellects and thoughts.
