Al-Marzuqi said: The meaning is: then there will come to me your best and most distinguished ones, who present an excuse. This is like saying: "So-and-so is of the remnant of his people," meaning among their most virtuous.

In the word "baqiyyah" there is another meaning, which is sparing them. The Arabs, when asking to stop fighting, say: "Spare us," and they say "al-baqiyyah, al-baqiyyah" (spare, spare) in the accusative as an incitement. Al-A'sha said:

"They said, 'Spare!' while the Indian [sword] was reaping them, and there was no sparing except vengeance, and they fled."

Miswar ibn Ziyadah al-Harithi said:

"I remind [him] of sparing toward one who has struck me, and my sparing is that I strive, not falling short."

The meaning is: God's sparing you and your deliverance from the punishment of annihilation is better for you than these hasty, evil-ending benefits. Thus it is an allusion to a warning of annihilation. All these meanings are appropriate here. Perhaps the speech of Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, included all of them, so the Qur'an related it with this comprehensive word.

The annexation of "baqiyyah" to the Name of Majesty (Allah), according to all these meanings, collectively and separately, is an annexation of honour and blessing. It is an annexation in the sense of the particle "li" (belonging to), because the remnant is from His grace or from what He commanded.

The meaning of ﴿if you are believers﴾ is: if you are those who believe in what I have been sent with to you; because they will not abandon their corruptions and perform what they were commanded except when they affirm that this is from God. Then the remnant of God will be better for them. So the point of the condition is that the remnant is good for them; that is, the remnant is good only for believers.

[p. 140]

He used the active participle, which is in truth the description of being characterized by the act at the present time, bringing it near for their belief by showing eagerness to achieve it immediately and hastening their belief so that the punishment does not suddenly seize them and the opportunity for remedy is lost.

The clause ﴿And I am not a guardian over you﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial phrase from the pronoun in "u'budu" (worship) and its like, meaning: do that by your own choice, because it is for your good, and I am not compelling you to do it.

Al-hafiz: the compeller, as in His statement: ﴿But if they turn away, We have not sent you as a guardian over them; your duty is only to convey [the message]﴾ [al-Shura: 48]. It was discussed earlier at His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And We did not make you a guardian over them﴾ [al-An'am: 107] in Surat al-An'am. The purpose of this is to draw down their hostility, lest they be repelled by the command. This is an exhaustive pursuit of encouragement and fine argumentation.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 11, verse 87:

﴿They said, "O Shu'ayb, does your prayer command you that we should abandon what our fathers worshipped, or that we should not do as we wish with our wealth? Indeed, you are the forbearing, the discerning one."﴾

Prayer (al-salah) was a pillar of all religions. The deniers and disbelievers had conspired in every nation to reject it and to mock its practitioner: ﴿Did they bequeath this to one another? Nay, they are a transgressing people﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 53]. So when prayer was the most distinctive of his practices that opposed their customs, they made it the target of their mockery, on the basis of what had reached them from him of matters opposed to their customs, relying on the correspondence between the cause and its effect in opposing customary practice. Their purpose was to ridicule him and to deride him, denying what he had brought them. Thus, attributing the command to the prayers is not literal, since all rational people know that actions do not command. The meaning is that his prayer commands him to make them abandon [the worship], i.e., it commands him to induce them to abandon what their fathers worshipped. For being commanded with the actions of another means that he is commanded to strive toward that by commanding them to do things.

و(ما) in His saying ﴿what our fathers worshipped﴾ is a relative pronoun referring to the objects of worship. Its meaning of abandoning them is abandoning their worship, as the verb ya'budu indicates. It is also possible that (ma) is a verbal-noun particle (masdariyyah), with the sense: "that we abandon the like of our fathers' worship."

The Jumhur read (أصَلَواتُكَ) in the plural form of salah. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Hafs and Khalaf read (أصَلاتُكَ) in the singular form.

The (أوْ) in His saying ﴿or that we should do as we wish with our wealth﴾ serves to divide what he commands them, because some of them do not trade, and so do not cheat in measure and weight; he is thus a distinct category set apart from the rest of the nation, being commanded to abstain from cheating. So His saying ﴿that we should do﴾ is coordinated with ﴿what our fathers worshipped﴾, meaning: that we abandon doing what we wish with our wealth, so that we become obedient to your command, doing what you command us to do and abandoning what you command us to abandon.

From this you will know that there is no need to make (أوْ) mean the conjunction of addition (waw al-jam'), as many exegetes have done, such as al-Baydawi and al-Kawashi, who took it as coordinated with (نَتْرُكُ) and then sensed that the meaning was not coherent, as al-Tabari said. He interpreted it in two ways: one reported from the people of Basra and the other from the people of Kufa; one of them is based on a supposed omitted element, and the other on an interpretation of the verb (تَأْمُرُكَ). Both are forced. Most of them resorted to diverting (أوْ) from its commonly known meaning, although they had room to avoid that. Many, such as the author of al-Kashshaf, remained silent about it. Al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi alluded to what we have made explicit.

The sentence ﴿Indeed, you are the forbearing, the discerning one﴾ is another resumptive expression of mockery. The sentence has been emphasized with the particle inna, the oath-lam, and the restrictive form in ﴿you are the forbearing, the discerning one﴾, thus containing four emphases.

Al-Halim (the forbearing), as an intensification of the mockery: possessor of forbearance, i.e., of intellect; and al-Rashid: one who manages wealth well.

قالَ يا قَوْمِ أرَيْتُمْ إنْ كُنْتُ عَلى بَيِّنَةٍ مِن رَبِّي ورَزَقَنِي مِنهُ رِزْقًا حَسَنًا وما أُرِيدُ أنْ أُخالِفَكم إلى ما أنْهاكم عَنْهُ إنْ أُرِيدُ إلّا الإصْلاحَ ما اسْتَطَعْتُ وما تَوْفِيقِيَ إلّا بِاللَّهِ عَلَيْهِ تَوَكَّلْتُ وإلَيْهِ أُنِيبُ

[Shu'ayb said: "O my people, tell me, if I am upon clear evidence from my Lord and He has provided me with good provision from Him, (then what?) And I do not intend to oppose you in what I forbid you from. I intend only reform, as far as I am able. My success is only through Allah. In Him I put my trust, and to Him I turn back."]

تَقَدَّمَ نَظِيرُ الآيَةِ في قِصَّةِ نُوحٍ وقِصَّةِ صالِحٍ عَلَيْهِما السَّلامُ.

The like of this verse has preceded in the story of Nuh and the story of Salih, peace be upon them both.

والمُرادُ بِالرِّزْقِ الحَسَنِ هُنا مِثْلُ المُرادِ مِنَ الرَّحْمَةِ في كَلامِ نُوحٍ وكَلامِ صالِحٍ - عَلَيْهِما السَّلامُ - وهو نِعْمَةُ النُّبُوَّةِ، وإنَّما عَبَّرَ شُعَيْبٌ - عَلَيْهِ السَّلامُ - عَنِ النُّبُوَّةِ بِالرِّزْقِ عَلى وجْهِ التَّشْبِيهِ مُشاكَلَةً (المُشاكَلَةُ: أنْ يُذْكَرَ الشَّيْءُ بِلَفْظِ غَيْرِهِ لِوُقُوعِهِ في صُحْبَتِهِ) لِقَوْلِهِمْ: ﴿أوْ أنْ نَفْعَلَ في أمْوالِنا ما نَشاءُ﴾ [هود: ٨٧] لِأنَّ الأمْوالَ أرْزاقٌ. وجَوابُ الشَّرْطِ مَحْذُوفٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَيْهِ سِياقُ الكَلامِ، أوْ يَدُلُّ عَلَيْهِ ﴿إنْ كُنْتُ عَلى بَيِّنَةٍ مِن رَبِّي﴾. والتَّقْدِيرُ: ماذا يَسَعُكم في تَكْذِيبِي، أوْ ماذا يُنْجِيكم مِن عاقِبَةِ تَكْذِيبِي، وهو تَحْذِيرٌ لَهم عَلى فَرْضِ احْتِمالِ أنْ يَكُونَ صادِقًا، أيْ فالحَزْمُ أنْ تَأْخُذُوا بِهَذا الِاحْتِمالِ، أوْ فالحَزْمُ أنْ تَنْظُرُوا في كُنْهِ ما نَهَيْتُكم عَنْهُ لِتَعْلَمُوا أنَّهُ لِصَلاحِكم.

The meaning of ﴿وما أُرِيدُ أنْ أُخالِفَكم إلى ما أنْهاكم عَنْهُ﴾ according to all the commentators (mufassirun) from the Followers and those after them is: "I do not intend, in what I have forbidden you from, to prohibit you from acts while I myself am doing them." That is, I would not forbid you from something while I myself do it. Al-Zamakhshari in al-Kashshaf made clear that this construction conveys this meaning in his saying: "It is said: 'So-and-so opposed me to such-and-such' when he intended it while you were turning away from it... and a man meets you coming away from the water, so you ask him about his companion, and he says: 'He opposed me to the water,' meaning that he went to it while arriving, and I am going away from it while departing." End of quote.

Its explanation: opposition indicates being characterized by the opposite of one's state. When it is mentioned with an object, it indicates being characterized by its opposite. Then the manner of opposition is specified by mentioning the thing over which the difference occurred, governed by the particle (ilā), which indicates reaching a thing, as in their saying "khalafanī ilā al-mā'" (he opposed me to the water), in which (ukhalifakum) implies the meaning of striving toward something. ﴿إلى ما أنْهاكُمْ﴾ is connected to the verb (ukhalifakum), and ﴿أنْ أُخالِفَكُمْ﴾ is the object of (urīdu).

So His saying ﴿أنْ أُخالِفَكم إلى ما أنْهاكم عَنْهُ﴾ means: that I would do the opposite of the actions I have forbidden you from, by turning you away from them while I myself go to them. The purpose is to show that he is commanded with that command which includes the community and himself, and that is the nature of the sacred laws. As our scholars said: the address to the community includes the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, unless there is evidence specifying him otherwise. Thus in this there is a demonstration that what he forbids them from also forbids himself. In this there is also an admonition to them regarding the benefit in the prohibition, and that his conduct is not the conduct of the tyrants who forbid acts while they themselves commit them, because such a thing indicates a lack of sincere advice in what they command and forbid, for if they wanted sincere advice and good in that, they would have chosen it for themselves. And to this meaning the rebuke in His saying, Exalted is He, points: ﴿أتَأْمُرُونَ النّاسَ بِالبِرِّ وتَنْسَوْنَ أنْفُسَكم وأنْتُمْ تَتْلُونَ الكِتابَ أفَلا تَعْقِلُونَ﴾ [البقرة: ٤٤]: that is, while you recite the Book of the general Law for you, will you not reason, so that you would know that you are more deserving of bringing good to your own selves.

What appears to me regarding the meaning of the verse is that by opposition is meant contrariness and contention. Either because he recognized from the signs of their denial that they supposed him to be seeking to dominate over them and to be arrogant, or because he wanted to uproot from their souls the thoughts of evil before they stir within them.

This interpretation of the verse is permitted by the usage of the construction and by the aims of the Messengers, and it is more comprehensive of meanings than the explanation of the earlier scholars. Therefore the explanation of the verse should not be restricted to what they said, because it does not correspond to the words of his people: ﴿أصَلاتُكَ تَأْمُرُكَ أنْ نَتْرُكَ ما يَعْبُدُ آباؤُنا أوْ أنْ نَفْعَلَ في أمْوالِنا ما نَشاءُ﴾ [هود: ٨٧], for they thought of him that he intended only to oppose them and to correct them, and they denied that he had any righteous purpose in what he called them to. So the requirement of refuting their suspicion was that he deny that he intends merely to oppose them, as evidenced by his saying right after it: ﴿إنْ أُرِيدُ إلّا الإصْلاحَ ما اسْتَطَعْتُ﴾.

So the meaning of his saying ﴿وما أُرِيدُ أنْ أُخالِفَكُمْ﴾ is that he does not intend mere opposition, like the case of critics who fault for the sake of fault, but he opposes them for a lofty purpose, which is to intend their reform. Among this usage is what occurred in the hadith when the delegation of Fazara came to the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him. Abu Bakr al-Siddiq said: "Appoint al-Aqra' ibn Habis." And Umar said: "Appoint so-and-so." Abu Bakr said to Umar: "You intended nothing but to oppose me." Umar said: "I intended nothing but to oppose you."

This interpretation has a sound basis in this verse. In this there is an indication that critics are of two kinds: one kind criticizes a thing and stops at the limit of criticism without rising to explain what would reform the thing criticized; and another kind criticizes in order to show the fault and then follows it with an explanation of what would correct the fault. On this basis, ﴿إلى ما أنْهاكم﴾ is connected to the verb (urīdu), and likewise ﴿أنْ أُخالِفَكُمْ﴾ is connected to (urīdu) with the omission of the preposition lām. The estimated meaning is: "I do not intend toward the prohibition for the sake of opposing you," that is, out of love of opposing you.

The clause ﴿إنْ أُرِيدُ إلّا الإصْلاحَ ما اسْتَطَعْتُ﴾ is an explanation of the clause ﴿ما أُرِيدُ أنْ أُخالِفَكم إلى ما أنْهاكم عَنْهُ﴾, because the negation of the intention of opposition to what he forbade them is general regarding what he wants to affirm of the opposites of the negated. So he clarified it by saying that the opposite intended to be affirmed is reform at all times within his ability, by achieving reform. So the restriction is a restriction by reversal (qasr qalb, i.e., restriction that corrects a mistaken belief).

The form of restriction served to emphasize this, because restriction would have occurred merely by limiting to negation and affirmation, as when one says: "I do not intend to oppose you; I intend reform," like the saying of Abd al-Malik ibn Abd al-Rahim al-Harithi or al-Samaw'al:

"Our souls flow over the edges of the swords, and they do not flow except over the edges."

When he had made clear to them the reality of his work, and in his explanation there was what would draw praise to himself, he followed it by returning the credit in that to Allah, and said: ﴿وما تَوْفِيقِي إلّا بِاللَّهِ﴾. So he named his intention of reform "success" (tawfiq) and made it from Allah; it does not occur at any time except through Allah, that is, through His will and His guidance. So the clause ﴿وما تَوْفِيقِي إلّا بِاللَّهِ﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun of (urīdu).

Tawfiq: making a thing accord with another, that is, matching it. For this reason they defined it as: the creation of the power that calls to obedience.

The clause ﴿عَلَيْهِ تَوَكَّلْتُ﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause from the name of majesty (Allah), or from the first-person pronoun in his saying "tawfiqī," because the noun here is like a part of the noun it is attached to, so that permits the circumstantial clause to come from the attached-to noun.

Tawakkul (trust in God) was discussed at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿فَإذا عَزَمْتَ فَتَوَكَّلْ عَلى اللَّهِ﴾ [آل عمران: ١٥٩] in Surat Al 'Imran.

Inabah (turning back in repentance) has been discussed just before, in His saying: ﴿إنَّ إبْراهِيمَ لَحَلِيمٌ أوّاهٌ مُنِيبٌ﴾ [هود: ٧٥].

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 11, verses 89–90:**

﴿O my people, let not my opposition bring upon you the like of what befell the people of Noah, or the people of Hud, or the people of Salih; and the people of Lot are not far from you.﴾ ﴿And ask forgiveness of your Lord, then turn to Him in repentance. Indeed, my Lord is Merciful and Loving.﴾

The subtle point (nukta) of repeating the address (nida') within a single speech to the same listeners has already been discussed, close by.

The discussion of ﴿let not ... bring you to commit a crime (la yajrimannakum)﴾ was given earlier, at His saying: ﴿And let not the hatred of a people, because they barred you from the Sacred Mosque, lead you to transgress﴾ [al-Ma'ida 5:2], at the beginning of al-'Uqud. Its meaning is: let it not earn for you (la yaksibannakum).

Al-shiqaq (opposition) is the verbal noun of shaqqahu, meaning he opposed him. It was discussed earlier, at His saying: ﴿That is because they opposed Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Anfal 8:13], at the beginning of al-Anfal.

The meaning is: let your enmity toward me not draw down upon you the affliction of the like of what befell the people of Noah, and so on to the end of the verse. The apparent sense of the speech is that it forbids opposition from drawing this consequence upon them. The intended purpose is

Page 147

to forbid them from making opposition a cause for turning away from considering his call, so that they would bring upon themselves a punishment like that which befell the nations before them. They would then imagine that they were outwitting him by their aversion, but they outwit only themselves.

The exposure of the bad intentions that impelled them to turn away from his call came right after he had displayed his good intention, when he said: ﴿I do not intend to do what I forbid you to do; I intend only reform, as far as I am able﴾ [Hud 11:88]. This struck the very mark of eloquent speech, since he accused them of acting contrary to how he dealt with them.

The clause ﴿and the people of Lot are not far from you﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the object pronoun in His saying: "that it befall you." The waw is the linking particle that connects the clause. The sense of the circumstantial clause here has a special suitability to the content of the clause, since the nearness of their time to the addressees is regarded as though it were one of the conditions of the addressees.

By distance is meant distance in time, place and lineage. The time of Lot, peace be upon him, was not far from the time of Shu'ayb, peace be upon him. The dwellings were close to theirs, since the settlements of Madyan lay near the Aqabah of Ayla, adjacent to Ma'an on the side of the Hijaz, while the dwellings of the people of Lot were in the region of Jordan extending to the Dead Sea. Madyan, son of Ibrahim, peace be upon them both, the forefather of the tribe named after him, had married a daughter of Lot.

The clause ﴿and ask forgiveness of your Lord﴾ is coordinated (ʿatf) with the clause ﴿let not my opposition ... ﴾.

The clause ﴿indeed my Lord is Merciful and Loving﴾ gives the reason for the command to seek His forgiveness and to turn to Him in repentance. It is a reason for what the command implies, namely the hope of His pardon for them if they seek forgiveness and repent.

He varied the attribution of the Lord: once to His own pronoun, and once to the pronoun of his people. This was to remind them that He is their Lord, so that they would not persist in turning away, and to honor the relation of the Lord to His creatures.

Al-Rahim has already been discussed.

Page 148

Al-Wadud is an intensive form (mithal mubalaghah) from al-wadd, which means love. It was discussed earlier, at His saying: ﴿They wish that you would disbelieve as they disbelieved﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:89], in Surat al-Nisa'. The meaning is that Allah has intense love for whoever draws near to Him through repentance.

**Ibn 'Ashur's commentary on Surah Hud (11), verse 91:**

﴿They said: "O Shu'ayb, we do not understand much of what you say, and we see you as weak among us. Were it not for your clan, we would have stoned you, and you are not mighty against us."﴾

*Al-fiqh* (فقه) means understanding. It was discussed earlier, at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So what is wrong with these people that they can hardly understand any statement?﴾ [An-Nisa: 78] in Surat an-Nisa', and at His saying: ﴿See how We explain the signs, that perhaps they may understand﴾ [Al-An'am: 65] in Surat al-An'am.

Their meaning here may be mere obstinate denial (*al-mubahatah*), as God relates of the disbelievers: ﴿They said, "Our hearts are under coverings against what you invite us to, and in our ears is deafness"﴾ [Fussilat: 5], and His saying about the Jews: ﴿They said, "Our hearts are uncircumcised"﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 88]. It is also possible that they meant "we do not comprehend it," because to them it was like the impossible, since it contradicted what they were accustomed to, as God relates of others by His saying: ﴿"Has he made the gods into one God? Indeed, this is a astonishing thing!"﴾ [Sad: 5]. The meaning is not that they did not understand his speech, because Shu'ayb (peace be upon him) was an eloquent speaker, and the Prophet (ﷺ) described him as "the orator of the prophets."

So the meaning is: "You say what we do not believe." This is a preface to condemning him and establishing that, in their view, he deserves blame and punishment, as in their saying: ﴿Were it not for your clan, we would have stoned you.﴾ For this reason they joined to it: ﴿and we see you as weak among us﴾, that is, "and indeed you are weak among us," meaning without strength or protection. The intended meaning is weakness in defending oneself if they sought to harm him, and this is something that can be seen, because its evidences and marks are visible.

The mention of the verb of seeing (*ru'yah*) here serves to affirm, as was discussed earlier at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We see you as nothing but a human like us, and we see that none follow you except the lowest of us﴾ [Hud: 27]. They spoke of it in a way that treats it as though they were not seeing it with their eyes, so they stated the verb of seeing explicitly. They reinforced it with *inna* and the *lam* of initiation, as an intensification, placing him in the position of one who is ignorant of what they know about this, or one who denies it. In this manner of speaking there is an indirect insult to his dullness, as in the verse of Hajal ibn Nadlah:

*"Indeed, the spears among your paternal cousins..."*

Among the corruptions of the exegeses is the interpretation of *da'if* (weak) as one who has lost his sight, and the claim that this is a Himyarite usage (*lughah himyariyyah*). From this they constructed the claim that Shu'ayb (peace be upon him) was blind, and from that they proceeded to raise the question of whether blindness is permissible for prophets, which is built on illusions. Nothing is known from any report or from the books of earlier peoples indicating that Shu'ayb (peace be upon him) was blind.

They joined to this their saying: ﴿Were it not for your clan, we would have stoned you﴾, which is the real purpose of the premises that preceded it. That is, nothing prevents us from stoning you except the standing of your clan among us, because you have made your stoning obligatory by your attack on our religion.

When *al-rahat* (رهط) is attributed to a man, it refers to his closest relatives, since they are not many. They applied to them the word *rahat*, whose original sense is a small group from three to ten. They did not say "your people" (*qawmaka*), because his people had rejected him. The clan of Shu'ayb (peace be upon him) were among the most devoted people of their religion, so they honored them by refraining from harming their relative, because they disliked whatever would harm him on account of his kinship. Were it not for that, his clan would not have supported him, since they do not support one whom the people of their religion resent. Moreover, his kin were only a small number, whose might was not feared; rather, the sparing of him was merely an act of honor toward his kinship, because they were sincere to their religion.

So the omitted predicate after *law-la* (لولا) is to be supplied with something that conveys the meaning of honor, by the indication of their saying: ﴿and you are not mighty against us﴾, and His saying: ﴿"Is my clan more mighty to you than God?"﴾ [Hud: 92]. When they denied that he was mighty, and since a man's might lies in his protectors, it became clear that the presence of his clan, which prevented them from stoning him, was a specific presence, namely the presence of honor and reverence. The sense is therefore: "Were it not that your clan are honored among us, we would have stoned you."

*Al-rajm* (الرجم) is killing by stoning, by throwing, and it is a degrading and humiliating death. This indicates that, in their customs, the penalty for one who abandons their religion was stoning.

The clause ﴿and you are not mighty against us﴾ serves to confirm the content of ﴿Were it not for your clan, we would have stoned you﴾, because once his strength in their minds is negated, it becomes clear that their restraint from stoning him, despite their belief that he deserved it, was solely for the sake of honoring his clan, and not out of fear of them.

This clause was joined (by *'atf*) to the one before it, even though the rule for a confirmatory clause is that it should be separated and not joined. This is because, while it confirms the content of the preceding clause, it also conveys a judgment that concerns the one addressed, so in this respect it was worthy of being joined to the clauses that describe his condition, such as ﴿we do not understand much of what you say﴾ and the clauses after it.

*Al-'izzah* (العزة) means strength, power, and dominance. *Al-'aziz* is derived from it, and its construction with the particle *'ala* (على) is because it carries the sense of hardship and weight upon the self, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It grieves him that you suffer﴾ [At-Tawbah: 128], that is, it is hard upon his soul. Thus the meaning of ﴿and you are not mighty against us﴾ is that your killing will not overwhelm us, nor will it weigh heavily on our souls, that is, because you are insignificant to us and despised in our eyes, and you have no one among us to support you. The might of a man over a tribe is not the overpowering of his person, since one individual does not overpower a group; rather his might is through his people and tribe, as al-A'sha said:

*"Indeed, might belongs only to the one who has the most numbers."*

So the meaning of ﴿and you are not mighty against us﴾ is that you cannot overpower us.

Their purpose in this speech is to warn him against persisting in opposing his clan, since they are about to depose him and permit themselves to stone him. These are very subtle meanings and a most wondrous conciseness.

The fronting of the predicate subject (*al-musnad ilayh*) before the predicate (*al-musnad*) in His saying: ﴿and you are not mighty against us﴾ does not serve to convey exclusivity or emphasis.

[p. 151]

﴿He said, "O my people, is my kinsfolk more powerful over you than God? And you have put Him behind your backs, disregarded. Indeed my Lord is encompassing of what you do."﴾

When they intended, by the words they addressed to him, to warn him against continuing to oppose their religion, he replied with a statement indicating that he had never relied on the might of his kinsfolk, but was instead trusting in God, who is mightier than every mighty one. The purpose of the report is therefore its implication, namely that he knows the content of this report and is not heedless of it. That is: "I know that my kinsfolk are more powerful over you than God is. So I do not need you to treat me as one who is not esteemed by you, or as one whose clan is a small group that you could not overpower if you wished to stone me."

Repeating the vocative "O my people" serves to draw attention to his speech and to show that he is discerning in it. The interrogative is one of denial (istinkari), meaning: "God is mightier than my kinsfolk." It is a kinayah (metonymy) for his reliance on God rather than on his kinsfolk, so the lack of might among his kinsfolk over them does not trouble him. This is also a threat to them, that God is his helper because He sent him; his might is thus the might of the one who sent him.

The clause ﴿and you have put Him behind your backs﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the name of God. That is: "God is mightier, while you have forgotten this."

Al-ittikhadh (taking, adopting) means making. It was discussed earlier in His words ﴿Do you take idols as gods?﴾ [al-An'am: 74] in Surah al-An'am.

Al-zihriyy, with a kasra on the ẓā', is a relative form derived from al-zahr (the back) contrary to the regular analogy, and alterations of words for the sake of forming the relative are numerous. What is meant by "zihriyy" is a kinayah for forgetting, or an isti'arah (metaphor), because a thing placed behind the back is forgotten through rarely being seen. It therefore resembles a thing set behind the back in this respect. Thus "ẓihriyyan" occurs as a circumstantial accusative emphasising the adverbial phrase in His words "behind your backs," intensifying the meaning of forgetting, because they were occupied with the idols rather than with knowing God or attending to His attributes.

The clause ﴿Indeed my Lord is encompassing of what you do﴾ is either a resumptive clause (istinaf) or a ta'lil (causal explanation) for the implication of the clause ﴿Is my kinsfolk more powerful over you than God?﴾, which is his reliance upon Him and his seeking help from Him.

[p. 152]

Al-muhit is the one described as the doer of the act of encompassing. The original sense of ihatah (encompassing) is one thing confining another from all its sides, like the encompassing of a container around what it contains, of a wall around a town, or of a bracelet around a wrist. In the Maqamat al-Haririyya (of al-Hariri) there is:

"And the mixed throngs have surrounded him, as a halo surrounds the moon,
and as sheaths surround the fruit."

It is used figuratively in the expressions "his knowledge encompassed such-and-such," and "he encompassed everything in knowledge," meaning the knowledge of everything that could be known in that matter. Then this usage became common, so the specifier (tamyiz) was omitted and the encompassing was attributed to the one who knows, meaning the comprehensiveness of his knowledge, i.e., the inclusion of his knowledge of everything that can be known in a given matter. He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿and He has encompassed what is with them﴾ [al-Jinn: 28], meaning His knowledge. From this is His saying here, ﴿Indeed my Lord is encompassing of what you do,﴾ and what is meant is the encompassing of His knowledge. This is an allusive threat, and that God is about to punish them for what He knows of their deeds.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 11, verse 93:

﴿And, O my people, act according to your position; indeed, I am acting. You will soon know who will receive a punishment that will disgrace him, and who is a liar. And watch; indeed, I am with you a watcher.﴾

He conjoined one call to another as an additional alertness, and the intent is to conjoin what follows the second call to what follows the first call.

The clause ﴿Act according to your position; indeed, I am acting. You will soon know﴾ has had the explanation of its counterpart in Surah al-An'am already discussed.

The imperative here is for threat. The meaning: act while firmly established in your position (makanah), that is, your state in which you are, i.e., act in whatever you wish to do to me.

The clause "indeed, I am acting" (inni 'amil) is resumptive (mustanaffah). The particle (sawfa) in this verse was not joined with the fa' (resultative particle), whereas in the verse of Surah al-An'am it was joined with the fa'; so the clause "sawfa ta'lamun" here is made resumptive:

an explanatory resumption (istinaf bayani), since when he opened to them with a threat, that would give rise in their souls to a question about what would result from this threat, and it is answered with the threat "sawfa ta'lamun." Because it is so, it was equivalent in outcome to the resultative fa' occurring in the verse of Surah al-An'am, but it is more eloquent in indicating the arising of the content of the resumptive clause from the content of the one before it. Thus in the address of Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, to his people there is a severity not found in the address commanded to the Prophet ﷺ in Surah al-An'am, following what Allah sent His Messenger Muhammad ﷺ with of gentleness toward them: ﴿So by mercy from Allah, you were gentle with them﴾ [Al 'Imran: 159]. Likewise the disparity between the two objects of (ta'lamun): here it is harsh and severe, ﴿who will receive a punishment that will disgrace him, and who is a liar﴾, while there it is gentle: ﴿to whom the good outcome of the abode belongs﴾ [al-An'am: 135].

"Man" (من) here is an interrogative suspending the verb of knowing from acting, i.e., you will know the answer to this question. And punishment ('adhab) is disgrace (khizy) because it is humiliation.

Al-irtiqab is at-taraqqub (watching/awaiting), and it is an ifti'al form from raqabahu, when he awaited him.

And al-raqib here is fa'il in the sense of fa'il (active participle), i.e., "indeed, I am with you a watcher"; that is, each of you awaits what Allah will requite him with, if he is a liar or a denier.

And when Our command came, We saved Shu'ayb and those who believed with him by a mercy from Us, and the Cry seized those who did wrong, so they were found prostrate in their homes, as though they had never dwelt there. Unquestionably, away with Madyan, just as Thamud were removed.

The conjunction (*'atf*) of "when Our command came" here, and in His words about the people of 'Ad, ﴿And when Our command came, We saved Hud﴾ [Hud: 58], is with *waw* in both places. Its counterparts in the story of Thamud, ﴿So when Our command came, We saved Salih﴾ [Hud: 66], and in the story of the people of Lot, ﴿So when Our command came, We made its highest part its lowest﴾ [Hud: 82], are with *fa'*. The reason is that in the stories of Thamud and the people of Lot, the time of the punishment with which their prophets had threatened their peoples was specified.

[Page 154]

In the story of Thamud: ﴿He said, "Enjoy yourselves in your homes for three days. That is a promise not to be denied"﴾ [Hud: 65]. In the story of the people of Lot: ﴿Indeed, their appointed time is the morning. Is not the morning near?﴾ [Hud: 81]. Thus the context called for the listener to await what befell them at that appointed time, and so *fa'* was the fitting particle, to make what befell them follow as a consequence of the threat concerning it. In the story of 'Ad and the story of Madyan, however, no time for the punishment is specified. The threat in both is general, from His words: ﴿and my Lord will bring in a people other than you﴾ [Hud: 57], and His words: ﴿Wait, indeed I am with you among those who wait﴾ [Hud: 93].

The discussion of the meaning of "when Our command came" was given earlier, up to His words ﴿Away with Madyan﴾, in the story of Thamud. The discussion of *bu'dan* (away with) was given earlier in the story of Noah, in His words: ﴿And it was said, "Away with the wrongdoing people"﴾ [Hud: 44].

As for His words ﴿just as Thamud were removed﴾, it is a comparison of the *bu'd* (removal), which is the extinction of Madyan, with the extinction of Thamud. The point of resemblance is the equality in the cause of their punishment by annihilation, namely the punishment of the Cry. It is also possible that the purpose of the comparison is a *istitrad* (digression, a rhetorical device) to censure Thamud, because they were the most audacious in opposing the messengers of God. So when the setting was ready to conclude the discourse on the stories of the extinct nations, it was fitting to mention again the most severe of them in disbelief and obstinacy, and so the destruction of Madyan was compared to their destruction.

The *istitrad* is a type of *badi'* (rhetorical embellishment). An example of it is the verse of Hassan concerning a digression in satire against al-Harith, the brother of Abu Jahl:

If what you told me was false, then you escaped as al-Harith ibn Hisham escaped.

He left his loved ones, not fighting to defend them,
and fled upon the head of a swift mare, with her bridle.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 11, verses 96–97:

Page 155

﴿And We certainly sent Moses with Our signs and a clear authority﴾ ﴿to Pharaoh and his chieftains, but they followed the command of Pharaoh, and the command of Pharaoh was not rightly guided.﴾

He joined one narrative to another. The story of Madyan was followed by mention of the sending of Moses, peace be upon him, because of the closeness of the time between the two and the strong connection between the prophets; Moses was sent during the lifetime of Shu'ayb, peace be upon them both, and he had married Shu'ayb's daughter.

The emphasis of the report with "qad" (certainly) is like the emphasis of the report about Noah, peace be upon him, in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We certainly sent Noah to his people﴾ [Hud: 25].

The "ba'" in (bi-ayatina, with Our signs) denotes accompaniment, since the manifestation of the signs coincided with the time of the sending to Pharaoh, which is the period of Moses's, peace be upon him, call to Pharaoh and his chieftains.

Al-sultan: the clear proof, i.e., that which manifests the truthfulness of the one who brings it, and it is either the rational argument or the divine support. The mention of Pharaoh and his chieftains has already occurred in Surat al-A'raf.

The mention of the sending of Moses, peace be upon him, was followed by mention of the chieftains' following the command of Pharaoh, because their following Pharaoh's command took place as a consequence of the sending; thus it is understood that Pharaoh had ordered them to reject that message.

The repetition of the name of Pharaoh the second time, rather than a pronoun, and the third time, is for the purpose of exposing them and publicly declaring his blame, namely the negation of right guidance from his command.

The sentence ﴿and the command of Pharaoh was not rightly guided﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to Pharaoh.

Al-rashid: an intensive form (fa'il) from rashada (of the pattern nasara and fariha), when one is characterized by hitting the correct course.

It is said: "Arshadaka Allah" (may God guide you). The attribute "rashid" was applied to the command as a metaphorical attribution (majaz 'aqli). Rather, the one who is rashid is the one who commands, in hyperbole regarding the command's containing what requires the absence of right guidance; so it is as if the command itself is the one described with lack of right guidance.

Page 156

The intended meaning is that Pharaoh's command was foolishness, since there is no intermediate position between right guidance and foolishness. But he turned away from describing his command as foolish to negating right guidance from it, to disparage those who followed his command, because the way of the sensible is to seek to follow what contains goodness; and they followed what has no sign of its soundness or of its deserving to be followed. So what deceived them into following it?

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 11, verses 98–99:**

﴿He will lead his people on the Day of Resurrection and bring them into the Fire. Wretched is the watering-place to which they are brought.﴾ ﴿They were pursued by a curse in this world, and on the Day of Resurrection. Wretched is the gift that is given.﴾

The clause ﴿yaqduMu qawmahu﴾ (He leads his people) may be in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to Fir'awn (Pharaoh), mentioned in the clause before it. It may also be a explanatory resumptive clause (isti'naf bayani).

Al-iradu (bringing to water) means making something arrive, that is, heading toward the water. The one who brings them to water is the forerunner (al-farit), also called al-fard.

Al-wirdu, with a kasra on the waw, means the water that is come to. It is a verbal noun used in the sense of a passive participle, like dhibh (what is slaughtered). In His saying ﴿fa-awradahumu al-nara wa-bi'sa al-wirdu al-mawrud﴾ there is a metaphor (isti'arah) in which bringing to water is applied to leading people toward punishment. This metaphor is sarcastic (tahakkumiyyah), because bringing to water is done for the benefit of being given drink, whereas leading one's people to the Fire is the opposite of that.

Yaqdumu is the present tense of qadama (with a fatha on the dal), meaning taqaddama in the transitive sense, when one goes before others.

The past form ﴿fa-awradahum﴾ is used to draw attention to the certainty of the occurrence of that bringing to water. Otherwise, the indication of His saying "on the Day of Resurrection" shows that it has not yet happened in the past.

The clause ﴿wa-bi'sa al-wirdu al-mawrud﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause. The implied pronoun that is the object of praise (al-damir al-makhsus bi-al-madh al-mahdhuf), which is omitted, serves as the connecting element. This is a stripping away of the metaphor (tajrid lil-isti'arah), as in His saying ﴿bi'sa al-sharab﴾ (Wretched is the drink) [al-Kahf: 29], because the water that is the basis of comparison cannot be blameworthy.

Al-itba' means attaching (al-ilhaq).

Al-la'nah (the curse) is the curse of punishment in this world and in the Hereafter.

"On the Day of Resurrection" is connected to "they were pursued." It is thus known that they were pursued by a curse on the Day of Resurrection, because the first curse was restricted by the prepositional phrase introduced by the locative particle fi (in). Therefore it is determined that the pursuit on the Day of Resurrection is by another curse.

The clause ﴿bi'sa al-rifdu al-marfud﴾ is a new resumed clause (isti'naf) expressing the censure of the curse. The thing being censured is omitted, and the mention of the curse indicates it, meaning: "Wretched is the gift, it being [the curse]."

Al-rifdu, with a kasra on the ra', is a noun on the pattern fi'l in the sense of maf'ul, like dhibh. That is, what is given support, that is, what is given. It is said: rafadahu when he gives him what helps him with wealth or the like.

Omitting the object of praise or censure is concise (ijaz), so that the censure is directed at one of the two curses without specifying which, because both are wretched.

Applying rifd to the curse is a sarcastic metaphor (isti'arah tahakkumiyyah), like the saying of 'Amr ibn Ma'dikarib:

"Their greeting among themselves is a painful blow."

Al-marfud, in its literal sense, means one who is given something. The gift is described as marfud because each of the two curses is supported by the other. Each one is therefore likened to someone who has been given a gift, and so is marfud. The word marfud was made masculine in agreement with rifd, because it was applied to it as a masculine noun.

Page 157

The implied pronoun that is the object of praise (al-damir al-makhsus bi-al-madh al-mahdhuf), which is omitted, serves as the connecting element. This is a stripping away of the metaphor (tajrid lil-isti'arah), as in His saying ﴿bi'sa al-sharab﴾ (Wretched is the drink) [al-Kahf: 29], because the water that is the basis of comparison cannot be blameworthy.

Al-itba' means attaching (al-ilhaq).

Al-la'nah (the curse) is the curse of punishment in this world and in the Hereafter.

"On the Day of Resurrection" is connected to "they were pursued." It is thus known that they were pursued by a curse on the Day of Resurrection, because the first curse was restricted by the prepositional phrase introduced by the locative particle fi (in). Therefore it is determined that the pursuit on the Day of Resurrection is by another curse.

The clause ﴿bi'sa al-rifdu al-marfud﴾ is a new resumed clause (isti'naf) expressing the censure of the curse. The thing being censured is omitted, and the mention of the curse indicates it, meaning: "Wretched is the gift, it being [the curse]."

Al-rifdu, with a kasra on the ra', is a noun on the pattern fi'l in the sense of maf'ul, like dhibh. That is, what is given support, that is, what is given. It is said: rafadahu when he gives him what helps him with wealth or the like.

Omitting the object of praise or censure is concise (ijaz), so that the censure is directed at one of the two curses without specifying which, because both are wretched.

Applying rifd to the curse is a sarcastic metaphor (isti'arah tahakkumiyyah), like the saying of 'Amr ibn Ma'dikarib:

"Their greeting among themselves is a painful blow."

Al-marfud, in its literal sense, means one who is given something. The gift is described as marfud because each of the two curses is supported by the other. Each one is therefore likened to someone who has been given a gift, and so is marfud. The word marfud was made masculine in agreement with rifd, because it was applied to it as a masculine noun.

﴿That is some of the news of the towns. We relate it to you: some of them are standing and some are mown down.﴾ ﴿We did not wrong them, but they wronged themselves. Their gods, whom they called upon besides God, did not avail them anything when the command of your Lord came. They added nothing but ruin.﴾

This is a resumption (istinaf, a new sentence that is not grammatically dependent on what precedes it) to emphasize the importance of the news that has been mentioned.

The demonstrative (ism al-isharah) refers to everything mentioned of the stories, from the story of Noah (peace be upon him) onward.

Al-anba' is the plural of naba', which means news or report. It was discussed in Surat al-An'am in the words of God: ﴿And there has certainly come to you some of the news of the messengers﴾ [al-An'am: 34]. The clause "We relate it to you" is a circumstantial clause (hal) describing the demonstrative. He used the present tense although the stories are past, in order to evoke the state of these stories in their eloquent vividness.

The clause ﴿some of them are standing and some are mown down﴾ is a parenthetical clause (mu'taridah), and it is a circumstantial clause describing "the towns."

"Standing" (qa'im) is an adjective for a omitted noun, which is indicated by the conjunction of "mown down" (wa-hasid). The meaning is: among them is standing crop and mown crop. This is an eloquent metaphor (tashbih baligh).

Al-qa'im is the crop standing independently on its stalk. Al-hasid is the crop that has been harvested. It is the form fa'il in the sense of maf'ul. Both are likened to what remains of the towns and what has been effaced. What is meant by the standing is that among the towns which God recounted in the Qur'an, some remain standing, such as the monuments of the land of Pharaoh, like the Pyramids, Abu al-Hawl (known as the Sphinx), and the Karnak temple in Egypt, and like the ruins of Nineveh, the city of the people of Jonah; Antioch, the town of the three messengers; Sana'a, the city of the people of Tubba'; and ruined towns like the abodes of 'Ad, the towns of the people of Lot, and the town of Madyan. The towns mentioned in this surah are not meant exclusively. The purpose of this clause is consideration (i'tibar).

[Page 159]

The pronoun of the third person in "We did not wrong them" refers to the towns in terms of their inhabitants, because they are the intended subject.

God, exalted is He, did not wrong them because what befell them of punishment was a recompense for the evil of their deeds. Thus they were the ones who wronged themselves, since they brought punishment upon themselves.

He based upon their wronging themselves the negation that their gods availed them anything. The reason for this consequence and sequence is that their wronging of themselves was manifested in their worship of idols. When they worshipped them, they worshipped them to be delivered from the calamities of events, and so that they would be intercessors for them with God. They were secure from being struck by severity in this world, relying on their idols to repel it from them. When their command came in the opposite of that, this opposite contradicted their expectation and their assessment.

The purpose of this sequence is an indirect warning to the polytheists among the Arabs against relying on the benefit of the idols. The polytheists were certain that those nations worshipped idols. How, then, could these people have borrowed the worship of idols from the earlier nations? They were certain that the annihilation they had witnessed the traces of had befallen those nations. Thus this is an admonition for them, if they were guided.

The clause ﴿and they added nothing but ruin﴾ is an addition and an ascent beyond the fact that they were not of benefit at the time of need. It means that their condition was not merely that they did not avail them, but that they increased them in ruin and loss, that is, they increased them in the causes of loss.

Al-tatbib is the verbal noun of tabbabahu, when he caused him to fall into tibab, which is loss. The apparent meaning of this is that their idols increased them in ruin when the command of God came, because it is conjoined to the verb restricted by "lamma" of temporal specification, which conveys that this occurred at the time the command of God came, namely the descent of punishment upon them.

The aspect of their increasing them in ruin at that time is that their insistence on hoping that the idols would rescue them from calamities prevented them, and prevented them from repentance upon hearing the threat of punishment.

It is also possible that the conjunction is for mere sharing in the attribute without its restriction, meaning: they increased them in ruin before the command of God came, in that their belief in them diverted them from reflecting upon the signs of

[Page 160]

the messengers, and their hope in the idols increased them in ruin. The false myths and the baseless virtues attributed to the idols were enticing them to commit abominations, error, degradation of morals, and corruption of thought, with audacity against the messengers of God, until the anger of God, which required the descent of His punishment upon them, became due.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 11, verse 102:

﴿And such is the seizing of your Lord when He seizes the cities while they are wrongdoing. Indeed, His seizing is painful and severe.﴾

The reference is to what was mentioned of the annihilation of those cities, which is indicated by His saying: (﴿the seizing of your Lord﴾). The implied meaning is: "And such is the seizing by which We seized those cities; it is the seizing of your Lord when He seizes the cities." The comparison is in the manner and in the outcome.

The purpose of this concluding statement is an indirect warning to the idolatrous Arabs, of Makkah and elsewhere.

Al-zulm (wrongdoing) here means shirk (polytheism). The clause ﴿Indeed, His seizing is painful and severe﴾ is in the position of explaining the content of ﴿And such is the seizing of your Lord﴾. In it there is an indication of the aspect of the resemblance.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 11, verses 103–104:**

﴿Surely in that is a sign for whoever fears the punishment of the Hereafter. That is a Day on which mankind will be gathered, and that is a Day that will be witnessed.﴾ ﴿We delay it only for a limited term.﴾

This is an explanation of the allusion (ta'ridh) and an explicit statement after an indirect hint. The meaning is: "Thus is the seizing of your Lord. So beware of Him, and beware of what is even more severe than it, which is the punishment of the Hereafter." The reference is to the earlier seizing. In this there is an approach to exhorting the Muslims, and an indirect praise of them, in that those like them are the ones who benefit from the signs and take heed from the lessons, as in His saying: ﴿And none understands them except those who have knowledge﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 43].

[Page 161]

He made the punishment of this world a sign indicating the punishment of the Hereafter, because God threatened the wrongdoing towns with the punishment of this world and the punishment of the Hereafter, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed for those who did wrong there is a punishment short of that﴾ [al-Tur: 47]. So when they witnessed the punishment of this world, its realization was a sign of the realization of the other punishment.

The clause ﴿That is a Day on which mankind will be gathered﴾ is a parenthetical clause (mu'taridah) that draws attention to the importance of this Day, to the extent that the speaker begins a statement for the sake of describing it.

The demonstrative ﴿That﴾ refers to the Hereafter, because what it refers to is the Day of Resurrection. So the masculine form of the demonstrative is in agreement with the meaning of "the Hereafter."

The lam in (﴿majmu'un lahu﴾, "on which ... will be gathered") is the lam of cause, meaning: mankind is gathered for its sake.

The predicate coming as a nominal sentence in reporting about the Day indicates the meaning of permanence, i.e., the gathering of mankind by God for that Day is a fixed matter. It indicates the firmness of the connection of the gathering with mankind, and the firmness of the gathering being for the sake of that Day, to the extent that this Day was given the title "the Day of Assembly," in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The Day He gathers you for the Day of Assembly﴾ [al-Taghabun: 9].

The conjoining of the clause ﴿And that is a Day that will be witnessed﴾ to the clause ﴿That is a Day on which mankind will be gathered﴾ serves to increase the awe of the Day by stating that it will be witnessed. The agent is omitted, since what is intended is that it will be witnessed by those who witness it, because the aim is not to specific witnesses. The report about it in this way indicates that they will witness it with a special witnessing, namely the witnessing of an awe-inspiring thing, since it is known that one would not intend to report about it merely by its being visible; rather, what is meant is that it is visible in a special sight.

It is also possible that "witnessed" (mashhud) means "established," i.e., it is witnessed as to its occurrence, as one says: "a witnessed truth," meaning there is testimony to it that cannot be denied, clear to the eye.

It is also possible that "witnessed" means "attended by many witnesses" because of its fame, as one says: "For so-and-so is a witnessed assembly," like the words of Umm Qays al-Dabbiyya:

[Page 162]

And a gathering where I have sufficed those who speak about it,
In a council of forelocks of horses, well attended.

This would be of the kind of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿How then, when We bring from every nation a witness, and bring you as a witness against these?﴾ [al-Nisa': 41] ﴿On that Day those who disbelieved will wish...﴾ [al-Nisa': 42], and the verse.

The clause ﴿We delay it only for a limited term﴾ is a parenthetical clause between the clause ﴿That is a Day on which mankind will be gathered﴾ and the clause ﴿The Day it comes, no soul will speak except by His permission﴾ [Hud: 105], etc. The intended purpose is to refute those who deny resurrection, who argue from the delay of its occurrence, at the time of their denial of it, supposing that their denial angers God, so He hastens it for them. This is out of their ignorance of the station of divinity. So God made clear to them that its delay is until a term He set for it from the day of the creation of the world, just as He set the terms of living beings. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they say, "When is this promise, if you are truthful?"﴾ [Saba': 29] ﴿Say, "For you is an appointment of a Day from which you cannot delay an hour, nor advance it."﴾ [Saba': 30].

The term (ajal) originally means the period one waits for in a matter. It is also applied to the end of that period, and this is what is meant here, by the indication of the lam, as it is meant in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So when their term comes﴾ [al-A'raf: 34].

The word (ma'dud) originally means "counted." Here it is used figuratively to mean "specified and fixed," such that it neither delays nor advances, because what is counted necessarily has definiteness; or it is used figuratively to mean "near."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 11, verses 105–108:

Page 163
﴿On the day it comes, no soul will speak except by His permission. Among them will be the wretched and the happy.﴾ ﴿As for those who were wretched, they will be in the Fire, where for them is groaning and wailing.﴾ ﴿Abiding therein for as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills. Indeed, your Lord is the Accomplisher of what He intends.﴾ ﴿As for those who were made happy, they will be in the Garden, abiding therein for as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills — a gift unbroken.﴾

The clause ﴿On the day it comes, no soul will speak﴾ is an elaboration of the implication of the clause ﴿That is a Day for which mankind will be gathered﴾ [Hud: 103], and it clarifies the magnitude of that Day regarding both evil and good, following that elaboration. The primary purpose of this clause is His saying: ﴿Among them will be the wretched and the happy﴾ and what follows it, while what precedes it serves as a preface to it, expressing the magnitude of that Day. The arrangement of the speech has come with an inversion of order, required by the parenthetical placement of the emphasis on the terror of the Day within the connected discourse, because that is more suited to the harmony of the speech's aims. Adverbs of time are suitable for connecting speech, just as coordinating particles and conditional particles are.

The word (yawm) in His saying (yawma ya'ti) is used in the sense of (ḥīn) "time" or (sā'ah) "hour". This is a common usage in Arabic with the words yawm and layla, as a broadening by applying them to a part of their time, since time cannot be free of occurring either in daytime or at night, so that is a yawm or a layla. When these two are used in this way, nothing is conveyed by them except the meaning of ḥīn, without specification of a duration, nor of daytime or nighttime. Do you not see the saying of al-Nābigha:

"They chose from the rivers of the day of Ḥalīma"

Here he attributed (anhār), the plural of (nahār), to (yawm). It is also related as: "from the times of the day of Ḥalīma."

And the saying of Tawba ibn al-Ḥumayyir:

"As if the heart, the night it was said: 'It is taken out in the morning ∗∗∗ with Layla al-Akhyaliyya or in the evening'"

Page 164
He meant the hour when it was said, "It is taken out in the morning with Layla," and therefore he said, "in the morning or in the evening," without observing what suits the word "night" regarding evening.

So His saying, exalted is He: "on the day it comes" means "at the time it comes." The pronoun in "it comes" refers to a "Day witnessed," which is the Day of Resurrection. What is meant by its coming is its occurrence and its arrival, as in His saying: "Do they await anything but that the Hour should come upon them?"

So His saying "on the day it comes" is an adverbial phrase related to His saying: "no soul will speak except by His permission."

The clause "no soul will speak" is an independent initial sentence. The adverb preceded its verb for the aforementioned purpose. The meaning is: no soul will speak at the time the witnessed Day arrives. The pronoun in "by His permission" refers to God, exalted is He, understood from the context and from the pronoun in "We defer it." The meaning is that no one speaks except with permission from God, as in His saying: "On the day when the Spirit and the angels stand in rows, none will speak except one whom the Most Merciful permits and who speaks rightly" [al-Naba': 38]. The purpose of this is to nullify the belief of the people of ignorance that the idols have a right to intercession with God.

"Soul" (nafs), being in a negative context, encompasses all souls, so it includes both the righteous and the wicked souls, and includes the speech of the intercessor and the speech of one who argues on his own behalf. The generality of souls is specified by the difference of their conditions. This specification conveys the classification of people in His saying: "to which mankind will be gathered" [Hud: 103], but it has come in this arrangement because of what intervened in that, a semblance of parenthetical insertion with His saying: "And We do not defer it except for a counted term" [Hud: 104], up to His saying "by His permission," and that is a wondrous composition.

Al-shaqiyy: (fa'īl) is an adjective of the attributive form from (shaqiya), when one is afflicted with misery and wretchedness, that is, bad condition and its harm, and what is repugnant to the nature of one characterized by it.

Al-sa'īd: the opposite of the shaqiyy, and it is one afflicted with happiness, which is the good, beneficial conditions suitable to the one characterized by them. The meaning: among them on that day are those who are in punishment and hardship, and among them are those who are in bliss and ease.

Page 165
Wretchedness and happiness are among the gradable concepts (mawāhī maqūla bi-al-tashkīk), so each of them has many degrees, varying in the strength of the attribute. This is a summary whose detail is: ﴿As for those who were wretched﴾ to its end.

Zafīr: expelling breaths with force and intensity due to the pressure of breathing. Shahīq is its opposite, which is drawing air into the chest with intensity due to the strong need for breathing.

Among their conditions in Hell, He singled out for mention the zafīr and shahīq, as a warning against the causes of the destination to the Fire, because mentioning these two states carries disfigurement of them, and that is more fearful for them than pain.

The meaning of "as long as the heavens and the earth endure" is permanence, because it has become like a proverb; otherwise the well-known heavens and earth will vanish on that day. He, exalted is He, said: "On the day the earth will be changed to other than the earth, and the heavens" [Ibrahim: 48]. Or it is intended: the heavens and earth of the Hereafter.

And ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾ is an exception from the periods encompassed by the adverb in His saying "as long as," meaning: except the periods in which God wills their non-eternity, and this entails the exception of some of those who abide, following the periods. This is based on the predominant usage of the relative "mā" as for non-rational beings. It is also permissible that it be an exception from the pronoun in "abiding" (khālidīn), because "mā" is frequently applied to the rational, as in His saying: "Marry what seems good to you of women" [al-Nisa': 3].
