The majority read "su'idu" (sa'idu) with a fatḥa on the sīn, while Ḥamza, al-Kisā'ī, Ḥafṣ from 'Āṣim, and Khalaf read it with a ḍamma on the sīn, as passive voice (mabnī lil-nā'ib), even though the original verb is intransitive with no object. But it is treated as transitive, meaning: one was done to such that he became the possessor of that state, as in their saying: "junna fulān" (so-and-so became possessed) when something was done to him that made him one with madness. Thus "su'idu" means "use'idu" (were made happy). It has also been said: "sa'ida" is transitive in the dialect of Hudhayl and Tamīm, who say: "sa'idahu Allāh" meaning "as'adahu Allāh" (God made him happy). It is also explained that its original form was "use'idu," and the hamza of increase was dropped, as they said "majnūb" (with a ba' at its end), and from it their saying: "rajul mas'ūd" (a fortunate man).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 11, verse 109:

Page 167
﴿So do not be in doubt concerning what these worship. They worship only as their fathers worshipped before. And indeed, We will give them their full share without reduction.﴾

This is a consequence (tafri') drawn from the preceding narratives, for they instill in the listener certainty about the falsehood of what the idol-worshippers hold to, and about the failure of what they hoped for from these idols of intercession in this world. The earlier wretchedness of their destruction in this world by the punishment of annihilation (al-isti'sal) indicates the evil of their condition in the Hereafter. Thus it is made a consequence: a prohibition to the listener from doubting the evil and corruption of polytheism.

The address in phrases such as ﴿So do not be in doubt﴾ is directed to any listener, not to a specific listener, whether or not he is one who might be suspected of doubting this, since the intended addressee is not specified.

It is also possible that the address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), and that "la taku" (do not be) is intended merely to affirm the report, for it has become like a proverb in the speech of the Arabs, like the expressions: "la shakka" (there is no doubt), "la mahalata" (there is no doubt), "la a'rifannaka" (I will not know you), and similar.

It is also possible that it is a reassurance (tathbit) for the Prophet (ﷺ) regarding what he encounters from his people of obstinacy in polytheism, meaning: do not be a doubter that you have encountered from your people denial similar to what the messengers encountered from their nations, for these people worship only as their fathers worshipped before, inheriting it from their predecessors among the perished nations.

The "fi" (in) is for figurative (majazi) containment.

Al-miryah (with a kasra on the mim) is doubt. Its verb has come in the pattern fa'ala, or tafa'ala and if'tala. It has not come in the bare pattern, because the root of al-mira' is disputation and contention, metaphorically taken from "maraytu al-shah" when I extract its milk. From this is their saying: "la yujara wa la yumara" (he is not disputed with and not contended with). In the Qur'an: ﴿Will you then dispute with him over what he sees?﴾ [al-Najm: 12]. The notion of contention (al-imtira') was mentioned earlier at His words: ﴿Then you still doubt﴾ [al-An'am: 2] at the beginning of al-An'am.

Page 168
The "ma" in His words "ma ya'budu" is a verbal-source (masdariyyah), meaning: do not be in doubt about the worship of these people. The reference of "these" (ha'ula') is to the idolaters of Quraysh.

I have traced the Qur'anic usage and found that it refers to them with this demonstrative (hadha) in about eleven places, and this is among what I was guided to and drew attention to at His words, exalted is He: ﴿And We bring you as a witness over these﴾ [al-Nisa': 41] in Surat al-Nisa'.

The meaning of doubt concerning their worship is nothing other than doubt concerning its matter, because their worship was known to the Prophet (ﷺ), so there is no sense in negating his doubt about it. Rather, what is intended is the negation of doubt about what may afflict him of doubt as to whether God will punish them in this world or leave them to the punishment of the Hereafter.

The clause ﴿They worship only as their fathers worshipped before﴾ is a resumed (mustanaf'ah) sentence, serving as a justification (ta'lil) for the absence of doubt about the outcome of their affair in this world.

The reason it is a cause is that, since their religion is identical to the religion of those who were before them from their fathers, and what God did to them has reached you, punishing them for their religion, you are certain that their recompense will be similar to the recompense of their predecessors, because God's wisdom requires equality in recompense for similar deeds.

The exception in His words ﴿except as their fathers worshipped﴾ is an exception from the generality of verbal-sources. The kaf of comparison stands in place of an omitted verbal-source. The estimate: except worship as their fathers worshipped.

"Fathers" is applied to the predecessors, namely 'Ad and Thamud. This is because the 'Adnani Arabs had as their mother a Jurhumite woman, who was the wife of Isma'il, and Jurhum were brothers of Thamud, and Thamud were brothers of 'Ad. Also, Quraysh had as their mother a Khuza'i woman, who was the wife of Qusayy. The worship of idols among the Arabs was brought to them by 'Amr ibn Luhayy, who was the grandfather of Khuza'ah.

He expressed the worship of the fathers with the present tense to indicate their continuity in that worship, meaning: except as their fathers habitually worshipped. The indication of past time is His words "min qabl" (before),

Page 169
as if it were said: except as their fathers were worshipping. The noun to which "qabl" is added is omitted, its estimate being "min qablihim" (before them), to make explicit that they were their predecessors in this error and that they followed them.

The clause ﴿And indeed, We will give them their full share﴾ is coordinated (atf) upon the clause of causation, and the coordinated element is the caused element, and the meaning of the kaf of comparison has governed it for this reason. So the meaning: And indeed, We will give them their share of the punishment just as We fulfilled it for their predecessors.

Tawfiyah (fulfilment) is the completion of a thing without deficiency.

Al-nasib: its origin is portion (al-hazz). Here "muwaffuhum" (We will give them in full) and "nasibahum" (their share) are used in a mocking (tahakkumi) manner, as if they had a gift they were asking for and it was given to them in full. So His words ﴿without reduction﴾ come as an emphatic circumstantial clause (hal) to confirm the fulfilment, increasing the mockery; for among the honouring of one promised a gift is that the promise be affirmed for him, and this is called glad tidings (bishara).

The intended meaning is their share of the punishment of the Hereafter, for God did not uproot them as He uprooted the earlier nations, by the blessing of the Prophet (ﷺ), when he said: "Perhaps God will bring forth from their loins one who will worship Him."

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 11, verse 110:**

﴿And We certainly gave Moses the Scripture, but it was disputed over.﴾

This is a parenthetical clause (i'tiraḍ) given to strengthen the Prophet ﷺ and console him: the People of the Scripture, who are in a better state than the people of polytheism, were given the Scripture and then disagreed about it, and they belong to one religious community. So do not grieve over your people's opposition to you. The sentence is joined by conjunction (ʿaṭf) to the sentence ﴿So do not be in doubt﴾ [Hud: 109].

Because of the sense of strengthening it contains, He made the next statement a consequence of it: ﴿So be upright as you have been commanded﴾ [Hud: 112].

His words "it was disputed over" mean: concerning the Scripture, which is the Torah. The disagreement about it consists of the disagreement of the people of the Torah over affirming some of it and nullifying some of it, over making some of it apparent and concealing some of it, such as the ruling on stoning; over interpreting parts of it according to their desires; and over attributing things to the Scripture as though they were from it. As He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So woe to those who write the Scripture with their own hands and then say, "This is from Allah"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 79]. This is the kind of thing that happens among some of them, not all of them, and so it entails disagreement among them between an affirmer and a denier. This disagreement, in its types and conditions, returns to disagreement about some part of the Scripture. So these meanings were gathered in a wonderful way by the transitive use of the particle (fī), which indicates a figurative sense of place (ẓarfiyya majaziyya) and is like "accompaniment." That is: it was disputed in a manner that accompanies it, i.e., accompanies the Scripture.

Because the purpose was not concerned with specifying the disputants, nor with blaming them, since among them are the blameworthy, who initiated the disagreement, and among them are the praiseworthy, who denounced the distorters, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Among them is a moderate community, but many of them—evil is what they do﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 66]. His statement will come: ﴿And indeed, your Lord will fully compensate them for their deeds﴾ [Hud: 111]. Rather, it was for warning against falling into the like of it.

The verb (ukhtulifa) is in the passive voice, because the only purpose is mention of the act, not of its doer.

\* \* \*

﴿And had it not been for a word that preceded from your Lord, it would have been decided between them﴾

This may be joined by conjunction to the sentence ﴿And indeed, We will fully pay them their share without reduction﴾ [Hud: 109], and the parenthetical clause would then end at His words "it was disputed over." In that case the pronoun in (baynahum, "between them") refers to the demonstrative in His words ﴿what these worship﴾ [Hud: 109]. That is: had it not been for what preceded from the wisdom of Allah, that He delay the punishment from them, it would have been decided between them; that is, Allah would have decided between them, destroying the polytheists and the opponents and granting victory to the believers.

In this case, (baynahum) is the deputy subject of (quḍiya, "was decided"). The sense is: the punishment would have befallen them, i.e., among them.

It may also be joined by conjunction to the sentence (fa-ukhtulifa fīhi, "so it was disputed over"). Then the pronoun in (baynahum) refers to what is understood from His words "it was disputed over," because that implies a group of disputants regarding the rulings of the Scripture. (Baynahum) is then connected to (quḍiya): that is, a judgment would have been made among them by making manifest the correct from the erroneous in the rulings of the Scripture. This becomes a warning against disagreement; that is, if it occurs, Allah grants respite to the disputants and leaves them in doubt. It is not part of Allah's way to decide among the disputants in a way that brings them to distinguish the true from the false. So you must beware of disagreement regarding your Scripture, for if you disagree you will remain in doubt and the recompense of your deeds will befall you.

The (kalimah, "word") is the eternal will of Allah and His custom regarding His creation. It is that He left people to the guidance of the Messengers to invite to Allah, and to reflect upon the signs, and then to exert complete effort in reaching the truth, and to strive for agreement and to reject disagreement, by directing sound understandings toward meanings, by mutual consultation, by insight into the truth, by fairness in debate and argument, and by making the truth their goal and effort their constant practice and habit. The wisdom of this is that distinguishing and being guided to the truth is a benefit and advantage for people, not for Allah. The full benefit of this is attained by their exerting their effort and employing their reflections, because that is a means to increasing their intellect and thinking. This has already been mentioned in His words, exalted is He: ﴿And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and justice﴾ [al-An'am: 115] in Surat al-An'am, and in His words: ﴿And Allah intends to establish the truth by His words﴾ [al-Anfal: 7] in Surat al-Anfal.

He described it as "preceding" because it is eternal, with regard to the knowledge's connection to its occurrence, and because it returns to a universal custom established from before.

The meaning of ﴿it would have been decided between them﴾ is that it would have been a judgment of annihilating the falsifier and preserving the truthful, as Allah judged between the Messengers and their deniers. However, Allah's will required otherwise with respect to the understanding of the community regarding its Scripture.

The pronoun in (baynahum) refers to the disputants implied by His words "it was disputed over," and the indication is clear.

The object of the judgment is omitted because it is evident; that is, it would have been decided between them concerning what they disputed, as He said in another verse: ﴿Indeed, your Lord will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection concerning that over which they used to differ﴾ [al-Sajdah: 25].

\* \* \*

﴿And indeed, they are in disquieting doubt concerning it﴾

This may be joined by conjunction to the sentence ﴿And indeed, We will fully pay them their share without reduction﴾ [Hud: 109]. Then the pronoun in (wa-innahum, "and indeed they") refers to what the pronoun in (mā yaʿbudūn, "what they worship") referred to in the verse; that is, indeed the polytheists are in doubt about the fulfillment of their share, because they do not believe in the Resurrection. This fits with His words ﴿And had it not been for a word that preceded from your Lord, it would have been decided between them﴾ according to the first and preferred of the two possibilities. Then the pronoun in (minhu, "concerning it") refers to (yawm, "day") in His words ﴿The Day when no soul will speak except by His permission﴾ [Hud: 105], and so on.

It may also be joined by conjunction to the sentence (fa-ukhtulifa fīhi, "so it was disputed over"). That is: "so its people disagreed concerning it," i.e., the People of the Scripture. Then the pronoun in (wa-innahum) refers to what the pronoun in (baynahum) referred to according to the second possibility; that is: they disagreed concerning their Scripture, and indeed they are in doubt.

As for the pronoun in (minhu, "concerning it"), it may refer to the Scripture: that is, they proceeded to what they proceeded to while in doubt and hesitation about their Scripture, i.e., without knowledge that produces certainty, such as the inductive examination of the legal proofs by our scholars, or knowledge that produces a probability close to certainty, like the conjecture of the mujtahid (qualified jurist) regarding what his effort has reached. This is because a sound inference derived from the Scripture is not considered disagreement regarding the Scripture, since the basis is agreed upon. So the basis of blame is disagreement regarding the text of the Scripture, not in deriving branches from its proofs. The pronoun in (minhu) may also refer to the Qur'an, understood from the context and from His words ﴿That is from the reports of the towns which We relate to you﴾ [Hud: 100].

(Al-Murib) means the one that causes doubt. Describing doubt with this word is an emphasis, like the saying "a dark night" (layl alyal) and "a poetic poem" (shiʿr shāʿir).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 11, verse 111:

Page 173

﴿And indeed, to all of them your Lord will surely pay in full for their deeds. Indeed, He is Acquainted with what they do.﴾

This is a concluding statement (tadhyil) appended to the preceding reports. The wa is parenthetical (i'tiradiyyah). The (in) is a lightened form of (inna, indeed) in the heavy form, according to the reading of Nafi', Ibn Kathir, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim, and its grammatical function (i'mal) is exercised on its noun, so that the noun after it is in the accusative. When the lightened (in) is followed by a nominal sentence, its government (i'mal) is frequent and its non-government (ihmal) is also frequent; this was said by al-Khalil, Sibawayh, and the grammarians of Basra, and it is the correct view. The rest read (inna) with the doubled nun, according to the original form.

The (kullan) carries tanwin as a replacement (iwad) for the genitive noun that has been omitted. The estimated sense is: "and indeed all of them," i.e., all those mentioned just above from among the people of the towns, and the polytheists alluded to, and those among the followers of Musa (peace be upon him) who differed concerning the Book.

The (lamma) is lightened in the reading of Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, and al-Kisa'i, so the lam that enters upon (ma) is the lam of initiation (lam al-ibtida') which enters upon the predicate of (inna). The second lam that enters upon (layuwaffiyannahum) is the lam of the answer to an oath (lam jawab al-qasam). The (ma) is an added particle for emphasis (za'idah li al-ta'kid). The separation between the two lams is to avert the disliked succession of two similar elements.

Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, 'Asim, Abu Ja'far, and Khalaf read (lamma) with a doubled mim. As for those who read (in) lightened and doubled the mim, namely Abu Bakr from 'Asim, then (in) is a lightened form of the heavy (inna). As for those who doubled the nun of (inna) and doubled the mim of (lamma), namely Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, Hafs from 'Asim, Abu Ja'far, and Khalaf, the justification of their reading and the reading of Abu Bakr is what al-Farra' said: it means (li-man ma), and one of the three mims was elided. He means that (lamma) is not a single word, although in its form it resembles the letter (lamma) in the orthography of the Mushaf, because he followed in it the form of pronunciation. Rather, it is composed of the lam of initiation and (min), the genitive particle, which is used to express the frequent repetition of an action, as in the verse of Abu Hayyah al-Numayri:

Page 174

"And indeed we, when we strike the ram with a blow upon its head, the tongue flies out from the mouth."

That is: we frequently strike the ram, i.e., the commander of the enemy's army, upon his head. And the saying of Ibn 'Abbas: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to encounter severe hardship from the revelation, and among what moved his tongue when the Qur'an was sent down upon him was that. So Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Do not move your tongue with it to hasten it﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 16], and so on." So the original of these words in the verse, according to these readings, is: "and indeed to all of them, min ma, layuwaffiyannahum." When the nun of (min) was changed into a mim for its assimilation into the mim of (ma), three mims accumulated, so the first mim was elided for lightness, which is the mim of (min), because there is evidence for it, namely the second mim, since the original of the second mim is the nun of (min). Thus it became (lamma).
The lam of (layuwaffiyannahum) is the lam of oath.

The sense of plurality in this verse is a metonymy (kinayah) for the non-escape of any group of those who differ concerning the Book from the infliction of the requital for their deeds upon them.

The meaning is: "And indeed all of them will surely meet the recompense of their deeds; not one of them will escape. And Allah's paying them their deeds in full is something Allah has established and has not been lenient about." This interpretation is the most preferred of the aspects on which this reading has been based, and it is narrated from al-Farra'; al-Mahdawi followed him, as did Nasr al-Shirazi the grammarian, and al-Baydawi adopted it. Abu Shamah, in his commentary on al-Shatibi's poem, brought the number of aspects to six, and others brought them to eight.

In the Tafsir of al-Razi: I heard some of the virtuous scholars say: When Allah, the Exalted, reported the full payment of recompense to those deserving it in this verse, He mentioned in it seven types of emphases. The first: the word (inna), which is for emphasis. The second: (kull), which is also for emphasis. The third: the lam that enters upon the predicate of inna. The fourth: the particle (ma) when we make it a relative pronoun according to the view of al-Farra'. The fifth: the implied oath. The sixth: the lam that enters upon the answer to the oath. The seventh: the emphatic nun in His saying: layuwaffiyannahum.

The full payment of their deeds means the full payment of the recompense of the deeds, i.e., giving the recompense in full: good for good deeds, and evil for evil deeds.

The clause ﴿Indeed, He is Acquainted with what they do﴾ is a resumptive statement and a justification for the full payment, because the all-encompassing knowledge of their deeds, together with the will to recompense them, necessitates that the recompense correspond to the deed in complete correspondence. And that is the realization of full payment.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 11, verse 112:

﴿So be steadfast as you have been commanded, and [so too] those who turn [to God] with you.﴾

Following on from the consolation contained in His words: ﴿And We gave Moses the Book, but it was disputed over﴾ [Hud: 110], and from the reassurance indicated by His words: ﴿So do not be in doubt about what these worship﴾ [Hud: 109], comes the exhortation to persevere in holding fast to Islam in an upright manner. He expressed this by "steadfastness" (istiqamah) to indicate perseverance in acting upon the teachings of Islam, a perseverance whose essence is remaining steadfast in it and guarding against altering it.

Since the disagreement over the Book of Moses, peace be upon him, arose only from the People of the Book, He joined to the command to the Prophet ﷺ to be steadfast in accordance with his Book a command to the believers to be steadfast in the same way as well. This is because deviation (i'wijaj) is among the causes of disagreement over the Book, through groups from the Community rising up to alter it in order to accommodate their desires. Moreover, the Community's deliberate opposition to the rulings of its own Book is nothing but a form of disagreement over it, since it is disagreement against its rulings. In a hadith: "Those before you were destroyed only by the abundance of their questions and their disagreement with their prophets." Thus steadfastness was necessarily a barrier against this, for steadfastness is acting upon the complete Shari'ah such that one does not deviate from it by the width of a finger-span (qid shibr). Its object is acting upon the Shari'ah

Page 176

after belief, because belief is a foundation, and steadfastness does not attach to it. The meaning of this has been indicated by the words of the Prophet ﷺ to Abu 'Amrah al-Thaqafi when he said to him: "O Messenger of God, tell me a saying about Islam about which I shall not ask anyone other than you. He said: Say, 'I have believed in God,' then be steadfast." He thus made steadfastness something that comes after belief.

The command was addressed to the Prophet ﷺ as an honouring of him, so that the words "as you have been commanded" might be built upon it, indicating that he is the first recipient of the legislative commands. This is an honouring of him in regard to the station of his messengership. Then He informed of it through addressing his community with His words: ﴿and those who turn [to God] with you﴾. The particle of comparison (ka) in His words "as you have been commanded" is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the steadfastness derived from "be steadfast." The meaning of comparing the steadfastness commanded to that which the Prophet ﷺ was commanded is that steadfastness is of the same kind as all else he was commanded, and it is the comparison of the general (mujmal) to the detailed (mufassal) in its detail, in that it should correspond to it. This meaning reverts to the ka being in the sense of "upon," as one says: "Be as you are," i.e., do not change, and let your future circumstances resemble this state of yours.

(Those who turn) is conjoined to the pronoun attached in "you have been commanded." The justification for the conjunction exists, namely the separation by the prepositional phrase.

"Those who turn" are the believers, since belief is a repentance from polytheism. "With you" is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to "turn," and is not attached to "turn," because the Prophet ﷺ was not among the polytheists.

His words ﴿So be steadfast as you have been commanded﴾ gathered the roots and branches of religious righteousness through His words "as you have been commanded."

Ibn 'Abbas said: No verse was revealed to the Messenger of God ﷺ that was harder or more difficult upon him than this verse. For this reason he said to his companions, when they said to him: "Grey hair has come to you quickly": "Hud and its sisters have made me grey." He was asked about what is in Hud, and he said: His words ﴿So be steadfast as you have been commanded﴾.

* * *

﴿And do not transgress. Indeed, He is Seeing of what you do.﴾

The address in His words "and do not transgress" is directed to the believers upon whom "and those who turn [to God] with you" applies.

Transgression (tughyan) originally means self-aggrandisement, boldness and lack of concern. It was discussed in His words, exalted is He: ﴿And He extends them in their transgression, wandering blindly﴾ [al-Baqarah: 15] in Surah al-Baqarah. What is meant here is boldness in opposing what they were commanded, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Eat of the good things with which We have provided you, and do not transgress therein, lest My anger descend upon you﴾ [Ta-Ha: 81]. Thus God forbade the Muslims from opposing the rulings of His Book, just as He forbade the Children of Israel.

Transgression encompasses the roots of corruptions, so the verse comprehends the establishment of benefits and the averting of harms. The prohibition of it therefore comprehends the sources of corruption from the corrupter's own self, and what remains of what is feared as contagion of corruption from one's associate is the object of the prohibition in His words after this: ﴿And do not incline toward those who did wrong, lest the Fire touch you﴾ [Hud: 113].

From al-Hasan al-Basri: God made the religion between two prohibitions: ﴿And do not transgress﴾ and ﴿And do not incline﴾ [Hud: 113].

The clause ﴿Indeed, He is Seeing of what you do﴾ is a resumptive clause warning whoever conceals transgression that God is aware of every deed that the Muslims do. For this reason the attribute "Seeing" (basir) was chosen from among the rest of the Most Beautiful Names, because its root indicates clear knowledge and its form indicates the strength of that knowledge.

**[Page 178]**

*Al-rukūn* means leaning toward and agreeing with something, and its verb is conjugated like *ʿalima* (*rakana*, *yarkunu*). It may be derived from *al-rukn*, meaning the side, with a *ḍamma* on the *rāʾ* and a *sukūn* after it, because a person who inclines brings his side close to the thing he is inclined toward. Here it is used figuratively for agreeing with someone. So, after forbidding them from transgression, He forbade them from drawing close to the polytheists, lest they lead them astray and make them slip away from Islam.

*Those who have done wrong* (*alladhīna ẓalamū*) are the polytheists. This verse is a foundation for *sadd al-dharāʾiʿ* (blocking the means to corruption), whether the corruption is certain or presumed.

*Al-massu* is used here in the sense of striking or befalling, as was explained earlier in His saying, ﴿Indeed, those who fear God, when an impulse from Satan touches them﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 201], at the end of *al-Aʿrāf*. The intended meaning is the Fire of punishment in Hell.

The clause ﴿and you have no protectors other than God﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*), meaning: you will not find anyone who strives for what benefits you.

*Thumma* indicates a *tarākhī rutbī* (a sequence of rank, i.e. a greater gradation), meaning: you will not find anyone who helps you, that is, anyone who lightens for you the touch of the punishment of the Fire or brings you out of it.

The phrase *min dūni Allāh* (other than God) is connected to *awliyāʾ* (protectors) because it is implicitly *taḍmīn* (imputing the sense of another word) to it the meaning of defenders and those who shield.

His saying, ﴿and do not transgress﴾ [Hūd: 112], and His saying, ﴿and do not incline toward those who have done wrong﴾, together encompass the two roots of the religion, which are faith and righteous action. Al-Ḥasan's statement mentioned just before this is relevant: God made the religion lie between two negations: ﴿and do not transgress﴾ [Hūd: 112] and ﴿and do not incline﴾.

[Page 179]

He moved from addressing the believers to addressing the Prophet ﷺ. This address encompasses the entire community, as indicated by the fact that what is commanded is among the obligations incumbent on all Muslims, especially since it is mentioned alongside what corresponds to the specified times of the five prayers. This is what the ḥadīth of Abū al-Yusr, cited below, requires.

The *ṭaraf* (extremity) of a thing is its end, either its beginning or its finish. Thus the dual form is explicit that the intended meaning is the beginning of the day and its end.

The *nahār* (daytime) is the period between dawn and the setting of the sun. It was named *nahār* because light "yanhar" (gushes forth) in it, that is, it emerges just as a river (*nahr*) flows forth.

The command to "establish" (*iqāmah*) indicates that it is an obligatory act, because *iqāmah* is performing an act in the manner it deserves. This requires that the intended meaning of *al-ṣalāh* here is the obligatory prayer. The two extremities are thus times for establishing the obligatory prayer. It is therefore known that what is commanded is the performance of a prayer at the beginning of the day, which is the Ṣubḥ (dawn prayer), and a prayer at its end, which is the ʿAṣr (afternoon prayer), though it has been said to be the Maghrib (sunset prayer).

The *zulaf* is the plural of *zulfah*, like *ghurfah* and *ghuraf*, and it means an hour close to its neighbouring hour. Thus it is known that what is commanded is the performance of prayer during "zulaf" of the night. Since the prayers commanded to be established within this period of time are not specified, this was general (*mujmal*), and so the Sunnah and the mass-transmitted practice (*al-ʿamal al-mutawātir*) clarified it: five prayers, namely Ṣubḥ, Ẓuhr, ʿAṣr, Maghrib and ʿIshāʾ. This was an explanation of many verses of the Qur'an which were general in specifying the times of the prayers, such as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Establish the prayer at the decline of the sun until the darkness of the night, and the recitation of dawn; indeed, the recitation of dawn is witnessed﴾ [al-Isrāʾ: 78].

The purpose is that the prayer should be the first of the Muslim's actions when he rises in the morning, which is the Ṣubḥ prayer, and the last of his actions when he enters the evening, which is the ʿIshāʾ prayer, so that the bad deeds occurring in between are effaced by the good deeds surrounding them. This points to the wisdom behind the disapproval of conversation after the ʿIshāʾ prayer, in order to encourage prayer, especially those prayers performed at times when negligence of them is likely. The obligation of these two prayers has been established by other evidences, and there is nothing in this verse that requires restricting the obligation to what is mentioned in it.

[Page 180]

The clause ﴿Indeed, good deeds remove bad deeds﴾ is brought as a justification for the command to establish the prayers, and the clause is emphasised by the particle *inna* for emphasis and to affirm the statement. The *inna* here conveys the meaning of causation and consequence. This causation indicates that God made good deeds remove bad deeds, and the causation implies the generality of the doers of good deeds, because it is the norm that the cause is more general than the effect, together with what the definite article on the plural noun implies of generality.

The removal of bad deeds includes preventing their occurrence, by making the soul's inclination to abandon bad deeds easy and light, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the prayer forbids indecency and wrongdoing﴾ [al-ʿAnkabūt: 45]. This is among the properties of all good deeds. It also includes erasing their sin when they occur, and this is among the properties of all good deeds, a bounty from God upon His righteous servants.

The scope of "bad deeds" here is taken to be minor sins that are of the category of *al-lamam* (minor lapses), applying the absolute of this verse to the qualified (*muqayyad*) verse: ﴿those who avoid major sins and indecencies, except minor lapses﴾ [al-Najm: 32], and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If you avoid the major sins that you are forbidden, We will remove from you your bad deeds﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 31]. From the totality of these verses it results that avoiding indecencies is what God made a cause for the forgiveness of minor sins, or that performing good deeds removes the effect of minor bad deeds. This has been discussed earlier at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If you avoid the major sins that you are forbidden, We will remove from you your bad deeds﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 31], in Sūrat al-Nisāʾ.

Al-Bukhārī narrated from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd, may Allah be pleased with him, that: "A man had touched a woman unlawfully by kissing her, and came to the Prophet ﷺ and mentioned that. Then there was revealed to him: ﴿And establish the prayer at the two ends of the day and in the first hours of the night﴾. The man said: 'Is this for me?' He said: 'It is for whoever among my community acts upon it.'"

Al-Tirmidhī narrated from Ibn Masʿūd, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "A man came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: 'I have been with a woman at the far end of the city, and I have done with her what is less than having intercourse with her, and here I am, so judge me as you wish.' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ did not return him any answer. The man left, and the Prophet sent a man after him and called him, and recited to him: ﴿And establish the prayer at the two ends of the day﴾ to the end of the verse. A man from the people said: 'Is this for him alone?' He said: 'No, rather it is for all people.'" Al-Tirmidhī said: "This is a ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ ḥadīth." Al-Tirmidhī also recorded two other ḥadīths, one from Muʿādh ibn Jabal and the other from Abū al-Yusr, who is the companion of the story, and he declared both weak.

It is apparent that the narration concerning this verse is what led Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatādah to say that this verse is Madanī, distinct from the rest of this sūrah, because it occurs in the narrations of al-Bukhārī and al-Tirmidhī: "Then it was revealed to him." If this is so, as the narrator mentioned, then this verse was appended to this sūrah in this place because of the connection with the occurrence before it of His saying: ﴿So be steadfast as you have been commanded﴾ [Hūd: 112], and after it His saying: ﴿And be patient, for indeed Allah does not waste the reward of the good-doers﴾ [Hūd: 115].

As for those who preferred that the whole sūrah is Makkī, they said: the verse was revealed concerning the command to establish the prayers, and that the Prophet ﷺ informed the one who asked about the unlawful kiss, and he had come repentant, to inform him with His saying: ﴿Indeed, good deeds remove bad deeds﴾. So the narrator's words "then it was revealed to him" are interpreted to mean that there was revealed to him the inclusion, in the generality of good and bad deeds, of the questioner's case and of all similar cases of committing sins other than indecencies.

This is supported by what is in al-Tirmidhī's narration from ʿAlqamah and al-Aswad from Ibn Masʿūd, that he said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited to him: ﴿And establish the prayer﴾," and they did not say: "then it was revealed to him."

His saying: ﴿That is a reminder for those who remember﴾, meaning: a reminder for the one whose nature is to take heed, and whose disposition is not to turn away from seeking guidance and good. This expressly conveys generality. His saying "That" (*dhālika*) is a reference to what was mentioned before it, from His saying: ﴿So be steadfast as you have been commanded﴾ [Hūd: 112].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 11, verse 115:

Page 182
﴿And be patient, for indeed Allah does not allow the reward of the doers of good to be lost.﴾ It is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon the clause ﴿So do not be in doubt about what these worship﴾ [Hud: 109] and what follows it, because it was brought in the manner of strengthening (al-tathbit) [the Prophet] in the face of the delay of the punishment of those who denied.

The occasion for the command to patience following the command to uprightness (al-istiqamah) and the prohibition against inclining toward those who did wrong is that the things commanded are never free of great hardship and of opposition to the desires of many souls. Therefore it was fitting that the command to patience come after that, so that patience would be [exercised] in all of this, each in its proper measure.

Addressing the Prophet ﷺ directly is an honouring of him. What is intended is he and his community (ummah), as indicated by the causal clause ﴿indeed Allah does not allow the reward of the doers of good to be lost﴾, because of its generality and because of the consequential particle (al-tafri'), which requires that both be combined: that patience is among the good deeds of the doers of good; otherwise the consequential particle would have no place. The emphatic particle (harf al-ta'kid) is brought in for the sake of emphasizing the information (al-khabar).

The reward was called "ajr" (wage) because it occurs as a recompense for deeds and is promised, so it resembles a wage (ajr).

[Page 183]

This is very closely connected to His words, exalted is He: ﴿Such is the seizing of your Lord﴾ [Hud: 102]. It may therefore be a consequence (tafri') of that verse, with what lies between them being a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraD) prompted by a digressive shift (al-intiqal al-istitradi) among closely connected meanings. The meaning is: "Why were there not, among those nations, people of virtue (ashab baqiyya) from good who forbade their people from corruption when there befell them what befell them?" This is a guidance to the obligation of forbidding evil (al-nahy 'an al-munkar). It may also be a consequence of His words, exalted is He: ﴿So remain upright as you have been commanded﴾ [Hud: 112]. The verse is then a consequence of the command to uprightness and the prohibition of transgression and of inclining toward those who did wrong. The meaning is: "Do not be like the nations before you, when they lacked anyone to forbid them from corruption on earth and to forbid them from denying the messengers, so they exceeded their bounds until the anger of God descended upon them, except a few of them. So if you abandon what you have been commanded, your condition will be like theirs." For this meaning the consequential particle fa' has been used, because the verse stands in the position of detail and causal explanation for the clause ﴿So remain upright as you have been commanded﴾ [Hud: 112] and what is conjoined to it. It is as if it were said: "And indeed, all of them, your Lord will surely pay them in full for their deeds. So why were there not among them people of virtue who forbade corruption on earth..." to the end. That is: "Beware lest you become as they were, and so befall you what befell them. Be upright, do not transgress, do not incline toward the wrongdoers, and establish prayer." Thus the arrangement of speech was altered to this style which is in the verse, for the variety of its benefits, its subtleties and the independence of its purposes, though they all lead to a general aim that encompasses them. This is among the most wondrous methods of inimitability (i'jaz), namely the returning of the final part to the beginning (radd al-'ajz 'ala al-sadr), without artifice and without apparent intent.

Close to this meaning is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "What I have forbidden you, avoid it; and what I have commanded you, do of it as much as you are able. For those before you were destroyed only by the multitude of their questions and their disputing with their prophets."

Lawla is a particle of urging (harf tahdid) meaning halla ("why not"). Urging toward what has already passed is not intended except to warn others against falling into what those before them fell into, and the lesson lies in what befell them.

Al-qurun: the nations (al-umam). This was discussed at the beginning of al-An'am.

Al-baqiyya: excellence and goodness. The term baqiyya was applied to excellence by way of metonymy (kinaya), which became established and circulated as a proverb, because the nature of a precious thing is that its owner does not neglect it.

Baqiyyat al-nas: their leaders and those of excellence among them. Ruwaysh ibn Kathir al-Ta'i said:

"If you commit sins, then your best (baqiyyatukum) come to me,
then no sin of yours is beyond my reach."

[Page 184]

From their proverbs: "In corners are hidden treasures, and among men are remnants (baqaya)." From here the term was applied to excellence and goodness in the qualities of people, so one says: "In so-and-so there is baqiyya." The meaning here is: people of excellence, religion and knowledge of the sharia. The intended ones are not the messengers themselves, but the followers of the messengers and the bearers of the laws, who forbade their peoples from corruption on earth.

Al-fasad: sins and the disorder of conditions. Their forbidding restrains them from recklessness in sins, so that their conditions are set right and weakness and dissolution do not come upon them, as befell the Children of Israel when they lacked anyone to forbid them. In this there is an honouring (tanwih) of the companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), for they were people of baqiyya among the Quraysh, who called them to faith until all of them believed. And they were people of baqiyya among other nations who mixed with them, calling them to faith and uprightness after entering it, and teaching the religion. As God, exalted is He, said of them: ﴿You are the best nation brought forth for mankind, enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong﴾ [Al 'Imran: 110].

In His words ﴿from the generations before you﴾ there is an allusion to good tidings that the Muslims will not be like that, which is implied by His words, exalted is He: "before you."

Ibn Jammaz related from Abu Ja'far the reading bi-qiyya, with a kasra on the ba' and sukun on the qaf and a light ya'. This is a dialectal form (lugha), which the authors of lexicographical books did not mention. Perhaps it was treated like the form hay'a (appearance), because it carries an imagined dignity and gravity.

Illa qalilan is a disjunctive exception (istithna' munqati') from "people of baqiyya." It entails an exception from "the generations," since the generations among whom there were people of baqiyya are not included in the ruling on the generations mentioned previously. It has the sense of a corrective (istidrak), because the sense of urging is directed at those generations in which there were no people of baqiyya, namely those whose lack of that category is being reproached. Of these generations, none is excepted, since all of them were not saved from the consequences of corruption. But since the meaning of urging may give the impression that all the generations that preceded the Muslims lacked people of baqiyya, while some of those generations did have people of baqiyya, the corrective was used to remove this misunderstanding. Thus the excepted party is not included in what was mentioned before, and therefore it is disjunctive. The sign of its disjunction is its being in the accusative, because the accusative of the exception after a negation, when the stated antecedent is not in the accusative, is an indication of treating it as disjunctive, since that is the more eloquent usage. Would the most eloquent speech come except in the most eloquent inflection? Had its connection been intended, it would have come in the nominative as a substitute (badal) of what was mentioned before it.

Min in His words ﴿from those whom We saved﴾ is explicative (bayaniyya), explaining the few, because those whom God saved from the generations are the few who forbade corruption, and they are the followers of the messengers.

In the explanation there is an indication that their forbidding of corruption was the cause of the salvation of those generations, because the forbidding is the cause of the cause, since forbidding causes abstention from sins, which is the cause of salvation.

His words ﴿those of them whom We saved﴾ indicate that there is an ellipsis by omission (ijaz hadhf) in the speech, its estimate being: "So they used to repent and desist from corruption on earth, and thus they were saved from the touch of the Fire, which has no repeller for them."

The clause ﴿But those who did wrong pursued﴾ is conjoined to what the exception conveys of the existence of a few who forbade corruption. It is therefore an explicit statement of the implication of the exception and a clarification of its generality. The meaning is: "And most of them did not forbid corruption, nor did they themselves desist, nor did their peoples; they pursued what they were given ease in," like His words, exalted is He: ﴿They prostrated, except Iblis, who refused and was arrogant and was among the disbelievers﴾ [al-Baqara: 34], as a detail of the implication of the exception.

In the verse there is a lesson and admonition for the disobedient among the Muslims, because they are never free of wronging themselves.

Pursuing what they were given ease in means being devoted to it and turning toward it, as a follower turns toward the one he follows.

Utrifu: they were given ease (al-taraf), which is the abundance and luxury that God facilitated for them. So it was God who gave them ease, but they did not thank Him.

[Page 186]

And they were criminals: that is, in pursuing ease, so they were not grateful. This confirms the meaning of pursuit, because taking up ease together with gratitude is not called pursuit; rather it is wholehearted devotion and cutting off, without admixture with anything else. In the speech there is another ellipsis by omission, the estimate being: "So the destruction of the criminals became binding upon them." By this the setting was prepared for His words after it: ﴿Your Lord would never destroy the towns unjustly﴾ [Hud: 117].

**Commentary of Ibn ʿAshur (al-Taḥrir wa al-Tanwīr) on Surah 11, verse 117:**

﴿Your Lord would never destroy the towns unjustly while their people were reforming.﴾

It is coordinated (*ʿaṭf*, grammatical coordination) with the clause ﴿and those who did wrong followed the luxury they had been given therein﴾ (Hud 11:116). This is because the content of the clause it is coordinated with implies that the criminals were exposed to the descent of punishment upon them, on account of their being described as wrongdoers and criminals. So it follows this with the statement that the descent of the punishment upon those it struck was not an injustice from God, Exalted is He. Rather, they brought destruction upon themselves through what they corrupted on earth, and God does not love corruption.

The form ﴿Your Lord would never destroy﴾ indicates the strong negation of the act, as was explained earlier at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿It is not for any human that God should give him the Book﴾ (Ali ʿImran 3:79), in Āl ʿImrān, and at His saying: ﴿He said, "Glory be to You! It is not for me to say what I have no right to say"﴾ (al-Māʾidah 5:116), at the end of al-ʿUqūd. So refer back to those two passages.

By "the towns" (*al-qurā*) is meant their people, in the manner of the figurative usage of *al-majāz al-mursal* (metonymy, where a part or related thing stands for the whole), as in His saying: ﴿and ask the town﴾ (Yusuf 12:82).

The *bāʾ* in ﴿unjustly﴾ is for *mulābasah* (accompaniment, the sense of being accompanied by something), and it is in the position of a *ḥāl* (circumstantial qualifier) relating to ﴿your Lord﴾. That is, He does not destroy people with a destruction accompanied by injustice.

The clause ﴿while their people were reforming﴾ is a *ḥāl* relating to ﴿the towns﴾. That is, God's destruction does not occur as an unjust act against a people who are reforming.

**[p. 187]**

The reformers (*al-muṣliḥūn*) are the opposite of the corrupters (*al-mufsidūn*) in His saying before it: ﴿who forbade corruption on earth﴾ (Hud 11:116), and His saying ﴿and they were criminals﴾ (Hud 11:116). So God does not destroy a people who are unjust toward them, but He destroys a people who are unjust toward themselves. He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿We would never destroy the towns unless their people were wrongdoers﴾ (al-Qaṣaṣ 28:59).

What is meant is the swift destruction that befalls them at a time other than the time of the arrival of its like, not the destruction decreed for all nations, which is the passing away of one nation and the rise of another within known periods, according to known laws (*sunan*, divine patterns).

**[Page 188]**

*Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 11, verses 118–119:*

﴿Had your Lord willed, He would have made mankind one community, but they will not cease to differ,﴾ ﴿except those on whom your Lord has mercy. For this He created them. And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled: "I will surely fill Hell with jinn and mankind, all together."﴾

When the censure of the nations who did not have among them anyone to forbid corruption, and so followed wrongdoing, was established, and when the report of their destruction, that it was not an injustice from God, and that had they been reformers they would not have been destroyed, was established, all of this could give rise to the illusion that the disobedience of the nations to what God willed for them is an escape from the grip of divine power. He therefore followed this with what removes that illusion: God is able to make them one community, united upon the truth and steadfast upon it, as He commanded them to be.

But the wisdom upon which the order of this world is founded required that the human intellect be susceptible to being swayed toward the path of error or the path of guidance, according to the degree of soundness of their thinking and reflection, and of their freedom from the veils of error. And since God, exalted is He, created minds fit for this, He made in them the acceptance of truth in accordance with the natural disposition (fitrah) (*fitrah*: the innate, sound human disposition), which is the soundness of minds from the accidents of ignorance and misguidance, and this is the complete natural disposition, indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Mankind was one community﴾ [al-Baqarah: 213].

*[Page 189]*

The discussion of it has already passed in surah al-Baqarah. He did not withhold guidance or counsel from them through the messengers, the callers to good, and those who instruct them from the followers of the messengers, who are the people of remnant (*ulu al-baqiyyah*) (*ulu al-baqiyyah*: those of virtue who forbid corruption on earth), who forbid corruption on earth. So among mankind there are those who are guided, and many of them are defiantly disobedient. Had He willed, He would have created human minds upon a unified inspiration from which they could not deviate, just as He created the perception of dumb animals upon an order they cannot transgress from the beginning of creation until the end of the world. Thus we find the state of the camel and the sheep in the time of Adam, peace be upon him, the same as their state in our time, and so it will remain until the world comes to an end. There is no doubt that God's wisdom required this order in the human intellect, because that is more fitting for the realization of God's purpose, exalted is He, through human endeavours in this worldly life, which is transient and mixed, so that they may move from it to the world of eternal and pure life: good if it is good, and evil if it is evil. Had man been created thus, righteous deeds would not require the reward of bliss, nor would corruption require the punishment of Hellfire. Therefore God certainly created humans upon an order whose nature is that difference arises among them in matters, among them the matter of righteousness and corruption on earth, which is the most important and the greatest of them, so that people may vary in the stages of ascent and aspire to the levels of nearness, and thus the individuals of this species become distinguished in every aspect of life, until one is counted as a thousand: ﴿That God may distinguish the wicked from the good﴾ [al-Anfal: 37].

This is the reason for the conjunction of the clause ﴿And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled: "I will surely fill Hell with jinn and mankind, all together"﴾ with the two clauses ﴿but they will not cease to differ﴾ and ﴿For this He created them.﴾

The object of the verb of willing is omitted, because what is intended by it equals the meaning of the response of the conditional clause, so it was omitted for brevity. The estimate is: "Had your Lord willed to make mankind one community, He would have made them so."

*Ummah* (community): a group of people united in some great matter of the affairs of life, such as homeland, language, lineage, or religion. It has already been discussed at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Mankind was one community﴾ [al-Baqarah: 213] in surah al-Baqarah. Thus *ummah* is interpreted in every context by what its annexation to something indicates of the causes of its formation, as one says: the Arab *ummah* and the Islamic *ummah*.

*[Page 190]*

The meaning of its being one is that all of mankind should be in agreement on following the religion of truth, as the context indicates. The meaning thus comes to: "Had your Lord willed, He would have made mankind a people of one religion, and they would have been one community in terms of pure religion."

It is understood from the condition of *law* (*law*: "had"/"if") that their being made one community in religion is negated, i.e., its continuation in unity in religion is negated, even though they existed at the beginning of creation in agreement, but they did not remain so until disagreement arose between the two sons of Adam, peace be upon him, in accordance with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Mankind was one community﴾ [al-Baqarah: 213], and His saying: ﴿And mankind were not but one community, then they differed﴾ [Yunus: 19] in surah Yunus. Thus it is known that mankind had differed in the past and so were not one community. Then it is not known whether their affair will return to agreement in religion. Therefore He followed this by stating that difference is perpetual among them, because it is part of what minds have been formed upon.

Since difference implies that it is a difference in religion, and that its meaning is deviation from truth to falsehood, because truth does not admit of plurality and difference, He followed the generality of ﴿but they will not cease to differ﴾ with an exception for those who remained steadfast upon the true religion and did not oppose it, by His saying: ﴿except those on whom your Lord has mercy﴾, i.e., He preserved them from difference.

From this it is understood that the blameworthy difference warned against is difference regarding the foundations of religion, which entails regarding the one who opposes it as outside the religion, even if he claims to be one of its followers. When this difference arises, it becomes obligatory upon the community to crush it and to exert effort in removing it from among them by every means of truth and justice: by guidance, good argument, and debate. If that does not succeed, then by fighting, as Abu Bakr did in fighting the Arabs who denied the obligation of zakat, and as 'Ali, may God honor his face, did in fighting the Harurites (*Harurites*: the early Kharijite sect) who declared the Muslims to be unbelievers. This verse is a stern warning against that difference.

As for its being followed by His saying: ﴿For this He created them﴾, it is an emphasis on the content of ﴿but they will not cease to differ﴾. The reference is to the difference derived from His saying: ﴿differing﴾, and the *lam* is for causation, because

*[Page 191]*

when He created them upon a nature that necessitates difference of opinions and inclinations, and He was willing according to what that nature requires and knowing of it, as we have explained just before, difference was a final cause for their creation. The final cause does not necessarily entail restriction to it; it suffices that it is an end of the act, and there may be many other ends along with it. Thus there is no contradiction between this and His saying: ﴿And I did not create jinn and mankind except that they should worship Me﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 56], because the restriction there is relative (*qasr idafi*) (*qasr idafi*: restriction relative to a specific counter-case), i.e., except in the state that they worship Me and do not associate others with Me. A relative restriction does not negate the existence of other states beyond what the restriction was intended to refute, as is clear to anyone who has studied the methods of Arabic eloquence.

The fronting of the object before its verb in His saying: ﴿For this He created them﴾ is not for restriction, but for emphasis on this cause. By this, the perplexity that arises in interpretation in reconciling the two verses is dispelled.

Then He followed that with His saying: ﴿And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled: "I will surely fill Hell with jinn and mankind, all together"﴾, because His saying: ﴿except those on whom your Lord has mercy﴾ indicates that those excepted from it are a people who differ in a difference for which there is no mercy. So it is a difference contrary to mercy, and the opposite of blessing is vengeance. Thus it is a difference that necessitated retribution.

The fulfilment of the Lord's word is a metaphor for truthfulness and realization, as has passed at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and justice﴾ [al-An'am: 115] in surah al-An'am. Thus those who differ are the portion of Hell.

*Kalimah* (word) here means speech. The "word of God" is His decree and His will. It is called a *word* figuratively, because it is the cause of the issuing of the word "Be" (*kun*), which is the command of creation. Its detail has already been given at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and justice﴾ [al-An'am: 115] in surah al-An'am.

The clause ﴿I will surely fill Hell﴾ is an explanation of the word in the sense of speech. That is an expression for the will, which is expressed by inner speech (*kalam nafsi*) (*kalam nafsi*: the inner speech of God, distinct from recited speech).

*[Page 192]*

It is also possible that the word is a speech which He addressed to the angels before the creation of mankind, so that ﴿I will surely fill Hell﴾ is then an explanation of *the word*.

*Min al-jinnah wa al-nas* (from the jinn and mankind) is partitive, i.e., "I will surely fill Hell from the two groups." And ﴿ajma'in﴾ (all together) is an emphasis for the inclusion of both kinds in the dual, not for the inclusion of all individuals, because that would contradict the sense of partitiveness conveyed by *min*.

**[Page 188]**

*Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 11, verses 118–119:*

﴿Had your Lord willed, He would have made mankind one community, but they will not cease to differ,﴾ ﴿except those on whom your Lord has mercy. For this He created them. And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled: "I will surely fill Hell with jinn and mankind, all together."﴾

When the censure of the nations who did not have among them anyone to forbid corruption, and so followed wrongdoing, was established, and when the report of their destruction, that it was not an injustice from God, and that had they been reformers they would not have been destroyed, was established, all of this could give rise to the illusion that the disobedience of the nations to what God willed for them is an escape from the grip of divine power. He therefore followed this with what removes that illusion: God is able to make them one community, united upon the truth and steadfast upon it, as He commanded them to be.

But the wisdom upon which the order of this world is founded required that the human intellect be susceptible to being swayed toward the path of error or the path of guidance, according to the degree of soundness of their thinking and reflection, and of their freedom from the veils of error. And since God, exalted is He, created minds fit for this, He made in them the acceptance of truth in accordance with the natural disposition (fitrah) (*fitrah*: the innate, sound human disposition), which is the soundness of minds from the accidents of ignorance and misguidance, and this is the complete natural disposition, indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Mankind was one community﴾ [al-Baqarah: 213].

*[Page 189]*

The discussion of it has already passed in surah al-Baqarah. He did not withhold guidance or counsel from them through the messengers, the callers to good, and those who instruct them from the followers of the messengers, who are the people of remnant (*ulu al-baqiyyah*) (*ulu al-baqiyyah*: those of virtue who forbid corruption on earth), who forbid corruption on earth. So among mankind there are those who are guided, and many of them are defiantly disobedient. Had He willed, He would have created human minds upon a unified inspiration from which they could not deviate, just as He created the perception of dumb animals upon an order they cannot transgress from the beginning of creation until the end of the world. Thus we find the state of the camel and the sheep in the time of Adam, peace be upon him, the same as their state in our time, and so it will remain until the world comes to an end. There is no doubt that God's wisdom required this order in the human intellect, because that is more fitting for the realization of God's purpose, exalted is He, through human endeavours in this worldly life, which is transient and mixed, so that they may move from it to the world of eternal and pure life: good if it is good, and evil if it is evil. Had man been created thus, righteous deeds would not require the reward of bliss, nor would corruption require the punishment of Hellfire. Therefore God certainly created humans upon an order whose nature is that difference arises among them in matters, among them the matter of righteousness and corruption on earth, which is the most important and the greatest of them, so that people may vary in the stages of ascent and aspire to the levels of nearness, and thus the individuals of this species become distinguished in every aspect of life, until one is counted as a thousand: ﴿That God may distinguish the wicked from the good﴾ [al-Anfal: 37].

This is the reason for the conjunction of the clause ﴿And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled: "I will surely fill Hell with jinn and mankind, all together"﴾ with the two clauses ﴿but they will not cease to differ﴾ and ﴿For this He created them.﴾

The object of the verb of willing is omitted, because what is intended by it equals the meaning of the response of the conditional clause, so it was omitted for brevity. The estimate is: "Had your Lord willed to make mankind one community, He would have made them so."

*Ummah* (community): a group of people united in some great matter of the affairs of life, such as homeland, language, lineage, or religion. It has already been discussed at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Mankind was one community﴾ [al-Baqarah: 213] in surah al-Baqarah. Thus *ummah* is interpreted in every context by what its annexation to something indicates of the causes of its formation, as one says: the Arab *ummah* and the Islamic *ummah*.

*[Page 190]*

The meaning of its being one is that all of mankind should be in agreement on following the religion of truth, as the context indicates. The meaning thus comes to: "Had your Lord willed, He would have made mankind a people of one religion, and they would have been one community in terms of pure religion."

It is understood from the condition of *law* (*law*: "had"/"if") that their being made one community in religion is negated, i.e., its continuation in unity in religion is negated, even though they existed at the beginning of creation in agreement, but they did not remain so until disagreement arose between the two sons of Adam, peace be upon him, in accordance with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Mankind was one community﴾ [al-Baqarah: 213], and His saying: ﴿And mankind were not but one community, then they differed﴾ [Yunus: 19] in surah Yunus. Thus it is known that mankind had differed in the past and so were not one community. Then it is not known whether their affair will return to agreement in religion. Therefore He followed this by stating that difference is perpetual among them, because it is part of what minds have been formed upon.

Since difference implies that it is a difference in religion, and that its meaning is deviation from truth to falsehood, because truth does not admit of plurality and difference, He followed the generality of ﴿but they will not cease to differ﴾ with an exception for those who remained steadfast upon the true religion and did not oppose it, by His saying: ﴿except those on whom your Lord has mercy﴾, i.e., He preserved them from difference.

From this it is understood that the blameworthy difference warned against is difference regarding the foundations of religion, which entails regarding the one who opposes it as outside the religion, even if he claims to be one of its followers. When this difference arises, it becomes obligatory upon the community to crush it and to exert effort in removing it from among them by every means of truth and justice: by guidance, good argument, and debate. If that does not succeed, then by fighting, as Abu Bakr did in fighting the Arabs who denied the obligation of zakat, and as 'Ali, may God honor his face, did in fighting the Harurites (*Harurites*: the early Kharijite sect) who declared the Muslims to be unbelievers. This verse is a stern warning against that difference.

As for its being followed by His saying: ﴿For this He created them﴾, it is an emphasis on the content of ﴿but they will not cease to differ﴾. The reference is to the difference derived from His saying: ﴿differing﴾, and the *lam* is for causation, because

*[Page 191]*

when He created them upon a nature that necessitates difference of opinions and inclinations, and He was willing according to what that nature requires and knowing of it, as we have explained just before, difference was a final cause for their creation. The final cause does not necessarily entail restriction to it; it suffices that it is an end of the act, and there may be many other ends along with it. Thus there is no contradiction between this and His saying: ﴿And I did not create jinn and mankind except that they should worship Me﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 56], because the restriction there is relative (*qasr idafi*) (*qasr idafi*: restriction relative to a specific counter-case), i.e., except in the state that they worship Me and do not associate others with Me. A relative restriction does not negate the existence of other states beyond what the restriction was intended to refute, as is clear to anyone who has studied the methods of Arabic eloquence.

The fronting of the object before its verb in His saying: ﴿For this He created them﴾ is not for restriction, but for emphasis on this cause. By this, the perplexity that arises in interpretation in reconciling the two verses is dispelled.

Then He followed that with His saying: ﴿And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled: "I will surely fill Hell with jinn and mankind, all together"﴾, because His saying: ﴿except those on whom your Lord has mercy﴾ indicates that those excepted from it are a people who differ in a difference for which there is no mercy. So it is a difference contrary to mercy, and the opposite of blessing is vengeance. Thus it is a difference that necessitated retribution.

The fulfilment of the Lord's word is a metaphor for truthfulness and realization, as has passed at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and justice﴾ [al-An'am: 115] in surah al-An'am. Thus those who differ are the portion of Hell.

*Kalimah* (word) here means speech. The "word of God" is His decree and His will. It is called a *word* figuratively, because it is the cause of the issuing of the word "Be" (*kun*), which is the command of creation. Its detail has already been given at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and justice﴾ [al-An'am: 115] in surah al-An'am.

The clause ﴿I will surely fill Hell﴾ is an explanation of the word in the sense of speech. That is an expression for the will, which is expressed by inner speech (*kalam nafsi*) (*kalam nafsi*: the inner speech of God, distinct from recited speech).

*[Page 192]*

It is also possible that the word is a speech which He addressed to the angels before the creation of mankind, so that ﴿I will surely fill Hell﴾ is then an explanation of *the word*.

*Min al-jinnah wa al-nas* (from the jinn and mankind) is partitive, i.e., "I will surely fill Hell from the two groups." And ﴿ajma'in﴾ (all together) is an emphasis for the inclusion of both kinds in the dual, not for the inclusion of all individuals, because that would contradict the sense of partitiveness conveyed by *min*.

[p. 192]

﴿And We relate to you from the news of the messengers that with which We strengthen your heart. And in this has come to you the truth, and an admonition and a reminder for the believers.﴾ This is a concluding summation (tadhyil) and a gathering-up (hawsalah) of what preceded it: the accounts of the towns and the accounts of the messengers.

The clause ﴿And We relate to you from the news of the messengers﴾ through to its end is a conjunction (ʿatf) of one report upon another and one narrative upon another. You may also take the wāw (and) as parenthetical (iʿtirāḍiyyah) or as introducing a new sentence (istiʾnāfiyyah). This serves as a preparation for the closing of the sūrah and a summation (faldhalakah) of the stories and admonitions that have been presented in it.

Kullan (كُلًّا) is in the accusative as the object of the verb naquss (نَقُصُّ). Its being placed before its verb serves to draw attention and to create an initial vagueness (ibhām) so that its explanation comes afterwards, making it more firmly fixed in the mind of the listener.

The tanwīn on kullan (كُلًّا) is the tanwīn of compensation (ʿiwaḍ) for a omitted genitive complement (muḍāf ilayhi), which is made clear by the words ﴿from the news of the messengers﴾. The sense is: "Every report about the messengers which We relate to you." Thus the phrase ﴿from the news of the messengers﴾ is an explanation (bayān) of the tanwīn that attached to kullan. And ﴿that with which We strengthen your heart﴾ is a substitute (badal) for kullan.

The word al-qaṣaṣ (القَصَصُ, narratives) occurs at His statement, exalted is He: ﴿We relate to you the best of narratives﴾ [Yūsuf: 3], at the beginning of the sūrah of Yūsuf.

Al-tathbīt (التَّثْبِيتُ, strengthening): its essential meaning is settling something in its place such that agitation and instability are removed. It has preceded in His statement, exalted is He: ﴿it would have been better for them and firmer in strengthening﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 66] in the sūrah of al-Nisāʾ, and in His statement: [p. 192 continued]
﴿So strengthen those who believed﴾ [al-Anfāl: 12] in the sūrah of al-Anfāl. Here it is used metaphorically (mustaʿār) for confirmation (taqrīr), like His statement: ﴿but so that my heart may be at rest﴾ [al-Baqarah: 260].

Al-fuʾād (الفُؤادُ, heart): it is applied to perception (al-idrāk), as is common in the speech of the Arabs.

The strengthening of the heart of the Messenger ﷺ means an increase in his certainty and his knowledge of what God has promised him, because everything that is repeated of the narratives of the prophets and the circumstances of their peoples with them increases him in remembrance and knowledge that his own situation runs in accordance with the ways (sunan) of the prophets. And he is increased in remembrance by the fact that his final outcome is victory over his enemies, and it renews consolation for what he encounters from his people of denial, and that increases him in patience. Patience (al-ṣabr) is the strengthening of the heart.

And the similarity of the conditions of the nations in the face of the call of their prophets, despite the differences of eras, increases him in knowledge that the levels of human intellects are varied, and that the acceptance of guidance is the ultimate point of the ascent of the intellect. So he knows that disagreement is an ancient trait (shanshanah) among human beings, and that the struggle between truth and falsehood is an ancient matter, and it is among the laws (nawāmīs, sing. nāmūs: established natural laws) upon which the human order has been constituted. Therefore the opposition of his people to him does not grieve him. And it increases him in knowledge of the exaltedness of his followers who accepted his guidance and held fast to his religion by its firmest handhold. So there came to him, in the likeness of the story of Mūsā (peace be upon him) and the disagreement of the People of the Book concerning it, a clarification of the truth, an admonition and a reminder for the believers, so that they would not fall into what the People of the Book fell into.

The indication in His statement "in this" (fī hādhihi) has been said to refer to the sūrah, and this is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās. This implies that this sūrah was more full of the news of the messengers than the sūrahs revealed before it, and on this basis it accords with the view of those who say it was revealed before the sūrah of Yūnus. The more apparent view is that the indication refers to the verse preceding it, which is ﴿Why were there not, among the generations before you, people of virtue who forbade corruption in the earth﴾ [Hūd: 116], up to His statement ﴿from the jinn and mankind, all together﴾. Thus these three verses would be the first to be revealed concerning the prohibition of wrongdoing.

Moreover, His statement ﴿and in this has come to you the truth﴾ is not explicit that a like of it had not come before these verses, so reflect.

[p. 193]

Perhaps what is meant by "the truth" (al-ḥaqq) is the assurance to the Messenger concerning the disagreement of his community about his book, by the indication of His statement ﴿Why were there not, among the generations before you, people of virtue﴾, which implies that those addressed are not in that position, as the indication to this was mentioned just previously.

Its definiteness (taʿrīf) is an indication to a truth known to the Prophet, either by his seeking it, or by his asking his Lord.

Al-mawʿiẓah (المَوْعِظَةُ, admonition) is the verbal noun of al-waʿẓ, which is reminding a person of what turns him away from a harmful action.

Al-dhikrā (الذِّكْرى, reminder) is simply reminding of what benefits. So this is an admonition to the Muslims that they might beware of that, and a reminder to them of the conditions of the nations so that they may draw analogies from them and reflect upon their circumstances. The indefiniteness of mawʿiẓah and dhikrā is for magnification (taʿẓīm).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 11, verses 121–122:

﴿Say to those who do not believe: "Act according to your position; indeed, we are acting."﴾ ﴿And wait; indeed, we are waiting."﴾ This is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon the clause ﴿And there has come to you in this the truth﴾ [Hud: 120], etc.; for since that (passage) included that in this story there is a reminder (dhikra) for the believers, he was commanded to address those who do not believe concerning what is in it with the address of one who has despaired of their benefiting from the reminder. This is the address of one who does not concern himself with their aversion, and whom their rallying against their falsehood and their opposition to the truth does not turn away from his call to the truth. Therefore, His saying ﴿Say to those who do not believe﴾ was a counterpart (ʿadil) to His saying ﴿and an admonition and a reminder for the believers﴾ [Hud: 120]. And this statement is one he was commanded to say on his own tongue and on the tongue of the believers.

His saying ﴿Act according to your position; indeed, we are acting﴾ is the same as what was related of Shuʿayb, peace be upon him, in this surah just before.

The pronouns in ﴿indeed, we are acting﴾ and ﴿indeed, we are waiting﴾ refer to the Prophet and the believers who are with him.

In God's command to His Messenger to say this on the tongue of the believers is a testimony from God to the truthfulness of their faith. It also contains the delegation to the head of the community to decide a matter on behalf of his community, in confidence that they will not reject his action, just as the Prophet ﷺ said to Hawazin when they came repentant and asking for the return of their captives and their property: "Choose one of the two: the captives or the wealth." When they chose the captives, the captives were returned to their families, and he did not consult the Muslims; rather, he made it so that whoever would make this agreeable for Hawazin would have his right to the first of the captives that came. The believers said: "We have made that agreeable."

His saying ﴿And wait; indeed, we are waiting﴾ is a threat and a warning, just as one says in warning: "You will see."
