Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 11, verse 123:

﴿And to Allah belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth, and to Him the whole matter is returned. So worship Him and rely upon Him. And your Lord is not unaware of what you do.﴾

This is a comprehensive statement, a *tadhyil* (concluding complement) that signals the surah's close, and so it is among the excellences of the closing passage. The *waw* here is either a conjunction linking one statement to another, or the *waw* of *i'tirad* (parenthetical insertion) at the end of a speech, and examples of this are many.

The *lam* in *lillah* indicates ownership, specifically the ownership of comprehensive knowledge. That is, to Allah belongs what is hidden from the knowledge of people in the heavens and the earth. This statement combines good news for the believers of what they have been promised of the hidden bounties, and a warning to the polytheists of what they have been threatened with of the hidden punishment, in this world and the next.

The fronting of the two prepositional phrases in ﴿And to Allah belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth, and to Him the matter is returned﴾ serves to express exclusivity: it is Allah alone, not other than Him, who owns the unseen of the heavens and the earth, because this is something in which none shares with Him. And it is to Allah alone, not to other than Him, that the whole matter is returned. This is an allusion (*ta'rid*) to the corruption of the opinions of those who worship other than Him, since whoever is not like this does not deserve to be worshipped, and whoever is like this is worthy of being singled out for worship.

The meaning of the return of the matter to Him is that the affair of management, of victory, of abandonment, and of other things, returns to Allah, that is, to His knowledge and His power, even if people calculate and prepare. For the matters have often turned out contrary to what the one preparing had prepared for. Often the mighty has become mighty by his might and then met with abandonment from a direction he did not expect, and perhaps those deemed weak have been in a position of honour and victory over those who possess honour and strength.

The definite article in *al-amr* (the matter) is the definite article of the genus, so it encompasses all matters. The emphasis of *al-amr* by *kulluh* (all of it) is to make the generality explicit.

Those other than Nafi' read *yurja'u* with the verb in the passive form, meaning that every person with a matter returns his matter to Allah. Nafi' read it with the active form, so that the matter itself is the subject of the return, that is, it returns to Allah.

According to both recitations, the return is a *tamthil* (figurative depiction) of the state of people's inability to manage matters according to their desires, by the image of someone who takes hold of a thing to manage it, then finds he is unable to manage it, so he returns it to the one worthy of managing it. Or it is a figurative depiction of the state of matters submitting to Allah's management and not to the management of those who attempt to manage them, by the image of a wanderer seeking a place to settle, then taking refuge and returning to the fitting abode. Thus it is a *tamthiliyyah makniyyah* (an implicit allegorical image), signalled by the verb *yurja'u* and its construction with *ila-hi*.

The consequence of the command to the Prophet ﷺ to worship Allah and rely upon Him, drawn from the return of the whole matter to Him, is evident, because Allah is the one worthy of being worshipped and of being relied upon in every important matter. This is an allusion that criticises those who worshipped other than Him and relied upon the intercession and benefit of the gods. The command to the Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace, also implies the command to persist in worship and reliance.

[Page 196]

The intended meaning is that he should worship Him alone, to the exclusion of others, and rely upon Him alone, to the exclusion of others, as indicated by ﴿and to Him the whole matter is returned﴾, and by the context of the consequence, since it is not conceivable that any part of worship or reliance be directed to another, given that every matter returns to Him. Therefore, no form indicating the restriction of worship to Him was used, since this is dispensed with by the obligation of the cause that restricts both to Him.

The sentence ﴿And your Lord is not unaware of what you do﴾ is a comprehensive summary, and it is a *tadhyil* to what preceded. The *waw* in it is like the *waw* in ﴿And to Allah belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth﴾, for His not being unaware of any deed means that He gives every doer the reward of his deed: if good, then good, and if evil, then evil. For this reason, the description of being unaware is attached to the deed and not to persons, as in ﴿not unaware of you﴾, to indicate that upon the deed there is a recompense.

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Hafs from 'Asim, Abu Ja'far, and Ya'qub read *ta'malun* (what you do) with a *ta'* (second person), as an address to the Prophet ﷺ, with the people included with him in the address. The others read it with a *ya'* (third person), so that the pronoun refers back to the disbelievers. In that case it is a consolation to the Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace, and a threat to the polytheists.

[Page 197]

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

**Surah Yusuf**

The sole name of this surah is the name of Surah Yusuf. Ibn Hajar mentioned in *al-Isabah*, in the biography of Rafi' ibn Malik al-Zuraqi, on the authority of Ibn Ishaq, that Abu Rafi' ibn Malik was the first to come to Medina with Surah Yusuf, that is, after he had pledged allegiance to the Prophet ﷺ at the 'Aqabah.

The reason for its naming is evident, since it narrates the whole story of Yusuf, peace be upon him, and his story is not mentioned in any other surah. His name is not mentioned in any other surah except Surah al-An'am and Surah Ghafir.

In this name there is also a distinction for it among the surahs that begin with the letters *Alif Lam Ra*, as we mentioned in the discussion of Surah Yunus.

It is a Meccan surah according to the view that should not be turned away from. It has been said that the first three verses are Medinan. Al-Suyuti said in *al-Itqan*: this is weak and is not to be heeded.

It was revealed after Surah Hud and before Surah al-Hijr.

It is the fifty-third surah in the order of revelation according to the majority view.

The story of no prophet in the Qur'an is told with the elaboration (*itnab*) with which the story of Yusuf, peace be upon him, is told in this surah.

[Page 198]

The number of its verses is one hundred and eleven, by agreement of the counters of the major cities (*ashab al-'adad*).

* * *

**Among the aims of this surah**

Al-Wahidi and al-Tabari narrated, one of them exceeding the other, on the authority of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas (may Allah be pleased with him), that he said: "The Qur'an was revealed and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited it to his companions for a time. Then the Muslims in Mecca said: 'O Messenger of Allah, if only you would relate to us.' So Allah revealed ﴿Alif Lam Ra. These are the verses of the clear Book. Indeed, We have sent it down as an Arabic Qur'an that you might understand﴾ [Yusuf: 1], the three verses."

The most important of its purposes is the explanation of the story of Yusuf, peace be upon him, with his brothers, what he encountered in his life, and the lessons in that from various aspects.

In it is the affirmation that some dreams may be a report of a hidden matter, and that is among the principles of prophecy, and it is from the principles of the eastern wisdom, as will come at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When Yusuf said to his father, "O my father, indeed I saw eleven stars"﴾ [Yusuf: 4], and the verses that follow.

And that the interpretation of dreams is a knowledge that Allah grants to whomever He wills of His righteous servants.

And the envy of relatives among themselves.

And the kindness of Allah toward whomever He chooses of His servants.

And the lesson of good outcomes, of fidelity, of trustworthiness, of truthfulness, and of repentance.

And the settlement of the Children of Israel and their sons in the land of Egypt.

And the consolation of the Prophet ﷺ with what Ya'qub and Yusuf, peace be upon them both, suffered from harm inflicted by their own family. The Prophet ﷺ encountered from his own family harm greater than what he encountered from distant disbelievers of his people, such as his uncle Abu Lahab, al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, and Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib. Although the latter embraced Islam later and his Islam was good, the impact of harm from relatives on the soul is greater than the impact of harm from distant people, as Tarafah said:

*And the wrong of one's kin is more painful to a man*
*Than the striking of the keen, Indian sword.*

He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, in Yusuf and his brothers are signs for the inquirers﴾ [Yusuf: 7].

In it is the lesson of the patience of prophets, such as Ya'qub and Yusuf, peace be upon them both, in the face of trials, and how the outcome was theirs.

In it is the lesson of the migration of the people of the Prophet ﷺ to the land in which Ya'qub, peace be upon him, and his family settled, which is an allusion to the fact that the Quraysh would migrate to Medina as emigrants following the migration of the Prophet ﷺ.

In it are lessons from the history and ancient civilisations of nations, their laws, their systems of government, their punishments, and their commerce. Also the enslavement of the foundling child, the enslavement of the thief, the conditions of prisoners, and the monitoring of measures.

Indeed, in this surah there is a distinctive style among the styles of the Qur'an's inimitability (*i'jaz*), namely the inimitability in the style of narrative, which was particularly marvelled at by the people of Mecca, as they heard from it among the tales of the Persians and the Romans. Al-Nadr ibn al-Harith and others used to tempt the Quraysh by claiming that what the Qur'an says about the affairs of past nations is "the fables of the ancients which Muhammad has written down" ﷺ.

Al-Nadr used to frequent al-Hirah, so he learned the stories of Rustam and Isfandiyar, the heroes of Persia. He would tell the Quraysh about them and say to them: "By Allah, I am better at narration than Muhammad. Come, let me tell you a better narrative than his." Then he would relate to them the reports of the Persians, some of which were lengthy in the manner of the Persian storytellers, so that he might impress his listeners with their fullness. This surah came in the style of comprehensive narration, as a challenge to them to produce its equal.

Yet, despite this, it has omitted much of the story of everything that has no great effect on the lesson. Therefore you find within the surah ﴿And thus We established Yusuf in the land﴾ twice, and ﴿Thus We planned for Yusuf﴾ [Yusuf: 76]. These are lessons from parts of the narrative.

And the wisdom interspersed through it in the sayings of the righteous, such as His saying: ﴿Upon Him I have relied, and upon Him let those who rely [upon Him] rely﴾ [Yusuf: 67], and His saying: ﴿Indeed, he who fears [Allah] and is patient, then indeed, Allah does not allow to be lost the reward of the doers of good﴾ [Yusuf: 90].
